| AWS CodeCommit | Automatic (IAM RSA key) | None: deploy with `cipi deploy` or CI |
| Anything else (Gitea, Forgejo…) | Manual | Manual |

No lock-in: any server that accepts SSH deploy keys works.

## Save a token 

The installer offers this step; you can also do it any time:

```bash
$ cipi git github-token ghp_xxx
$ cipi git gitlab-url https://gitlab.example.com   # self-hosted only
$ cipi git gitlab-token glpat-xxx
$ cipi git bitbucket-token                  # or email:token
$ cipi git azure-token 
$ cipi git origin-token 
$ cipi git codecommit-token   
$ cipi git remove-github                           # remove-gitlab, -bitbucket, …
```

| Provider | Minimum permissions |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub | Fine-grained: Administration + Webhooks, read & write. Classic: `repo` |
| GitLab | `api` |
| Bitbucket | Manage repository access keys and webhooks |
| Azure DevOps | Code (read & write) |
| CodeCommit | IAM `UploadSSHPublicKey` (max 5 SSH keys per IAM user) |

Tokens are stored encrypted on the server ([Vault](https://cipi.sh/docs/vault)).

## What happens automatically 

| Event | Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi app create` | Adds the deploy key and webhook, then **tests** that the key can read the branch |
| `cipi app edit --repository=` | Removes them from the old repository, adds them to the new one, tests again |
| `cipi app delete` | Removes them from the repository |

| Command | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi git status` | Connected providers and per-app key/webhook IDs |
| `cipi git check [app]` | Can each key read its repository and branch? Exits 1 if not |
| `cipi git refresh [app]` | Re-create keys and webhooks (after deletions or a new token) |
| `cipi git refresh --rotate-keys` | New deploy keys for every app |
| `cipi git refresh --rotate-secret` | New webhook secrets |

## Manual setup 

Without a token, or for an unsupported server:

```bash
$ cipi deploy myapp --key                          # add as a read-only deploy key
$ cipi deploy myapp --webhook                      # payload URL and secret
$ cipi deploy myapp --trust-host=git.example.com:2222   # self-hosted, custom port
```

> [!note] With [CrowdSec](https://cipi.sh/docs/crowdsec) enabled, GitHub and Bitbucket webhook ranges are allowlisted automatically. For other providers, allow a blocked range with `cipi crowdsec allow `.

## Private packages: auth.json 

`shared/auth.json` is linked into every release like `.env`, so Composer finds credentials for private packages (Packagist.com, Satis, GitHub) on every deploy.

```bash
$ cipi auth create myapp      # creates it (mode 640) and opens the editor
$ cipi auth edit myapp        # JSON is validated on save
$ cipi auth show myapp
$ cipi auth delete myapp
```

Non-interactive flags (`--file=`, `--json`, `--force`) serve scripts and the panel; REST `GET|POST|PUT|DELETE /api/apps/{name}/auth`.

## Common problems 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `git check` fails | Deploy key not added, or added to the wrong repository |
| Self-hosted Git on another port | `cipi deploy myapp --trust-host=git.example.com:2222` |
| Private Composer packages | Add credentials with `cipi auth` (`auth.json`) |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Do I need a provider token? | No, but with one Cipi adds and rotates deploy keys and webhooks for you. |
| Can I use HTTPS URLs? | Use SSH URLs (`git@…`): deploy keys are read-only and per app. |


## Auto-deploy on push

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy

Push to your branch and the app is live a minute later. The Git provider calls a signed webhook on your app; the deploy itself runs on the server as the app user. CI needs no SSH key and the server opens no extra port.

## How it works 

```flow
git push | to the deploy branch
> You push commits to the app's deploy branch (`main` by default). Pushes to other branches are acknowledged and ignored.
Provider → /cipi/webhook | signed request over HTTPS
> GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea or Azure DevOps call the app's webhook URL over HTTPS, signed with the app's secret.
Verify & queue | signature, branch; answers 200 at once
> Cipi checks the signature and the branch. If both are right it leaves a small trigger and answers 200 immediately, so the provider never times out.
Cron, within a minute | starts the deploy as the app user
> A cron job checks for triggers every minute and starts the deploy as the app's own Linux user, never as root.
Deploy | the normal zero-downtime pipeline
> From here it's a normal deploy: new release, Composer, migrations, atomic swap, workers restarted. You get the usual notification. A push that arrives during a deploy waits for it; a commit whose deploy failed is not retried by itself.
```

The webhook only drops a trigger file; it never runs the deploy itself. That keeps the HTTP answer instant (providers time out after ~10 s) and the deploy in the same safe context as `cipi deploy`.

| Receiver | Used by | Verifies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-install) (`cipi/agent`) | Laravel apps | GitHub/Bitbucket HMAC, GitLab/Azure token, Gitea/Forgejo signature |
| Built-in receiver | Node apps | GitHub/Bitbucket HMAC, GitLab/Azure token |

## Set it up 

```bash
# in your Laravel project
$ composer require cipi/agent && git commit -am "Add Cipi Agent" && git push
# on the server: one manual deploy, so the route exists
$ cipi deploy myapp
$ cipi git status                 # webhook already created?
$ cipi deploy myapp --webhook     # if not: URL and secret to add by hand
```

| Provider | Payload URL | Secret | Events |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | `https://myapp.com/cipi/webhook` | the token from `--webhook` | push |
| GitLab | same | Secret token: same value | Push events |

Only pushes to `CIPI_DEPLOY_BRANCH` deploy; others get `skipped`. Cipi keeps it in step with `cipi app edit --branch`. Use HTTPS ([cipi ssl install](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl)) so the secret never travels in clear text.

Verify with a small commit:

```bash
$ cipi deploy myapp --status
$ cipi app logs myapp --type=deploy
```

Every webhook deploy lands in the [audit ledger](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit) with pusher, commit, delivery ID and source IP.

## From any tool, not only Git 

The agent's webhook also accepts the secret as a Bearer token, so anything that can send an HTTP request can queue a deploy: a CI job, a scheduler, a chat bot.

```bash
$ curl -fsS -X POST https://myapp.com/cipi/webhook \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main","pusher":{"name":"release-bot"}}'
{"status":"queued","app":"myapp","provider":"webhook","branch":"main", …}
```

It queues the deploy and answers at once; it doesn't wait for the result. When a pipeline must know whether the deploy worked, use SSH or the API instead: [CI/CD pipelines](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#connect).

## Troubleshooting 

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 404 | Agent not deployed yet | `cipi deploy myapp` after adding `cipi/agent` |
| 403, invalid signature | Secret mismatch | Copy the token from `cipi deploy myapp --webhook` again |
| 200 but no deploy | Another branch was pushed | Check `CIPI_DEPLOY_BRANCH` |
| Push queued, deploys later | A deploy was running | Nothing: it deploys when that one ends (`cipi deploy myapp --status` says *queued*) |
| 200 but the same commit doesn't deploy again | It failed before and is [paused](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploying#paused) | Push a fix, or `cipi deploy myapp` |
| Two deploys per push | Webhook and pipeline both active | Keep [one trigger](https://cipi.sh/docs/how-deploys-work) |

## Common problems 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Push doesn't deploy | Pushed to another branch, or the webhook was removed: `cipi deploy myapp --webhook` |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Webhook or CI? | Webhook for most apps; CI when tests must pass first. [Guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow). |


## CI/CD pipelines

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines

Pipeline mode lets your CI decide **when** an app goes live: usually right after the tests pass, sometimes after a backup or a manual approval. The server still does the deploy itself, exactly as with `cipi deploy`. Your pipeline only gives the order and reads the result.

This page has everything you need: how to connect CI to the server safely, a deploy command that never makes things worse, and ready-to-copy recipes for every popular CI.

```flow
Choose how CI calls | SSH, API or webhook | #connect
> Pick one of three ways for the pipeline to reach the server. The API is the safest; SSH is the quickest to set up.
Store the secrets | key or token in CI | #secrets
> Save the key or token in your CI's secret store. Never commit it to the repository.
Turn the webhook off | one trigger per app | #webhook-off
> If the app also deploys on push, the pipeline and the webhook would both deploy. Turn the webhook off.
Copy a recipe | GitHub, GitLab, Jenkins… | #recipes
> Copy the recipe for your CI, change the app name and the URL, and push.
Check it | one test push | #verify
> Push a small change and watch the pipeline: tests, deploy, health check, done.
```

## How a pipeline deploy works 

```flow
Push | to the branch
> You push to `main` (or merge a pull request). The pipeline starts.
Test | php artisan test
> The pipeline installs the dependencies and runs your tests on its own machines. If a test fails, it stops here and nothing reaches the server.
Deploy | SSH or API → cipi deploy
> The pipeline asks the server to deploy. The server pulls the latest commit of the branch from Git, builds the release and switches to it. The pipeline waits for the answer.
Check | health URL answers 200
> The pipeline calls a health URL of the app (for example Laravel's `/up`). If it answers, the job is green.
Roll back | only if the check fails
> If the new release is live but the app doesn't answer, the pipeline rolls back to the previous release and turns red, so you notice.
```

> [!warning] **Don't roll back when the deploy command fails.** When `cipi deploy` fails while building the release (Composer, assets, migrations), nothing is published and the previous release is still serving. Rolling back at that point would go one release further back, to older code. Roll back only when the deploy succeeded and the health check then fails, as every recipe on this page does.

## 1. Choose how CI calls the server 

| | SSH | API ([cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) or `curl`) | Agent webhook |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What CI runs | `ssh cipi@server "sudo cipi deploy shop"` | `cipi-cli prod deploy shop` | `curl -X POST https://shop.example.com/cipi/webhook …` |
| What the secret can do | Run **any** `cipi` command as root (including deleting apps) | Only what the token allows: with `deploy-manage`, deploy, roll back, unlock and read status | Only queue a deploy of that one app |
| Waits for the result | Yes | Yes | No: it answers "queued" and the deploy starts within a minute |
| Server needs | Port 22 open to CI | [`cipi api`](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) installed | [`cipi/agent`](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-install) in the app (Laravel) |
| Choose it when | You want the quickest setup on one server | You want the least privilege, or several servers | Your tool can only send an HTTP request |

> [!tip] Our recommendation: the **API** for production. A leaked API token with only `deploy-manage` can redeploy your app; a leaked SSH key for the `cipi` user can do anything Cipi can do.

## 2. Store the secrets 

Every recipe uses the same names, so you can copy them as they are.

| Secret | What it is | How to get it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SERVER_HOST` | The server's IP or hostname | Your provider's dashboard |
| `SERVER_SSH_KEY` | A private key used only by CI | `ssh-keygen` below |
| `SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS` | The server's public host key, so CI knows it's talking to your server | `ssh-keyscan` below |
| `CIPI_API_URL` | Your API address, e.g. `https://api.example.com` | `cipi api status` |
| `CIPI_API_TOKEN` | A token with only `deploy-manage` | `cipi api token create` below |
| `CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN` | The app's webhook secret | `cipi deploy shop --webhook` |
| `HEALTH_URL` | A URL that answers 200 when the app works, e.g. `https://shop.example.com/up` | Your app ([health checks](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks)) |

### An SSH key for CI 

Create a new key on your laptop. Never reuse your personal key or the app's deploy key.

```bash
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ci-deploy" -f ./ci_deploy -N ""
$ cat ./ci_deploy.pub        # 1. copy this line
$ ssh cipi@your-server "sudo cipi ssh add ''"   # 2. authorize it on the server
$ cat ./ci_deploy            # 3. paste the whole file into the CI secret SERVER_SSH_KEY
$ rm ./ci_deploy ./ci_deploy.pub   # 4. delete the local copies
```

Then save the server's host key. Run this from a machine that has already connected to the server, and check that the fingerprint matches the one the server shows:

```bash
$ ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 your-server             # → the CI secret SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS
$ ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 your-server | ssh-keygen -lf -
# on the server, the same fingerprint must appear:
$ ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
```

> [!note] Running `ssh-keyscan` inside the pipeline on every build works, but it trusts whatever answers on that address. A saved `SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS` is what stops a pipeline from sending your deploy to an impostor.

### An API token for CI 

```bash
# on the server, once
$ cipi api token create --name=ci-shop --abilities=deploy-manage --expires=2027-12-31
```

The token is shown once: save it as `CIPI_API_TOKEN`. If you restrict the API by IP (`cipi api ip-whitelist`), remember that hosted runners (GitHub, GitLab.com, Bitbucket) change IP on every build: allow their published ranges or use a self-hosted runner with a fixed IP.

## 3. Turn the webhook off 

If the app also deploys on push, every push would deploy twice: once from the webhook, once from the pipeline, and the second one hits the deploy lock and fails.

| Provider | Where |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub | Repository → **Settings → Webhooks** → the `/cipi/webhook` hook → untick **Active** |
| GitLab | Project → **Settings → Webhooks** → delete the `/cipi/webhook` hook |
| Bitbucket | Repository → **Repository settings → Webhooks** → delete or disable it |
| Gitea / Forgejo | Repository → **Settings → Webhooks** → untick **Active** |
| Azure DevOps | Project settings → **Service hooks** → disable the Cipi hook |

> [!note] `cipi git refresh` and `cipi app webhook recreate` create the webhook again. If you run them later, turn it off again.

## 4. The deploy step, explained once 

Every recipe below runs one of these, depending on how CI calls the server.

**Over SSH**, everything runs on the server in one command:

```bash
ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy shop && \
  { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null \
    || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `sudo cipi deploy shop` | Builds and publishes the new release. If it fails, the command stops here: nothing was published, and the job fails |
| `&& { curl … /up` | Only if the deploy succeeded: calls the app up to 6 times, 5 seconds apart |
| `\|\| { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }` | Only if the app doesn't answer: goes back to the previous release and fails the job |

**Over the API**, with cipi-cli:

```bash
cipi-cli profiles add prod --endpoint "$CIPI_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_API_TOKEN"
cipi-cli prod deploy shop
curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null \
  || { cipi-cli prod deploy rollback shop -y; exit 1; }
```

`cipi-cli deploy` waits for the deploy and exits with an error if it fails. It waits about nine minutes at most: for longer builds, follow the deploy with `cipi-cli prod deploy status shop`.

> [!tip] Already using Cipi's own [automatic rollback](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks#auto-rollback) (`rollback_on_unhealthy: true`)? Then keep the `curl` check, so the job turns red, but drop the CI rollback: Cipi has already rolled back, and a second rollback would go one release too far.

## 5. Recipes 

| CI | Jump to |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub Actions | [SSH](#github) · [API](#github-api) |
| GitLab CI/CD (cloud or self-hosted) | [Recipe](#gitlab) |
| Bitbucket Pipelines | [Recipe](#bitbucket) |
| Azure Pipelines | [Recipe](#azure) |
| Gitea Actions, Forgejo Actions | [Recipe](#gitea) |
| CircleCI | [Recipe](#circleci) |
| Laravel Envoy | [Recipe](#envoy) |
| Any CI with `curl` | [API with curl](#curl) · [Agent webhook](#webhook-ci) |
| Jenkins | [Jenkins page](https://cipi.sh/docs/jenkins) |
| AWS CodeDeploy | [AWS CodeDeploy page](https://cipi.sh/docs/aws-codedeploy) |

Replace `shop` with your app name and `https://shop.example.com/up` with your health URL. The test job is an example: keep the one you already have.

### GitHub Actions 

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Test and deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production      # one deploy at a time, queued in order
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with:
          php-version: "8.4"     # the version your app uses
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
      - run: php artisan test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production      # optional: required reviewers, protected secrets
    steps:
      - name: Set up SSH
        run: |
          mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SERVER_SSH_KEY }}" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
          printf '%s\n' "${{ secrets.SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS }}" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts
      - name: Deploy, check, roll back if unhealthy
        run: |
          ssh cipi@${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }} "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

### GitHub Actions with the API 

No SSH at all, and a token that can only deploy.

```yaml
  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    env:
      CIPI_API_URL: ${{ secrets.CIPI_API_URL }}
      CIPI_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CIPI_API_TOKEN }}
      HEALTH_URL: https://shop.example.com/up
    steps:
      - name: Install cipi-cli
        run: |
          base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
          curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
          sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
          sudo install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
      - name: Deploy, check, roll back if unhealthy
        run: |
          cipi-cli profiles add prod --endpoint "$CIPI_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_API_TOKEN"
          cipi-cli prod deploy shop
          curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null \
            || { cipi-cli prod deploy rollback shop -y; exit 1; }
```

### GitLab CI/CD 

Works the same on GitLab.com and self-hosted GitLab. Add the secrets under **Settings → CI/CD → Variables**, marked *Masked* and *Protected*.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [test, deploy]

test:
  stage: test
  image: composer:2
  script:
    - composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
    - cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
    - php artisan test

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine:latest
  resource_group: production         # one deploy at a time
  environment: production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache openssh-client
    - eval $(ssh-agent -s)
    - echo "$SERVER_SSH_KEY" | tr -d '\r' | ssh-add -
    - mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh
    - echo "$SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts
  script:
    - ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

### Bitbucket Pipelines 

Bitbucket can hold the SSH key for you: **Repository settings → Pipelines → SSH keys**. Generate or paste the CI key there, copy its public key to the server with `sudo cipi ssh add`, and add your server under **Known hosts** (Bitbucket fetches its fingerprint; compare it with the server's). The key is then available to every step without any secret in the file.

```yaml
# bitbucket-pipelines.yml
pipelines:
  branches:
    main:
      - step:
          name: Test
          image: composer:2
          script:
            - composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
            - cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
            - php artisan test
      - step:
          name: Deploy
          deployment: production
          script:
            - ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

### Azure Pipelines 

Create an SSH service connection first: **Project settings → Service connections → New → SSH**, host = your server, user = `cipi`, private key = the CI key. Call it `cipi-production`.

```yaml
# azure-pipelines.yml
trigger:
  branches:
    include: [main]

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

stages:
  - stage: Test
    jobs:
      - job: test
        steps:
          - script: |
              composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
              cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
              php artisan test
            displayName: Run tests

  - stage: Deploy
    dependsOn: Test
    jobs:
      - deployment: deploy
        environment: production        # add an "Exclusive lock" check for one deploy at a time
        strategy:
          runOnce:
            deploy:
              steps:
                - task: SSH@0
                  displayName: Deploy, check, roll back if unhealthy
                  inputs:
                    sshEndpoint: cipi-production
                    runOptions: commands
                    commands: sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }
                    failOnStdErr: false   # Cipi prints progress on stderr; the exit code decides
```

> [!note] Keep `failOnStdErr: false`. Cipi writes progress messages to stderr, and with the default the task would fail even on a perfect deploy.

### Gitea Actions and Forgejo Actions 

Both run GitHub Actions syntax. Copy the [GitHub Actions recipe](#github) into:

| Forge | File |
| --- | --- |
| Gitea | `.gitea/workflows/deploy.yml` (Gitea also reads `.github/workflows/`) |
| Forgejo | `.forgejo/workflows/deploy.yml` |

Two changes: set `runs-on:` to a label your runner offers (the label you gave it when you registered it), and add the secrets under **Settings → Actions → Secrets** of the repository. For push to deploy without CI, Gitea and Forgejo also work with the agent webhook ([Auto-deploy on push](https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy)).

### CircleCI 

Add the CI private key under **Project settings → SSH keys → Additional SSH keys** (hostname = your server) and copy the fingerprint CircleCI shows. Put `SERVER_HOST` and `SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS` in **Project settings → Environment variables**.

```yaml
# .circleci/config.yml
version: 2.1

jobs:
  test:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/php:8.4
    steps:
      - checkout
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
      - run: php artisan test

  deploy:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/base:current
    steps:
      - add_ssh_keys:
          fingerprints:
            - "SHA256:paste-the-fingerprint-here"
      - run: mkdir -p ~/.ssh && echo "$SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
      - run: ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"

workflows:
  test-and-deploy:
    jobs:
      - test
      - deploy:
          requires: [test]
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main
```

### Laravel Envoy 

[Envoy](https://laravel.com/docs/envoy) runs SSH tasks from your laptop or from CI. With Cipi, one task is enough: the server does the rest.

```blade
{{-- Envoy.blade.php --}}
@servers(['production' => 'cipi@203.0.113.10'])

@task('deploy', ['on' => 'production'])
    sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }
@endtask
```

```bash
$ composer require laravel/envoy --dev
$ php vendor/bin/envoy run deploy
```

### Any CI: the API with curl 

For CIs without a ready recipe, or when you'd rather not install cipi-cli. Needs `curl` and `jq`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
H="Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_API_TOKEN"

job=$(curl -fsS -X POST "$CIPI_API_URL/api/apps/shop/deploy" -H "$H" -H "Accept: application/json" | jq -r .job_id)
echo "Deploy job $job"

status=pending
for i in $(seq 1 180); do                       # up to 15 minutes
  status=$(curl -fsS "$CIPI_API_URL/api/jobs/$job" -H "$H" -H "Accept: application/json" | jq -r .data.status) || status=unknown
  case "$status" in completed|failed) break ;; esac
  sleep 5
done

if [ "$status" != completed ]; then
  echo "Deploy $status"; exit 1                 # failed or still running: nothing to roll back
fi

curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null || {
  curl -fsS -X POST "$CIPI_API_URL/api/apps/shop/deploy/rollback" -H "$H" -H "Accept: application/json"
  echo "Unhealthy: rollback requested"; exit 1
}
echo "Deployed and healthy"
```

The deploy answers `202` with a `job_id`; `GET /api/jobs/{id}` returns `pending`, `running`, `completed` or `failed` (with the output once finished). See the [REST API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api).

### Any CI: the agent webhook 

When a tool can only send an HTTP request (a chat bot, a scheduler, a low-code platform), call the app's own webhook. It accepts the webhook secret as a Bearer token, queues the deploy and answers immediately.

```bash
curl -fsS -X POST "https://shop.example.com/cipi/webhook" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_WEBHOOK_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"ref":"refs/heads/main","after":"'"$COMMIT_SHA"'","pusher":{"name":"ci"}}'
# {"status":"queued","app":"shop","provider":"webhook","branch":"main",...}
```

| Field | Optional? | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | Yes | If set, it must be the app's deploy branch, otherwise the answer is `skipped` |
| `after` | Yes | The commit (7 to 40 hex characters), recorded in the [deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit) |
| `pusher.name` | Yes | Who asked, recorded in the audit |

This path needs the [`cipi/agent`](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-install) package in a Laravel app. It does **not** wait for the deploy: the server starts it within a minute, and the result arrives through [deploy notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-notifications). Don't put the token in the URL (`?token=`): URLs end up in logs.

## 6. Check it works 

```bash
# push a small change, then on the server:
$ cipi deploy shop --status        # running, queued or idle
$ cipi deploy shop --audit         # the last entry says origin "cipi-cli" (SSH) or "panel" (API)
$ cipi app logs shop --type=deploy
```

## Patterns 

### Several apps from one pipeline 

```bash
ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy api && sudo cipi deploy frontend"
```

Deploy them one after the other, in the order they depend on each other. Each app has its own lock, so they could also run in parallel, but a failure is easier to read in sequence.

### Several servers 

With cipi-cli, add one profile per server and deploy each:

```bash
cipi-cli profiles add eu --endpoint "$CIPI_API_URL_EU" --token "$CIPI_API_TOKEN_EU"
cipi-cli profiles add us --endpoint "$CIPI_API_URL_US" --token "$CIPI_API_TOKEN_US"
cipi-cli eu deploy shop && cipi-cli us deploy shop
```

### Add more steps 

| Add | How | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A backup before the release | `sudo cipi backup run shop` in a step before the deploy | [Backups](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) |
| A database snapshot before migrations | `sudo cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot` (once; then every deploy) | [Safe deploy](https://cipi.sh/docs/safe-deploy) |
| Check `cipi.yml` in the test job | `php artisan cipi:yml validate --json` | [cipi.yml tooling](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml) |
| Slack or Telegram on every deploy | Server-side notifications, no CI code | [Deploy notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-notifications) |
| A live URL for every branch | Create and remove apps from CI | [Preview environments](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments) |

> [!tip] A setup many teams use: push to deploy on **staging** (instant feedback), pipeline on **production** (tests, backup, deploy, check). Compare the two in [Agent vs pipeline](https://cipi.sh/guides/agent-vs-pipeline-deploys).

## Common problems 

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | The CI public key isn't on the server | `sudo cipi ssh add ""` |
| `Host key verification failed` | `SERVER_KNOWN_HOSTS` is empty or from another server | Save it again with `ssh-keyscan` and compare the fingerprint |
| `sudo: a terminal is required` | The SSH user isn't `cipi` | Connect as `cipi@…`, the user allowed to run `sudo cipi` without a password |
| Every push deploys twice | The webhook is still active | [Turn it off](#webhook-off) |
| *A deploy of 'shop' is running* | Two pipelines at once, or a webhook deploy in flight | Add a concurrency limit and keep one trigger per app; a lock left by an interrupted deploy is removed by the next deploy (Cipi 5.13.0+) |
| `401` or `403` from the API | Token expired, wrong ability, or IP not allowed | `cipi api token list`; ability `deploy-manage`; `cipi api ip-whitelist show` |
| cipi-cli "timed out after polling" | The build takes more than about nine minutes | The deploy continues on the server: `cipi-cli prod deploy status shop` |
| Azure task fails on a good deploy | `failOnStdErr` is on | Set `failOnStdErr: false` |
| CI green, old code live | The pipeline used the agent webhook, which only queues | Use SSH or the API when CI must wait for the result |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Does CI build the app and upload it? | No. CI runs the tests; the server pulls the code from Git and builds the release itself. Nothing is uploaded. |
| Which commit goes live? | The latest commit of the app's branch when the server builds the release. With one deploy at a time per branch (the `concurrency`, `resource_group` and lock settings above), that's the commit your tests checked. |
| Can the CI key do anything else? | Over SSH, the `cipi` user can run any `cipi` command as root, which includes deleting apps. That's why the API with a `deploy-manage` token is the safer choice for production. |
| Do I need the agent for pipelines? | No. SSH and the API work for every app. The agent is only needed for the webhook path. |
| How are migrations run? | By the deploy, on the server, inside the new release and before it goes live. CI doesn't run them. |
| Can I require an approval before production? | Yes, with your CI's environments: GitHub *required reviewers*, GitLab *protected environments*, Azure *approvals*, Jenkins `input`. |


## Jenkins

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/jenkins

Jenkins can drive Cipi deploys like any other CI: a `Jenkinsfile` runs your tests and, if they pass, asks the server to deploy. The server pulls the code from Git and builds the release itself, so Jenkins never needs to copy files or know where the app lives on disk.

```flow
Credentials | key or token in Jenkins | #credentials
> Store an SSH key (or an API token) and the server's host key as Jenkins credentials.
Jenkinsfile | test, deploy, check | #jenkinsfile
> Add a Jenkinsfile to the repository: a Test stage, then a Deploy stage that runs only on `main`.
Trigger | Git notifies Jenkins | #trigger
> Make your Git server tell Jenkins about every push, so the pipeline starts by itself.
Webhook off | one trigger per app | #webhook-off
> Turn the Cipi webhook off for the app, so the push doesn't also deploy directly.
First run | push and watch | #verify
> Push a small change and follow it in Jenkins and with `cipi deploy shop --status`.
```

## What you need 

| Where | What |
| --- | --- |
| Jenkins | A Pipeline or **Multibranch Pipeline** job, the **SSH Agent** plugin (for the SSH way) and the **Credentials Binding** plugin (installed with the suggested plugins) |
| Jenkins agent | `ssh` and `curl`; for the API way, [`cipi-cli`](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client); for the test stage, PHP and Composer or Docker |
| Cipi server | Port 22 open to Jenkins (SSH way) or [`cipi api`](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) installed (API way) |

## 1. Credentials 

**Manage Jenkins → Credentials → (global) → Add credentials**:

| ID | Kind | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cipi-ci-key` | SSH Username with private key | Username `cipi`, the private key of a new CI key ([how to create it](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#ssh-key)) |
| `cipi-known-hosts` | Secret file | A file with the server's host key, from `ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 your-server` |
| `cipi-api-token` | Secret text | An API token with only `deploy-manage` (API way) |

Authorize the CI key on the server once: `sudo cipi ssh add ""`.

## 2. The Jenkinsfile 

### Over SSH 

```groovy
// Jenkinsfile
pipeline {
    agent any

    options {
        disableConcurrentBuilds()            // one build of this branch at a time
        timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES')
    }

    environment {
        APP        = 'shop'
        SERVER     = 'cipi@203.0.113.10'
        HEALTH_URL = 'https://shop.example.com/up'
    }

    stages {
        stage('Test') {
            agent {
                docker {
                    image 'composer:2'      // or any image with PHP and Composer
                    reuseNode true
                }
            }
            steps {
                sh 'composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist'
                sh 'cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate'
                sh 'php artisan test'
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps {
                withCredentials([file(credentialsId: 'cipi-known-hosts', variable: 'KNOWN_HOSTS')]) {
                    sshagent(credentials: ['cipi-ci-key']) {
                        sh '''
                          ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile="$KNOWN_HOSTS" "$SERVER" \
                            "sudo cipi deploy $APP && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors $HEALTH_URL >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy $APP --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
                        '''
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

What the deploy line does, in order: deploy; only if the deploy succeeded, call the health URL up to six times; only if the app doesn't answer, roll back and fail the build. If the deploy itself fails, nothing was published and nothing is rolled back. [Why](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#deploy-step).

> [!note] The `sh '''…'''` blocks use single quotes on purpose: the shell, not Groovy, reads `$APP` and the credentials. That keeps secrets out of Jenkins' Groovy interpolation warnings and out of the build log.

### Over the API, without SSH 

Install `cipi-cli` on the Jenkins agent once ([download](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases)), then replace the Deploy stage:

```groovy
        stage('Deploy') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            environment {
                CIPI_API_URL   = 'https://api.example.com'
                CIPI_API_TOKEN = credentials('cipi-api-token')
            }
            steps {
                sh '''
                  export HOME="$(mktemp -d)"     # the cipi-cli profile lives only for this build
                  cipi-cli profiles add prod --endpoint "$CIPI_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_API_TOKEN"
                  cipi-cli prod deploy "$APP"
                  curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null \
                    || { cipi-cli prod deploy rollback "$APP" -y; exit 1; }
                '''
            }
        }
```

The token can only deploy, roll back, unlock and read the deploy status. Jenkins masks it in the console output.

### Ask for approval before production 

Add a stage before Deploy. Someone with access to the job clicks **Deploy** in Jenkins; if nobody does within an hour, the build stops.

```groovy
        stage('Approve') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps {
                timeout(time: 1, unit: 'HOURS') {
                    input message: 'Deploy shop to production?', ok: 'Deploy'
                }
            }
        }
```

## 3. Start the pipeline on every push 

| Git server | How Jenkins hears about pushes |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub | Install the GitHub plugin, then add a repository webhook to `https://jenkins.example.com/github-webhook/` (event: push) |
| GitLab | Install the GitLab plugin and add a project webhook to the URL the job shows under **Build Triggers** |
| Bitbucket, Gitea, others | Their Jenkins plugin, or the Multibranch option **Periodically if not otherwise run** (for example every 2 minutes) |

This webhook goes to **Jenkins**, not to your app. It's a different hook from Cipi's `/cipi/webhook`.

## 4. Turn the Cipi webhook off 

Otherwise every push deploys twice: once directly through the app's webhook, once from Jenkins. In GitHub: **Settings → Webhooks** → the `/cipi/webhook` hook → untick **Active**. Other providers: [CI/CD pipelines](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#webhook-off).

## 5. First run 

```bash
# push a small change to main, then on the server:
$ cipi deploy shop --status      # running, queued or idle
$ cipi deploy shop --audit       # origin "cipi-cli" (SSH) or "panel" (API)
```

## A rollback button 

A small separate Pipeline job (for example "shop – rollback") gives your team a button that doesn't require SSH access:

```groovy
pipeline {
    agent any
    stages {
        stage('Rollback') {
            steps {
                input message: 'Roll shop back to the previous release?', ok: 'Roll back'
                withCredentials([file(credentialsId: 'cipi-known-hosts', variable: 'KNOWN_HOSTS')]) {
                    sshagent(credentials: ['cipi-ci-key']) {
                        sh 'ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile="$KNOWN_HOSTS" cipi@203.0.113.10 "sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback"'
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

A rollback switches code only: database migrations stay as they are. See [Deploy & roll back](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploying).

## Common problems 

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `No such DSL method 'sshagent'` | SSH Agent plugin missing | Install it from **Manage Jenkins → Plugins** |
| `Host key verification failed` | The known-hosts file is empty or from another server | Save it again with `ssh-keyscan` and compare the fingerprint |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | The CI key isn't authorized on the server | `sudo cipi ssh add ""` |
| Deploy stage skipped | Not a Multibranch job, so `branch 'main'` never matches | Use a Multibranch Pipeline, or remove the `when` line |
| Two deploys per push | The Cipi webhook is still active | [Turn it off](#webhook-off) |
| *A deploy of 'shop' is running* | Two builds at once, or a webhook deploy in flight | Keep `disableConcurrentBuilds()`; a lock left by an interrupted deploy is removed by the next deploy (Cipi 5.13.0+) |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Does Jenkins copy the code to the server? | No. The server pulls it from Git with its own read-only deploy key. Jenkins only says when. |
| Can I keep my existing Jenkins test stages? | Yes. Keep them and add the Deploy stage at the end. |
| Can one Jenkins deploy many servers? | Yes. One credential per server, or one cipi-cli profile per server. See [several servers](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#multi-server). |
| Is the CI key dangerous? | Over SSH, the `cipi` user can run any `cipi` command. For production, the API way with a `deploy-manage` token is safer. |

The whole setup, step by step from an empty Jenkins: [Deploy Laravel from Jenkins](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-jenkins-deploy).


## AWS CodeDeploy

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/aws-codedeploy

[AWS CodeDeploy](https://aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/) can orchestrate releases on Cipi servers: it decides when, on which servers and in which order, and Cipi does the deploy on each server. It fits teams that already manage releases in AWS (CodePipeline, CodeBuild, IAM approvals) or that want to roll a release across several Cipi servers one at a time.

> [!info] Cipi doesn't need CodeDeploy. If you only want "tests pass, then deploy", a [CI pipeline](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines) is simpler. Use CodeDeploy when AWS is already where your releases are managed.

## How it fits together 

CodeDeploy normally copies a bundle of files onto the server. With Cipi, the server already knows how to fetch and build the app from Git, so the CodeDeploy bundle stays tiny: an `appspec.yml` and two scripts. CodeDeploy runs the scripts; the scripts call Cipi.

```flow
Release starts | CodePipeline, CI or console
> A deployment is created: by CodePipeline, by your CI with `aws deploy create-deployment`, or by hand in the console.
Agent picks it up | outbound HTTPS only
> The CodeDeploy agent on the Cipi server polls AWS over HTTPS (port 443, outgoing). No inbound port opens.
ApplicationStart | scripts/deploy.sh → cipi deploy
> CodeDeploy runs `scripts/deploy.sh`, which runs `cipi deploy shop`. Cipi pulls the branch from Git, builds the release and switches to it with zero downtime.
ValidateService | scripts/validate.sh
> CodeDeploy runs `scripts/validate.sh`: it calls the health URL and, if the app doesn't answer, rolls back with Cipi and fails the deployment.
Next server | one at a time or all at once
> With several servers in the deployment group, CodeDeploy moves to the next one according to the deployment configuration, and stops if one fails.
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Servers | EC2 instances, or any Cipi server registered as an **on-premises instance** (Hetzner, OVHcloud, bare metal…) |
| Operating system | The CodeDeploy agent 2.x supports Ubuntu Server 24.04 and 26.04 LTS, on x86_64 and arm64 |
| Network | The agent only makes outgoing HTTPS calls to AWS: Cipi's firewall needs no change |
| Cost | No CodeDeploy charge on EC2; AWS charges per on-premises instance update (check the [current price](https://aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/pricing/)) |

## 1. Install the CodeDeploy agent on the Cipi server 

Follow AWS's guide for Ubuntu: [Install the CodeDeploy agent for Ubuntu Server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/codedeploy-agent-operations-install-ubuntu.html). For agent 2.x it comes down to:

```bash
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y wget
$ cd /tmp
$ wget https://aws-codedeploy-eu-central-1.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/latestv2/install   # use your Region
$ chmod +x ./install && sudo ./install auto
$ systemctl status codedeploy-agent      # "The AWS CodeDeploy agent is running."
```

**On EC2**, attach an instance profile that can read the deployment bundles (for example the AWS managed policy for CodeDeploy EC2 instances, plus read access to your S3 bucket).

**Outside AWS**, register the server as an on-premises instance (with an IAM user or, better, an IAM role session) and give it a tag such as `app=shop`. AWS explains both ways in [Working with on-premises instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/instances-on-premises.html).

## 2. Create the application and the deployment group 

In the CodeDeploy console (or with the AWS CLI):

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Application | `shop`, compute platform **EC2/On-premises** |
| Deployment group | `production` |
| Targets | The tag you gave the server(s), e.g. `app=shop` |
| Deployment configuration | `CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime` for several servers, `AllAtOnce` for one |
| Load balancer | Off (Cipi switches releases without downtime on each server) |
| **Rollbacks** | **Off**: see below |

> [!warning] **Turn CodeDeploy's automatic rollback off.** CodeDeploy rolls back by deploying the previous bundle again. With Cipi, that would run `cipi deploy` again, and Cipi always deploys the latest commit of the branch: you would get the new code a second time, not the old one. The `validate.sh` script below rolls back with Cipi instead, which really returns to the previous release.

## 3. The bundle: appspec.yml and two scripts 

Put these in a `codedeploy/` folder in the repository.

```yaml
# codedeploy/appspec.yml
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /
    destination: /opt/codedeploy-cipi/shop
hooks:
  ApplicationStart:
    - location: scripts/deploy.sh
      timeout: 1800
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/validate.sh
      timeout: 300
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# codedeploy/scripts/deploy.sh: CodeDeploy runs it as root
set -euo pipefail
/usr/local/bin/cipi deploy shop
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# codedeploy/scripts/validate.sh: health check, Cipi rollback if the app is down
set -uo pipefail
APP=shop
HEALTH_URL=https://shop.example.com/up

if ! curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null; then
  echo "Unhealthy: rolling back with Cipi"
  /usr/local/bin/cipi deploy "$APP" --rollback
  exit 1
fi

# Revisions from GitHub carry the commit CodeDeploy was asked to release.
if [ -n "${BUNDLE_COMMIT:-}" ]; then
  live=$(sudo -u "$APP" git -C "/home/$APP/current" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || true)
  [ "$live" = "$BUNDLE_COMMIT" ] || echo "Note: live commit $live, requested $BUNDLE_COMMIT (a newer push reached the branch)"
fi
echo "Healthy"
```

Make both scripts executable before committing: `chmod +x codedeploy/scripts/*.sh`.

| Hook | Why this one |
| --- | --- |
| `ApplicationStart` | Runs after CodeDeploy has placed the bundle; it's where the app "starts", so it's where Cipi deploys |
| `ValidateService` | CodeDeploy's place for "is it working?". A non-zero exit fails the deployment and stops it before the next server |

If the deploy fails while building the release, `deploy.sh` fails, nothing was published, and `validate.sh` never runs: there's nothing to roll back.

## 4. Start a deployment 

From the console (**Create deployment**), from CodePipeline, or from any CI with the AWS CLI.

**From an S3 bundle** (works with any Git host):

```bash
$ aws deploy push --application-name shop \
    --s3-location s3://my-deploy-bundles/shop/$COMMIT_SHA.zip --source codedeploy
$ aws deploy create-deployment --application-name shop --deployment-group-name production \
    --s3-location bucket=my-deploy-bundles,key=shop/$COMMIT_SHA.zip,bundleType=zip
```

**From GitHub** (after connecting CodeDeploy to GitHub in the console). Note that CodeDeploy then uses the whole repository as the bundle: keep `appspec.yml` at the repository root in this case, with the paths of the scripts changed to match.

```bash
$ aws deploy create-deployment --application-name shop --deployment-group-name production \
    --github-location repository=you/shop,commitId=$COMMIT_SHA
```

To wait for the result in CI: `aws deploy wait deployment-successful --deployment-id `.

## 5. Turn the Cipi webhook off 

If the app also deploys on push, every push would deploy before CodeDeploy does. Turn the `/cipi/webhook` hook off in your Git provider. Where: [CI/CD pipelines](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#webhook-off).

## With CodePipeline 

A typical pipeline: **Source** (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or CodeCommit) → **Build** (CodeBuild runs `php artisan test` and outputs the `codedeploy/` folder as the artifact) → **Deploy** (CodeDeploy, deployment group `production`). Add a **Manual approval** action before Deploy for production.

## Common problems 

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deployment stuck in "Pending" | The agent isn't running or can't reach AWS | `systemctl status codedeploy-agent`; check outgoing HTTPS |
| `ScriptFailed` in ApplicationStart | `cipi deploy` failed | Read the deploy log: `cipi app logs shop --type=deploy`. Nothing was published |
| `ScriptFailed` in ValidateService | The app didn't answer and Cipi rolled back | Check the release that failed: `cipi deploy shop --log` |
| "appspec.yml not found" | The bundle root is wrong | With S3, `--source codedeploy`; with GitHub, `appspec.yml` at the repository root |
| New code deployed again after a failure | CodeDeploy's automatic rollback is on | Turn it off in the deployment group |
| Permission denied on the scripts | Scripts not executable in Git | `chmod +x codedeploy/scripts/*.sh` and commit |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Does CodeDeploy copy my app to the server? | No. It copies only the small `codedeploy/` bundle. Cipi pulls the app from Git with its own deploy key. |
| Can I use it on servers outside AWS? | Yes, as on-premises instances: they need the agent and outgoing HTTPS to AWS. |
| Can I deploy a specific commit? | Cipi deploys the latest commit of the branch. `validate.sh` tells you when it differs from the commit you asked for. |
| Can CodeDeploy update several Cipi servers? | Yes. Put them in the same deployment group; `OneAtATime` updates one server, checks it, then the next. |
| Does this replace Cipi's own health check? | No, they work together. You can also keep Cipi's [post-deploy check](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) for notifications. |

Step by step from an empty AWS account: [Deploy Laravel with AWS CodeDeploy](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-aws-codedeploy).


## cipi.yml

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/yml

`cipi.yml` describes, in your repository, how the server should run the app: aliases, PHP settings, databases, workers, scheduler, health check, backups, routes, deploy options, crons. Server configuration gets reviewed, versioned and deployed like code.

```flow
Commit cipi.yml | next to your code
> Put `cipi.yml` at the root of the repository, next to `composer.json`, and commit it like code.
Deploy | the file ships with the release
> Deploy as usual: the file arrives on the server inside the release.
Plan | see exactly what would change
> `cipi yml plan myapp` lists every change it would make and every blocker. Nothing changes yet.
Apply | all or nothing, never half
> `cipi yml apply myapp` makes all the changes, or none if any fails. With `cipi yml auto myapp on`, this happens after every deploy.
```

## Commands 

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi yml generate myapp [--save]` | Write the app's current setup as a ready-to-commit file |
| `cipi yml example myapp` | A commented template that validates as is |
| `cipi yml validate myapp` | Parse and check; change nothing |
| `cipi yml plan myapp [--json]` | Show every change that would be made |
| `cipi yml apply myapp [--yes]` | Apply it |
| `cipi yml auto myapp on\|off\|status` | Apply automatically after every successful deploy |
| `cipi yml post-deploy myapp` | Run the `deploy.post` steps now |

Start from what you have: `cipi yml generate myapp > cipi.yml`, commit, and `plan` reports nothing to do. Validate locally or in CI with [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml): `php artisan cipi:yml validate`.

The file is read from the live release (`current/` or, for custom apps, `htdocs/`), then `shared/`. Every vhost refuses to serve it.

## The file 

```yaml
version: 1

app:
  php: "8.6"                       # must be installed
  aliases: ["www.myapp.com", "*.myapp.com"]   # replaces the current list
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 50M, memory_limit: 512M }
  limits: { memory_limit: 512M, fpm_max_children: 10 }

databases:                         # extra databases: myapp or myapp_*
  - name: myapp_reporting
  - name: myapp_analytics
    engine: pgsql

workers:
  horizon: false                   # true replaces the queues below
  reverb: false
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: emails, processes: 1, tries: 5, timeout: 300 }

schedule: true
search: false                      # Meilisearch for Scout

health:
  url: "https://myapp.com/up"      # must be one of the app's domains
  expect: 200
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true

deploy:
  branch: main
  keep_releases: 5
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
  post:
    - artisan cache:clear

ssl: { force_https: true }
env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, MAIL_HOST] }   # names only, never values

crons:
  - { every: 30m, run: artisan queue:prune-batches }

backup:
  profiles:                        # names: myapp or myapp-*
    - { name: myapp-db, scope: db, every: 30m, keep: 48, destinations: [local] }
    - { name: myapp-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
    - { name: myapp-files, scope: files, every: 6h, keep: 8, destinations: [s3], exclude_paths: [storage/app/uploads] }  # 5.13.0+
```

| Section | Same as | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app.php`, `app.ini` | [cipi php / ini](https://cipi.sh/docs/php) | Per-app; server-wide ini stays with `cipi ini` |
| `app.aliases` | [cipi alias](https://cipi.sh/docs/domains) | Authoritative: a removed alias is removed |
| `app.limits` | [cipi app limits](https://cipi.sh/docs/limits) | Out-of-range values block the plan instead of being clamped |
| `databases` | [cipi db](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) | Credentials go to `shared/cipi-databases.env`, never to the repo |
| `workers`, `schedule` | [Queues](https://cipi.sh/docs/workers), [Reverb](https://cipi.sh/docs/reverb), [Scheduler](https://cipi.sh/docs/scheduler) | Laravel apps only |
| `search` | [cipi search](https://cipi.sh/docs/search) | Needs `cipi search install` by root first |
| `health` | [Health checks](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) | Probed every 5 minutes and after every deploy |
| `deploy` | [deploy-config](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-script) | `branch` takes effect from the next deploy |
| `ssl.force_https` | `cipi ssl force` | Can only be turned on from the file |
| `env.required` | | A missing variable blocks the plan |
| `crons` | | Allowlisted runners only; your other cron lines are untouched |
| `backup.profiles` | [cipi backup](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) | The file owns the profiles it created; `exclude_paths` ([5.13.0+](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups#exclude-paths)) is validated like `--exclude-paths` |

## Routes: www, basic auth, redirects, proxies 

```yaml
app:
  aliases: ["www.myapp.com"]
  www: to-root                     # to-root | from-root | none
  basic_auth:
    users:
      - admin                      # keeps the password set on the server
      - { name: preview, password_hash: "$2y$12$…" }   # bcrypt or SHA-512 only
redirect: { to: "https://new.example.com", code: 301, keep_path: true }
redirects:
  - { from: /old-page, to: /new-page }
  - { from: /blog/, to: "https://blog.myapp.com/", code: 308 }
proxies:
  - { prefix: /api/, upstream: "http://127.0.0.1:3000", strip_prefix: true }
```

Routes apply as one change: one vhost rewrite, one `nginx -t`, reverted as a whole if Nginx refuses it. **No passwords in the repository**: users are names or strong hashes.

## Staging and production from one repository 

Each app has an environment label (`production` by default; set with `--env` on create, clone or edit). An app reads `cipi-.yml` first and falls back to `cipi.yml`.

| File | Read by | Typically |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cipi-staging.yml` | apps with `--env=staging` | `deploy: { branch: develop }` |
| `cipi.yml` (or `cipi-production.yml`) | production apps | `deploy: { branch: main }` |

```bash
$ cipi app clone shop --domain=staging.shop.com --name=shop-stg --env=staging
$ cipi yml plan shop-stg     # deploy branch: main → develop (from the next deploy)
```

The **server** decides which file an app reads, never the file itself: a commit cannot point production at the staging file. An invalid `cipi-.yml` does not fall back silently; the error names it.

## Node apps: `node:` 

```yaml
node:
  framework: next                  # next nuxt sveltekit astro remix vite
  mode: ssr                        # spa | static | ssr
  version: 22
  start: npx next start -H 127.0.0.1
```

Applied by the deploy itself, from the release being deployed, so the commit that changes the build is built with it. Requires `cipi yml auto myapp on`.

## Post-deploy steps: `deploy.post` 

Commands run from the live release after every successful deploy, webhook included. They need no auto-apply.

```yaml
deploy:
  post:
    - artisan scout:import --force
    - composer dump-autoload -o
    - node scripts/warm-cache.mjs
    - { run: artisan, command: view:cache }
  post_on_failure: warn            # or abort: cipi deploy fails too
```

| Allowed runners | Refused |
| --- | --- |
| `artisan`, `composer`, `npm`, `npx`, `yarn`, `pnpm`, `php`/`node` + a script inside the release | shells, pipes, `;`, `..`, `artisan tinker`, unknown commands |

Order of a deploy: build → swap → `cipi yml apply` (if auto) → `deploy.post` → health check → notification.

## Auto-apply 

Nothing on the server changes from the file until you run `cipi yml auto myapp on`. Then every successful deploy (CLI, panel, API or webhook) reconciles. A release without the file is a no-op; an invalid or blocked file is reported (`yml_fail`) and **never partially applied**, and the deploy itself still succeeds.

## Why it is safe to accept over Git 

Anyone who can push controls the file, so it is fail-closed:

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Configure only | It can never create, rename or delete an app |
| Namespaced | Databases and backup profiles must belong to the app |
| Own domains only | The health check can't aim the server at internal addresses |
| No shell | Only allowlisted runners; unknown keys are errors |
| Small YAML subset | Anchors, aliases, tags, merges and block scalars are refused |
| Strict proxies | Cipi's own ports, link-local and cloud-metadata addresses are refused |
| Server-only settings | Disk limit and which environment file is read can't be changed from the file |

> [!warning] With auto-apply on, push access to the repository means control over this app's configuration. Treat write access accordingly.


## Customize the pipeline

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-script

Most apps never touch the deploy recipe: the options below cover the common needs and are kept safely across updates. For anything else, add your own Deployer tasks.

## Deploy options 

```bash
$ cipi app deploy-config myapp                                  # show
$ cipi app deploy-config myapp --keep-releases=10
$ cipi app deploy-config myapp --no-migrate --no-optimize
$ cipi app deploy-config myapp --horizon-terminate --queue-restart
$ cipi app deploy-config myapp --extra-artisan=view:clear,event:cache
$ cipi app deploy-config myapp --node-build='npm ci && npm run build'
$ cipi app deploy-config myapp --predeploy-snapshot
```

| Option | Effect | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--keep-releases` | Releases kept for rollback | 5 |
| `--migrate` / `--no-migrate` | `migrate --force` | on |
| `--optimize` / `--no-optimize` | `artisan optimize` | on |
| `--storage-link` | `storage:link` | on |
| `--queue-restart`, `--horizon-terminate` | Reload workers / Horizon | on |
| `--extra-artisan` | More Artisan commands after migrations | none |
| `--node-build` | Front-end build before the swap (npm, yarn, pnpm, bun) | none |
| `--predeploy-snapshot` | Database dump before migrations | off |

Saving regenerates `deploy.php` from Cipi's template. Also via REST (`GET|PUT /api/apps/{name}/deploy-config`), MCP and the panel's Deploy tab. The same settings can live in [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml).

## Custom Deployer tasks 

The recipe is `/home/myapp/.deployer/deploy.php`. Add tasks **at the bottom**, below the Cipi-managed blocks:

```php
// ── Custom tasks (keep below Cipi-managed blocks) ──
task('app:warm', function () {
    run('{{bin/php}} {{release_path}}/artisan app:warm-cache');
});
after('artisan:migrate', 'app:warm');
```

| Hook point | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `after('deploy:shared', …)` | Builds that need `.env` (e.g. Vite reads `VITE_*`) |
| `after('artisan:migrate', …)` | Seeders, cache warm-up |
| `before('deploy:symlink', …)` | Last checks before going live |
| `after('deploy:symlink', …)` | Notifications, cache purges |

The default order: prepare → vendors → shared → (build) → migrate → optimize → storage link → **symlink** → restart workers → cleanup.

> [!warning] Changing PHP or branch with `cipi app edit` regenerates `deploy.php`. Keep custom tasks in one clearly marked block at the bottom and back it up, or prefer `deploy-config` and [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml), which are never lost.

Test every change with a normal deploy; `cipi deploy myapp --rollback` is always one command away, and the log is in `cipi app logs myapp --type=deploy`.


## Safe deploy & DB snapshots

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/safe-deploy

A safe deploy has a restore point taken **before** new code and migrations touch production. Cipi gives you two levels; use one or both.

| Level | How | Restores | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Database snapshot | `--snapshot` or `--predeploy-snapshot` | The database | On the server |
| Full backup | `cipi backup run` in a pipeline stage | Database + files (`shared/`: `.env`, uploads) | S3 or any S3-compatible bucket |

```flow
Tests pass | CI
> Your CI runs the tests. Only a green build goes on.
Snapshot / backup | restore point
> A database snapshot (`--snapshot`, or `predeploy_snapshot`) or a backup gives you a point to go back to if a migration goes wrong.
Deploy | atomic swap
> The release is built separately and switched in atomically.
Health check | automatic rollback if broken
> The health check verifies the live site; if it's broken, the previous release comes back automatically.
```

## Database snapshot before every deploy 

```bash
$ cipi deploy shop --snapshot             # dump first; warn and continue if it fails
$ cipi deploy shop --snapshot-required    # dump first; abort the deploy if it fails
$ cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot # always, for every trigger (CLI, webhook, CI)
```

Dumps go to `/var/log/cipi/backups/`, the same place as [cipi db backup](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases).

> [!warning] `cipi deploy --rollback` restores **code**, not data. To undo a migration, restore the snapshot: `cipi db restore shop /var/log/cipi/backups/shop_.sql.gz`.

## Full backup in a pipeline 

A webhook deploys as soon as you push, so an off-site backup step belongs in a [CI pipeline](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines). Configure S3 once with `cipi backup configure`.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (jobs only)
  backup:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: cipi
          key: ${{ secrets.SERVER_SSH_KEY }}
          script: sudo cipi db backup shop && sudo cipi backup run --profile=shop-nightly
  deploy:
    needs: backup
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: cipi
          key: ${{ secrets.SERVER_SSH_KEY }}
          script: "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

`test` → `backup` → `deploy`: if one fails, the next never runs. If the deploy fails while building, nothing is published and the previous release keeps serving; if the new release is live but doesn't answer, the step rolls it back. [Why it's written this way](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#deploy-step).

## Restore 

```bash
$ ls -lh /var/log/cipi/backups/shop_*.sql.gz
$ cipi db restore shop /var/log/cipi/backups/shop_20261103_143012.sql.gz
$ cipi deploy shop --rollback
# from S3
$ cipi backup list --profile=shop-nightly
$ cipi backup fetch shop-nightly 2026-11-03_020000 --dest=/root/restore
```

Local snapshots are kept until you remove them; see [Backups](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) for retention rules that prune automatically.


## Deploy audit ledger

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit

Every deploy, rollback and failure is written to a tamper-evident ledger, whoever started it: the CLI, the panel, a webhook, an AI agent, cron or someone typing `dep deploy` over SSH. Useful for incident reviews and for auditors.

```bash
$ cipi deploy myapp --audit                    # last 90 days
$ cipi deploy myapp --audit --days=365 --json
$ cipi compliance deploys                      # verify the chain, find gaps
```

## What a record proves 

The app's deploy recipe calls a root-owned helper at each outcome. Root **verifies** facts itself instead of trusting the caller:

| Field | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Event | `published`, `failed`, `rollback` |
| Release and commit | Read from disk by root |
| Origin | From the process chain: `cipi-cli`, `panel`, `webhook`, `app-queue`, `ssh`, `cron`, `root-shell`… |
| Operator | The login user ID set by PAM (the user can't change it) |
| IP | The SSH client address |
| Claimed | What only the app can say (e.g. who clicked deploy in an MCP client), kept apart from verified facts |

## The ledger 

`/var/log/cipi/deploys.jsonl` is root-only. Each line carries a sequence number and the SHA-256 of the previous line, and is also sent to syslog (`cipi-deploy`), so log forwarding keeps an independent copy off the server.

| `cipi compliance deploys` | When |
| --- | --- |
| **Fails** | The hash chain is broken |
| **Warns** | An app's recipe lost its hook, its sudo rule is missing, or Deployer knows a release the ledger never saw |

The panel shows the ledger on each app's Deploy tab; the API serves it at `GET /api/apps/{name}/deploy/audit`.

`cipi deploy myapp --audit --json` (and so the API and the panel) adds a `subject` to each record: the first line of the commit's message, read from the app's own Git clone when you ask (Cipi 5.14.0+). It is **not** in the ledger and no hash covers it: the record proves which commit went live, the clone says what it's called. A commit the clone no longer has gets none.

> [!note] The chain proves nothing older than the newest record was changed. Root could still rewrite the whole file, which is why the syslog copy matters. File edits over SFTP are not deploys; [malware scan](https://cipi.sh/docs/malware-scan) integrity covers those.


## Preview environments

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments

A preview environment is a **live copy of your app for one branch**: its own URL with HTTPS, its own database, its own workers. You open a pull request, a link appears; you push again, the preview updates; you merge or close it, the preview disappears with its data.

For Cipi, a preview is simply **one more app on a server**, created and deleted by a short script. No special mode, no container platform: the same isolation, deploys and rollback as production.

```flow
Prepare a server | DNS, Git token, API | #setup
> One time: a server for previews, a wildcard DNS record, a Git token and an API token.
Add the script | .cipi/preview.sh | #script
> Commit one script to the repository. It creates, updates and deletes the preview of a branch.
Try it locally | from your laptop | #local
> Run it once from your laptop to see a preview come up.
Automate | GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket… | #recipes
> Call the same script from your CI when a pull request opens and closes.
Clean up | merged and deleted branches | #cleanup
> Previews of closed pull requests are deleted; a nightly sweep removes the ones nobody closed.
```

## How a preview works 

```flow
Pull request opened | or the script run by hand
> A developer opens a pull request for `feature/cart`. CI runs `.cipi/preview.sh up feature/cart`.
Name it | stable per branch
> The script turns the branch into a stable app name (`pv3a1f9c2e4b`) and a readable address (`feature-cart-3a1f9c2e4b.preview.example.com`). Same branch, same names, every time.
Create | app, database, HTTPS, first deploy
> If the preview doesn't exist yet: `cipi app create` on that branch, a Let's Encrypt certificate, the first deploy, the database seeders.
Update | every push to the branch
> Every later push deploys the preview again, with the usual zero-downtime deploy, usually through the preview's own webhook.
Delete | when the pull request closes
> `.cipi/preview.sh down feature/cart` deletes the app: Linux user, files, database, certificate, and the deploy key and webhook in the repository.
```

Each preview is a complete, isolated Cipi app:

| Every preview gets | Like production? |
| --- | --- |
| Its own Linux user, PHP-FPM pool and files | Yes: one preview can't read another |
| Its own database (MariaDB or PostgreSQL) and Valkey | Yes: empty, then migrated and seeded |
| HTTPS with its own Let's Encrypt certificate | Yes |
| Queue workers and the scheduler | Yes, adjustable with `cipi-preview.yml` |
| Zero-downtime deploys, rollback, logs, audit | Yes |
| Backups | No, unless you add them |

## How a preview gets updated 

After the first deploy, new pushes to the branch must reach the preview. There are two ways, the same two as for [any deploy](https://cipi.sh/docs/how-deploys-work):

| | Webhook (default) | Deploy from the script |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How | Cipi gives each preview its own webhook; a push to the branch deploys it within a minute | CI runs the script on every push, and the script deploys |
| Use it when | The app has [`cipi/agent`](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-install) (Laravel), or it's a Node app | The app has no agent, or the preview is behind basic auth |
| CI work per push | None | One deploy step |
| Set with | `PREVIEW_MODE=webhook` | `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` |

> [!warning] **Basic auth blocks the webhook.** A preview protected with a password answers `401` to the Git provider too, so the webhook can't deploy it. For password-protected previews use `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy`. To keep previews private without that limit, put them behind [Cloudflare Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust), which lets `/cipi/webhook` through.

## 1. One-time setup 

| What | How | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A server for previews | A separate Cipi server is best ([install](https://cipi.sh/docs/installation)) | Previews use RAM and CPU, and the token that creates and deletes them shouldn't be able to touch production |
| Wildcard DNS | `A *.preview.example.com → preview server IP` | Every preview gets a subdomain without touching DNS again |
| A Git token on the server | `cipi git github-token …` (or GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure) | Cipi adds a read-only deploy key and the webhook for each preview, and removes them on delete. See [Git providers](https://cipi.sh/docs/git) |
| The API | `cipi api api.preview.example.com` | The script talks to the server through the API, not SSH |
| A token for previews | See below | Only what previews need |
| PHP | `cipi php install 8.4` (the version your app uses) | Previews are created with it |

```bash
# on the preview server
$ cipi api token create --name=previews \
    --abilities=apps-view,apps-create,apps-delete,apps-env,apps-artisan,deploy-manage,ssl-manage,yml-manage \
    --expires=2027-12-31
```

Save the token as `CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN` and the API address as `CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL` in your CI. The token can create and delete apps on that server: one more reason to keep previews away from production.

> [!note] Using the production server for previews works too. Then remember that `apps-delete` covers production apps as well: the script below only ever deletes the `pv…` names it computes, but the token itself could delete anything.

## 2. The script 

Commit this as `.cipi/preview.sh` and make it executable (`chmod +x .cipi/preview.sh`). It runs on your laptop or in CI, needs [`cipi-cli`](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) and `git`, and talks to the preview server through the API.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .cipi/preview.sh: create, update or delete the preview of one branch.
#   .cipi/preview.sh up   [branch]    create it, or update it (PREVIEW_MODE=deploy)
#   .cipi/preview.sh down [branch]    delete it with its database
#   .cipi/preview.sh url  [branch]    print its address
#   .cipi/preview.sh name [branch]    print its app name (pv…)
# Settings (environment variables):
#   PREVIEW_DOMAIN      required, e.g. preview.example.com
#   PREVIEW_REPOSITORY  SSH clone URL; default: the "origin" remote
#   PREVIEW_PHP         default 8.4
#   PREVIEW_MODE        webhook (default) or deploy
#   CIPI_PROFILE        cipi-cli profile of the preview server; default "preview"
set -euo pipefail

ACTION=${1:-up}
BRANCH=${2:-$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)}
BASE=${PREVIEW_DOMAIN:?Set PREVIEW_DOMAIN, e.g. preview.example.com}
PHP=${PREVIEW_PHP:-8.4}
MODE=${PREVIEW_MODE:-webhook}
PROFILE=${CIPI_PROFILE:-preview}

# Cipi needs an SSH clone URL: turn https://host/owner/repo into git@host:owner/repo.git
to_ssh() {
  case "$1" in
    https://*) local u=${1#https://}; u=${u#*@}; u=${u%.git}; printf 'git@%s:%s.git' "${u%%/*}" "${u#*/}" ;;
    *) printf '%s' "$1" ;;
  esac
}
REPO=$(to_ssh "${PREVIEW_REPOSITORY:-$(git remote get-url origin)}")

# Stable names: the same repository and branch always give the same app and address.
sha1() { if command -v sha1sum >/dev/null; then sha1sum; else shasum -a 1; fi; }
ID=$(printf '%s#%s' "$REPO" "$BRANCH" | sha1 | cut -c1-10)
SLUG=$(printf '%s' "$BRANCH" | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sed -E 's/[^a-z0-9]+/-/g; s/^-+//; s/-+$//' | cut -c1-40 | sed -E 's/-+$//')
APP="pv${ID}"                                  # Linux user: lowercase letters and digits only
DOMAIN="${SLUG:+$SLUG-}${ID}.${BASE}"

cli() { cipi-cli "$PROFILE" "$@"; }
exists() { cli apps show "$APP" >/dev/null 2>&1; }

case "$ACTION" in
  url)
    echo "https://${DOMAIN}"
    ;;
  name)
    echo "$APP"
    ;;
  up)
    if exists; then
      if [ "$MODE" = deploy ]; then
        cli deploy "$APP"
      else
        echo "Preview ${APP} exists: its webhook deploys every push to ${BRANCH}."
      fi
    else
      cli apps create --user "$APP" --domain "$DOMAIN" --php "$PHP" \
        --repository "$REPO" --branch "$BRANCH" --env preview >/dev/null   # keeps the DB password out of CI logs; errors still show
      cli apps env set "$APP" --set MAIL_MAILER=log    # previews never e-mail real people
      cli ssl install "$APP"
      cli yml auto "$APP" on -y                        # applies cipi-preview.yml, if the repo has one
      cli deploy "$APP"
      cli apps artisan "$APP" -- db:seed --force || echo "Seeding skipped"
    fi
    echo "https://${DOMAIN}"
    ;;
  down)
    if exists; then
      cli apps delete "$APP" -y
    else
      echo "No preview for ${BRANCH}."
    fi
    ;;
  *)
    echo "Usage: $0 up|down|url|name [branch]" >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
esac
```

What it computes, for the branch `feature/Cart-v2` of `git@github.com:acme/shop.git`:

| Value | Example | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ID` | `3a1f9c2e4b` | First 10 characters of the SHA-1 of repository + branch: stable, and unique across repositories |
| `APP` | `pv3a1f9c2e4b` | Cipi app names are lowercase letters and digits, 3 to 32 characters, starting with a letter |
| `DOMAIN` | `feature-cart-v2-3a1f9c2e4b.preview.example.com` | Readable slug (max 40 characters) + the ID, so two branches never collide |

The last line the script prints is always the preview URL, so CI can read it with `tail -1`.

### Without the API: over SSH 

If the preview server has no API, the same steps run over SSH as the `cipi` user, who may run `sudo cipi …` without a password. Set `PREVIEW_HOST`, give CI an SSH key for the `cipi` user ([how](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#ssh-key)), and swap each API call of the script for its SSH twin:

```bash
srv() { ssh cipi@"$PREVIEW_HOST" sudo cipi "$@"; }
exists() { srv app show "$APP" >/dev/null 2>&1; }
```

| In the script | Over SSH |
| --- | --- |
| `cli apps create --user "$APP" …` | `srv app create --user="$APP" --domain="$DOMAIN" --php="$PHP" --repository="$REPO" --branch="$BRANCH" --env=preview` |
| `cli apps env set "$APP" --set MAIL_MAILER=log` | `srv app env "$APP" --set=MAIL_MAILER=log` |
| `cli ssl install "$APP"` | `srv ssl install "$APP"` |
| `cli yml auto "$APP" on -y` | `srv yml auto "$APP" on` |
| `cli deploy "$APP"` | `srv deploy "$APP"` |
| `cli apps artisan "$APP" -- db:seed --force` | `srv app artisan "$APP" db:seed --force` |
| `cli apps delete "$APP" -y` | `srv app delete "$APP" --force` |

The API version gives CI less power (a token limited to what previews need, instead of a key that can run any `cipi` command): prefer it.

## 3. Try it from your laptop 

```bash
# once: install cipi-cli and add the preview server as a profile
$ cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint https://api.preview.example.com --token "1|…"

# on any branch of your project
$ export PREVIEW_DOMAIN=preview.example.com
$ .cipi/preview.sh up
Creating app 'pv3a1f9c2e4b'...
…
https://feature-cart-3a1f9c2e4b.preview.example.com

$ .cipi/preview.sh url feature/cart      # the address of any branch
$ .cipi/preview.sh down                  # delete the preview of the current branch
```

Handy for a demo branch you want to show a client today, without any CI.

## 4. Recipes 

| Tool | Creates on | Deletes on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [GitHub Actions](#github) | Pull request opened or reopened | Pull request closed or merged |
| [GitLab CI/CD](#gitlab) | Push to any branch except the default one | Branch deleted, merge, or the **Stop** button |
| [Bitbucket Pipelines](#bitbucket) | Pull request created or updated | The nightly [cleanup](#cleanup) or a manual pipeline |
| [Gitea and Forgejo Actions](#gitea) | Pull request opened | Pull request closed |
| [Jenkins](#jenkins) | Build of a pull request (change request) | The nightly [cleanup](#cleanup) |
| Any other CI | A job running `.cipi/preview.sh up` | The nightly [cleanup](#cleanup) |

All recipes install cipi-cli the same way:

```bash
base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
sudo install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli    # without sudo in root containers
cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN"
```

### GitHub Actions 

The preview link appears in the pull request as a **View deployment** button.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/preview.yml
name: Preview
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, reopened, synchronize, closed]

concurrency:
  group: preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

env:
  PREVIEW_DOMAIN: preview.example.com
```
