```yaml
  PREVIEW_REPOSITORY: git@github.com:${{ github.repository }}.git
  PREVIEW_PHP: "8.4"
  PREVIEW_MODE: webhook                 # "deploy" if the app has no cipi/agent or uses basic auth
  BRANCH: ${{ github.head_ref }}

jobs:
  up:
    if: github.event.action != 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: preview
      url: ${{ steps.preview.outputs.url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install cipi-cli
        env:
          CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL: ${{ secrets.CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL }}
          CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
          curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
          sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
          sudo install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
          cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN"
      - id: preview
        run: echo "url=$(.cipi/preview.sh up "$BRANCH" | tail -1)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  down:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install cipi-cli
        env:
          CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL: ${{ secrets.CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL }}
          CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
          curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
          sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
          sudo install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
          cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN"
      - run: .cipi/preview.sh down "$BRANCH"
```

| Detail | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `BRANCH` passed through `env` | The branch name is never pasted into the shell script, so a branch called `` `rm -rf` `` stays a string |
| `head.repo.full_name == github.repository` | No previews for pull requests from forks: they don't get your secrets, and they shouldn't run on your server |
| `concurrency` per pull request | Two quick pushes don't create the same preview twice |
| `synchronize` | Needed only with `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy`; in webhook mode the job just confirms the preview exists |

### GitLab CI/CD 

GitLab calls them **review apps** and has everything built in: the environment link in the merge request, a **Stop** button, automatic stop when the branch is deleted or after a timeout.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [review]

variables:
  PREVIEW_DOMAIN: preview.example.com
  PREVIEW_REPOSITORY: git@gitlab.com:$CI_PROJECT_PATH.git     # your GitLab host if self-hosted
  PREVIEW_PHP: "8.4"
  PREVIEW_MODE: webhook

.cipi-cli: &cipi-cli
  image: debian:stable-slim
  before_script:
    - apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq curl git ca-certificates >/dev/null
    - base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
    - curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
    - sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
    - install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
    - cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN"

review:
   preview.env
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: preview.env
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: $PREVIEW_URL
    on_stop: stop_review
    auto_stop_in: 2 weeks

stop_review:
  /dev/null 2>&1 && cipi-cli preview apps delete "pv$ID" -y || echo "Nothing to delete"
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    action: stop
```

The stop job doesn't check out the repository (the branch may be deleted), so it computes the app name inline, with the same rule as the script. Mark `CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN` as *Masked*; don't mark it *Protected*, or feature branches won't see it.

### Bitbucket Pipelines 

Bitbucket runs pipelines when a pull request is created or updated, but has no "pull request closed" trigger: deletion is done by the nightly [cleanup](#cleanup), or by hand with a custom pipeline.

```yaml
# bitbucket-pipelines.yml
definitions:
  steps:
    - step: &preview-up
        name: Preview
        script:
          - base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
          - curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
          - sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
          - install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
          - cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN"
          - export PREVIEW_REPOSITORY="git@bitbucket.org:$BITBUCKET_REPO_FULL_NAME.git"
          - .cipi/preview.sh up "$BITBUCKET_BRANCH"

pipelines:
  pull-requests:
    '**':
      - step: *preview-up
  custom:
    delete-preview:                    # Run pipeline → custom: delete-preview, on the branch
      - step:
          name: Delete preview
          script:
            - base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
            - curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
            - sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
            - install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
            - cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN"
            - export PREVIEW_REPOSITORY="git@bitbucket.org:$BITBUCKET_REPO_FULL_NAME.git"
            - .cipi/preview.sh down "$BITBUCKET_BRANCH"
```

Set `PREVIEW_DOMAIN` (and the two API variables, secured) under **Repository settings → Repository variables**. Bitbucket shows the URL in the step log, last line.

### Gitea and Forgejo Actions 

Both run the [GitHub Actions recipe](#github) as it is, with three changes: save it as `.gitea/workflows/preview.yml` or `.forgejo/workflows/preview.yml`, set `runs-on:` to a label of your runner, and point `PREVIEW_REPOSITORY` at your forge's SSH address (for example `git@git.example.com:${{ github.repository }}.git`).

> [!note] Cipi adds deploy keys and webhooks by itself on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps. On Gitea and Forgejo it can't, so each preview of a **private** repository needs its deploy key added by hand (`sudo cipi deploy pv… --key` on the server prints it), and pushes reach it only with `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy`. Fully automatic previews there work for public repositories.

### Jenkins 

In a Multibranch Pipeline with pull request discovery, add a stage that runs only for change requests:

```groovy
stage('Preview') {
    when { changeRequest() }
    environment {
        PREVIEW_DOMAIN         = 'preview.example.com'
        PREVIEW_REPOSITORY     = 'git@github.com:acme/shop.git'
        CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL   = 'https://api.preview.example.com'
        CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN = credentials('cipi-preview-token')
    }
    steps {
        sh '''
          export HOME="$(mktemp -d)"
          cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN"
          .cipi/preview.sh up "$CHANGE_BRANCH"
        '''
    }
}
```

Jenkins has no step that runs when a pull request closes: schedule the [cleanup](#cleanup) as a nightly job. More on Jenkins: [Jenkins](https://cipi.sh/docs/jenkins).

## 5. Clean up 

Previews whose branch is gone should go too. This script lists the previews on the server and deletes those whose branch no longer exists in the repository. Run it nightly from any CI scheduler (GitHub `schedule`, GitLab pipeline schedules, Bitbucket schedules, Jenkins `cron`) or from your laptop.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .cipi/preview-cleanup.sh: delete previews whose branch no longer exists
set -euo pipefail
PROFILE=${CIPI_PROFILE:-preview}
REPO=${PREVIEW_REPOSITORY:?set PREVIEW_REPOSITORY to the SSH clone URL}

heads=$(git ls-remote --heads origin)            # fails, and stops the script, if Git can't be reached
cipi-cli "$PROFILE" apps list --json \
  | jq -r --arg repo "$REPO" '.data[] | select(.env == "preview" and (.app | startswith("pv")) and .repository == $repo) | "\(.app) \(.branch)"' \
  | while read -r app branch; do
      if grep -q "refs/heads/${branch}$" <<< "$heads"; then
        echo "keep   $app ($branch)"
      else
        echo "delete $app ($branch)"
        cipi-cli "$PROFILE" apps delete "$app" -y
      fi
    done
```

It only touches apps that are labelled `preview`, named `pv…` and built from this repository, so production apps and other projects' previews are never in its list.

## 6. Make previews useful 

### A configuration just for previews 

Previews are created with `--env preview`, so they read **`cipi-preview.yml`** first and fall back to `cipi.yml`. The script turns on automatic apply, so the file is applied after every deploy.

```yaml
# cipi-preview.yml
version: 1
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 1 }   # one worker is plenty for a review
schedule: false                          # no scheduled jobs on previews
deploy:
  keep_releases: 2                       # less disk per preview
```

See [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml) for every key.

### Data to look at 

| Option | How |
| --- | --- |
| Seeders (default) | The script runs `db:seed --force` once, after the first deploy |
| A realistic dump without personal data | Create one with the [anonymizer](https://cipi.sh/docs/anonymizer), then `sudo cipi db restore pv3a1f9c2e4b dump.sql.gz` on the preview server |
| Never | A copy of production. A preview is easier to reach than production and shouldn't hold real customers' data |

### Keep previews private 

| Option | Works with | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cloudflare Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) | Both update modes | Login with your company accounts; `/cipi/webhook` stays reachable |
| Basic auth (`app.basic_auth` in `cipi-preview.yml`, or `cipi basicauth enable`) | `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` only | Blocks the Git webhook too |
| Unguessable names only | Both | The ID in the address is not a secret: search engines and link scanners can still find a preview |

### E-mails, payments, third parties 

The script sets `MAIL_MAILER=log`, so previews never e-mail anyone. Do the same for anything with side effects: test keys for payment providers, sandbox webhooks, a separate S3 bucket. Set them once with `cipi-cli preview apps env set pv… --set KEY=value`, or add them to the script's create branch.

## Limits to know 

| Limit | Value | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server resources | Each preview is a PHP pool, a worker and a database | A 4 GB server runs about a dozen small previews; delete stale ones |
| Let's Encrypt | 50 new certificates per registered domain every 7 days | Use a separate domain for previews (`acme-preview.dev`) so production renewals never compete |
| GitHub webhooks | 20 per repository for the push event, production included | Above about 18 open previews, new previews get no webhook: close stale pull requests, or use `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` |
| Names | App name up to 32 characters; DNS label up to 63 | The script keeps both well under |

## Common problems 

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Invalid username` | A hand-made name with `-` or capitals | Let the script compute it: `pv` + 10 hex characters |
| Preview created but not updating | No agent in the app, or basic auth on | Add `cipi/agent`, or set `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` |
| "Could not add the webhook" on create | GitHub's 20-webhook limit, or the Git token lacks webhook rights | Close stale previews; check the token ([Git providers](https://cipi.sh/docs/git)) |
| Certificate fails | Wildcard DNS missing, or the Let's Encrypt weekly limit | `dig +short x.preview.example.com`; use a separate preview domain |
| Deploy key can't read the repository | No Git token on the preview server | `cipi git github-token …` on the preview server, then `.cipi/preview.sh down` and `up` again |
| `403` from the API | The token lacks an ability | Recreate it with the list in [setup](#setup) |
| A preview half-created (the script stopped) | A step failed after `apps create` | `.cipi/preview.sh down`, fix the cause, `.cipi/preview.sh up` |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Is a preview a real Cipi app? | Yes: same isolation, deploys, logs and rollback as production. It's only labelled `preview` and named `pv…`. |
| Do previews need a wildcard certificate? | No. Each preview gets its own certificate over HTTP; only the DNS record is a wildcard. |
| Can previews run on the production server? | Yes, but a separate server keeps reviews from slowing production and keeps the preview token away from production apps. |
| Do tests run before a preview updates? | In webhook mode the preview updates on every push, tests or not: that's usually what reviewers want. With `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy`, put the preview job after your tests. |
| What happens to the database when the preview is deleted? | It's deleted with the app, together with the files, the certificate and the deploy key and webhook in the repository. |
| How do I see all previews? | `cipi-cli preview apps list`, or `sudo cipi app list` on the server: they're the `pv…` apps. |

The why and the team workflows: [What preview environments can do for your team](https://cipi.sh/guides/preview-environments-for-teams).


## Deploy notifications

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-notifications

Know about every deploy, success or failure, without watching logs. The simplest way is the server itself: it notifies for **every** trigger, webhook deploys included.

## From the server (recommended) 

```bash
$ cipi notification add slack ops --url=https://hooks.slack.com/services/…
$ cipi notification add telegram team --token= --chat-id=
$ cipi notification test
```

| Event | Sent when |
| --- | --- |
| `deploy_success` | After the post-deploy health check passes |
| `deploy_fail` | The deploy failed; the live release is unchanged |
| `deploy_rollback` | A rollback ran (manual or automatic) |

Messages include app, branch, release, commit and author, duration and health verdict. Channels: email (SMTP, Resend, SES), Slack, Discord, Mattermost, Google Chat, Telegram, ntfy, Pushover, signed webhook. See [Notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications).

## From CI 

When the message should come from the pipeline (with the CI run link), add a step after `cipi deploy`:

```yaml
# GitHub Actions, after the deploy step
      - name: Notify Slack
        if: always()
        run: |
          STATUS=${{ job.status == 'success' && '✅ deployed' || '❌ FAILED' }}
          curl -s -X POST "${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL }}" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
            -d "{\"text\":\"*myapp* $STATUS · ${{ github.ref_name }} by ${{ github.actor }}\"}"
```

```yaml
# GitLab CI
deploy:
  script:
    - ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy myapp" && R="✅ deployed" || R="❌ FAILED"
    - curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}/sendMessage" -d chat_id="$TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID" -d text="myapp $R on $CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME"
    - '[ "$R" = "✅ deployed" ] || exit 1'   # a failed deploy published nothing: no rollback needed
```

> [!tip] Telegram chat ID: add the bot to the group, open `https://api.telegram.org/bot/getUpdates` and read `chat.id`.


## Domains & aliases

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/domains

An app has one **primary domain** and any number of **aliases**. One certificate covers them all.

```bash
$ cipi domains            # every domain of every app, in one table
```

| Column | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| DOMAIN, APP, KIND | The name, its app, `primary` or `alias` |
| TYPE, PHP, DOCROOT, BRANCH | How the app is served and deployed |
| LAST DEPLOY | When the live release was published |
| SSL | `✓`/`✗` per name |
| suffix | `⏸ suspended` for suspended apps |

To rename the primary domain: `cipi app edit myapp --domain=new.example.com` ([Manage apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/manage-apps#edit)).

## Aliases 

```bash
$ cipi alias add myapp www.myapp.com
$ cipi alias add myapp myapp.it
$ cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'     # wildcard: quote it
$ cipi alias list myapp
$ cipi alias remove myapp myapp.it
```

The vhost keeps serving HTTPS while you change aliases. `alias add` tells you whether the new name is already covered by the certificate or which command adds it (usually `cipi ssl install myapp`; for a wildcard `--dns=cloudflare`, see [Wildcard domains](https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains)).

## www and apex 

Pick one canonical host and 301 the other to it. Search engines see one site, and the certificate covers both.

```bash
$ cipi www force-to-root myapp      # www.myapp.com → myapp.com
$ cipi www force-from-root myapp    # myapp.com → www.myapp.com
$ cipi www status myapp
$ cipi www clear myapp
```

The missing counterpart is added as an alias automatically. ACME challenges stay reachable, so renewals keep working. In [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml#cli-yml-routes): `app.www: to-root`.

## In the web panel 

Aliases, certificates and www/apex redirects, from the browser. The [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) is optional; everything here also works from the CLI.

## Common problems 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Alias added but the site shows another app | DNS points elsewhere, or the browser cached a redirect: check `dig`, try a private window |
| HTTPS warning on the new alias | Re-run `cipi ssl install myapp` so the certificate covers it |
| Wildcard alias doesn't get a certificate | Wildcards need DNS validation: [wildcard domains](https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains) |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| How many domains per app? | As many aliases as you like; one certificate covers up to 100 names. |
| www or not? | Pick one with `cipi www`; the other redirects to it. |
| Behind Cloudflare? | Read [Cloudflare in front of Laravel](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-proxy-ssl-wildcard). |


## SSL certificates

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl

Free Let's Encrypt certificates for every app, renewed automatically. One command covers the primary domain and every alias.

## Commands 

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi ssl install myapp` | Issue or reissue (all names in one certificate); forces HTTPS; sets `APP_URL` |
| `cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare` | Issue through Cloudflare DNS: wildcards, proxy on, no port 80 needed |
| `cipi ssl install myapp --http` | Back to HTTP validation |
| `cipi ssl force myapp` | Re-apply the HTTP → HTTPS redirect without reissuing |
| `cipi ssl status` | Certificates, expiry, and per app the names not covered |
| `cipi ssl renew` | Force renewal of everything |

## Two ways to validate 

| | HTTP-01 (default) | DNS-01 via Cloudflare |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs | DNS pointing at the server, port 80 open | A Cloudflare API token (Zone → DNS → Edit) |
| Wildcards | No | Yes |
| Behind Cloudflare proxy | Depends on Cloudflare rules | Always works |
| Renewal | Automatic | Automatic, with the same token |

```bash
$ cipi ssl dns set --token=CF_TOKEN
$ cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare [--wildcard]
```

A certificate is always renewed the way it was issued, and Nginx reloads after each renewal (twice-daily timer plus a weekly safety cron). Cipi writes the HTTPS block itself, so aliases, redirects, Octane, Reverb, basic auth or suspension never drop HTTPS.

## Several Cloudflare accounts 

Hosting clients with their own Cloudflare accounts? Give each token a name:

```bash
$ cipi ssl dns set --name=client-a --token=TOKEN_A
$ cipi ssl install shop --dns=cloudflare --account=client-a
$ cipi ssl dns list           # accounts and what renews with each (tokens never shown)
$ cipi ssl dns remove client-a
```

Tokens are root-only files in `/etc/cipi/cloudflare/`. Removing an account is refused while a certificate still renews with it, so nothing expires silently.

> [!warning] Behind the Cloudflare proxy set SSL/TLS to **Full (strict)**. *Flexible* creates a redirect loop with Cipi's HTTPS redirect. With [Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) tunnels, Cloudflare terminates HTTPS and Cipi adapts automatically.

## Common problems 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Certificate fails over HTTP | DNS not pointing at the server, or port 80 closed: check `dig` and the provider firewall |
| `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` behind Cloudflare | SSL/TLS mode is Flexible: set Full (strict) |
| Renewal failed alert | `cipi ssl status`; a domain that moved away blocks renewal of the whole certificate: remove its alias |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Do certificates renew by themselves? | Yes, twice daily checks, the same way they were issued. |
| Wildcards? | Yes, through Cloudflare DNS: `cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare`. |
| Is it free? | Yes, Let's Encrypt. |


## Wildcard domains

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains

One app answering on every `.myapp.com`, with one certificate for all of them. It takes two separate things:

| Part | How | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Routing** | `cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'` (or a wildcard primary) | Works with any DNS |
| **Certificate** | `cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare` | Let's Encrypt issues wildcards over DNS only; Cipi automates Cloudflare |

## Which setup is yours 

| Your DNS | Certificate | Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloudflare, proxied (orange) — best for SaaS | Let's Encrypt via DNS-01, or [Cloudflare Origin CA](#origin-ca) | **Full (strict)** |
| Cloudflare, DNS only (grey) | Let's Encrypt via DNS-01 | not used |
| Another provider | Move DNS to Cloudflare (free), list the subdomains, or bring your own certificate | — |
| Cloudflare Tunnel ([cipi zt](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust)) | Not needed: Cloudflare terminates HTTPS | set by the tunnel |

## With Cloudflare, step by step 

```flow
DNS records | A @ and A * → server
> In Cloudflare, create `A @` and `A *` records pointing at the server's IP, **both with the same proxy status**. The `*` record sends every subdomain to the server.
API token | Zone → DNS → Edit
> Create a Cloudflare API token with only **Zone → DNS → Edit** on that zone and save it with `cipi ssl dns set --token=…`.
Wildcard alias | routes subdomains
> `cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'` (with quotes) tells Nginx to send every subdomain to this app.
Certificate | DNS-01, ~1 minute
> `cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare` proves ownership with a temporary DNS record and gets the wildcard certificate in about a minute. It works with the proxy on or off.
Proxy settings | Full (strict), real IPs
> If the records are proxied (orange cloud): SSL/TLS **Full (strict)**, no rule that sets Flexible, `cipi zt enable` for real visitor IPs and `trustProxies` in Laravel.
```

```bash
$ cipi ssl dns set --token=YOUR_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN
$ cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'
$ cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare
$ cipi ssl status
$ curl -sI https://tenant1.myapp.com | head -1
```

Renewals happen by themselves with the same token, through DNS, so they don't depend on the proxy, on Cloudflare rules or on port 80. `--wildcard` adds `myapp.com` + `*.myapp.com` to the certificate even without a wildcard alias (handy for many explicit subdomains); it does not route anything.

## How the proxy fits in 

| | DNS only (grey cloud) | Proxied (orange cloud) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visitors connect to | Your server | Cloudflare, which connects to your server |
| Certificate visitors see | Cipi's Let's Encrypt certificate | Cloudflare's edge certificate (Universal SSL, automatic) |
| Certificate on the server | Cipi's, checked by browsers | Cipi's, checked by Cloudflare in **Full (strict)** |
| SSL/TLS mode in Cloudflare | Ignored | **Full (strict)** |
| Server IP | Public | Hidden behind Cloudflare |
| CDN, WAF, DDoS protection | No | Yes |
| IP seen by Nginx and Laravel | The visitor's | Cloudflare's, until you [configure real IPs](#real-ip) |

With the orange cloud every request makes **two HTTPS hops**: browser → Cloudflare (edge certificate) and Cloudflare → server (Cipi's certificate). Both must be valid for every tenant name, and both cover one level: `myapp.com` and `*.myapp.com`.

> [!tip] Start grey. When `https://tenant1.myapp.com` works with the grey cloud, switch `@` and `*` to orange together. One change at a time makes errors easy to place.

## DNS records 

In **DNS → Records**:

| Type | Name | Content | Proxy status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | `@` | server IPv4 | Proxied or DNS only |
| A | `*` | server IPv4 | **Same as `@`** |
| AAAA | `@`, `*` | server IPv6 | Only if the server really answers on IPv6; same status |

- **Keep `@` and `*` on the same proxy status.** Mixed statuses make the apex and the tenants behave differently (different certificates, different IPs in logs), and errors become hard to place.
- **The wildcard only fills gaps.** A name with a record of its own (`api`, `www`, `mail`) doesn't use `*`. That's how you point `api.myapp.com` elsewhere, but it also means a stray record silently takes a tenant name away.
- **Proxied wildcards are on every plan**, Free included.
- **Mail stays grey.** `MX`, SPF, DKIM and DMARC records are unaffected by `*`, but hostnames for mail servers (`mail.`, `smtp.`) must be DNS only: the proxy carries only HTTP(S).
- **No AAAA you can't serve.** Cloudflare may prefer IPv6 to reach the origin: a wrong AAAA gives intermittent 52x errors.
- Wait until the zone shows **Active** in Cloudflare before issuing the certificate: with the old nameservers still answering, the DNS challenge fails.

## The API token 

**My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token**, template **Edit zone DNS**:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Permissions | Zone → DNS → Edit |
| Zone Resources | Include → Specific zone → `myapp.com` |
| Client IP Address Filtering | Empty, or only the server's IP |

Use an **API token**, never the Global API Key (full access to the whole account). The token is stored root-only in `/etc/cipi/cloudflare/`; a client with its own Cloudflare account gets a named token (`--name=client-a`, then `--account=client-a`, see [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl#accounts)).

## SSL/TLS settings, when proxied 

**SSL/TLS → Overview**, encryption mode:

| Mode | Cloudflare → your server | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Off | No HTTPS at all | Don't |
| Flexible | **HTTP** | **Redirect loop**: Cipi redirects HTTP to HTTPS, Cloudflare asks again over HTTP, forever |
| Full | HTTPS, certificate **not** checked | Works, but an attacker in between wouldn't be noticed |
| **Full (strict)** | HTTPS, certificate **checked** against the hostname | **Use this** |

Then **SSL/TLS → Edge Certificates**:

| Setting | Set to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Universal SSL | Active | The edge certificate for `myapp.com` and `*.myapp.com` |
| Always Use HTTPS | On | Cloudflare redirects HTTP itself, before reaching the server |
| Minimum TLS Version | 1.2 | Drops only very old clients |
| Automatic HTTPS Rewrites | On | Fixes leftover `http://` links |
| HSTS | Only **after** every tenant works over HTTPS | With `includeSubDomains` it covers all tenants, and browsers remember it for months |

> [!warning] Rules override the global mode. A Configuration Rule or Page Rule that sets SSL to **Flexible** for some hostnames gives redirect loops only on those names, typically "the apex works, tenants loop". Check **Rules** before anything else.

## Let's Encrypt or Cloudflare Origin CA 

| | Let's Encrypt via DNS-01 | Cloudflare Origin CA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Command | `cipi ssl install myapp --dns=cloudflare` | `cipi zt origin-cert myapp` |
| Trusted by | Browsers and Cloudflare | **Only Cloudflare** |
| Grey cloud | Works | Browsers reject it |
| Validity | 90 days, renewed automatically | Up to 15 years |
| Token | DNS token (`cipi ssl dns set`) | Zero Trust token with Zone · SSL and Certificates ([Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust#cli-zt-origin-cert)) |

Let's Encrypt is the safer default: it keeps working if you ever switch a record to grey. Origin CA fits servers that are permanently behind the proxy or the tunnel.

## Real IPs and a closed origin 

Behind the orange cloud every request comes from a Cloudflare IP. Left as is, Nginx logs, Fail2ban, CrowdSec and Laravel (`$request->ip()`, rate limiting, login throttling) see the same few addresses for every visitor.

1. **Nginx**: [`cipi nginx real-ip cloudflare`](https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx#real-ip) sets Nginx's real IP from Cloudflare's ranges (refreshed every night) and teaches Fail2ban and CrowdSec the same ranges. No token and no tunnel (Cipi 5.14.0+; with a [Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) tunnel, `cipi zt enable` does the same). From here `$request->ip()` is already the visitor's.
2. **Laravel**: trust the proxy in `bootstrap/app.php`, so the scheme and host Cloudflare forwards are believed too:

```php
->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
    $middleware->trustProxies(at: '*');
})
```

3. **Optional, close the origin**: `cipi zt lock http --yes` allows 80/443 only from Cloudflare, so nobody can skip the WAF by calling the server's IP. It refuses while an app still renews over HTTP; with `--dns=cloudflare` renewals are unaffected. Don't lock if some records are grey.

> [!warning] `trustProxies(at: '*')` is safe only when the server can't be reached except through Cloudflare (step 3, or a [tunnel](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust)). With 80/443 open to the world, list [Cloudflare's IP ranges](https://www.cloudflare.com/ips/) instead of `*`, or anyone can fake their IP.

## Caching, WebSockets and limits 

| Topic | What to know |
| --- | --- |
| HTML cache | Cloudflare doesn't cache HTML by default: keep it that way. Never "Cache Everything" on tenant pages: users would see each other's pages |
| Static files | Cached per hostname, so each tenant has its own copy. To share one copy, serve assets from one host (`ASSET_URL=https://myapp.com`) |
| WebSockets | [Reverb](https://cipi.sh/docs/reverb) works through the proxy on 443, on every plan |
| Upload size | 100 MB per request on Free and Pro: larger uploads go straight to object storage with signed URLs |
| Request timeout | About 100 seconds: long exports and imports belong in queues |
| Webhooks | Don't challenge `/cipi/webhook` with Bot Fight Mode or WAF rules, or push-to-deploy stops |

## Check it 

```bash
# Through Cloudflare: expect HTTP/2 200 and "server: cloudflare"
$ curl -sI https://tenant1.myapp.com | grep -Ei '^(http|server)'
# Straight to the server, skipping Cloudflare: checks Cipi's certificate and vhost
$ curl -sI --resolve tenant1.myapp.com:443:SERVER_IP https://tenant1.myapp.com | head -1
# Names on the server's certificate: expect myapp.com and *.myapp.com
$ echo | openssl s_client -connect SERVER_IP:443 -servername tenant1.myapp.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName
```

If the second command works and the first doesn't, the problem is in Cloudflare (mode, rules, DNS). If both fail, it's on the server (alias, certificate).

## Cloudflare errors decoded 

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` | SSL/TLS mode Flexible (globally or in a rule) | Full (strict), then check Rules |
| 525 SSL handshake failed | No app has that hostname, or it has no certificate yet | Add the alias / issue the certificate |
| 526 Invalid SSL certificate | The certificate doesn't cover the hostname, or expired | `cipi ssl status`, then reissue |
| 521 Web server is down | Nginx stopped, or 80/443 closed to Cloudflare | `cipi status`, [firewall](https://cipi.sh/docs/firewall) |
| 522 Connection timed out | Wrong IP in the record, provider firewall, or an AAAA the server doesn't answer | Fix the records, allow 80/443 |
| Certificate issuance fails | Zone not Active yet, token without DNS Edit on that zone, or IP filter on the token | Check zone status and token |
| Apex works, tenants don't (or the reverse) | `@` and `*` with different proxy status, or a rule on some hosts | Align the records, review Rules |
| One tenant name goes elsewhere | That name has its own DNS record, which beats `*` | Remove the record |
| Every visitor has the same IP | Real IP not configured | [Real IPs](#real-ip) |
| 413 on uploads | Plan's request size limit | Direct-to-storage uploads |
| Deep names fail (`a.b.myapp.com`) | Universal SSL and the wildcard certificate cover one level | Keep tenants one label deep, or Advanced Certificate Manager plus a `*.b.myapp.com` certificate |

The whole Cloudflare setup, not only wildcards, is in [Cloudflare in front of Laravel](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-proxy-ssl-wildcard).

## Without Cloudflare 

| Option | When |
| --- | --- |
| Move DNS to Cloudflare, records "DNS only" | Recommended: free, traffic unchanged |
| List each subdomain as an alias, HTTP-01 | Few, known tenants (max 100 names per certificate) |
| Bring your own certificate with your provider's certbot plugin | Route 53, DigitalOcean, OVH, Gandi… |

```bash
# bring your own: name the certificate after the app's primary domain
$ apt install python3-certbot-dns-route53
$ certbot certonly --dns-route53 -d myapp.com -d '*.myapp.com' --cert-name myapp.com
$ cipi alias add myapp '*.myapp.com'    # Cipi finds and serves it
```

Don't run `cipi ssl install` on that app afterwards: it would reissue over HTTP without the wildcard.

## Multi-tenant tips 

- **Exact names win**: with `*.myapp.com` on one app, `api.myapp.com` can still be another app.
- **Unknown hosts are closed** by the [default server](https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx#cli-nginx), not sent to your tenant resolver.
- **Laravel**: resolve the tenant from the `Host` header; set `SESSION_DOMAIN=.myapp.com` only to share logins across subdomains.
- **Need isolation per tenant** (own database, backups, server)? Create one Cipi app per tenant through the [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) instead.


## Redirects & proxies

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/redirects-proxies

Move pages or whole sites without losing visitors or search ranking, and route a path to another service. Rules live in Cipi's state and survive every vhost change.

## Redirect a whole app 

Every name the app answers to (primary, aliases, www) goes to the target in **one hop**.

```bash
$ cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com            # 301, path and query kept
$ cipi redirect set oldsite --to=https://new.com --302 --no-path
$ cipi redirect disable oldsite      # serve the app again, keep the target
$ cipi redirect enable oldsite
$ cipi redirect unset oldsite
```

Status codes: `--301` (default), `--302`, `--307`, `--308`. The old name's certificate keeps renewing, so HTTPS visitors get a valid redirect too.

## Redirect paths 

```bash
$ cipi redirect add myapp /old-pricing /pricing
$ cipi redirect add myapp /blog/ https://blog.example.com/
$ cipi redirect add myapp /docs/ https://docs.example.com --308 --no-path
$ cipi redirect list myapp
$ cipi redirect remove myapp /old-pricing
```

| `from` | Matches | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/old` (no trailing slash) | Exactly that path; query kept | `/old?x=1` → `/new?x=1` |
| `/blog/` (trailing slash) | The prefix; the rest is appended | `/blog/x?y` → `https://blog.example.com/x?y` |
| with `--no-path` | Everything to the target as is | `/blog/x` → `https://blog.example.com/` |

Path redirects and proxies keep working while an app redirect is on, so a moved site can keep `/api/` in place.

## Proxy a path to another service 

Hand `/api/`, `/events/` or `/docs/` to a Node or Go service, a legacy app or another origin.

```bash
$ cipi proxy add myapp /api/ http://127.0.0.1:3000 --strip-prefix
$ cipi proxy add myapp /events/ http://127.0.0.1:4000 --no-buffering --timeout=3600
$ cipi proxy add myapp /docs/ https://docs-origin.example.com --preserve-host
$ cipi proxy list myapp
$ cipi proxy remove myapp /api/
```

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| (none) | URI unchanged: `/api/users` → `upstream/api/users` |
| `--strip-prefix` | `/api/users` → `upstream/users`, with `X-Forwarded-Prefix` |
| `--preserve-host` | Send the visitor's `Host` |
| `--timeout=N` | Upstream timeout in seconds |
| `--no-buffering` | For Server-Sent Events, long polling, streaming |

Every proxy carries WebSocket upgrade and `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-*` headers; basic auth, when on, covers it too.

## Safety rails 

| Guard | Protects against |
| --- | --- |
| Strict charset for paths and URLs | Injecting Nginx directives |
| Reserved paths (`/`, ACME, `/robots.txt`, `/cipi/webhook`, Reverb's `/app`) | Breaking certificates, webhooks or WebSockets |
| Loop and overlap detection | Redirect loops; a redirect and a proxy on the same prefix |
| Loopback guard | Proxying to Cipi's own ports (SSH, databases, Valkey, Octane, Reverb) without `--force`; the panel and cipi.yml can never force |
| `nginx -t` before reload | A bad rule: config and state are restored, exit code 1 |

Changes fire `redirect_change` / `proxy_change` [notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications). Also available in the panel, the API and [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml#cli-yml-routes).


## Nginx

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx

Cipi runs Nginx from nginx.org's mainline repository, hardened and kept patched. This page covers the security report, upgrades, the default server, the visitor's address behind Cloudflare and an app's own directives.

## Security report 

```bash
$ cipi nginx security
```

| Reports | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Installed version vs. the oldest with every known fix | Are you exposed to a published CVE? |
| Whether the running binary is the one on disk | An upgrade isn't real until the old workers are gone |
| Every config file that turns HTTP/2 on | Most recent HTTP/2 CVEs need it |

Cipi's vhosts use `listen 443 ssl;` and never enable HTTP/2, which removes a whole class of vulnerabilities from a standard Cipi server. [How Cipi handled the nginx 1.31.9 CVEs](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching) walks through a real case.

## Upgrades 

Nginx is excluded from unattended upgrades so it never restarts unexpectedly. Patch it on your terms:

```bash
$ cipi nginx upgrade [--yes]      # now
$ cipi autoupdate on nginx        # or nightly, automatically
```

```flow
apt upgrade nginx | your nginx.conf kept
> Nginx is upgraded with apt; your `nginx.conf` and every vhost are kept.
nginx -t | must pass
> `nginx -t` must pass with the new binary before anything reloads. If it fails, the old Nginx keeps running.
Reload | graceful
> A graceful reload: new workers start, old ones finish their requests. No connection is dropped.
Check binary | restart if old workers linger
> Cipi checks that the running binary is the new one, and restarts if old workers linger, so the fix is really active.
```

If a long-lived connection (a WebSocket) keeps an old worker on the replaced binary, Cipi restarts Nginx instead of reloading (well under a second of interruption). A server found on Ubuntu's archive Nginx is moved to nginx.org mainline in one simulated-first transaction: if anything can't be done, nothing changes.

## Default server 

```bash
$ cipi nginx default-server status|on|off
```

On by default: requests for unknown hostnames, on HTTP and HTTPS, get an empty reply (444) instead of reaching one of your apps or a tenant resolver.

## Behind Cloudflare: the visitor's real IP 

A domain proxied by Cloudflare (the orange cloud) reaches Nginx from Cloudflare's addresses: the access log, Fail2ban, CrowdSec and your app all see Cloudflare instead of the visitor. One command fixes it for the whole server (Cipi 5.14.0+):

```bash
$ cipi nginx real-ip cloudflare     # on
$ cipi nginx real-ip status         # --json for scripts
$ cipi nginx real-ip off            # back to the address of each connection
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | Gives Nginx Cloudflare's IPv4 and IPv6 ranges and `CF-Connecting-IP`: a request from one of the ranges gets the visitor's address |
| **Why it can't be forged** | A request from anywhere else keeps the address of its connection, so sending the header straight to your server does nothing. Domains not behind Cloudflare are unaffected |
| **In the app** | With PHP-FPM the visitor's address is `REMOTE_ADDR`: `$request->ip()`, rate limiting and login throttling work with no change in Laravel. Octane and Node apps get it in `X-Forwarded-For`, as they already do for a direct visitor |
| **Fail2ban and CrowdSec** | Never ban Cloudflare's ranges (that would take every proxied site down), and `cipi crowdsec enable` no longer needs `--force` behind the proxy |
| **Kept current** | The ranges are Cloudflare's public list — no token — fetched again every night; if the fetch fails, the previous ones stay |

`nginx -t` runs before the reload: if Nginx refuses (another `real_ip_header` in your `nginx.conf`, say), the file is taken back and you get Nginx's reason. A `real_ip` configuration Cipi didn't write is left alone.

> [!info] A firewall ban stops direct connections only. A visitor who comes through Cloudflare is blocked at Cloudflare (WAF rules), not on the server. With a [Zero Trust tunnel](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust), `cipi zt enable` already sets the same thing and the two share one file.

## Your own directives 

Cipi generates each vhost (`/etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp`) and writes it again whenever aliases, PHP, SSL, basic auth, redirects or proxies change — so an edit of that file never lasts. What lasts is a text of your own per app: Cipi keeps it and includes it in the app's server block.

```bash
$ cipi nginx edit myapp                    # in $EDITOR; tested and live when you save
$ cipi nginx show myapp                    # --json for scripts
$ cipi nginx set myapp --file=myapp.conf   # the same from a file (- for stdin)
$ cipi nginx reset myapp                   # remove them
```

```nginx
client_max_body_size 512M;

location ^~ /downloads/ {
    add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
    access_log off;
}

location ~* \.(?:woff2?|ttf)$ {
    add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin "*";
    expires 1y;
}
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where it lives** | In the app's settings, so it follows [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/docs/sync), and in `/etc/nginx/cipi-custom/myapp.conf`, included before `location /` in every kind of vhost: Laravel, Octane, custom, Node |
| **What it's for** | Headers, caching, upload size, timeouts, rewrites, `location` blocks of your own |
| **What it can't do** | Redefine a location Cipi already defines (`/`, `\.php$`, the ACME path): Nginx says *duplicate location* and nothing changes. For reverse proxies and redirects use [`cipi proxy` and `cipi redirect`](https://cipi.sh/docs/redirects-proxies) |
| **Limits** | 32 KB per app. A suspended app keeps its text; it's back in the vhost when you unsuspend |

```flow
Save | your text
> The text is saved with the app's settings and its vhost is written again with the `include`.
nginx -t | must pass
> Nginx tests the whole configuration. If it's already broken before your change, Cipi stops and touches nothing.
Reload | graceful
> Passed: a graceful reload, no connection dropped.
Refused | everything back
> Failed: the settings and the vhost go back to what they were and you get Nginx's reason by line (`line 3: unknown directive "foo"`). `cipi nginx edit` offers the editor again on your text.
```

### From the API, the SDK and cipi-cli 

The same text can be read and replaced through the [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api#endpoints-nginx) (`GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE /api/apps/{name}/nginx`), the [PHP SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk#domains) (`$cipi->nginx()`) and [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client#nginx) from your laptop (`cipi-cli nginx edit myapp` opens your own editor).

> [!security] Through the API **a subset of Nginx's language** is accepted, and the server decides, not the client. With the whole language a token would be root: Nginx opens an `access_log` or `error_log` path and reads an `include` as root, `server_name` takes another app's domain, `listen` opens a port, a `*_pass` reaches another app's PHP socket or a database on the loopback.

| From the API | |
| --- | --- |
| **Accepted** | `location`, `if`, `return`, `rewrite`, `set`, `try_files`, `error_page`, `add_header`, `expires`, `gzip*`, `client_max_body_size` and the timeouts, `allow` / `deny`, `autoindex`, `types`, `sub_filter`, the `fastcgi_*` and `proxy_*` buffers and timeouts, `access_log off`, `auth_basic off`, `root` and `alias` under `/home/myapp/` |
| **Refused** | A log path, `include`, `listen`, `server_name`, every `*_pass`, certificates, `auth_basic_user_file`, a path outside the app's home, and anything not on the list — by name, with its line |
| **The whole language** | `cipi nginx edit myapp` at the server, as root |

`cipi nginx set myapp --file=… --strict` applies the API's check at the terminal, to try a text before sending it from a script.


## PHP versions & php.ini

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/php

Run several PHP versions side by side, give each app its own, and keep all of them patched. Cipi installs from packages.sury.org (fastest with security releases), then the ondrej PPA, then Ubuntu.

## Versions 

```bash
$ cipi php list                # versions, patch level, security state, default
$ cipi php install 8.4         # add a version (8.3–8.6)
$ cipi php switch 8.6          # server default (CLI, panel pools)
$ cipi php remove 8.1          # refused while it's the default or an app uses it
$ cipi app edit myapp --php=8.6  # move one app, zero downtime
```

| Version | Status on Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| 8.6 | Default on new servers once the repository has every extension Cipi needs |
| 8.3, 8.4, 8.5 | Installable and assignable |
| 7.4–8.2 (old servers) | Listed, restartable, removable; never offered to an app |

Each app's deploys, Composer, cron and workers always use **the app's** PHP, never the server default.

## A new PHP minor 

When a new minor comes out, the extension packages (`redis`, `memcached`, `imagick`) follow a few days later. Cipi handles the gap:

| Situation | Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| PHP packaged, some extensions not yet | Installs it, records what's missing, adds each extension as soon as it's published (nightly) |
| Only a release candidate available | Installs it and labels it **prerelease** |
| Assigning a version still missing extensions | Refused with the list of what's missing; `--force` if the app doesn't use them |
| A lock file that rejects the new PHP | The deploy fails and the live release stays: update the dependency, commit, deploy |

## Security patches 

PHP is excluded from Ubuntu's unattended upgrades: Cipi patches it itself **every night at 03:30**, restarts only the affected PHP-FPM services and reports the result.

```bash
$ cipi php upgrade      # patch now and print the patch level
```

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `patched` | At or past the latest security release Cipi knows |
| `VULNERABLE` | A fix exists but isn't installed yet (exit code 1; the nightly job alerts until fixed) |
| `distro` | Ubuntu build: fixes backported without a version bump |
| `END OF LIFE` | No more fixes from PHP: move apps off it |
| `prerelease` | Release candidate, not compared |

[Octane](https://cipi.sh/docs/octane) apps run the PHP inside their FrankenPHP binary, which apt never touches; `cipi php upgrade` lists them too and `cipi frankenphp upgrade` fixes them.

## Hardening 

Every pool Cipi writes (apps, webhook receivers, panel) locks down settings that recent PHP advisories used as attack paths, and Octane apps load the same rules:

```ini
php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off
php_admin_flag[fatal_error_backtraces] = off
```

They are set as admin flags, so neither `.user.ini` nor `ini_set()` can turn them back on. Vhosts never enable `fastcgi_keep_conn`. Real-world walkthrough: [How Cipi handles PHP and nginx CVEs](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching).

## php.ini settings: `cipi ini` 

Change PHP settings without hunting for the right file. Server-wide changes reach **PHP-FPM and CLI**, so web requests, workers, Artisan and cron agree.

```bash
$ cipi ini list [--app=shop]                  # effective values and where each comes from
$ cipi ini set upload_max_filesize=50M        # server-wide
$ cipi ini set memory_limit=512M --app=shop   # one app only (wins)
$ cipi ini unset memory_limit --app=shop
$ cipi ini reset [--app=shop]
$ cipi ini keys                               # what can and can't be set
```

| Behaviour | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Raising `upload_max_filesize` raises `post_max_size`/`memory_limit` if they'd cap it | One command, a working upload limit |
| Nginx `client_max_body_size` flagged when it would cap it | No mystery 413 errors |
| `open_basedir`, `auto_prepend_file`, `extension`… refused | They are part of app isolation |
| Every change fires the `ini_set` notification | Nothing changes on a shared server without a trace |

Per-app settings can also live in [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml) as `app.ini`.

## Common problems 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Assigning a version is refused | An extension isn't published yet for it: the message lists which; `--force` if unused |
| `VULNERABLE` in `cipi php list` | Run `cipi php upgrade` now |
| Wrong `php -v` in the shell | That's the server default; apps use their own |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Can apps use different versions? | Yes, each app has its own. |
| How do I upgrade an app? | [Upgrade PHP without downtime](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-version-upgrade). |


## Node.js

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/nodejs

Official Node.js builds for [Node apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/node-apps) and for Laravel asset builds. Every download is verified against nodejs.org's `SHASUMS256.txt`; only even (LTS) majors are offered.

## Commands 

```bash
$ cipi node install 24            # x64 or arm64, checksum-verified
$ cipi node list                  # majors, default, apps on each
$ cipi node upgrade 22 --restart  # latest patch; SSR apps restart blue/green
$ cipi node default 22            # server-wide Node for builds, app run, deploy.post
$ cipi node default system        # back to the distribution package
$ cipi node remove 20             # refused while in use
```

## Which Node is used 

| Layer | Picks the Node used by |
| --- | --- |
| Server default (`cipi node default`) | Laravel `--node-build`, `cipi app run … npm`, `deploy.post`, new Node apps |
| Per Laravel app (`cipi app edit myapp --node-version=24`) | That app's builds only |
| Per Node app (`--node-version`) | That app's runtime |

Runtimes live in `/opt/cipi/node/` behind an atomic symlink per major, so `cipi node upgrade` moves every app on that major at once. Files you installed yourself in `/usr/local/bin` are never overwritten. The panel can install, upgrade and remove runtimes and choose the server default too (Cipi 5.9.0+, ability `node-runtimes-manage`), and restart Node apps.


## Databases

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/databases

Each Laravel app gets its own database and user, so no app can read another's data. MariaDB is the default; PostgreSQL can be added and chosen per app or per database, and port 3306 can run [MySQL instead of MariaDB](#mysql).

## Engines 

```bash
$ cipi db install pgsql             # add PostgreSQL next to MariaDB
$ cipi db default mariadb|pgsql     # default when --engine is omitted
$ cipi db engines [--json]          # which server runs on 3306, too
$ cipi db uninstall pgsql           # destroys its data: asks first
```

| | MariaDB | PostgreSQL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Port | 3306 (localhost) | 5432 (localhost) |
| Installed | Always | `cipi db install pgsql` |
| Laravel `DB_CONNECTION` | `mysql` | `pgsql` |
| Why choose it | [Design decisions](https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions#why-mariadb) | [Design decisions](https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions#why-postgresql) |

## MySQL instead of MariaDB 

MariaDB stays the default. Since 5.13.0, a server can run **MySQL** on port 3306 instead — only as an explicit choice, from the command line, and **only on a server with no databases on 3306 yet**:

```bash
$ cipi db switch mysql            # asks first (--yes in scripts)
$ cipi db engines                 # mariadb  running  3306  MySQL
$ cipi db switch mariadb          # back, on the same terms
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| When | No database, no app and nothing in the registry on 3306. The data is never converted: no in-place upgrade exists between the two, and what a dump can't carry (MariaDB's `uuid`/`inet6` types, sequences, SQL only one of them understands) would surface later, in your apps |
| Which MySQL | From the Ubuntu archive: 8.0 on 24.04 (security fixes backported by Ubuntu), 8.4 LTS on 26.04. No extra repository or key |
| Checked first | A `mysql-server` package is available, and removing MariaDB would remove nothing but its own packages and client libraries. Otherwise nothing changes |
| What it does | Stops MariaDB, keeps its data directory aside (`/var/lib/mysql.mariadb-`), purges it, installs MySQL with the same root password (`caching_sha2_password`) and Cipi's tuning (`/etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/99-cipi.cnf`). If the install fails, MariaDB comes back with its data |
| What stays the same | The engine is still called `mariadb` (`--engine=mariadb`, `cipi.yml`, backups, API) and apps keep `DB_CONNECTION=mysql`. At the terminal the messages of `cipi db` say `mysql` (5.14.0+), a name `--engine=` accepts too. `cipi db upgrade`, autoupdate, `cipi service`, `cipi monitor`, credentials and labels follow the server that runs |
| Not in the panel or API | Replacing a database server is an operator decision; the [panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) shows *MySQL* where it runs. A `db_switch` [notification](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications) is sent |

Step by step, with what to check in your code first: [Run Laravel on MySQL instead of MariaDB](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-mysql-instead-of-mariadb).

**A server already in use** moves the way an app moves anywhere: a new server, `cipi db switch mysql` there before its first app, then [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/docs/sync). The old server stays as it was, which is your way back. Dumps cross between the two: restoring into MySQL drops MariaDB's sandbox line and maps its UCA 14 collations to MySQL's `0900` ones (and back into MariaDB); rows are never touched.

## Databases 

```bash
$ cipi db create --name=analytics --engine=pgsql
$ cipi db create --name=wpblog --app=blog     # belongs to the "blog" app
$ cipi db link wpblog blog                    # or link an existing one
$ cipi db list [--json]                       # sizes and owning app
$ cipi db backup myapp
$ cipi db restore myapp backup.sql.gz
$ cipi db password myapp                      # new password, .env updated
$ cipi db delete analytics
```

Each database has its own user and password. Linking is a label: a linked database is listed with its app (in the CLI and the panel) and is **kept** when the app is deleted; only a Laravel app's own database goes with it. Connect from TablePlus or DBeaver with the `mariadb+ssh://` URL (`mysql+ssh://` on MySQL) shown at creation: no database port is ever exposed.

## Restores you can trust 

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Stops at the first failing statement | Clear error, exit 1, no "restored" lie |
| PostgreSQL restore in one transaction | A truncated or failing dump rolls back; your data stays |
| Empty dumps refused | A backup of nothing never wipes a database |
| Newer `pg_dump` into older server | Unknown `SET` lines are dropped so it still restores |
| Files from an app's home opened as that user | A malicious symlink can't make root read other files |

## Upgrades 

Database engines are excluded from unattended upgrades, so they never restart under you. Patch when you choose (brief restart):

```bash
$ cipi db upgrade [mariadb|pgsql] [--yes]
```

Or schedule it with [cipi autoupdate](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades).

## In the web panel 

Every database on every server, with backup, restore and password rotation. The [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) is optional; everything here also works from the CLI.

## Common problems 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Access denied for user` | Password changed by hand: `cipi db password myapp` updates database and `.env` together |
| Restore stops with an error | Cipi stops at the first failing statement: read it, fix the dump or the target |
| Can't connect from TablePlus | Use the SSH tunnel settings (`mariadb+ssh://` URL from creation); no database port is open |

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| MariaDB or PostgreSQL? | Both supported; see [Laravel on PostgreSQL](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-postgresql). |
| Can I use MySQL? | Yes, in place of MariaDB on a new server: `cipi db switch mysql` before the first app ([above](#mysql)). MariaDB stays the default. |
| Can I open the database port? | Avoid it; use SSH tunnels. If you must, allow one IP with `cipi firewall allow 3306 --from=…`. |
| Need a copy without personal data? | [Anonymized dumps](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps). |


## Valkey

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/valkey

Valkey is the open-source (BSD, Linux Foundation) continuation of Redis: same protocol, same `phpredis` driver, same `REDIS_*` variables. Cipi gives **each Laravel app its own instance**, so no app can read or flush another's cache, sessions or jobs.

| Per-app instance | |
| --- | --- |
| Service | `cipi-valkey@myapp`, running as the app's user |
| Network | `127.0.0.1`, its own port (from 6400) and password |
| Config / data | `/etc/cipi-valkey/myapp.conf`, `/var/lib/cipi-valkey/myapp` |
| Cost | About 10 MB of RAM when idle |
| `.env` | `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT`, `REDIS_PASSWORD` already written |

## Use it in Laravel 

New apps keep cache, sessions and queues in their database. Switch whatever you want to Valkey:

```bash
$ cipi app env myapp --set=CACHE_STORE=redis
$ cipi app env myapp --set=SESSION_DRIVER=redis
$ cipi app artisan myapp config:cache
$ cipi worker restart myapp
```

Queues on Valkey run under Horizon: set `QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis` and `cipi worker horizon enable myapp` ([Horizon](https://cipi.sh/docs/workers#horizon)). Plain `queue:work` workers read the `database` connection.

## Manage instances 

```bash
$ cipi valkey list
$ cipi valkey isolate shop                     # move an app off the shared instance
$ cipi valkey isolate --all
$ cipi valkey isolate shop --maxmemory=256mb --policy=allkeys-lru
$ cipi valkey restart shop
$ cipi valkey flush-shared                     # once no app uses it: empty + new password
```

```flow
Maintenance on | app returns 503
> The app briefly returns 503 (a few seconds) so nothing writes during the move.
Workers stop | nothing writes
> Its workers stop too.
Copy keys | with their expiry
> Every key is copied from the shared instance to the app's own, with its expiry time.
Switch .env | config cache rebuilt
> The app's `REDIS_*` variables are switched to its own instance and the config cache is rebuilt.
Back online | seconds later
> The app comes back online. If the copy failed, it stays on the shared instance, unchanged.
```

If the copy fails, the app stays exactly where it was. Apps whose Redis points elsewhere are left alone. Clones and synced apps get their own instance. `cipi pending` lists apps still on the shared instance.

> [!note] `cipi app create --valkey=shared` keeps one app on the server-wide instance. Valkey is excluded from unattended upgrades; patch it with [stack upgrades](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades).


## Search (Meilisearch)

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/search

Full-text search for Laravel Scout, self-hosted: no Algolia account, no per-record billing. Meilisearch runs natively (a single binary with systemd), listens on localhost only, and every app gets a key that can touch **its own indexes and nothing else**. Off until you install it.

```bash
$ cipi search install             # binary, config, hardened unit; checks /health
$ cipi search enable myapp        # scoped key + SCOUT_* in .env
$ cipi app artisan myapp scout:import "App\Models\Product"
$ cipi search status [--check]
$ cipi search disable myapp [--purge-indexes]
```

Step-by-step with a real model: [Laravel Scout with Meilisearch on Cipi](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scout-meilisearch).

> [!tip] Small dataset? Scout's `database` driver or PostgreSQL full-text need no extra service. `cipi search status` says so on servers without Meilisearch.

## Isolation by design 

```flow
App myapp | SCOUT_PREFIX=myapp-
> Cipi gives each app an index prefix based on its name (`myapp-`), written to `.env` as `SCOUT_PREFIX`. You can't choose one that collides with another app.
Scoped key | indexes myapp-* only
> The app's Meilisearch key can only act on indexes starting with its prefix. Another app's index answers 403.
Meilisearch | 127.0.0.1, no public port
> Meilisearch itself listens on `127.0.0.1` only: nobody can query it from the internet.
```

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Prefix written by Cipi, not chosen by you | App names can't overlap, so prefixes can't either |
| Key limited to Scout's actions on `myapp-*` | No key management, no other app's indexes (a stray index name gets 403) |
| Master key in a root-only file, never on a command line | App users can't read it from `/proc` |
| Delete or clone an app | Its key is revoked / the clone gets a new key and prefix, never production's |
| Memory check before install | Refused below 512 MB available, warned below 1 GB |

## Commands 

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi search list` | Apps with search and their prefixes |
| `cipi search key show\|rotate myapp` | Show or replace an app's key (`.env` updated) |
| `cipi search key rotate --master` | New master key; every app's `.env` is rewritten in the same run |
| `cipi search upgrade [--version=]` | Upgrade in place; the old binary returns if the store is refused |
| `cipi search remove [--keep-data]` | Uninstall |

The panel can show status and enable/disable search per app; installing, upgrading, rotating and removing stay on the CLI.


## Services

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/services

See and control every service Cipi runs. Nginx always reloads gracefully, so restarting it never drops a request.

## Commands 

```bash
$ cipi service list [nginx] [--json]
$ cipi service restart              # everything
$ cipi service restart nginx        # graceful reload
$ cipi service restart php          # every PHP-FPM version
$ cipi service start fail2ban
$ cipi service stop supervisor      # asks first
$ cipi service upgrade              # installed vs available versions
$ cipi service upgrade valkey [--yes]
```

## Service names 

| Name | Service |
| --- | --- |
| `nginx` | Web server |
| `php` or `php8.6-fpm` | All PHP-FPM versions, or one |
| `mariadb` (or `mysql`, where [`cipi db switch mysql`](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases#mysql) ran), `postgresql` (`pgsql`) | Databases |
| `valkey-server` (`redis`, `valkey`) | Shared Valkey |
| `supervisor` | Workers, Octane, Horizon, Reverb |
| `fail2ban` | Brute-force protection |
| `meilisearch` (`search`), `cloudflared` | Only when installed |

`upgrade all` is refused on purpose: patch one service at a time and watch it come back. REST: `GET /api/services`, `POST /api/services/{name}/restart`.

## When to restart what 

| Symptom | Restart | Effect on visitors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Changed an Nginx setting by hand | `cipi service restart nginx` | None: graceful reload |
| Changed `php.ini` by hand | `cipi service restart php8.6-fpm` | A short pause for apps on that version |
| Workers ignore new code | `cipi worker restart myapp` (one app) | None |
| Database unresponsive | `cipi service restart mariadb` | Seconds of errors: last resort |

Prefer the narrowest restart: one app's workers before Supervisor, one PHP version before all of them.

## Questions 

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Does `restart nginx` drop connections? | No. Cipi reloads Nginx gracefully: open requests finish on the old workers. |
| Why is `upgrade all` refused? | One service at a time lets you see which one misbehaves after an upgrade. Nightly patches are covered by [stack upgrades](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades). |
| Can the panel restart services? | Yes, through the [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) (`POST /api/services/{name}/restart`). Stopping services stays on the CLI. |


## Packages

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/packages

Tools and libraries some Laravel packages need on the host, through a **closed allowlist**: never a root apt shell. Nothing is installed until you ask. Most come from Ubuntu's own repositories; a few, which Ubuntu doesn't ship, are [upstream releases](#upstream) pinned by version and SHA-256. Since 5.14.0 the catalog has twenty entries, Browsershot's and the [security scanners](#sec) of Hackly included, and the [web panel](#panel) installs and removes them too.

## Commands 

```bash
$ cipi package list [--json]
$ cipi package install browsershot
$ cipi package install libreoffice
$ cipi package install webp            # one apt package of a group
$ cipi package remove ffmpeg
$ cipi package remove pandoc --yes     # no prompt; required without a terminal (5.14.0+)
```

## Available packages 

| Package | Installs | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `image-optimizers` | jpegoptim, optipng, pngquant, gifsicle, webp | `spatie/laravel-image-optimizer` |
| `avif` | `avifenc` | AVIF in `spatie/laravel-image-optimizer` (5.14.0+) |
| `ffmpeg` | `ffmpeg`, `ffprobe` | `pbmedia/laravel-ffmpeg` (run it in a queue worker, never in a request) |
| `imagemagick` | `convert` / `magick` CLI | Code that shells out to ImageMagick (the PHP extension is already installed) |
| `poppler-utils` | `pdftotext`, `pdftoppm` | `spatie/pdf-to-text`, feeding PDFs to search |
| `browsershot` | The libraries and fonts Chrome needs to start | `spatie/browsershot`, `spatie/laravel-pdf` with Browsershot (5.14.0+, [below](#browsershot)) |
| `fonts-cjk` | Noto CJK fonts | Chinese, Japanese and Korean text in PDFs and images (5.14.0+) |
| `pdftk` | `pdftk` (pdftk-java) | `mikehaertl/php-pdftk`: fill forms, merge, split (pulls a headless Java runtime; 5.14.0+) |
| `libreoffice` | `soffice`, Writer and Calc without a GUI | DOCX, XLSX and ODT to PDF with `soffice --headless --convert-to pdf` (5.14.0+) |
| `pandoc` | `pandoc` | `ueberdosis/pandoc`: Markdown, HTML, DOCX, ODT, EPUB (5.14.0+) |
| `tesseract` | `tesseract`, English, Italian, German, French and Spanish | `thiagoalessio/tesseract_ocr` (5.14.0+) |

`cipi package list` marks each entry installed, **partial** (some apt packages missing — `install` completes it) or not installed; `--json` adds what each brings (`binaries`), whether it is tools or libraries (`kind`) and what a partial install lacks (`missing`). Install shows what apt will do (packages, disk space) and asks first; afterwards Cipi checks each binary is on the `PATH`. It refuses to start with less than 1 GB free.

Every entry has to be **stateless** (binaries, libraries, fonts: no daemon, no port, no credentials), **from an Ubuntu repository** (Ubuntu ships its security updates) or an [upstream release pinned in Cipi](#upstream), and backed by a real Laravel or PHP package. Why the catalog is closed, and why that lets the panel use it: [design decisions](https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions#packages). Anything with a daemon, a port or state is a service, not a package: see [search](https://cipi.sh/docs/search) and [databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases). Names that changed between Ubuntu releases (the 24.04 `t64` libraries) are resolved on the server, so the same entry works on 24.04 and later.

## Security scanners 

[Hackly](https://github.com/andreapollastri/hackly) scans the domains and repositories of a team: it runs a dozen open-source scanners and keeps their findings. On a Cipi server, the `sec-*` entries install them:

| Package | Source | Installs | Hackly uses it for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sec-recon` | Ubuntu | `nmap`, `dig`, `whois` | Port scans, DNS and WHOIS, mail security |
| `sec-gitleaks` | Ubuntu | `gitleaks` | Secrets in repositories |
| `sec-nuclei` | upstream 3.11.1 | `nuclei` | DAST, path discovery, pentests |
| `sec-zap` | upstream 2.17.0 | OWASP ZAP (`zap.sh`) and a Java runtime from Ubuntu | Baseline and pentest scans |
| `sec-nikto` | upstream 2.6.1 | `nikto`, Perl modules from Ubuntu | Pentests. Ubuntu's Nikto is 2.1.5 (2014), with no JSON reports |
| `sec-wpscan` | upstream 3.8.28 | `wpscan`, Ruby from Ubuntu | WordPress targets |
| `sec-trivy` | upstream 0.76.2 | `trivy` | Dependency vulnerabilities (SCA) |
| `sec-semgrep` | upstream 1.185.0 | `semgrep` | Static analysis (SAST) |
| `sec-checkov` | upstream 3.3.26 | `checkov` | Infrastructure as code |

```bash
$ for p in sec-recon sec-gitleaks sec-nuclei sec-zap sec-nikto sec-wpscan sec-trivy sec-semgrep sec-checkov; do
    sudo cipi package install "$p" --yes
  done
$ cipi app artisan hackly hackly:check-binaries
```

A command name works as well (`cipi package install nuclei`). Hackly finds them on the `PATH` (`/usr/local/bin`): no `.env` changes. Install only what the scans you run need — ZAP takes about 1 GB of RAM while it scans, so keep it off a small server that also serves production apps.

> [!warning] Scan only what you're allowed to. Hackly checks DNS ownership before a scan; the tools themselves don't.

Each scanner keeps its own licence. WPScan's isn't an open-source one: testing your own systems and penetration testing are free, selling it as a service needs a commercial licence from its authors. Nmap has its own too (the NPSL: the GPL with extra terms).

## Upstream releases 

Ubuntu has no nuclei, ZAP, WPScan, Trivy, Semgrep or Checkov, and its Nikto is too old. Those entries are **upstream releases pinned in Cipi**:

| Pinned | How |
| --- | --- |
| One version per entry | The server never resolves "latest"; a newer version arrives with a Cipi release |
| The download, by SHA-256 | nuclei and ZAP archives, Trivy's `.deb`. A file that doesn't match its pin is refused and deleted, nothing installed. The pins come from upstream's own checksums and manifests, checked against the files |
| A git tag, by commit | Nikto: the `2.6.1` tag must point at the pinned commit |
| Python and Ruby tools, by version | Semgrep and Checkov from PyPI, WPScan from RubyGems, each in a directory of its own; their dependencies are resolved by pip and gem |

Each lives in `/opt/cipi/packages//`, `current` points at the live version, and its commands are linked into `/usr/local/bin`. A command already there that Cipi didn't install (a script's, Hackly's own installers') is left alone: remove it, or replace it with `--force` at the server's shell, never from the panel. The apt packages an entry needs (a Java runtime, Ruby, Perl modules) come and go with it; one that another package already brought (Java, for `pdftk`) is kept for the entry too, so removing `pdftk` doesn't take it away under ZAP. Build tools (WPScan's `build-essential`) are removed right after the build, and an install that fails puts back what apt installed for it. One `install` or `remove` runs at a time: a second one waits.

Upstream entries aren't updated by unattended-upgrades. When a Cipi release pins a newer version, `cipi package list` marks the entry outdated and `cipi self-update` names it; installing it again updates it (the new version first, `current` swapped, the old one removed):

```bash
$ cipi package list                    # ◐ sec-nuclei   3.10.0 installed, 3.11.1 available
$ sudo cipi package install sec-nuclei --yes
```

## Browsershot 

Browsershot drives Chrome through Puppeteer, and Puppeteer downloads **its own Chrome** for the version it was tested with. What the server lacks is the shared libraries and fonts that Chrome needs to start; that is the `browsershot` entry:

```bash
$ sudo cipi package install browsershot            # once per server
$ cipi app run shop npm install puppeteer          # per app: Chrome comes with it
```

Better still, keep `puppeteer` in the app's `package.json`, so every deploy installs it. Point Browsershot at the app's Node and npm if they aren't on the `PATH` of PHP-FPM (`setNodeBinary()`, `setNpmBinary()`), and render in a queue worker, not in the request: a page takes seconds and hundreds of MB of RAM.

There is **no `chromium` entry on purpose.** On Ubuntu 24.04 `chromium-browser` is a transitional package that installs the snap, with `snapd`: a daemon, outside the allowlist's rules, and a Chrome that isn't the one Puppeteer expects. `wkhtmltopdf` isn't there either: archived upstream, on an unpatched Qt WebKit. Use Browsershot (or `libreoffice` for office documents) instead.

## Removing 

`cipi package remove` takes **only what no other package needs**: for an upstream entry, its directory, its links and the apt packages only it needed. Before asking, it shows what goes: the entry's packages, and the dependencies that become unused because of them. Dependencies that were already unused before stay where they are; `--autoremove` takes them too, at the server's shell.

When something else on the server depends on a tool entry (software you installed by hand on top of `ffmpeg`, say), the removal stops and names it: nothing is changed. `--force` at the server's shell removes them as well. A tool another package pulled in (`dig`, for `ubuntu-standard`) was never the entry's: it stays.

For a library entry (`browsershot`, `fonts-cjk`) the libraries are often shared: the ones other software still uses stay installed, and when every one of them is still in use nothing is removed, with the reason. Apps that use a removed entry stop working, so the prompt asks first; without a terminal (the panel, a script) it needs `--yes`.

## From the panel 

The server page of the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-overview) has a **Packages** tab: the whole catalog, each entry with what it brings (`ffmpeg, ffprobe`, or *Libraries*), what a partial install lacks, the pinned version of an *Upstream* entry (and **Update to x.y.z** when an older one is installed), and since panel 4.6.0 ([API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api#endpoints-packages) 1.44, Cipi 5.14.0 on the server) **Install**, **Complete install** and **Remove**, confirmed and run as jobs.

Changing needs **Manage** on the server, and the token the `packages-manage` ability. The panel takes only ids the page lists, and the server's catalog is closed whatever is sent: the panel passes `--yes`, its `--force` and `--autoremove` are ignored and the disk check holds. The [MCP server](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp) lists the catalog but doesn't install or remove.


## Stack upgrades

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades

Security patches for the whole stack, without surprise restarts. Ubuntu's unattended upgrades would restart Nginx or a database whenever they run; Cipi takes those packages over and patches them at a quiet hour, one at a time, checking each one.

| Component | Patched by | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ubuntu (kernel, libraries…) | unattended-upgrades | Daily |
| PHP | [cipi php upgrade](https://cipi.sh/docs/php#security) | Daily, 03:30 |
| Nginx, MariaDB (or MySQL), PostgreSQL, Valkey, Node.js, Composer, FrankenPHP | `cipi autoupdate` | Nightly, 04:20 |
| Reboot for a new kernel | `cipi reboot auto` | Off unless you turn it on |

## Nightly patches: `cipi autoupdate` 

```bash
$ cipi autoupdate                    # what's on, how the last run went
$ cipi autoupdate off mariadb        # patch this one yourself
$ cipi autoupdate on
$ cipi autoupdate run [name]         # now
```

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Patch releases only (`--only-upgrade`) | No major jumps overnight |
| Your config files are kept; `nginx -t` before reload | A patch never breaks the config |
| Node runtimes checked against SHA-256; Composer rolled back if it won't start | Verified binaries only |
| One at a time, databases last; skipped during a dump or deploy | No restart in the middle of your work |
| Octane builds stay on their PHP minor, health-checked, rolled back if silent | [FrankenPHP pinning](https://cipi.sh/docs/octane#cli-frankenphp) |
| Each upgrade notified; failures alert and show in `cipi pending` | You always know |

Log: `/var/log/cipi/autoupdate.log`.

## By hand 

```bash
$ cipi nginx upgrade [--yes]
$ cipi db upgrade [mariadb|pgsql] [--yes]     # mariadb: MySQL's packages where it runs
$ cipi service upgrade valkey [--yes]
$ cipi service upgrade                 # installed vs available
```

Package patterns are pinned (a loose match can't drag PHP in), vendor repositories are re-asserted if missing, and a lock prevents two upgrades from overlapping. These are not exposed to the panel: patching a database is an operator decision.

## What needs you: `cipi pending` 

A server can be fully patched and still run last month's kernel. `cipi pending` lists what an update can't do by itself, each with the command to run:

```bash
$ cipi pending [--json]
```

| Item | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Reboot required | New kernel installed, old one running |
| Below a security release | PHP, Nginx, Composer, Node.js |
| Old binary still running | Nginx upgraded on disk, workers not yet replaced |
| Updates waiting | A component with autoupdate off, or whose last run failed |
| Unmanaged code | PHP extensions built by hand or with PECL |
| App hygiene | Horizon installed but not running; apps on the shared Valkey |

Checked every morning; mailed when the list changes, and weekly while something stays on it. `cipi status` shows it too.

## Reboots 

```bash
$ cipi reboot                         # needed? since when? which kernel?
$ cipi reboot now [--yes]
$ cipi reboot auto on --at=04:45      # only on nights one is required
```

Automatic reboots notify, warn two minutes ahead, and wait for the next night while a package install, dump, deploy or other `cipi` command is running.


## Server commands & updates

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/server-commands

The everyday commands for the server itself.

| Command | Shows or does |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi status` | CPU, RAM, disk, services, PHP versions, apps, pending items |
| `cipi disk` | Disk usage of the server and each app ([Disk usage](https://cipi.sh/docs/disk)) |
| `cipi pending` | What needs a human ([Stack upgrades](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades#pending)) |
| `cipi version` | Installed Cipi version |
| `cipi help [topic]` | Every command, grouped |

## Credentials 

```bash
$ cipi credentials                       # root, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Valkey, Meilisearch, backup key
$ cipi credentials export > cipi.csv     # CSV for any password manager
$ cipi reset root-password
$ cipi reset db-password [--engine=pgsql]
$ cipi reset valkey-password             # restarts the shared Valkey
```

Run the export from your laptop (`ssh cipi@server sudo cipi credentials export > cipi.csv`) so no copy stays on the server. Every show or export is logged and notified (`credentials_show`). Secrets are stored encrypted ([Vault](https://cipi.sh/docs/vault)).

## Updating Cipi 

```bash
$ cipi self-update --check
$ cipi self-update
```

```flow
Download | from GitHub
> `cipi self-update` downloads the new version of Cipi from GitHub.
Back up | /opt/cipi.bak.
```
