Simplest: `cipi api token create --name=laptop --full-access`. Keep server and API current with `cipi self-update` so every command is available.


## PHP SDK

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk

`cipi/sdk` is the **PHP client for the Cipi API**. From a Laravel app, a Symfony service or a plain script, one token calls the same surface as [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) and the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui): apps, deploys, `cipi.yml`, domains, databases, backups and the server. It runs on your machine over HTTPS: no SSH, no shelling out to `cipi`.

```bash
$ composer require cipi/sdk
```

PHP 8.2+ with `ext-curl` and `ext-json`; Laravel optional. Source: [github.com/cipi-sh/sdk](https://github.com/cipi-sh/sdk) (MIT). The server needs [`cipi api`](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) and a token with only the abilities this code needs.

## Client 

```php
use Cipi\Sdk\Cipi;

$cipi = Cipi::connect(
    baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com',   // "/api" suffix optional
    token: getenv('CIPI_TOKEN') ?: '',
);

$apps = $cipi->apps()->list();
$job  = $cipi->deploys()->start('shop');  // 202 + job_id
$done = $cipi->wait($job);                // polls until completed or failed
```

Reads return the JSON body as an array; writes return a job you can `wait()` on. Plain `http://` is refused unless you pass `['allow_http' => true]` (for a local panel).

## Laravel 

Auto-discovered on Laravel 11, 12 and 13.

```bash
$ php artisan vendor:publish --tag=cipi-config
```

```bash
CIPI_BASE_URL=https://api.example.com
CIPI_TOKEN=
CIPI_TIMEOUT=30
```

```php
use Cipi\Sdk\Laravel\Facades\Cipi;

Cipi::apps()->list();
```

Or type-hint `Cipi\Sdk\Cipi`. The container holds one server; for another, call `Cipi::connect()` with its URL and token. Symfony and others register `Cipi::connect()` in their own container.

> [!tip] Install it next to [`cipi/agent`](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp) and the app's MCP server gains panel tools: `panel_rollback`, `panel_deploy_audit`, `panel_db_backup`, `panel_job`, `panel_status`.

## Apps 

```php
$cipi->wait($cipi->apps()->create([
    'user'       => 'shop',
    'domain'     => 'shop.example.com',
    'repository' => 'git@github.com:acme/shop.git',
    'branch'     => 'main',
    'php'        => '8.6',
    'env'        => 'production',
    'node_build' => 'npm ci && npm run build',
]));

$cipi->apps()->update('shop', ['php' => '8.6']);
$cipi->apps()->suspend('shop');  $cipi->apps()->unsuspend('shop');
$cipi->apps()->recreateWebhook('shop', rotateSecret: true);
$cipi->wait($cipi->limits()->update('shop', ['fpm_max_children' => 10, 'disk_limit_gb' => 5]));

$cipi->basicAuth()->enable('shop', 'admin');
$cipi->wait($cipi->artisan()->run('shop', 'migrate --force'));
$cipi->wait($cipi->run()->execute('shop', 'composer install --no-dev'));
$cipi->logs()->get('shop', 'deploy');
```

Create accepts the fields of `POST /api/apps`: `user` and `domain` required, plus `repository`, `branch`, `php`, `env`, `custom`, `octane`, `engine`, `node_build`, or Node fields. Invalid values throw `ValidationException` (422).

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `env` | `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}$`, default `production`; picks `cipi-.yml` |
| `node_build` | Starts with `npm`, `npx`, `yarn`, `pnpm`, `bun` or `node`; `&&` and `;` allowed; no pipes, redirects or substitutions; max 200 characters |
| `limits()` | FPM children, `memory_limit`, Octane workers, queue workers, `disk_limit_gb` (soft, `null` removes it) |

After create (and edits that change repository or branch) the job result carries `repository_access`:

```php
$job = $cipi->wait($cipi->apps()->create($attributes));
$access = $job['data']['result']['repository_access'] ?? null;
if ($access && $access['status'] !== 'ok') {      // ok, nobranch or denied
    // $access['error'] is git's line, $access['hint'] the server command that fixes it
}
```

## Deploys, jobs and cipi.yml 

```php
$cipi->wait($cipi->deploys()->start('shop'));
$cipi->deploys()->rollback('shop');
$cipi->deploys()->unlock('shop');               // also resumes a paused commit (Cipi 5.13.0+)
$cipi->deploys()->audit('shop', days: 30);
$cipi->deploys()->status('shop', tail: 50);   // running, queued, interrupted, idle; paused_commit
$cipi->deploys()->history('shop', limit: 10);
$cipi->deploys()->last();                     // last run of every app
$cipi->deployConfig()->update('shop', ['keep_releases' => 5, 'migrate' => true]);

$cipi->jobs()->wait($job, timeoutSeconds: 120, intervalSeconds: 1.0);
```

`wait()` times out after 300 s by default and throws `JobFailedException` (payload on `$e->job`) when a job fails.

```php
$plan = $cipi->yml()->status('shop')['data'];      // file, env, valid, in_sync, changes, blockers
foreach ($plan['changes'] as $change) {
    echo $change['summary'], PHP_EOL;              // e.g. "PHP 8.5 → 8.6"
}
if ($plan['blockers'] === []) {
    $job = $cipi->jobs()->wait($cipi->yml()->apply('shop'), throwOnFailure: false);
    $outcome = $job['data']['result']['outcome'];  // applied, unchanged, partial, blocked, invalid, no-file
}
$cipi->yml()->enableAuto('shop');
```

> [!warning] With auto-apply on, anyone who can commit can change the app's aliases, PHP settings, limits, workers, deploy recipe, schedule, databases and backups. Ask for confirmation before enabling it for someone. Reads need `yml-view`, writes `yml-manage`.

## Domains and SSL 

```php
$cipi->aliases()->add('shop', 'www.shop.example.com');
$cipi->www()->forceToRoot('shop');
$cipi->redirects()->set('shop', 'https://example.com', 301, keepPath: true);
$cipi->redirects()->add('shop', '/blog/', 'https://blog.example.com', 301, true);
$cipi->proxies()->add('shop', prefix: '/api/', upstream: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000', stripPrefix: true);
$cipi->ssl()->install('shop');
$cipi->ssl()->install('shop', dns: 'cloudflare', account: 'prod', wildcard: true);
$cipi->ssl()->setDnsAccount($cloudflareToken, 'prod');   // sync, never returned
```

Redirects and proxies are tested with `nginx -t` and reverted on failure; the proxy loopback guard can't be bypassed.

```php
$cipi->nginx()->show('shop')['data']['config'];                     // the app's own directives
$cipi->nginx()->update('shop', "client_max_body_size 512M;\n");     // sync: nginx -t, then reload
$cipi->nginx()->reset('shop');
```

`nginx()` reads and replaces [an app's own Nginx directives](https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx#custom) (API 1.44+, Cipi 5.14+). A refused text is a `ValidationException` (422) and changes nothing; from the API [a subset of the language](https://cipi.sh/docs/nginx#custom-api) is accepted. Node apps: `node()->status($app)`, `node()->restart($app)`.

## Env, databases and backups 

```php
$cipi->env()->update('shop', ['APP_ENV' => 'production'], ['TELESCOPE_ENABLED']);  // merge, unset
$cipi->env()->reorder('shop', $keysInOrder);   // every key once (API 1.43+, Cipi 5.13.0+)
$cipi->authJson()->replace('shop', ['http-basic' => ['repo.example.com' => ['username' => 'token', 'password' => $secret]]]);

$cipi->wait($cipi->databases()->create('shop_reports', 'pgsql', app: 'shop'));
$cipi->databases()->backup('shop');
$cipi->databases()->password('shop');
$cipi->databases()->link('legacy', 'shop');
$cipi->databases()->engines();                // engine, status, port; server/label: MySQL where it runs
$cipi->wait($cipi->databases()->restoreLocal('shop', __DIR__.'/shop.sql.gz'));   // chunked upload
```

`restoreLocal()` streams the dump in chunks (not bound by `memory_limit`) and cancels the upload if anything is refused. The panel deletes uploads when the restore ends.

```php
$cipi->backups()->createProfile('nightly', [
    'scope' => 'all', 'every' => '1d', 'destinations' => ['s3'], 'keep_days' => 14, 'encrypt' => true,
    'exclude_paths' => ['storage/app/uploads'],    // API 1.43+, Cipi 5.13.0+
]);
$cipi->backups()->status()['data']['uncovered'];   // what no enabled profile takes
$cipi->backups()->run('nightly');                  // starts and returns, not a job
$cipi->wait($cipi->backups()->verify('nightly'));
```

Destinations and their keys are configured on the server and never returned.

## Server 

```php
$cipi->server()->status();
$cipi->php()->install('8.6');
$cipi->ssh()->add($publicKey);
$cipi->services()->restart('php8.6-fpm');
$cipi->health()->update('shop', 'https://shop.example.com/up', 200);
$cipi->search()->enable('shop');
$cipi->disk()->usage();
$cipi->metrics()->series('shop', ['req', 'http_5xx'], '7d');   // ~240 points of [ts, avg, max]
$cipi->metrics()->uptime('shop', '30d');
$cipi->metrics()->setHeartbeat('https://hc-ping.com/', every: 1);
$cipi->notifications()->add('telegram', 'oncall', ['token' => $bot, 'chat_id' => '-1001234', 'test' => true]);   // 1.9+
$cipi->notifications()->update('oncall', ['chat_id' => '-1009999']);   // the token is kept
$cipi->notifications()->setTriggers(['deploy_success' => false]);
$cipi->wait($cipi->node()->upgrade(24, restart: true));
$cipi->wait($cipi->packages()->install('browsershot'));   // API 1.44+, Cipi 5.14+
$cipi->ipWhitelist()->replace(['203.0.113.10'], ensureClientIp: true);
$cipi->request('GET', '/apps/shop');               // any endpoint not wrapped yet
```

Monitor, Zero Trust and disk usage are read-only, as on the API. [Optional packages](https://cipi.sh/docs/packages) are listed, installed and removed (`packages()->list()`, `install()`, `remove()`): the catalog is closed and lives on the server.

## Security 

| Protection | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Transport | HTTPS with verification; redirects never followed, so the token stays on your host |
| Token | Only in the `Authorization` header; whitespace or control characters rejected (no header injection); stripped from exceptions and `var_dump` |
| Retries | Reads may retry `429`/`503` with a short `Retry-After`; writes never |
| Limits | Responses over 16 MiB refused; 30 s timeout, 10 s connect |

```php
$cipi = Cipi::connect($url, $token, [
    'timeout' => 30, 'connect_timeout' => 10, 'max_retries' => 2,
    'max_response_bytes' => 16777216, 'allow_http' => false,
]);
```

One token per application, smallest ability set, kept in the environment, never committed. A missing ability is a 403, never a silent no-op.

## Errors 

| Status | Exception |
| --- | --- |
| 401 | `AuthenticationException` |
| 403 | `AuthorizationException` (missing ability, or IP allowlist) |
| 404 | `NotFoundException` |
| 409 | `ConflictException` |
| 422 | `ValidationException` (`errors()` with Laravel's bag) |
| 429 | `RateLimitException` (`retryAfter`) |
| 5xx | `ServerException` |
| none | `TransportException`, `ConfigurationException`; from `wait()`: `JobFailedException`, `TimeoutException` |

```php
try {
    $cipi->wait($cipi->deploys()->start('shop'));
} catch (JobFailedException $e) {
    $job = $e->job;
} catch (AuthorizationException $e) {
    // token lacks deploy-manage
}
```


## WHMCS module

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/whmcs

Sell Laravel and PHP hosting on your own servers. The official **WHMCS provisioning module** ([github.com/cipi-sh/whmcs](https://github.com/cipi-sh/whmcs), MIT) maps the WHMCS lifecycle to the [Cipi API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api): orders create apps, suspensions take them offline, terminations remove them. A self-contained drop-in, no Composer dependencies.

```flow
Order paid | WHMCS Create Account
> A customer pays an order in WHMCS and the product's module runs Create Account.
POST /api/apps | isolated app on Cipi
> The module calls the Cipi API (`POST /api/apps`), which creates an isolated app: user, database, PHP pool, vhost.
Auto-SSL | Let's Encrypt (optional)
> Optionally a Let's Encrypt certificate is issued once DNS points at the server.
Lifecycle | suspend, change package, terminate
> Suspend, unsuspend, change package and terminate in WHMCS call the matching Cipi API actions.
```

## Requirements 

WHMCS 8.x, a Cipi server with [`cipi api`](https://cipi.sh/docs/api), and a token with these abilities:

| Ability | For |
| --- | --- |
| `apps-view` | Test Connection, App Info |
| `apps-create` | Create Account |
| `apps-edit` | Change Package |
| `apps-suspend` | Suspend, Unsuspend |
| `apps-delete` | Terminate |
| `deploy-manage` | Deploy, Rollback, Unlock |
| `ssl-manage` | Install SSL, Auto-SSL |

## Install 

```tree
your-whmcs/
└── modules/servers/cipi/
    ├── cipi.php
    └── lib/CipiApiClient.php
```

1. Copy `modules/servers/cipi/` into your WHMCS root.
2. **System Settings → Servers → Add New Server**: type *Cipi (Laravel hosting)*, hostname = API base URL (no trailing slash), password = token, Secure = yes.
3. Create a hosting product on that server and set its module settings:

| Setting | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PHP Version | 8.3, 8.4, 8.5, 8.6 | server default |
| App Type | `laravel` or `custom` | `laravel` |
| Git Repository (SSH) | Required for Laravel, optional for custom | — |
| Git Branch | Branch to deploy | `main` |
| Auto SSL | Certificate right after creation | No |

| App type | Cipi equivalent | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `laravel` | `cipi app create` | Laravel apps with Deployer releases, workers, database |
| `custom` | `cipi app create --custom` | WordPress, static sites, SPAs, any PHP; Git optional (SFTP-only hosting) |

## Lifecycle 

| WHMCS action | API call | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Test Connection | `GET /api/apps` | Token and reachability |
| Create Account | `POST /api/apps` | Provision, wait for the job, optional SSL |
| Suspend | `POST /api/apps/{name}/suspend` | 503 maintenance page, nothing deleted |
| Unsuspend | `POST /api/apps/{name}/unsuspend` | Normal vhost back |
| Change Package | `PUT /api/apps/{name}` | PHP, repository, branch |
| Terminate | `DELETE /api/apps/{name}` | Remove the app |

Admin buttons on the service page: **Install SSL**, **Deploy**, **Rollback Deploy**, **Unlock Deploy**, **App Info**. If Auto-SSL fails, the app is still created and a warning is logged. Every call is logged with `logModuleCall()` (Utilities → Logs → Module Log).

## Extend it 

The bundled `CipiApiClient` covers apps, deploys, SSL, aliases, databases and jobs, for your own hooks:

```php
require_once ROOTDIR . '/modules/servers/cipi/lib/CipiApiClient.php';
$client = new CipiApiClient('https://api.example.com', $token);
$client->addAlias('myapp', 'alias.example.com');
$client->createDatabase('myapp_extra');
$client->backupDatabase('myapp');
```

Designing the products (Laravel-ready VPS, managed app, instance per customer), plan limits from a WHMCS hook and pricing: [Cipi and WHMCS for hosting providers](https://cipi.sh/guides/hosting-providers-laravel-whmcs).

> [!note] The module adds no client-area tab. One-time secrets Cipi generates (SSH and database passwords, deploy key, webhook) aren't pushed to WHMCS: deliver them with a hook or your support workflow. For richer tooling use the [PHP SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk).


## Cipi vs alternatives

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/vs-alternatives

Server tools fall into five families. Cipi sits in the first, but runs **on your own server, for free**, with a CLI, an optional panel, an API and MCP. This page tells you honestly where it fits and where something else is a better choice. Head-to-head pages: [all comparisons](https://cipi.sh/alternatives).

| Family | Examples | You pay | Who runs the control plane |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Server panels** for your VPS | **Cipi**, Laravel Forge, Ploi, RunCloud, Cleavr, Vito Deploy, CloudPanel | Cipi: nothing; SaaS panels: per server per month | Cipi and Vito: you; the rest: the vendor |
| **Managed PaaS** | Laravel Cloud, Ploi Cloud, Render, Sevalla, fortrabbit | Usage or resources | The vendor, on its cloud |
| **Self-hosted Docker PaaS** | Coolify, Dokku, Easypanel | Nothing | You, with containers |
| **Deploy tools** | Kamal | Nothing | You; provisioning is up to you |
| **Hosting panels** | cPanel, Plesk, DirectAdmin, HestiaCP, aaPanel | Licence (cPanel, Plesk, DirectAdmin) or nothing | You, built for shared hosting |

## What Cipi is 

> [!tip] **Free, MIT, on your VPS.** One installer turns Ubuntu into a hardened server; every app is an isolated cell with its own user, PHP pool, database and certificate. Zero-downtime Git deploys, versioned server settings in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml), backups, monitoring and security updates. Driven by a CLI, an optional [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui), a [REST API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) and [MCP servers](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp). Laravel-first, with [custom](https://cipi.sh/docs/custom-apps) and [Node](https://cipi.sh/docs/node-apps) apps for everything else.

## At a glance 

| | Cipi | Forge | Ploi | Vito Deploy | Coolify | Laravel Cloud |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost of the tool | **Free** | from $12/server/mo | €8–30/server/mo | Free | Free | Usage-based |
| Runs on | Your VPS | Vendor SaaS | Vendor SaaS | Its own VPS | Your server | Vendor cloud |
| Root on the server | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Native Laravel stack (FPM, Octane) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Containers | Managed |
| Settings versioned in the repo | `cipi.yml` | No | No | No | Partly (compose) | Partly |
| Full CLI, scriptable | Yes | API + CLI | API | API | API | API + CLI |
| Web dashboard | Optional, self-hosted | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| MCP for AI assistants | Per app and per server | No | No | No | No | No |
| Config encrypted at rest | Vault (AES-256) | Not advertised | Not advertised | Not advertised | Not advertised | Managed |
| Your infrastructure data leaves the server | Never | Yes (US SaaS) | Yes (EU SaaS) | No | No | Yes |

Prices from each product's public pages; check them before deciding, they change.

## Server panels 

### Laravel Forge 

The benchmark: built by the Laravel team, polished and battle-tested at huge scale, with multi-cloud provisioning, teams and monitoring. **Choose Forge** if you want the most mature hosted dashboard and provider integrations. **Choose Cipi** to stop paying per server, keep management on the server itself (no SaaS to be reachable), version server settings in `cipi.yml`, script everything from the CLI and drive it from AI assistants. [Cipi vs Forge](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-forge).

### Ploi 

A Forge-like SaaS panel from the Netherlands, natively GDPR-friendly, with a clean UI and built-in backups and monitoring. **Choose Ploi** for a cheaper hosted GUI with EU data handling. **Choose Cipi** when you want no third party at all, no plan limits, and the CLI, API and MCP surface. Not to be confused with [Ploi Cloud](#vs-ploi-cloud). [Cipi vs Ploi](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-ploi).

### Vito Deploy 

The closest in spirit: free, open source, self-hosted, a GUI built with Laravel, teams and plugins. Vito runs as its own Laravel app with a database, usually on a dedicated VPS; Cipi lives on the server it manages and adds the panel only if you want it. Cipi adds `cipi.yml`, MCP, an encrypted vault, server sync, a deploy audit trail and automatic security patching. [Cipi vs Vito Deploy](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-vito-deploy).

### RunCloud, Cleavr, ServerPilot, moss.sh 

Hosted panels from roughly $8 to $49 per server per month. RunCloud and ServerPilot lean towards WordPress and generic PHP; Cleavr and moss.sh support Laravel through a hosted GUI (moss.sh caps deploys on its free tier). Cipi gives you Laravel-aware automation (Deployer releases, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane) for nothing. [RunCloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-runcloud) · [Cleavr](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cleavr) · [ServerPilot](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-serverpilot) · [moss.sh](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-moss).

### CloudPanel 

Free and polished, for PHP, Node, Python and static sites. A generic multi-stack panel with no Laravel release or worker management. Pick it if Python sites matter to you; pick Cipi for Laravel depth. [Cipi vs CloudPanel](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cloudpanel).

## Managed PaaS 

You don't touch a server; you pay for resources and accept the platform's limits. To put numbers on the choice (what a variable bill must buy you to beat a fixed one, and when Kubernetes pays off), see [VPS, Kubernetes or a managed platform](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-vs-kubernetes-vs-managed-paas).

| Platform | Strength | Choose Cipi when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Laravel Cloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-cloud) | Autoscaling, scale-to-zero, managed databases and edge, from the Laravel team | You want a fixed bill, root and a portable stack |
| [Ploi Cloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-ploi-cloud) | EU PaaS for Laravel, PHP and Node, memory-based pricing | You'd rather own the VPS and pay the provider only |
| [Render](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-render) | Multi-language, previews, private networking, compliance options | Your apps are Laravel/PHP and you want no usage invoice |
| [Sevalla](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-sevalla) | Apps, databases and storage under one managed bill | You want native Laravel on your own Ubuntu |
| [fortrabbit](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-fortrabbit) | PHP-specialised managed hosting with a long track record | You want root, Octane, Horizon and Reverb under your control |

## Self-hosted Docker PaaS 

[Coolify](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify), [Dokku](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-dokku) and [Easypanel](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-easypanel) deploy containers on your server, free. Great when you host many stacks and already think in Docker. Cipi runs a **native** Nginx + PHP-FPM/Octane + MariaDB/PostgreSQL stack with no container layer: less overhead, simpler debugging, and Laravel's lifecycle (releases, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb) built in.

## Deploy tools 

[Kamal](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-kamal) ships containers over SSH to servers you've already prepared. It doesn't install the web server, PHP, databases, firewall, certificates, backups or workers. Cipi does all of that, and deploys. Choose Kamal if you have Docker infrastructure and need only the deploy step.

## Hosting panels 

[cPanel](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cpanel), [Plesk](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-plesk) and [DirectAdmin](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-directadmin) are built for selling shared hosting: e-mail, FTP, DNS and many customer sites, under a licence. Right for hosting resellers, heavy for a team deploying its own apps. Hosting companies that want to add Laravel-native products next to them: [Cipi and WHMCS for hosting providers](https://cipi.sh/guides/hosting-providers-laravel-whmcs).

HestiaCP (the maintained fork of the abandoned VestaCP) is a free, lighter alternative for e-mail, DNS and many websites, with no Laravel tooling. aaPanel is a free, plugin-based multi-stack panel popular in Asia-Pacific, GUI-centric, also without Laravel automation.

GridPane, xCloud and ServerAvatar focus on WordPress and WooCommerce: staging clones, multisite, WordPress caching. For WordPress fleets, evaluate them on their merits. Cipi runs WordPress as a custom app when it sits next to your Laravel apps.

20i is a hosting company (reseller, WordPress, VPS, domains, e-mail, 24×7 support). It covers a full hosting catalogue; Cipi replaces it only for "deploy my apps on a VPS I own". Cipi vs 20i.

## How to choose 

```flow
Own a VPS? | no → managed PaaS
> If you don't want to manage a server at all, not even with a tool, a managed PaaS (Laravel Cloud, Render…) is the simpler choice.
Laravel or PHP apps? | many stacks → Docker PaaS
> If you run many stacks (Go, Python, Rails) with Docker, a Docker PaaS (Coolify, Dokku…) fits better. Cipi is for Laravel, PHP and Node.
Want to pay per server? | yes → Forge or Ploi
> If you prefer a hosted dashboard and pay per month, Forge or Ploi do that well.
Otherwise | Cipi
> If you own a server, deploy Laravel/PHP apps and want it free, open source and scriptable: Cipi.
```


## Design decisions

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions

## Why not local? 

Cipi is a **production server provisioner**: it turns a fresh Ubuntu VPS into an internet-facing host. It doesn't run on a laptop, in local Docker, or behind a home NAT, by design.

| A Cipi server needs | Because |
| --- | --- |
| A public IPv4 address, no NAT | Domains must resolve to it and Git providers must reach its webhooks |
| Full virtualization or bare metal (KVM, VMware, Hyper-V, Xen HVM) | Shared-kernel containers (OpenVZ, LXC) can't run the services and firewall Cipi manages; the installer detects them and stops |
| Ports 22, 80 and 443 reachable | SSH, Let's Encrypt validation and HTTPS |

> [!warning] Don't install Cipi inside Docker Desktop, OrbStack, Colima, WSL or a local VM expecting a working stack: certificates won't issue, domains won't resolve and webhooks can't arrive. A small VPS is enough for staging.

Every production provisioner has the same constraint. What Cipi doesn't ask for is the difference: no agent phoning home, no external control plane, no cloud account.

**Locally**, use [Laravel Herd](https://herd.laravel.com/), [Sail](https://laravel.com/docs/sail) or `php artisan serve`, then push to a Cipi server for staging and production.

## Why no Docker? 

Cipi installs Nginx, PHP-FPM, MariaDB or PostgreSQL, Valkey and Supervisor **as native Ubuntu packages**, managed by systemd, and seals apps off from each other with Linux users. There are no containers, no images and no Docker daemon on a Cipi server. That's deliberate: for one server running Laravel and PHP apps, Docker adds a layer that has to be secured, patched and debugged, without giving anything the OS doesn't already provide.

| | With Docker | On a Cipi server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ease of use** | A second system to learn on top of Linux: images, Compose files, networks, volumes, registries. Every task goes through Docker first | One command per task (`cipi app create`, `cipi deploy`, `cipi ssl install`). Underneath, a plain Ubuntu server: nothing to translate |
| **An extra layer** | Docker sits between you and every component: to change a `php.ini` or an Nginx rule you edit an image or a mount, then recreate | The component is the one on the host: `/etc/nginx`, `/etc/php`, managed by Cipi and visible to you |
| **SSH and SFTP** | SSH lands on the host, not in the app: then `docker exec` into a container that usually has no SSH, no editor and no SFTP | [`ssh myapp@server`](https://cipi.sh/docs/app-ssh) drops you into the app as its own user, with `artisan`, `composer`, logs and SFTP for your IDE |
| **Remote databases** | The database lives on a container network. To reach it from TablePlus or DBeaver you publish its port (bypassing the firewall, see below) or chain an SSH tunnel into the container network | Native MariaDB or PostgreSQL on localhost: connect over SSH with the `mariadb+ssh://` URL shown at creation. [No database port is ever exposed](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| **Ports and firewall** | Published ports (`-p 3306:3306`) are opened by Docker's own iptables rules, ahead of UFW: a firewall that says "deny" doesn't apply to them | One firewall. UFW, Fail2ban, CrowdSec and `cipi zt lock` see and govern every port |
| **Security patches** | A CVE in PHP or OpenSSL means rebuilding every image that contains it and redeploying every app. Images pinned months ago keep old libraries | PHP patched **every night at 03:30** from packages.sury.org, Nginx from nginx.org, the rest by unattended-upgrades. One update fixes every app |
| **Privileges** | `dockerd` runs as root, and anyone in the `docker` group is root in practice | No daemon with root access to manage. Apps run as their own unprivileged users |
| **Isolation** | Containers share the host kernel; a misconfigured mount or a privileged container breaks the boundary | Per-app Linux user (home `750`), PHP-FPM pool with `open_basedir`, database user and Valkey instance |
| **Restarts and reloads** | A config change usually means recreating the container. Restarting or upgrading `dockerd` stops every container, unless live-restore is configured | `systemctl reload`: Nginx and PHP-FPM pick up changes without dropping connections. Nightly patching restarts only the affected PHP-FPM service |
| **Workers** | Restart policies only know "the process exited" | Supervisor restarts workers, Horizon, Reverb and Octane individually, with logs per program |
| **Native components** | Bridge networks, NAT, `docker-proxy` and an overlay filesystem between the request and PHP | Unix sockets between Nginx, PHP-FPM, the database and Valkey. Nothing in between |
| **Resources** | The daemon plus a runtime and a copy of the userland per container; heavy on a 1–2 GB VPS | One shared runtime. Cipi sizes MariaDB's buffer pool from the server's RAM |
| **Data** | Databases on volumes; one `docker compose down -v` deletes them | Data in the standard directories, backed up by [`cipi backup`](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups), encrypted and verified |
| **Deploys** | Build an image, push it to a registry, pull it, swap containers behind a proxy | `git push`: [Deployer](https://cipi.sh/docs/how-deploys-work) builds a release and swaps a symlink atomically, with one-command rollback |
| **Debugging** | `docker exec` into a minimal image, with logs per container | `systemctl`, `journalctl`, `/var/log`, `strace`: the tools and tutorials every sysadmin already knows |

> [!warning] The firewall point is the one that bites. Docker writes its own iptables rules for published ports, and they're evaluated before UFW. A database container published on `3306` is reachable from the internet even with `ufw deny 3306`. Docker's own documentation calls Docker and UFW incompatible. On a Cipi server, what the firewall says is what's open.

**What you don't lose.** The things people use Docker for on a server are already there: per-app isolation, one version of PHP per app ([8.3 to 8.6](https://cipi.sh/docs/php) side by side), a database per app, reproducible settings in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml) committed to the repository, and zero-downtime deploys with rollback.

**When Docker is the better fit.** Many stacks on one host (Go, Python, Rails next to PHP), images built once in CI and shipped unchanged, or a team that already thinks in containers. Then a Docker PaaS such as [Coolify](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify) or [Dokku](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-dokku) suits you better: see the [comparison](https://cipi.sh/docs/vs-alternatives#docker). **Locally**, Docker is great: [Sail](https://laravel.com/docs/sail) or [init](https://init.web.ap.it/) on your laptop, Cipi on the server. Cipi itself doesn't install inside a container: the installer detects Docker, LXC, OpenVZ or WSL and stops.

## Why a closed package catalog? 

Some Laravel packages call a program on the host: Browsershot needs the libraries Chrome starts with, `laravel-ffmpeg` needs `ffmpeg`, OCR needs `tesseract`. Cipi could offer `apt install `. It doesn't: a panel or a token that installs any package is a root shell with extra steps. [`cipi package`](https://cipi.sh/docs/packages) has a **closed catalog** instead, and every entry has to earn its place:

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Stateless: programs, libraries, fonts | No daemon, no port, no credentials, nothing to back up or to patch outside apt |
| From an Ubuntu repository, or an upstream release pinned in Cipi | Ubuntu ships the security updates, and the server applies them unattended. What Ubuntu doesn't ship (the security scanners Hackly runs) is pinned to one version and its SHA-256: nothing resolves "latest" on the server, and a file that doesn't match is refused |
| A real Laravel or PHP package behind it | "Might be handy" is not a reason |

Chromium is the rejection that shows why the rules matter. On Ubuntu 24.04 `chromium-browser` installs the snap, with `snapd`: a daemon, and a Chrome that isn't the one Puppeteer was tested with. So the `browsershot` entry installs the libraries and fonts, and Chrome comes with Puppeteer, per app. `wkhtmltopdf` is out too: archived upstream, its WebKit unpatched.

**Because the set is closed, the panel and the API may install and remove entries** (Cipi 5.14.0), the pinned upstream ones included. The worst a stolen session or token can do is install `ffmpeg` or a scanner whose bytes Cipi pinned, or remove it, and a removal takes only what no other package needs. A pinned version is also why an upstream entry isn't patched unattended: a newer one comes with a Cipi release, and the operator installs it. `--force`, `--autoremove` and anything outside the catalog stay at the server's shell. The [MCP server](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp) only lists the catalog: what is installed on the host changes when a person asks, in the panel or at the CLI, as with the [firewall](https://cipi.sh/docs/firewall#panel).

## Why MariaDB by default? 

MariaDB (port `3306`) is the default because it fits most Laravel apps with zero friction. [PostgreSQL](#why-postgresql) is one command away and can run next to it.

| Reason | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Drop-in for Laravel | `mysql` driver, same `DB_*` keys, same migrations; works with TablePlus, DBeaver, Sequel Ace |
| Built for web concurrency | Strong optimizer and a native thread pool in the community edition, good with PHP-FPM connection churn |
| Tuned to your VPS | Cipi sizes `innodb_buffer_pool_size` from RAM (256 MB on 1 GB hosts up to 4 GB on 16 GB+) |
| Simple licensing | GPL community server, no enterprise feature gates, no Oracle dual-licensing to navigate |
| Native packaging | Installed from MariaDB.org or Ubuntu; Cipi adds users, backups and vault credentials on top |

Need **MySQL** itself (an app that relies on MySQL-only behaviour, a team standard)? Since 5.13.0, `cipi db switch mysql` replaces MariaDB on a new server, before its first app — an explicit choice, never a default, and never a conversion of existing data ([MySQL instead of MariaDB](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases#mysql)).

## Why PostgreSQL as an option? 

```bash
$ cipi db install pgsql                       # port 5432, side by side with MariaDB
$ cipi app create shop --engine=pgsql
```

Choose PostgreSQL per app when the product needs more than tables:

| Need | PostgreSQL gives you |
| --- | --- |
| Rich data | JSONB, arrays, ranges, UUID, full-text search, CHECK and exclusion constraints |
| Indexing | B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, partial and expression indexes |
| Extensions | `pgcrypto`, `pg_trgm`, PostGIS, `pgvector` for embeddings and RAG |
| Concurrency | MVCC: readers don't block writers; long reports and busy writes coexist |
| Portability | The standard of managed databases, BI tools and data pipelines |

The same `cipi db` workflow covers both engines: create, list, backup, restore, password rotation.

## Why Valkey? 

| Reason | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Drop-in | Same protocol on `6379`, same `phpredis`, same `REDIS_*` keys; Laravel doesn't notice |
| Truly open source | BSD-licensed, stewarded by the Linux Foundation after Redis moved to source-available licences |
| Native on Ubuntu | `valkey-server` from the Universe repository, no third-party PPAs |
| Automatic migration | Servers moved from Redis to Valkey on `cipi self-update`, same password and data |

The licence of every component Cipi installs, and why it matters on a server: [Open source licences, explained](https://cipi.sh/guides/open-source-licences).

## Why Laravel first? 

Knowing the framework lets Cipi automate what generic panels leave to you: the release layout, `.env` handling, queue workers, the scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane, health routes. Every assumption maps to a known structure, so there's no guesswork. Anything that isn't Laravel still runs as a [custom app](https://cipi.sh/docs/custom-apps) (WordPress, Symfony, static sites) or a [Node app](https://cipi.sh/docs/node-apps).

| Laravel brings | Cipi turns it into |
| --- | --- |
| Queues and Horizon | Supervisor workers, `cipi worker horizon enable` |
| Reverb | Supervisor process, Nginx `/app` proxy, `REVERB_*` keys: `cipi app reverb enable` |
| Octane | FrankenPHP apps side by side with FPM: `cipi app create --octane` |
| Scheduler | One cron per app, nothing to configure |
| Scout | Meilisearch on the server: `cipi search` |
| Secure defaults and a long support cycle | Apps you can leave in production for years |

Taylor Otwell's mantra is **"we must ship"**. Cipi exists for the same reason: to remove the server work between a developer and a live application.

## Why "ci-pi"? 

Cipi is the Italian reading of the letters C and P: Control Panel. A nod to the project's Italian roots, and to what it does under the hood: manage Nginx, PHP-FPM, databases, Supervisor, certificates and the firewall for you.

The mascot is a penguin, a reference to **Tux**, the Linux mascot drawn by Larry Ewing in 1996. Same species, different attitude: minimal, hand-sketched, happier in the terminal than in the spotlight.


## History

URL: https://cipi.sh/docs/history

Cipi was created by [Andrea Pollastri](https://web.ap.it), a developer since 2005 working on Laravel, system administration and security, with experience at companies like Docebo and Musement. He built it out of a practical need: a fast, scriptable way to put Laravel apps on his own VPS without handing control to a SaaS panel. The private tool became an open-source project with over 1,000 GitHub stars and servers running it around the world.

Seven years, five major versions, one idea that never changed: **your server, your apps, no bill for the tool.**

v0.1June 2019The ideaA handful of shell scripts that set up Nginx, PHP, MariaDB and Supervisor on a fresh Ubuntu VPS. No UI, no package. Just bash.
v1–v22019–2020A Laravel control panelThe scripts were wrapped in a Laravel web panel hosted on the same server: create apps, deploy, configure Nginx from the browser. A year of iteration added SMTP, database backups, service management and dozens of fixes, and Cipi became a stable choice for small-team Laravel hosting.
v32021API, PHP 8, real-time UIRebuilt on Laravel 8 with a documented REST API, PHP 8, live CPU and RAM charts, a cron editor, Supervisor and GitHub management. The 3.1 series was the most polished release of the web-UI era, and many teams ran it for years. It also raised the question that shaped what followed: was a browser panel still the right interface, when deploys were moving to SSH, CI pipelines and automation?
v42026The rewrite: CLI-first, Laravel-firstThe web UI was dropped and Cipi became a CLI operated over SSH, with every part of the stack tuned for Laravel. MariaDB replaced MySQL, Deployer brought zero-downtime releases, each app got its own Linux user and deploy key, and GitHub and GitLab webhooks, S3 backups, encrypted server sync, a REST API and MCP servers for AI agents arrived. Late v4 added optional PostgreSQL and the return of a web panel, this time as an optional add-on.
v52026, todayA complete, free platform on your own serverv5 turned the CLI into a full replacement for paid server panels, without giving up what made it simple. One command installs a hardened server; apps are isolated cells with their own user, PHP pool, database and certificate; deploys are atomic, audited and rolled back in one step.

## Cipi today 

| Area | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| Apps | Laravel on PHP-FPM or Octane (FrankenPHP), Node apps (SPA, static, SSR), and custom PHP apps such as WordPress or Symfony |
| Deploy | Zero-downtime releases, Git push from six forges, preview environments, a hash-chained audit trail, health-checked rollbacks |
| `cipi.yml` | The app's server settings versioned in its repository: PHP, workers, schedule, domains, databases, backups, per environment |
| Runtime | Multiple PHP versions side by side, MariaDB (or MySQL) and PostgreSQL, Valkey, Meilisearch, Horizon and Reverb, optional host tools (Browsershot, ffmpeg, LibreOffice, OCR) |
| Operations | Backup profiles to S3 with verification, server monitor, health checks, metrics and uptime history with a heartbeat, disk usage, alerts by e-mail, Slack, Telegram and webhooks |
| Security | Per-app isolation, encrypted vault, firewall and CrowdSec, Cloudflare Zero Trust, malware scans, automatic PHP and Nginx security updates |
| Interfaces | The CLI, an optional web panel with roles and SSO, a REST API, cipi-cli, a PHP SDK, WHMCS and MCP servers for AI assistants |

Every version is listed in the [changelog](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cipi/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md). Announcements go out first on the [Telegram channel](https://t.me/cipicloud).


## Companion tools & community

## Companion tools 

Cipi deploys and runs your apps. Exception tracking, analytics or object storage are separate jobs, better done by separate tools. These projects cover the gaps around a Cipi server: same author, open source, all optional. Cipi depends on none of them.

### Around the server 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**conn**](https://conn.web.ap.it/) | SSH connection manager: save connections under aliases, connect with `conn to ` | One alias for the `cipi` admin user and one per app user, instead of remembering hosts and ports |
| [**Johnny**](https://johnny.web.ap.it/) | S3-compatible object storage on your own VPS (Garage + Caddy), with a web panel, CLI and API | On a **separate** VPS, as the S3 destination for [`cipi backup`](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) or a Laravel disk: off-site, still yours |

### Monitoring and analytics 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**Boogle**](https://boogle.web.ap.it/) | Self-hosted exception tracker and uptime monitor for Laravel | [`cipi monitor`](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) watches the server, Boogle the application from outside. Error payloads stay on your infrastructure |
| [**IndieStats**](https://indiestats.web.ap.it/) | Privacy-friendly web analytics on Laravel: no cookies, no consent banner | Deploy it with `cipi app create` on a subdomain and track every site without sending visitor data anywhere |

### Application security 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**Checkpoint**](https://checkpoint.web.ap.it/) | Laravel security audit in one Artisan command: vulnerable dependencies, leaked secrets, injection risks | Cipi hardens the server, Checkpoint the code. Run it in CI before the deploy |
| [**Hackly**](https://hackly.web.ap.it/) | Authorized attack-surface and code scanning (Laravel/PHP SAST and SCA) with a Filament panel | A continuous vulnerability view across projects; runs on a Cipi server, pairs with [`cipi compliance`](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance) |

### Building Laravel apps 

| Tool | What it does | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**init**](https://init.web.ap.it/) | One command for a complete local Laravel + Filament stack on macOS, with Docker, SSL and a real subdomain | Start locally, push to Git, and let Cipi take over: [Git setup](https://cipi.sh/docs/git), [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml), zero-downtime deploys |
| [**Larapilot**](https://larapilot.web.ap.it/) | Spec-driven AI workflow for Laravel via Laravel Boost: from product idea to reviewed code | Larapilot shapes the code; the [agent's MCP server](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp) and the [Cipi API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) let the same AI see and operate the running app |
| [**Studio**](https://studio.web.ap.it/) | Self-hosted, browser-based hub for teams building Laravel: each person's Claude Code writes and ships code, admins decide per project who sees and approves what, with previews, Git repositories, connectors, passwords and backups | Runs on its own Ubuntu VPS. Studio is where the team writes and reviews code; Cipi is where it goes live |

# Guides


## Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS with zero downtime

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps

This guide takes a fresh VPS to a live Laravel app with HTTPS, a queue worker, the scheduler and deploys on every `git push`. It uses [Cipi](https://cipi.sh/), a free, open-source tool that installs and runs the whole stack on your own server.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Release** | One deployed copy of your code, in its own timestamped folder |
| **`current`** | A link to the live release; switching it is the deploy |
| **Deploy key** | A read-only SSH key that lets the server clone one repository |
| **Webhook** | A URL your Git provider calls on every push, which starts a deploy |
| **Worker** | A background process that runs queued jobs |

New to servers? Read [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics) first: ten minutes, no jargon.

```flow
Server | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 | #server
Install | one command, ~10 min | #install
App | isolated user, DB, PHP | #app
Deploy | atomic release from Git | #deploy
HTTPS | Let's Encrypt | #https
```

**You need:** a VPS with a public IPv4 (1 GB RAM is enough to start, 2 GB is comfortable), a domain whose DNS you control, and your Laravel project in a Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps or any server that accepts SSH deploy keys).

## 1. Create the server 
Pick any provider that gives you a full virtual machine with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 LTS: Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS, Vultr, Linode, OVHcloud, Scaleway. Provider-specific walkthroughs: [AWS EC2](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-ec2), [Lightsail](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-lightsail), [DigitalOcean](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-digitalocean), [Hetzner](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-hetzner).

Open ports **22, 80 and 443** in the provider's firewall if it has one. Then point your domain's `A` record at the server's IP; DNS can propagate while you install.

## 2. Install Cipi 
SSH in as root (or a sudo user) and run the installer:

```bash
$ ssh root@203.0.113.10
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

It asks for your SSH public key, shows what it will do, and only then installs Nginx, PHP, MariaDB, Valkey, Supervisor, Node, Certbot, the firewall and fail2ban, and hardens SSH. Save the credentials it prints: they're shown once.

## 3. Log in as cipi

Root login is now disabled. Connect as `cipi` with your key; Cipi commands run with `sudo`, no password.

```bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10
$ sudo cipi status
```

## 4. Create the app 
```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.6
```

Or run `sudo cipi app create` alone and answer the wizard. Cipi creates a Linux user `shop`, a database and user `shop`, a PHP-FPM pool, an Nginx vhost, a queue worker, the scheduler cron and an `ed25519` deploy key.

| You get | Where |
| --- | --- |
| `.env` with every credential | `/home/shop/shared/.env` |
| Releases | `/home/shop/releases/`, live one linked at `current/` |
| Logs | `/home/shop/logs/` |
| One-time summary | DB password, deploy key, webhook URL and token |

## 5. Connect the repository

Add the deploy key from the summary as a **read-only deploy key** (GitHub: Settings → Deploy keys), and the webhook URL and token if you want push-to-deploy. If you gave Cipi a Git token, it already did both. Check access:

```bash
$ sudo cipi git check shop
```

## 6. Deploy 
```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

```tree
/home/shop/
  current -> releases/20261123_101500   ← live
  releases/
    20261123_101500/
    20261122_174210/                     ← rollback target
  shared/
    .env
    storage/
  logs/
```

Each deploy clones into a new release folder, runs `composer install`, links `.env` and `storage`, runs migrations, builds assets if you set a build command, then switches `current` with one atomic symlink and restarts workers. Visitors never see a half-deployed app.

## 7. Turn on HTTPS 
```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop
```

The certificate covers the domain and every alias and renews by itself. `APP_URL` becomes `https://`. Behind the Cloudflare proxy, use `--dns=cloudflare` and set SSL/TLS to Full (strict).

## 8. Deploy on every push

With the webhook in place, every push to `main` deploys. Prefer tests first? Turn the webhook off and deploy from [GitHub Actions](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow). Want the server settings (PHP, workers, backups) versioned in the repository? Add a [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml).

## What to do next

| Goal | Command or guide |
| --- | --- |
| Roll back | `sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback` |
| More queue workers or Horizon | [Horizon and queues](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues) |
| Nightly backups to S3 | [Back up to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) |
| Faster responses | [Laravel Octane with FrankenPHP](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-octane-frankenphp) |
| Alerts on Telegram or Slack | [Monitoring and alerts](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts) |
| A browser UI for the team | [Web panel and API](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-gui-and-api) |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` on deploy | The deploy key isn't on the repository: `sudo cipi deploy shop --key`, add it, `sudo cipi git check shop` |
| Composer fails on the PHP version | The app's PHP is older than `composer.lock` needs: `sudo cipi app edit shop --php=8.6` |
| 500 error after the first deploy | Read the log: `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=laravel`; usually a missing `.env` key |
| Certificate fails | DNS doesn't point at the server yet: `dig +short shop.example.com` |
| Push doesn't deploy | Webhook missing or wrong branch: `sudo cipi deploy shop --webhook`, check `CIPI_DEPLOY_BRANCH` |
| A deploy hangs or was interrupted | `sudo cipi deploy shop --status`; the next deploy removes a stale lock, `--unlock` clears it now |
| Assets 404 | No build command: `sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --node-build='npm ci && npm run build'` |


## Move a Laravel app from Forge (or Ploi) to Cipi

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-from-laravel-forge

This guide moves one Laravel app from a Forge (or Ploi) server to a new server running Cipi. The old server keeps running until the very last step, so you can stop at any point and nothing breaks.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Cut-over** | The moment traffic moves to the new server (a DNS change) |
| **TTL** | How long the world caches a DNS answer. Lower it before the move |
| **Dump** | A file with the whole database, used to copy it |
| **Rollback plan** | How to go back: point DNS at the old server again |

```flow
Prepare | lower TTL, new server | #before
Build | app, .env, workers | #create
Rehearse | copy data, test | #rehearse
Cut-over | final dump, DNS | #cutover
Keep old | a week, then delete | #rollback
```

## Forge and Ploi features, in Cipi 

| Forge / Ploi | Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| Server provisioning | `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh \| bash` on a fresh VPS |
| Site | `cipi app create` (Laravel, Node or custom) |
| Deploy script | Built-in steps plus `cipi app deploy-config`, `deploy.post` in `cipi.yml` |
| Quick deploy | Push-to-deploy webhook, created with the app |
| Environment | `cipi app env` (`/home//shared/.env`) |
| Daemons / queue workers | `cipi worker add`, `cipi worker horizon enable` |
| Scheduler | On by default per app |
| Databases | `cipi db` (MariaDB, PostgreSQL) |
| SSL (Let's Encrypt) | `cipi ssl install` |
| Backups | `cipi backup` (local and S3, encrypted) |
| Monitoring, health checks | `cipi monitor`, health checks with auto-rollback |
| Team access | Panel roles, API tokens with abilities |
| Monthly plan | None: MIT licensed |

## Before you start 

- Access to the Forge server (`ssh forge@OLD_IP`) and your DNS.
- The app's repository and branch.
- A new VPS with a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 ([choose one](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics)).
- A day before: lower the DNS TTL of the domain to 300 seconds.

## 1. Install Cipi on the new server 

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Install the PHP version the app uses today, and PostgreSQL if it's on Postgres:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4
$ sudo cipi db install pgsql          # only if needed
```

## 2. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.4
```

The summary shows a **deploy key**. Add it to the repository (GitHub → Settings → Deploy keys, read-only). With a Git provider token saved, Cipi does it for you.

## 3. Copy the .env 

On the old server, print it:

```bash
$ ssh forge@OLD_IP "cat /home/forge/shop.example.com/.env"
```

Copy **your own keys** (Stripe, mail, S3, Pusher, APIs) into the new app and keep Cipi's values for the database and Redis. One exception: `APP_KEY` must be the **old** one, or encrypted data and sessions become unreadable.

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=APP_KEY=base64:OLD_KEY…
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=STRIPE_SECRET=sk_live_…
$ sudo cipi app env shop                  # or paste the rest in the editor
```

| Keep from Cipi | Bring from Forge |
| --- | --- |
| `DB_*`, `REDIS_*`, `CIPI_*` | `APP_KEY`, mail, payments, storage, third-party APIs |
| `APP_URL` (switched to https by `cipi ssl install`) | Custom keys your code reads |

## 4. Deploy once 

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

Migrations create an empty schema; the data comes next. If your Forge deploy script ran extra commands, add them:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --extra-artisan=event:cache,icons:cache
$ sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --node-build='npm ci && npm run build'
```

## 5. Rehearse the data copy 

Database, from the old server to the new one:

```bash
# on the old server
$ mysqldump --single-transaction --quick -u forge -p shop | gzip > /tmp/shop.sql.gz
# from your laptop
$ scp forge@OLD_IP:/tmp/shop.sql.gz . && scp shop.sql.gz cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
# on the new server
$ sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql.gz
```

Uploaded files in `storage/app` (skip this if they're on S3):

```bash
$ rsync -az forge@OLD_IP:/home/forge/shop.example.com/storage/app/ /tmp/shop-storage/
$ sudo rsync -a /tmp/shop-storage/ /home/shop/shared/storage/app/ && sudo chown -R shop:shop /home/shop/shared/storage/app
```

Test without touching DNS: add `NEW_IP shop.example.com` to your laptop's `/etc/hosts` and browse. Remove the line when done.

## 6. Workers, scheduler, certificate 

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=2   # one per Forge daemon queue
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop                     # if Forge ran Horizon
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop                           # already on
```

Or write it all in a [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml), so the setup lives with the code:

```yaml
workers:
  horizon: false
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: emails, processes: 2 }
schedule: true
```

The certificate needs DNS pointing at the new server, so it comes right after the cut-over.

## 7. Cut-over 

```flow
Old: artisan down | stop writes
> On the Forge server, `php artisan down`: visitors see the maintenance page and nothing writes to the old database any more.
Final dump | restore on new
> Take the last dump, copy it, and restore it on Cipi with `sudo cipi db restore shop …`.
DNS | A record → NEW_IP
> Change the `A` record to the new server's IP. With a 300-second TTL, most visitors move within minutes.
SSL | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, `sudo cipi ssl install shop` issues the certificate.
Check | old server stays down
> Browse the site, place a test order. Leave the old server down, with its workers stopped, so nothing runs twice.
```

```bash
# old server
$ php /home/forge/shop.example.com/artisan down
# dump, copy, restore as in step 5
# DNS: change the A record to NEW_IP, then on the new server
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop
```

Stop the old server's workers and scheduler (Forge → Daemons, Scheduler) so they don't process jobs against the old database.

## 8. Rollback plan 

Until you delete the old server, going back is one DNS change plus `artisan up` there. Keep it a week, then cancel it.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `The MAC is invalid` | The new app has a different `APP_KEY`: set the old one |
| Images missing | `storage/app` not copied, or `storage:link` missing: redeploy |
| Deploy fails on Composer | PHP version differs from Forge: `cipi app edit shop --php=8.x` |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` on deploy | Deploy key not added to the repository |
| Certificate fails | DNS not pointing at the new server yet: `dig +short shop.example.com` |
| Jobs processed twice | Old server's workers still running: stop them |


## VPS, SSH and DNS for Laravel developers who never ran a server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics

Deploying to your own server sounds harder than it is. You need three skills: **get a server**, **log in with SSH**, and **point a domain at it**. This guide explains each from zero, then hands over to the [first deploy guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **VPS** | A virtual private server: a slice of a physical machine you rent by the hour or month, with its own IP and full control |
| **Ubuntu LTS** | The Linux version Cipi runs on (24.04 or 26.04). LTS = 5 years of security updates |
| **IP address** | The server's number on the internet, e.g. `203.0.113.10` |
| **SSH** | An encrypted way to log in and type commands on the server |
| **SSH key** | A pair of files: the private one stays on your laptop, the public one goes on the server. Safer than a password |
| **DNS** | The internet's phonebook: turns `shop.example.com` into an IP |
| **A record** | A DNS entry: "this name → this IPv4 address" |

```flow
Your laptop | SSH key
> You create an SSH key on your laptop. The private half never leaves it.
VPS | Ubuntu, public IP
> You rent a VPS with Ubuntu LTS and a public IP, giving the provider your public key.
Cipi | installs the stack
> One command installs Cipi and the whole stack.
Domain | A record → IP
> At your DNS provider, an `A` record points your domain at the server's IP.
Visitors | https://shop.example.com
> Visitors reach your app over HTTPS.
```

## 1. Choose a server 

| Need | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| Best price in Europe | [Hetzner](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-hetzner) |
| Simple, worldwide | [DigitalOcean](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-digitalocean), [Vultr, Linode, OVHcloud](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-vultr-linode-ovhcloud) |
| Already on AWS | [Lightsail](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-lightsail) or [EC2](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-ec2) |

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Image | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS or 26.04 LTS, nothing pre-installed |
| Size | 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM for a comfortable start |
| Region | Close to your users |
| Login | Your SSH key (next step) |

## 2. Create an SSH key 

On macOS, Linux or Windows (PowerShell), the same command:

```bash
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@laptop"
# press Enter for the default path, then choose a passphrase
$ cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3Nza… you@laptop
```

```tree
~/.ssh/
  id_ed25519        ← private: never share, never upload
  id_ed25519.pub    ← public: paste it into the provider
```

Paste the **public** line into the provider's "SSH keys" field when you create the server.

## 3. Log in 

```bash
$ ssh root@203.0.113.10
```

The first time, SSH asks whether you trust the server's fingerprint: type `yes`. You're in when the prompt changes to `root@…`. Now install Cipi ([installation](https://cipi.sh/docs/installation)):

```bash
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Early on, the installer asks for the public key that will open the `cipi` user: paste the same `id_ed25519.pub` line (you can add a second machine's key too). After the install, root login is disabled. From then on you log in as `cipi`:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10
```

Make it shorter with an entry in `~/.ssh/config`:

```text
Host shop
  HostName 203.0.113.10
  User cipi
```

Then `ssh shop` is enough.

## 4. Point your domain 

At your registrar or DNS provider (Cloudflare, Namecheap, OVH…), add:

| Type | Name | Value | TTL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | `shop` (or `@` for the bare domain) | `203.0.113.10` | Auto / 300 |
| A | `www` | `203.0.113.10` | Auto / 300 |
| AAAA | same names | the server's IPv6, if it has one | Auto |

Check it from your laptop:

```bash
$ dig +short shop.example.com
203.0.113.10
```

On Cloudflare, keep the cloud **grey** ("DNS only") until the certificate is issued, then you can turn the proxy on with SSL/TLS **Full (strict)**.

## 5. What Cipi does for you 

| Job | Without Cipi | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Install Nginx, PHP, MariaDB, Valkey, Supervisor | Hours of setup | One command |
| Firewall, Fail2ban, key-only SSH | Easy to get wrong | On by default |
| One user, database and pool per app | Rarely done | Every app |
| HTTPS certificates and renewals | certbot by hand | `cipi ssl install` |
| Security patches | Remember to log in | Nightly, automatic |
| Deploys with rollback | Scripts | `cipi deploy`, on push |

Next: [deploy your first Laravel app](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | Wrong user or key: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 cipi@IP`; check the key was added at creation |
| `Connection timed out` | Wrong IP, or the provider's firewall blocks 22: allow 22, 80, 443 |
| `REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED` | You rebuilt the server: `ssh-keygen -R 203.0.113.10` |
| `dig` shows nothing or an old IP | Record not saved or still cached: wait the TTL, check the name |
| Browser shows the provider's parking page | DNS still points at the registrar: change the A record |


## Cipi in the enterprise: where it fits, what it gives, what to add

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-enterprise

Enterprises usually meet Laravel through the side door: a Filament back-office here, a customer portal there, an agency delivering a project that now has to be hosted somewhere approved. Each lands on whatever the team found first. Cipi offers a **standard way** to host all of them, on infrastructure the organisation chooses, with the controls an auditor asks about built in.

## In 30 seconds 

| Cipi fits when | Look elsewhere when |
| --- | --- |
| You host Laravel and PHP apps on VMs you control (cloud, local provider, your own data centre) | You need autoscaling and multi-zone failover as a managed service |
| Data must stay in a given country, provider or network | Your standard is containers on Kubernetes for everything |
| You want one fixed infrastructure cost and no per-seat or per-server licence | You need a vendor contract with an SLA and a support desk |
| Auditors ask for evidence on access, changes, patching and backups | SAML-only identity, or an OS other than Ubuntu LTS, is a hard requirement |

```flow
Why | sovereignty, cost | #why
Fit | use cases | #fit
Controls | for auditors | #controls
Gaps | what to add | #gaps
Vendor Q&A | procurement | #questionnaire
Roll-out | pilot to fleet | #rollout
Cost | what you pay | #cost
```

## Why enterprises look at self-hosting again 

| Driver | What it means for hosting |
| --- | --- |
| **Data sovereignty** | Privacy law, sector rules (finance, health, public sector) and customer contracts increasingly specify *where* data lives and *who* can reach it. A server you choose, in a region you choose, with no third-party control plane, is the simplest answer |
| **Regulation of ICT risk** | Frameworks such as NIS2 and, for financial entities, DORA ask organisations to manage risks from their ICT suppliers. Every SaaS in the deploy path is one more supplier to assess |
| **Cost control** | Per-seat and usage-based tools grow with headcount and traffic. A fixed VPS price and a free tool don't ([the numbers](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-vs-kubernetes-vs-managed-paas#tests)) |
| **Vendor risk** | Price changes, licence changes, acquisitions and outages at a vendor become your problem. An open source tool with no service behind it removes that dependency ([licences](https://cipi.sh/guides/open-source-licences)) |
| **Shadow IT** | Teams that can't get hosting quickly will find it themselves. A standard, approved path is the cure |

## Where Cipi fits 

| Use case | How Cipi is used |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal tools and back-offices** | Many Laravel/Filament apps on a few servers, each isolated, behind SSO or [Cloudflare Access](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) |
| **Customer portals and APIs** | Production on dedicated servers, staging on shared ones, deploys from CI through scoped tokens |
| **Agency and supplier projects** | The supplier pushes to Git; the organisation owns the server, the data and the deploy history |
| **Regulated data** | Servers in the required country or provider; backups encrypted on the server before they leave, to a bucket you choose |
| **Business units with their own budgets** | One server (or more) per unit, all visible in one panel with roles |
| **Legacy PHP next to Laravel** | WordPress, Symfony and other PHP as isolated [custom apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/custom-apps), patched like the rest |

## The controls auditors ask about 

What Cipi does out of the box, grouped the way security questionnaires and ISO 27001 / SOC 2 audits group it:

| Area | What Cipi provides |
| --- | --- |
| **Identity and access** | Key-only SSH for the admin user, root login off, alerts on logins and `sudo`. Panel with [SSO over OpenID Connect](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-sso) (Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace, Keycloak…), two-factor, roles per server (View, Manage) and per app (View, Deploy, Edit, Environment, Logs, Commands, Delete), single-use invite links |
| **Least privilege for automation** | [API tokens](https://cipi.sh/docs/api#tokens) with listed abilities (`deploy-manage` alone deploys) and expiry dates, behind an [IP allowlist](https://cipi.sh/docs/api#cipi-api-ip-whitelist). The API calls an allowlist of `cipi` commands through sudo; destructive host operations stay on the CLI |
| **Segregation** | Each app is its own Linux user (home `750`), PHP-FPM pool with `open_basedir`, database user and Valkey instance. A compromised app can't read the others |
| **Change management** | Server settings in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml), reviewed in pull requests, planned and applied all or nothing. A repository can't raise its own disk limit or touch another app's backups |
| **Audit trail** | A [hash-chained deploy ledger](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit): every deploy, rollback and failure, with origin (CLI, panel, webhook, CI, AI agent, SSH), operator, IP and commit, verified by root and copied to syslog |
| **Vulnerability management** | Ubuntu security updates daily; PHP, Nginx, databases and Valkey patched nightly, one service at a time; optional ClamAV scans and CrowdSec; [Hackly](https://cipi.sh/guides/hackly-security-scanning) and [Checkpoint](https://cipi.sh/guides/checkpoint-laravel-sast-ci) for the code |
| **Network** | UFW allowing 22, 80 and 443 only, Fail2ban, optional [Cloudflare Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) that closes the origin's ports entirely |
| **Secrets** | Configuration, tokens and passwords encrypted at rest (AES-256), readable by root only; backups and sync archives encrypted before they leave |
| **Backup and recovery** | [Backup profiles](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) to any S3-compatible storage, encrypted, verified, with staleness alerts; warm standby servers with [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/docs/sync) |
| **Monitoring** | Server monitor and health checks with alerts to e-mail, Slack, Discord, Google Chat, Telegram, signed webhooks and more; [metrics](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-metrics-server-app-uptime) kept by the minute; OpenMetrics for your Prometheus |
| **Privacy** | Fixed [log retention](https://cipi.sh/docs/log-retention): logs with IP addresses 90 days, application and security logs 12 months; [anonymized database dumps](https://cipi.sh/docs/anonymizer) for developers |
| **Evidence** | [`cipi compliance report`](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance): 17 controls checked read-only and mapped to ISO 27001:2022 Annex A and SOC 2, with raw evidence and checksums |

```bash
$ sudo cipi compliance                    # pass / warn / fail per control
$ sudo cipi compliance report --days=365  # bundle for the auditor
$ sudo cipi compliance controls           # mapping to ISO 27001 and SOC 2
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --audit --days=365 --json
```

> [!tip] Record the checksum of each compliance bundle **outside** the server (a ticket, the GRC tool). It proves later that the bundle wasn't altered.

## What to add around it 

Being honest about the gaps is what makes a rollout succeed:

| Gap | How enterprises fill it |
| --- | --- |
| **No vendor support or SLA** | Name an internal platform owner (two, for holidays) and keep a runbook; or contract a local partner who knows Linux and Laravel. The stack is standard, so any experienced Linux administrator can work on it |
| **No autoscaling or clustering** | Size servers for peak; split heavy apps onto their own servers; keep a warm standby with `cipi sync`; put critical data on a managed database if you need automatic failover |
| **Logs stay on the server** | Forward syslog to the SIEM (Splunk, Elastic, Microsoft Sentinel) with your usual agent; the compliance report checks that forwarding is configured |
| **OIDC, not SAML** | Most identity providers offer OIDC next to SAML for the same users (Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace) |
| **Ubuntu LTS only** | Treat it as an appliance OS: Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 on full VMs, nothing else installed by hand |
| **Public IPv4 needed** | Required for certificates and webhooks; after setup, [`cipi zt lock`](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) closes 22, 80 and 443 to the internet and traffic arrives through a Cloudflare Tunnel |
| **Certifications for the tool itself** | Your controls are audited, not the tool. Use a certified infrastructure provider for the VMs and `cipi compliance` for the evidence on top |

## Answers for the vendor questionnaire 

Procurement and security teams ask the same questions of every supplier. For Cipi:

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Does the software send data to the vendor? | No. No telemetry, no account, no control plane. Alerts and backups go only to destinations you configure |
| Where is data stored? | On your servers, and in the backup buckets you choose. Backups are encrypted on the server before upload |
| Who can access the servers? | Your accounts only: SSH keys you add, panel users you invite, tokens you create |
| Licence and cost? | MIT for every component; no licence fee, no per-seat or per-server pricing |
| Is the source available? | Yes, all of it, on [GitHub](https://github.com/cipi-sh). What runs as root is readable on the server |
| How are vulnerabilities reported and fixed? | Private reports through GitHub's vulnerability reporting ([security.txt](https://cipi.sh/.well-known/security.txt)); fixes ship in the latest release, installed with `cipi self-update` |
| How are changes documented? | A detailed [changelog](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cipi/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md) per release, with the tests each release adds |
| What if the project is discontinued? | Servers keep working without it; the code can be forked; the server is standard Ubuntu |
| Can we exit? | Yes: apps are ordinary Laravel apps, data is in standard MariaDB, MySQL or PostgreSQL, files in standard directories |

## Roll it out in five steps 

```flow
Pilot | one real, non-critical app
> Pick an internal tool with real users but limited impact. Install Cipi on a fresh VM, deploy it, run it for a month. Measure deploy time, incidents and hours spent.
Baseline | the golden server
> Write down the standard: Ubuntu version, VM size, Cipi version, backup destination and profiles, notification channels, CrowdSec on or off, Zero Trust on or off. Script it: `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | SSH_PUBKEY="…" bash`, then the same `cipi` commands every time.
Guardrails | access and change rules
> Panel with SSO and roles; API tokens per pipeline with only the abilities they need and an expiry date; branch protection on repositories with `cipi.yml`; `cipi yml auto` only where pushing to main is already controlled.
Evidence | from day one
> Schedule `cipi compliance --json` (exit 1 on any failure) and a monthly `cipi compliance report`; forward syslog; keep the bundles' checksums in your GRC tool.
Scale | the fleet
> Add servers per business unit or per environment, all in one panel. Use cipi-cli profiles and the PHP SDK for automation, and `cipi sync` to rebalance or move providers.
```

## What it costs 

| Line | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Cipi, panel, API, CLI, SDK, WHMCS module | €0, MIT |
| Servers | Your VM or VPS prices, fixed |
| Backup storage | Your S3-compatible bucket |
| People | The platform owner's time: routine work (patching, renewals, backups, alerts) is automated; incidents, upgrades you schedule and onboarding remain |

The comparison that matters is not "free versus paid", but **fixed infrastructure plus some owned time** against **subscriptions, usage and supplier risk**. The [VPS, Kubernetes or managed platform](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-vs-kubernetes-vs-managed-paas) guide shows how to put numbers on it.


## For hosting providers: Laravel-ready hosting with Cipi and WHMCS

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/hosting-providers-laravel-whmcs

Ask a Laravel developer where they host, and the answer is rarely "my hosting provider". It's a VPS plus Forge or Ploi, or a managed platform. The reason isn't price: standard hosting plans don't run what a Laravel app needs. Cipi turns any Ubuntu server into Laravel-native hosting, and its WHMCS module automates the products. This guide is for the hosting company that wants that business.

```flow
The gap | what's missing | #gap
Products | three to sell | #products
WHMCS | module, servers | #whmcs
Limits | per plan | #limits
Customers | SSH, Git, panel | #access
Operate | the fleet | #operate
Price | margins | #pricing
```

## The gap: what Laravel needs and standard hosting misses 

| A Laravel app needs | Typical shared or cPanel hosting | On a Cipi server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long-running queue workers, Horizon | Often not allowed, or killed | Supervisor programs per app, restarted on deploy |
| The scheduler every minute | Cron with limits on frequency | One cron per app, on by default |
| Git deploys without downtime | FTP uploads, or `git pull` in place | Releases with an atomic symlink swap, rollback in one command, webhooks from six Git forges |
| Composer and Node builds | Limited SSH, old tool versions | Composer 2 and Node on the server, build steps in the deploy |
| A choice of PHP version per app | One or a few versions | PHP 8.3 to 8.6 side by side, per app |
| Redis-compatible cache and queues | Rare on shared plans | A Valkey instance per app |
| WebSockets (Reverb), Octane | Not available | `cipi app reverb enable`, `cipi app create --octane` |
| Document root on `public/` | Workarounds with `.htaccess` | Nginx configured for Laravel |
| Isolation from other customers | Shared users or containers of varying quality | A Linux user, PHP-FPM pool, database user and Valkey instance per app |

Few providers offer this out of the box. That's the opportunity: a Laravel-friendly product is a reason to choose you, not just a cheaper VPS.

## Three products you can build 

| Product | Customer gets | You run | WHMCS automation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Laravel-ready VPS** | A whole VPS with Cipi installed, and root | The VPS only | Your existing VPS module, plus Cipi installed at first boot |
| **Managed Laravel app** | One isolated app on your servers: SSH/SFTP as its own user, Git deploys, database, SSL | The servers, patching, backups, monitoring | The Cipi module: order → app, unpaid → suspended, cancelled → removed |
| **App instance per customer** | A ready instance of a Laravel product (yours, or a client's SaaS) on its own domain | Same as above | The Cipi module with the product's Git repository in the product settings: every order deploys the same codebase |

### Laravel-ready VPS: install Cipi at first boot 

Pass the customer's key and run the installer from cloud-init (or your virtualisation panel's post-install script). Without a terminal, the installer asks nothing:

```yaml
#cloud-config
runcmd:
  - [bash, -c, 'wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | SSH_PUBKEY="ssh-ed25519 AAAA… customer@laptop" bash > /var/log/cipi-install.log 2>&1']
```

The VM must be full virtualisation (KVM, VMware, Hyper-V, Xen HVM) with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04; the installer stops on LXC or OpenVZ.

## Architecture 

```stack
WHMCS | orders, invoices, suspensions
Cipi module | modules/servers/cipi
Cipi API | one per server, HTTPS + token
cipi CLI | the same code as over SSH
Isolated apps | user, PHP pool, database, Valkey
```

Each Cipi server runs its own [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api), on its own hostname, with a token for WHMCS. WHMCS sees each server as a *server* in a *server group*; the module calls the API to create, suspend, unsuspend, change and terminate apps. Your staff can see the whole fleet in the optional [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui).

## 1. Prepare each server 

```bash
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash             # fresh Ubuntu 26.04
$ sudo cipi api api.node1.host.example                   # DNS check, install, certificate
$ sudo cipi api token create --name=whmcs \
    --abilities=apps-view,apps-create,apps-edit,apps-suspend,apps-delete,deploy-manage,ssl-manage,aliases-view,aliases-create,aliases-delete \
    --expires=2027-12-31
```

| Ability | Used by |
| --- | --- |
| `apps-view` | Test Connection, App Info |
| `apps-create` | Create Account |
| `apps-edit` | Change Package, and the [limits hook](#limits) |
| `apps-suspend` | Suspend, Unsuspend |
| `apps-delete` | Terminate |
| `deploy-manage` | Deploy, Rollback, Unlock buttons |
| `ssl-manage` | Install SSL, Auto SSL |
| `aliases-view`, `aliases-create`, `aliases-delete` | List, Add and Remove Alias buttons |

Then let only your own machines reach the API: `sudo cipi api ip-whitelist add ` (and the address of your panel, if you run one). Set up off-site [backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) and [notifications](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts) before the first customer arrives.

## 2. Install the module and add the servers 

```tree
your-whmcs/
└── modules/servers/cipi/
    ├── cipi.php
    └── lib/CipiApiClient.php
```

```flow
Copy the module | into WHMCS
> Download it from [github.com/cipi-sh/whmcs](https://github.com/cipi-sh/whmcs) and copy `modules/servers/cipi/` into your WHMCS root. No Composer, no dependencies.
Add the server | System Settings → Servers
> Module *Cipi (Laravel hosting)*; hostname = the API's base URL without a trailing slash; password = the token; tick *Secure* so certificates are verified. Set *Maximum No. of Accounts* to cap apps per server. Use *Test Connection*.
Group the servers | fill method
> Create a server group per region or tier and choose *Add to the least full server*, so new orders spread across nodes.
Create the product | Module Settings
> A hosting product on that group, module *Cipi (Laravel hosting)*: PHP version, app type (`laravel` or `custom`), Git repository and branch (for `laravel`), Auto SSL. Ask for a domain on order.
Automate the lifecycle | Automation Settings
```
