```flow
> Turn on suspension and termination for overdue invoices. A suspended app serves a static 503 page and keeps all its data; unsuspending brings it back as it was.
```

| Module setting | `laravel` app | `custom` app |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What's created | A Laravel app with releases, workers, scheduler and its database | A PHP site in `htdocs/`: WordPress, static, any PHP |
| Git repository | Required (the product's repository) | Optional: empty means SFTP-only hosting |
| Good for | *App instance per customer*, or customers who connect their own repository after creation | Classic PHP and WordPress hosting with real isolation |

| WHMCS action | What happens on the server |
| --- | --- |
| Create Account | App created (user from the WHMCS username, primary domain from the order), job awaited, optional Let's Encrypt certificate |
| Suspend / Unsuspend | 503 maintenance page / normal vhost back; nothing deleted, certificates keep renewing |
| Change Package | PHP version, repository and branch from the new product |
| Terminate | App removed |
| Admin buttons | Install SSL, Deploy, Rollback Deploy, Unlock Deploy, List/Add/Remove Alias, App Info |

Every call is written to WHMCS's module log (Utilities → Logs → Module Log). If Auto SSL fails because DNS doesn't point at the server yet, the app is still created and the failure is logged: run *Install SSL* later.

> [!note] The module's PHP dropdown is a list in `cipi_ConfigOptions()`. Keep it aligned with the versions installed on your servers (`sudo cipi php list`), and install a version on every server of the group before selling it.

## 3. Plans and limits 

Limits stop one customer from starving the others. Set them per app with `cipi app limits`, or through the API (`PUT /api/apps/{name}/limits`) from a WHMCS hook, so each product applies its plan automatically:

| Plan (example) | PHP-FPM children | `memory_limit` | Queue workers | Soft disk limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starter | 5 | 256M | 1 | 5 GB |
| Pro | 10 | 512M | 2 | 20 GB |
| Business | 20 | 1G | 4 | 50 GB |

```php
 limits (the fields of PUT /api/apps/{name}/limits)
    $plans = [
        11 => ['fpm_max_children' => 5,  'memory_limit' => '256M', 'worker_procs' => 1, 'disk_limit_gb' => 5],
        12 => ['fpm_max_children' => 10, 'memory_limit' => '512M', 'worker_procs' => 2, 'disk_limit_gb' => 20],
        13 => ['fpm_max_children' => 20, 'memory_limit' => '1G',   'worker_procs' => 4, 'disk_limit_gb' => 50],
    ];
    $limits = $plans[(int) ($p['pid'] ?? 0)] ?? null;
    if ($limits === null) {
        return;
    }

    // The app name the module derives from the WHMCS username
    $app = substr(preg_replace('/[^a-z0-9]/', '', strtolower((string) $p['username'])), 0, 32);
    $base = rtrim((string) $p['serverhostname'], '/');
    if (!preg_match('#^https?://#i', $base)) {
        $base = 'https://' . $base;
    }

    $ch = curl_init($base . '/api/apps/' . rawurlencode($app) . '/limits');
    curl_setopt_array($ch, [
        CURLOPT_CUSTOMREQUEST => 'PUT',
        CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER => true,
        CURLOPT_TIMEOUT => 30,
        CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER => [
            'Accept: application/json',
            'Content-Type: application/json',
            'Authorization: Bearer ' . $p['serverpassword'],
        ],
        CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS => json_encode($limits),
    ]);
    $raw = curl_exec($ch);
    $code = (int) curl_getinfo($ch, CURLINFO_HTTP_CODE);
    curl_close($ch);

    // 202 = queued as a job on the server
    logModuleCall('cipi', 'ApplyLimits', ['app' => $app] + $limits, $raw, "HTTP {$code}", [$p['serverpassword']]);
});
```

| Limit | Controls | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fpm_max_children` | Concurrent PHP requests | The app's [metrics](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-metrics-server-app-uptime) count how often it hits the cap: a ready-made upsell signal |
| `memory_limit` | PHP's per-request memory | |
| `worker_procs` | Queue worker processes | |
| `octane_workers` | Octane workers, for Octane apps | |
| `disk_limit_gb` | Soft limit for files + database | Alerts at 90% and over the limit; never blocks the site. A repository's `cipi.yml` can't raise it |

For one-off changes, staff can use the CLI (`sudo cipi app limits shop --disk=20`), the panel, or the [PHP SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk): `$cipi->limits()->update('shop', ['fpm_max_children' => 10])`.

## 4. How customers work 

| Customer needs | How |
| --- | --- |
| Shell, Composer, Artisan, SFTP | [`ssh shop@node1.host.example`](https://cipi.sh/docs/app-ssh): the app's own user, kept out of other apps' files by permissions, with SFTP for their IDE |
| Deploys from Git | The app's deploy key added to their repository, then `git push` with the webhook ([auto-deploy](https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy)) |
| Database access | TablePlus or DBeaver over SSH with the `mariadb+ssh://` URL; no database port is ever open |
| Server settings | A [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) in their repository: workers, schedule, PHP settings, backups. You decide whether it's applied automatically |
| A dashboard | Invite them to the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-overview) with access to **their app only** (view, deploy, logs, environment…): a client area without building one |
| Help | Your support, with the same commands you use |

Deliver one-time secrets (passwords, deploy key, webhook URL) through your onboarding: the module deliberately doesn't store them in WHMCS.

## 5. Operate the fleet 

| Task | With Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| Patching | Ubuntu security updates daily, PHP nightly, Nginx, databases and Valkey through [autoupdate](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades), one service at a time. Reboots when you schedule them |
| Monitoring | The [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) alerts your ops channel on disk, services, workers, certificates, 5xx and load; [metrics](https://cipi.sh/docs/metrics) show which app is the noisy neighbour |
| Backups | A server-wide nightly profile to off-site storage, plus frequent database profiles; `cipi backup status` lists any app nothing covers |
| Security | Per-app isolation, CrowdSec, optional malware scans, Cloudflare Zero Trust for the admin side |
| Rebalancing | Move an app or a whole node with [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) |
| B2B customers' audits | [`cipi compliance report`](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance): evidence mapped to ISO 27001 and SOC 2 |

## 6. Price it 

Cipi adds no licence cost per server, per account or per site, so the margin is the difference between your price and your infrastructure and support.

```text
monthly margin per server = apps on the server × price per app − server cost − support time
```

An example with round numbers, to adapt to your own costs and capacity tests: a node that costs you €60 a month, hosting 20 small Laravel apps sold at €12, brings €240 of revenue and €180 before support. The customer gets a Laravel-native product without a server to manage or a panel to subscribe to; you get a margin no per-account licence eats into.

| Lever | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Measure real capacity | Load-test your node type with a typical Laravel app before fixing apps-per-server |
| Sell what Laravel developers value | Queues, Horizon, Reverb, scheduler, zero-downtime deploys, PHP 8.6: put them on the product page |
| Upsell on signals | Pool saturation, disk at 90%, sustained CPU: offer the next plan before the customer notices |
| Keep plans simple | Three tiers, the same limits on every node |

## What Cipi is not, for a host 

| Not included | Do instead |
| --- | --- |
| E-mail hosting, DNS servers, reseller accounts | Keep your existing products, or partner for them |
| A client-area tab in WHMCS | Panel invites per app, or your own hook with the [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) |
| Hard quotas | Soft limits with alerts, by design |
| Containers (LXC, OpenVZ) or operating systems other than Ubuntu LTS | Full VMs with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 |


## Open source licences, explained: what they allow, and why Cipi's stack is built on them

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/open-source-licences

Your hosting stack is the last place you want a surprise. A licence is the contract that says what you may do with each piece of it, what you must do in return, and how much its owner can change your situation later. This guide explains the families in plain words, looks at the licence changes that caught teams out, and shows how Cipi's choices are made to keep you out of that story.

> [!info] This is an engineer's overview, not legal advice. For a specific contract or product, ask a lawyer who knows software licensing.

```flow
Families | MIT to SSPL | #families
Definition | the guarantees | #definition
Changes | what happened | #changes
Cipi | all MIT | #cipi
Stack | by component | #stack
Trust | read, patch, fork | #transparency
Your app | its deps | #your-app
```

## The licence families, in plain words 

| Family | Examples | You may | You must | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Permissive** | MIT, BSD-2/3-Clause, Apache-2.0, PostgreSQL, PHP License | Use, modify, sell, embed in closed products | Keep the copyright and licence notice (Apache-2.0: also state changes, keep NOTICE) | Almost nothing. Apache-2.0 adds an explicit patent licence |
| **Weak copyleft** | LGPL, MPL-2.0 | Use in closed products | Share changes to *those* files or that library | Mixing code at file level (MPL) or static linking (LGPL) |
| **Strong copyleft** | GPL-2.0, GPL-3.0 | Use, modify, run anywhere | If you **distribute** the program or a derivative, do it under the GPL with source | Shipping GPL code inside a product you sell as a binary |
| **Network copyleft** | AGPL-3.0 | Use, modify | If you modify it and users reach it **over a network**, offer them your source | Patched AGPL servers offered as a service |
| **Source-available** | BSL/BUSL, SSPL, Elastic License, RSAL | Read the code, use it within the licence's limits | Respect the restrictions (often: no competing hosted service) | Not open source; terms set by one company and changeable for future versions |

Two things are worth knowing about copyleft. It is triggered by **distribution** (or, for AGPL, network use of a modified version), not by running software: a server running GPL databases doesn't make your Laravel app GPL. And it protects *users' freedoms* rather than restricting them: it stops anyone from taking the code closed.

## What "open source" actually guarantees 

"Open source" has a definition, maintained by the Open Source Initiative. Among its criteria: free redistribution, source code available, derived works allowed, and **no discrimination against persons, groups or fields of use**. That last one is why source-available licences don't qualify: forbidding "offering the software as a service" discriminates a field of use.

For infrastructure, the definition turns into four practical guarantees:

| Guarantee | Why it matters on a server |
| --- | --- |
| You can read it | You (or an auditor) can check what runs as root |
| You can change it | A fix doesn't have to wait for the vendor |
| You can share it | A community can maintain it if the original owner stops |
| Nobody can forbid your use case | Hosting clients, competing with someone, selling services: all allowed |

## When licences change 

Single-company projects can release **future versions** under a different licence. It has happened to some of the best-known infrastructure software:

| Year | Project | Change | What the community did |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2018 | MongoDB | AGPL-3.0 → SSPL | Distributions dropped it from their archives |
| 2021 | Elasticsearch, Kibana | Apache-2.0 → SSPL / Elastic License | AWS and others forked **OpenSearch** (Elastic later added the AGPL as an option, in 2024) |
| 2023 | Terraform, Vault (HashiCorp) | MPL-2.0 → BSL 1.1 | **OpenTofu** and **OpenBao** forks, under the Linux Foundation |
| 2024 | Redis | BSD-3-Clause → RSALv2 / SSPLv1 | **Valkey** fork, BSD-3-Clause, under the Linux Foundation (Redis later added the AGPL as an option) |

The lessons are the same each time. Versions already released keep their licence, so a fork can always start from the last open one. The cost falls on users who must re-evaluate, migrate or freeze versions, usually in a hurry. And the risk is highest where **one company owns all the rights** and earns from a hosted version of the same software.

## Cipi's own licences 

Every part of Cipi is released under the **MIT licence**, the most permissive common open source licence:

| Repository | What it is | Licence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [cipi-sh/cipi](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cipi) | The server CLI and installer | MIT |
| [cipi-sh/agent](https://github.com/cipi-sh/agent) | Laravel package: webhook deploys, health, MCP, anonymized dumps | MIT |
| [cipi-sh/api](https://github.com/cipi-sh/api) | REST API and MCP server for the server | MIT |
| [cipi-sh/gui](https://github.com/cipi-sh/gui) | Optional web panel | MIT |
| [cipi-sh/cli](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli) | `cipi-cli` for your laptop | MIT |
| [cipi-sh/sdk](https://github.com/cipi-sh/sdk) | PHP SDK | MIT |
| [cipi-sh/whmcs](https://github.com/cipi-sh/whmcs) | WHMCS provisioning module | MIT |

What MIT means for you, concretely: no fee, no account, no per-server or per-site limit, commercial use allowed (agencies, hosting companies, SaaS), modifications allowed, private forks allowed. The only obligation is to keep the copyright and licence notice in copies of the code. What it doesn't give you is a warranty: the licence disclaims it, as every open source licence does. Support comes from the docs, GitHub and the community, and [the enterprise guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-enterprise) covers what to put around it in a larger organisation.

## The stack, component by component 

Cipi installs well-known open source components from their official packages, and chooses them with licences in mind:

| Component | Role | Licence | Installed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ubuntu LTS | Operating system | Mostly GPL and other OSI licences | Base |
| Nginx (nginx.org packages) | Web server | BSD-2-Clause | Always |
| PHP (packages.sury.org) | Runtime | PHP License (BSD-style, permissive) | Always |
| MariaDB Server | Database on port 3306 | GPL-2.0 | Default |
| MySQL Community | Alternative on port 3306 | GPL-2.0 | Only with `cipi db switch mysql` |
| PostgreSQL | Database on port 5432 | PostgreSQL License (permissive) | Optional |
| Valkey | Cache, sessions, queues | BSD-3-Clause | Always |
| Supervisor | Queue workers, Horizon, Reverb, Octane | BSD-style | Always |
| Deployer | Zero-downtime releases | MIT | Always |
| Composer, Node.js | Builds | MIT | Always |
| Certbot | Let's Encrypt certificates | Apache-2.0 | Always |
| UFW, Fail2ban | Firewall, bans | GPL-3.0, GPL-2.0 | Always |
| CrowdSec | Shared threat intelligence | MIT | Optional |
| ClamAV | Malware scan | GPL-2.0 | Optional |
| Meilisearch | Search for Laravel Scout | MIT (Community Edition) | Optional |
| FrankenPHP | Octane runtime | MIT | Optional |

Three choices worth noting:

| Choice | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| **Valkey instead of Redis** | Same protocol, same `phpredis`, same `REDIS_*` keys, but BSD-licensed and stewarded by the Linux Foundation. Servers moved automatically on `cipi self-update` ([why](https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions#valkey)) |
| **MariaDB by default** | A GPL community server with no enterprise edition gating features and no dual licensing to navigate; MySQL stays available as an explicit choice ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-mysql-instead-of-mariadb)) |
| **No source-available component** | Nothing in this stack carries a "no competing service" clause, so you can host clients, sell hosting or build a platform on it |

None of these components is AGPL. Cipi installs them from their official packages and configures them, it doesn't ship modified copies, so running them creates no licence obligation for you as the operator of the server.

The [optional packages](https://cipi.sh/docs/packages) are a different matter: third-party tools installed only when you ask, each under its own licence. Most are open source. Among the [security scanners](https://cipi.sh/docs/packages#sec), WPScan (`sec-wpscan`) is not: it is free to test your own systems and for penetration testers, but needs a commercial licence to be sold as a service. Nmap (`sec-recon`) has a licence of its own, the NPSL: the GPL with extra terms. Read a tool's licence before you build a paid service on it.

## Transparency: you can read what runs as root 

| What you can check | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Every command Cipi runs | Bash and PHP in `/opt/cipi/lib` on your server, the same code as on GitHub |
| Every change between versions | The [changelog](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cipi/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md), written to explain *why*, with the tests each release adds |
| What leaves the server | Nothing by default: no telemetry, no account, no control plane. Alerts and backups go only where you configure them |
| What the panel and API may do | A sudo allowlist of `cipi` commands (`/etc/sudoers.d/cipi-api`), readable on the server |
| Who deployed what | A hash-chained [deploy ledger](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit), copied to syslog |
| How the server measures up | [`cipi compliance`](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance), which says plainly what it can't prove |

A closed SaaS panel asks you to trust a dashboard. An open source tool on your own server lets you verify instead.

## Security: why openness helps 

Open source doesn't make software secure by itself. It makes security **checkable**, and it changes who you depend on:

| Property | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| Auditable | You, your security team or an external auditor can review the code that has root on your servers |
| Patched upstream | Components come from their official repositories (Ubuntu, nginx.org, packages.sury.org, MariaDB.org), so fixes arrive with the vendor's own release; Cipi applies PHP and stack patches nightly |
| No vendor in the path | No external control plane to breach, and no outage at a vendor that takes your deploys down |
| Responsible disclosure | Private vulnerability reports on GitHub, with a [security.txt](https://cipi.sh/.well-known/security.txt) on this site |
| Reproducible | The same standard packages on every server: what's secure on one is secure on all |
| No surprise relicensing at the core | MIT for Cipi, permissive or copyleft OSI licences for the stack, no single-vendor source-available component |

## Continuity: if the project stops tomorrow 

| If… | Then |
| --- | --- |
| cipi.sh went offline | Your servers keep running: nothing on them calls home. Deploys, backups, renewals and alerts work as before |
| Development stopped | The last version keeps working; MIT lets anyone fork and maintain it |
| You want to leave Cipi | The server is standard Ubuntu with standard packages, configs in their usual places. Any sysadmin can take it over |

That's the practical value of a licence nobody can take away, on software that doesn't depend on a service.

## Check your own app 

The same reasoning applies to your Laravel app's dependencies:

```bash
$ composer licenses                        # every PHP package and its licence
$ composer licenses --format=json > licences.json
$ composer require --dev cyclonedx/cyclonedx-php-composer
$ composer CycloneDX:make-sbom             # a software bill of materials
```

| Look for | Why |
| --- | --- |
| AGPL packages in a SaaS you modify | The network clause may apply to your changes |
| Source-available packages | Check their restrictions against your business model |
| "proprietary" or unknown licences | Ask the vendor, or replace them |
| Abandoned packages | A licence doesn't patch vulnerabilities: combine with [security scanning](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-security-checklist) |


## Cipi on a VPS, Kubernetes or a managed platform: how to choose

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-vs-kubernetes-vs-managed-paas

There are four common ways to run a Laravel app in production. They differ less in what the app can do than in **who runs the servers** and **how the bill is built**. This guide compares them, then gives you three tests to decide, with your own numbers, whether a variable bill is worth its premium.

## In 30 seconds 

| If… | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Traffic is fairly steady, you want a fixed bill, root access and no lock-in | **Cipi on a VPS** |
| Nobody on the team will own a Linux server, or peaks are many times the average, or you need managed failover | **A managed platform** (Laravel Cloud, Ploi Cloud, Sevalla, Render, fortrabbit) |
| Many services and teams share one platform, and a platform team already runs it | **Kubernetes** |
| You want a SaaS panel driving your VPS and don't mind a subscription | Forge or Ploi ([comparisons](https://cipi.sh/alternatives)) |

```flow
Models | who runs what | #models
Who does what | self vs managed | #responsibilities
Bills | fixed vs variable | #bills
Fixed wins | hidden costs | #predictable
Three tests | your numbers | #tests
K8s | when it pays | #kubernetes
Choose | signals, mixes | #choose
```

## The four models 

| | Cipi on a VPS | SaaS panel + VPS | Managed platform (PaaS) | Kubernetes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Who runs the servers** | You, with Cipi automating the routine | You, driven by the vendor's panel | The vendor | You (or your platform team), the cloud runs the control plane |
| **How you pay** | VPS price, fixed. Cipi is free (MIT) | VPS price + subscription | Plan + usage (compute, database, bandwidth, builds…) | Control plane + nodes + load balancers + traffic |
| **Root access** | Yes | Yes | No | On nodes, if not serverless |
| **Scaling** | Resize the server, or spread apps over servers | Same | Automatic, sometimes to zero | Automatic, if you configure it |
| **Laravel specifics** | Built in: releases, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane | Built in | Built in (Laravel-focused platforms) | You build them: images, workers, CronJobs, migrations |
| **Lock-in** | None: standard Ubuntu stack, any provider | Low: servers are yours, the panel isn't | Databases, queues and storage are platform resources | Low on the app, high on the platform's YAML and add-ons |
| **Typical team** | Developers, agencies, small and mid-size companies, internal IT | Same, preferring a hosted UI | Teams that never want to see a server | Organisations with a platform team |

Many managed platforms are Kubernetes underneath (Ploi Cloud, for example, deploys to managed Kubernetes clusters): with a PaaS you pay someone to run that layer for you.

## Self-hosted vs managed: who does what 

"Managed" doesn't mean "nothing to do", and "self-hosted" doesn't mean "do it all by hand". This is the honest split:

| Task | Cipi on a VPS | Managed platform | Kubernetes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OS and security patches | Automatic (unattended-upgrades), reboots when you choose | Vendor | Node images: you or the cloud |
| PHP, Nginx, database patches | Automatic, nightly, one service at a time | Vendor | You rebuild images |
| TLS certificates | Automatic (Let's Encrypt) | Vendor | cert-manager, which you install |
| Backups | Built in: encrypted, verified, off-site | Vendor (check retention and restore options) | You choose and run a tool |
| Monitoring and alerts | Built in: monitor, health checks, metrics, heartbeat | Vendor dashboards | You install a stack |
| Scaling | You resize or add servers | Automatic | Automatic, after you tune it |
| Failover across zones | You plan it (warm standby with `cipi sync`) | Vendor, on higher plans | You design it |
| Incident at 3 a.m. on the infrastructure | **You** | Vendor (and you, waiting) | **You** |
| Bugs, slow queries, bad deploys | You | You | You |
| Security of your code | You | You | You |
| Cost control | One number | You, through limits and alerts | You, through FinOps |

The rows that stay yours in every column (code, queries, deploys) are where most incidents come from. Managed platforms take away the infrastructure rows; Cipi automates most of the same rows, and leaves the decisions and the pager with you.

## How the bills are built 

A **fixed** bill has one line: the server. Bigger traffic makes the server busier, not the invoice longer.

A **variable** bill multiplies prices by usage. A typical one has a base plan plus: compute per second per replica, database compute and storage, cache, bandwidth per GB, build minutes, log retention, sometimes per-seat fees. Published prices in November 2026, as examples (check the vendors' pages before deciding):

| Platform | How it charges |
| --- | --- |
| [Laravel Cloud](https://laravel.com/cloud/pricing) | Starter $5, Growth $20, Business $200 a month, **plus usage**; $5 of usage credit included; scale-to-zero; spending limits per organisation |
| [Sevalla](https://sevalla.com/pricing/) | Usage-based, from $5 a month; application bandwidth $0.10 per GB |
| [Ploi Cloud](https://ploi.cloud/pricing) | Usage-based, on managed Kubernetes; managed MySQL/PostgreSQL from €14 a month; object storage €10 per 250 GB |
| [Amazon EKS](https://aws.amazon.com/eks/pricing/) | $0.10 per cluster per hour (about $73 a month) for the control plane, $0.60 (about $438) on an outdated Kubernetes version; nodes, load balancers and traffic on top |
| [DigitalOcean Kubernetes](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/kubernetes/details/pricing) | Control plane free, high availability $40 a month; nodes on top |
| AWS traffic to the internet | First 100 GB a month free, then $0.09 per GB |
| **Cipi on a VPS** | The VPS price. Most VPS plans include a terabyte or more of traffic |

Fixed isn't frozen either: [Hetzner raised its cloud prices](https://docs.hetzner.com/general/infrastructure-and-availability/price-adjustment/) twice in 2026. But a VPS price is one number, announced in advance, easy to compare across providers, and Cipi is the same on all of them.

## Why a predictable bill is worth more than it looks 

**You can quote it.** An agency that bills clients a fixed hosting fee turns every variable line into margin risk. A company budget wants one number per year, not a range.

**It grows with you, not with accidents.** A variable bill grows with things you don't choose: an aggressive crawler, a bot pulling your images, a queue job stuck in a retry loop, an autoscaler that reaches its maximum during an attack. On a VPS these make the server slower and fire an alert; on usage billing they also make an invoice. Two terabytes of unexpected traffic at $0.09–0.10 per GB is about $180–200, in one month.

**Spending limits cap the bill, not the cause.** When the cap is reached, the app degrades or stops: the same thing a VPS does when it's full. The difference is that, up to the cap, you paid more per unit of capacity.

**Every decision stops being a pricing decision.** Add a queue worker, keep logs longer, cache more, run a nightly report: on a fixed bill you decide on technical grounds. On a variable bill each choice is also a cost forecast.

**Leaving stays cheap.** A Cipi server is standard Ubuntu with standard packages; another provider is one [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) away. Once an app depends on a platform's serverless database, managed queues and storage, leaving costs engineering time, and that cost belongs in the comparison.

## Three tests: what must a variable bill buy you? 

Call **F** the fixed monthly cost of the Cipi setup (the VPS sized for your peak, backup storage, maybe a standby server) and **V** your realistic monthly bill on the managed platform, from its own calculator. The **premium** is **P = V − F**. Here's what P has to pay for.

### Test 1 — Time: is it buying hours? 

```text
break-even hours per month = P ÷ your hourly cost
```

| Premium P | Hourly cost €60 | Hourly cost €90 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| €50 / month | 0.8 h | 0.6 h |
| €200 / month | 3.3 h | 2.2 h |
| €500 / month | 8.3 h | 5.6 h |

The managed platform must save you **at least that many hours every month**. Count honestly: on a Cipi server patching, certificate renewals, backups, verification and alerting run by themselves. What's left is reading alerts, the upgrades you decide to do, and incidents. If that's below the break-even, the premium isn't buying time; it's buying comfort, which is fine, as long as you know it.

### Test 2 — Elasticity: do your peaks pay for it? 

You size a VPS for your **peak**; a usage bill charges your **average**. Call **m** the platform's markup: the monthly price of an always-on instance on the platform divided by the price of a VPS with the same vCPU and RAM.

```text
usage billing is cheaper only when  peak ÷ average  >  m
```

| Your traffic | Peak ÷ average | Usually cheaper |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business app, office hours | 2–3× | VPS |
| E-commerce, normal weeks | 2–4× | VPS |
| Ticket sales, launches, TV spots | 10–50× during the event | Usage billing, or a VPS resized for the event |
| Side project, idle most of the day | very high (average near zero) | Scale-to-zero, unless it shares a VPS with other apps |
| Staging and previews | very high | On Cipi they share an existing server at no extra cost |

These are typical shapes; measure yours. `sudo cipi metrics show --app=shop --range=30d` gives the minimum, average and peak of an app's CPU and requests per minute over the last month.

Two corrections make the test fairer. A Cipi server hosts many apps for one price, so compare **per server, not per app**: ten small sites on one VPS have a marginal cost close to zero. And a VPS can be **resized for a known event** and back, which turns a predictable peak into a predictable one-off cost.

### Test 3 — Risk: is it buying availability? 

```text
justified if  12 × P  ≤  (cost of one hour down) × (hours of downtime it avoids per year)
```

With P = €200 (€2,400 a year) and an hour of downtime costing you €300, the platform must avoid **8 hours of downtime a year** that you would otherwise have. Compare like with like: single-server commitments from VPS providers commonly sit between 99.5% and 99.99% (Hetzner's is 99.9%, about 8.8 hours a year), so check what the managed platform commits to on the plan you'd actually buy. What changes the number more is your **recovery time**: on Cipi, health checks with automatic rollback undo a bad release in seconds, the [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) and the [heartbeat](https://cipi.sh/docs/metrics#heartbeat) tell you the server is in trouble, and a warm standby fed by `cipi sync` every few hours is a DNS change away.

If your downtime costs thousands per hour and you need multi-zone failover without designing it yourself, test 3 says "managed", and you should listen.

### The verdict 

| A variable bill earns its premium when | Measured as |
| --- | --- |
| It saves more hours than it costs | Test 1: hours saved × hourly cost > P |
| Your peaks are much higher than your average | Test 2: peak ÷ average > m |
| It avoids downtime you can't avoid otherwise | Test 3: downtime avoided × cost per hour > 12 × P |
| Nobody can own a server, and you won't hire or contract someone who can | A team decision, not a number |

If none of these holds, the fixed bill wins, usually by a wide margin, and keeps winning as you grow, because a busier server costs the same.

## Kubernetes: when it pays off 

Kubernetes is an excellent platform for running **many services, owned by many teams**, on a shared pool of machines. For a Laravel monolith with queues and a scheduler, most of its value goes unused and most of its cost remains.

| Kubernetes makes sense when | It's overhead when |
| --- | --- |
| Dozens of services in several languages | One or a few Laravel or PHP apps |
| A platform team already runs clusters for the company | The developers would also become the platform team |
| You need bin-packing and self-healing across many nodes | One or two servers carry the load |
| Images are built once in CI and promoted unchanged through environments | `git push` and a release folder are enough |
| A company standard requires it | Nobody asked for it |

What you build yourself for Laravel on Kubernetes: images per release, web and worker Deployments, the scheduler (a CronJob or one replica of `schedule:work`), migrations as a Job before the rollout, sessions and cache in Valkey or Redis, uploads on object storage, Horizon and Reverb processes, ingress and certificates. And what you pay: the control plane where it's billed, at least two or three nodes for availability, load balancers, NAT gateways and traffic on the big clouds, plus regular cluster upgrades to stay on supported versions (Kubernetes ships about three minor versions a year; on EKS a version leaves standard support after 14 months and the cluster fee rises sixfold).

Cipi deliberately doesn't use containers on the server ([why](https://cipi.sh/docs/design-decisions#docker)). If containers are your standard, a self-hosted Docker platform such as [Coolify](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify) or [Dokku](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-dokku) is a lighter step than Kubernetes.

## Choose: signals and sensible mixes 

| Signal | Points to |
| --- | --- |
| "We need to know the hosting cost for next year" | Cipi on a VPS |
| "Our customers' data must stay in this country, with this provider" | Cipi on a VPS there |
| "We run 30 client sites and bill a fixed hosting fee" | Cipi on a few VPSs ([for agencies and hosts](https://cipi.sh/guides/hosting-providers-laravel-whmcs)) |
| "Nobody here will ever SSH into a server" | Managed platform |
| "Two days a year we get 40× the traffic" | Managed platform, or Cipi with a planned resize |
| "We have a platform team and 50 microservices" | Kubernetes, with Laravel apps on it or next to it |
| "We need a SOC 2 report from our hosting vendor" | Managed platform, or a certified provider for the VPS plus [`cipi compliance`](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance) evidence for your own controls |

Mixes that work well:

| Mix | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Cipi for the app, a managed database for the data | Fixed bill for compute, managed failover and point-in-time restore where it matters most. Point the app's `DB_*` settings at it; its backups are then the database provider's |
| Cipi for Laravel apps, Kubernetes for the rest of the company | Each tool where it's simplest |
| Production on Cipi, a second Cipi server as warm standby | Recovery in minutes for the price of one more VPS |
| Cloudflare in front of Cipi | CDN, cache and DDoS filtering at the edge; with [Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) the origin can close its ports |

## What you get with Cipi 

| Advantage | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Free and open source** | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server, per-site or per-seat fees ([licences](https://cipi.sh/guides/open-source-licences)) |
| **A fixed, predictable bill** | One VPS price, whatever the traffic does |
| **Nothing between you and your server** | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans or goes down |
| **Laravel built in** | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback |
| **Isolation by default** | Each app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance |
| **Configuration as code** | [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) keeps workers, cron, domains and backups in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing |
| **Security on autopilot** | Nightly PHP and stack patches, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec and malware scans, encrypted secrets |
| **Operations included** | Encrypted, verified backups; monitor, health checks and [metrics](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-metrics-server-app-uptime); alerts on Slack, Telegram, e-mail and more |
| **Evidence for audits** | A hash-chained deploy ledger and [`cipi compliance`](https://cipi.sh/docs/compliance) mapped to ISO 27001 and SOC 2 |
| **Portable** | Any provider, any region; move with `cipi sync` |
| **Automation and AI** | CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and MCP servers with guardrails |

And what you give up, so the comparison stays fair: no autoscaling, no vendor to call at 3 a.m., Ubuntu LTS only, and the server is yours to own.


## Install Cipi on AWS EC2

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-ec2

EC2 gives you a full virtual machine, which is exactly what Cipi needs. This walkthrough uses the AWS console; the same settings work from Terraform or the CLI.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Instance / server** | The virtual machine you rent |
| **Image** | The operating system it starts with: pick plain Ubuntu LTS, nothing pre-installed |
| **Public IP** | The address visitors and DNS point to; make it static so it survives rebuilds |
| **Provider firewall** | Rules in the provider's console, before traffic reaches the server. Cipi adds its own (UFW) on the server |
| **SSH key** | How you log in: the public half goes to the provider, the private half stays on your laptop ([basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics)) |

## Before you start 

- An account with the provider and a payment method.
- An SSH key on your laptop (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`), see [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).
- A domain whose DNS you can edit.

```flow
Launch | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS | #launch
Security group | 22, 80, 443 | #ports
Elastic IP | stable public address | #elastic-ip
Install | one command | #install
DNS | A record → Elastic IP | #dns
```

## 1. Launch the instance 
In **EC2 → Launch instance**:

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| AMI | **Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS** (or 26.04 LTS), from Canonical |
| Instance type | 2 GB RAM or more to be comfortable |
| Key pair | Your existing key, or create one and download it |
| Storage | 30 GB gp3 or more (releases, logs and local backups live here) |
| Network | A public subnet, **Auto-assign public IP** on |

## 2. Open the ports 
Create a security group with inbound rules:

| Port | Source | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22 (SSH) | Your IP, or anywhere if you'll rely on Cipi's fail2ban and keys | Administration |
| 80 (HTTP) | Anywhere (IPv4 and IPv6) | Let's Encrypt validation, redirects |
| 443 (HTTPS) | Anywhere (IPv4 and IPv6) | Your apps |

Cipi also runs its own firewall (UFW) on the instance; the two layers don't conflict.

## 3. Attach an Elastic IP 
**EC2 → Elastic IPs → Allocate**, then **Associate** it with the instance. The public IP of an instance changes on stop/start; your DNS shouldn't.

## 4. Install Cipi 
EC2 logs you in as `ubuntu` (a sudo user), not root:

```bash
$ ssh -i ~/Downloads/my-key.pem ubuntu@203.0.113.10
$ sudo -i
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

When the installer asks for your SSH public key, paste the **public** half of the key you'll use from now on (`cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` on your laptop). After the install you log in as `cipi`:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10
$ sudo cipi status
```

## 5. Point DNS and create the first app 
Create an `A` record (Route 53 or your DNS provider) for your domain to the Elastic IP, then follow [Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps) from step 4.

## AWS services that fit well

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Off-site backups | An S3 bucket as destination: `sudo cipi backup configure` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3)) |
| Outgoing mail | Amazon SES SMTP credentials in the app's `.env` |
| Code on AWS | CodeCommit works with Cipi's automatic deploy keys |
| Snapshots of the whole disk | EBS snapshots, on top of Cipi's database and file backups |

> [!tip] Outbound port 25 is restricted on EC2 by default. Use SES or another provider on port 587 for app mail and for Cipi's [notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/notifications).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Installer stops: container detected | You picked a container product (LXC/OpenVZ): choose a KVM virtual machine |
| Installer stops: unsupported OS | Use a plain Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 LTS image, not a marketplace app |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` after the install | Log in as `cipi`, not `root` or `ubuntu`, with the key you pasted in the installer |
| Certificate fails | Port 80 closed in the provider firewall, or DNS not pointing at the server yet |
| Site unreachable on 443 | Add 443 to the provider firewall (IPv4 and IPv6) |
| Notification e-mail never arrives | Port 25 is blocked by most providers: use an SMTP service on 587 |


## Install Cipi on Amazon Lightsail

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-lightsail

Lightsail is AWS with a fixed monthly price: a good fit for one to a handful of apps. Use the **OS-only** Ubuntu blueprint so Cipi can own the stack.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Instance / server** | The virtual machine you rent |
| **Image** | The operating system it starts with: pick plain Ubuntu LTS, nothing pre-installed |
| **Public IP** | The address visitors and DNS point to; make it static so it survives rebuilds |
| **Provider firewall** | Rules in the provider's console, before traffic reaches the server. Cipi adds its own (UFW) on the server |
| **SSH key** | How you log in: the public half goes to the provider, the private half stays on your laptop ([basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics)) |

## Before you start 

- An account with the provider and a payment method.
- An SSH key on your laptop (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`), see [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).
- A domain whose DNS you can edit.

## 1. Create the instance

**Lightsail → Create instance**:

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Platform | Linux/Unix |
| Blueprint | **OS Only → Ubuntu 24.04 LTS** (not LAMP or a Bitnami app) |
| SSH key | Your own key, or the default one Lightsail generates |
| Plan | 2 GB RAM is comfortable; 1 GB works for a small app |

## 2. Static IP and firewall

- **Networking → Create static IP** and attach it to the instance.
- In the instance's **Networking** tab, IPv4 firewall: keep SSH (22) and HTTP (80), **add HTTPS (443)**. Do the same for IPv6 if you use it.

## 3. Install Cipi

```bash
$ ssh ubuntu@203.0.113.10
$ sudo -i
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Paste your own public key when asked. From then on: `ssh cipi@203.0.113.10` and `sudo cipi …`.

## 4. DNS and first app

Point an `A` record at the static IP (Lightsail DNS zones work), then create and deploy the app as in [the main guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).

## Growing out of it

| When | Do |
| --- | --- |
| You need more RAM | Snapshot the instance and create a bigger one from it, or move apps with [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) |
| You need VPC, autoscaling groups, RDS in private subnets | Move to [EC2](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-aws-ec2) |

> [!note] Lightsail's own snapshots copy the whole disk. Keep Cipi's [S3 backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) too: they're per app, encrypted and restorable on any server.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Installer stops: container detected | You picked a container product (LXC/OpenVZ): choose a KVM virtual machine |
| Installer stops: unsupported OS | Use a plain Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 LTS image, not a marketplace app |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` after the install | Log in as `cipi`, not `root` or `ubuntu`, with the key you pasted in the installer |
| Certificate fails | Port 80 closed in the provider firewall, or DNS not pointing at the server yet |
| Site unreachable on 443 | Add 443 to the provider firewall (IPv4 and IPv6) |
| Notification e-mail never arrives | Port 25 is blocked by most providers: use an SMTP service on 587 |


## Install Cipi on a DigitalOcean Droplet

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-digitalocean

A Droplet is a full KVM virtual machine: exactly what Cipi needs.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Instance / server** | The virtual machine you rent |
| **Image** | The operating system it starts with: pick plain Ubuntu LTS, nothing pre-installed |
| **Public IP** | The address visitors and DNS point to; make it static so it survives rebuilds |
| **Provider firewall** | Rules in the provider's console, before traffic reaches the server. Cipi adds its own (UFW) on the server |
| **SSH key** | How you log in: the public half goes to the provider, the private half stays on your laptop ([basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics)) |

## Before you start 

- An account with the provider and a payment method.
- An SSH key on your laptop (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`), see [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).
- A domain whose DNS you can edit.

## 1. Create the Droplet

**Create → Droplets**:

| Setting | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| Image | **Ubuntu 24.04 (LTS) x64** or 26.04 |
| Size | Basic, 2 GB RAM is comfortable for a few apps |
| Authentication | **SSH key** (add yours) |
| Extras | Monitoring agent optional; Cipi has its own [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) |

## 2. Firewall and IP

- **Networking → Firewalls**: inbound TCP 22, 80, 443 from all IPv4 and IPv6; attach to the Droplet. Optional: Cipi's own firewall already protects the host.
- **Networking → Reserved IPs**: assign one if you may rebuild or resize the Droplet.

## 3. Install

```bash
$ ssh root@203.0.113.10
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

The installer disables root login and creates the `cipi` user with your key. Then:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@203.0.113.10
$ sudo cipi status
```

## 4. DNS and first app

Add an `A` record (DigitalOcean DNS or your registrar) to the Droplet's IP and continue with [Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).

## DigitalOcean extras that fit

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Off-site backups | **Spaces** is S3-compatible: use it as a `cipi backup` destination |
| Managed database | Point `DB_*` at a Managed MySQL/PostgreSQL cluster if you prefer |
| Behind a load balancer | Terminate TLS on the balancer or pass through to Cipi's certificates |

## Off-site backups on Spaces 

Create a Space in another region and a Spaces access key, then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup destination add spaces --bucket=acme-backups \
    --key=… --secret=… --endpoint=https://ams3.digitaloceanspaces.com --region=ams3
$ sudo cipi backup destination test
```

[Full backup guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Installer stops: container detected | You picked a container product (LXC/OpenVZ): choose a KVM virtual machine |
| Installer stops: unsupported OS | Use a plain Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 LTS image, not a marketplace app |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` after the install | Log in as `cipi`, not `root` or `ubuntu`, with the key you pasted in the installer |
| Certificate fails | Port 80 closed in the provider firewall, or DNS not pointing at the server yet |
| Site unreachable on 443 | Add 443 to the provider firewall (IPv4 and IPv6) |
| Notification e-mail never arrives | Port 25 is blocked by most providers: use an SMTP service on 587 |

## Push to deploy or CI pipeline? Agent vs pipeline deploys for Laravel

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/agent-vs-pipeline-deploys

Every Cipi deploy runs on your server and does the same thing: pull the branch from Git, build a new release, migrate, switch to it with zero downtime, check it. The only question is **who presses the button**: your Git provider, every time you push (agent mode), or your CI, when the tests pass (pipeline mode).

## In 30 seconds 

| | Push to deploy (agent) | CI pipeline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starts | On every push to the branch | When the pipeline's deploy job runs |
| Tests before going live | No | Yes |
| Setup | 2 minutes, mostly automatic | 10 to 30 minutes, once |
| Secret outside the server | None | An API token or an SSH key in CI |
| Best for | Side projects, staging, small teams, fast iteration | Production with real users, teams, regulated apps |

**Our verdict:** push to deploy for staging and personal projects; a pipeline for production once other people depend on the app. Many teams run both: webhook on staging, pipeline on production.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Deploy branch** | The Git branch an app follows, `main` by default. Only pushes to it deploy |
| **Webhook** | A URL your Git provider calls after every push. Cipi's is `https://your-app/cipi/webhook` |
| **Agent** | [`cipi/agent`](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-install), a Composer package that receives the webhook in a Laravel app |
| **Pipeline** | The steps your CI runs on each push: install, test, then deploy |
| **Deploy lock** | Cipi lets only one deploy per app run at a time |

## How push to deploy works 

```flow
git push | to main
> You push to the deploy branch.
Signed webhook | provider → your app
> GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea, Forgejo or Azure DevOps call `/cipi/webhook` on your app, signed with a secret only they and your server know.
Agent queues | answers in milliseconds
> The agent checks the signature and the branch, leaves a small trigger file for the server and answers immediately.
Server deploys | within a minute
> A cron job on the server picks up the trigger and runs the normal deploy as the app user.
```

What makes it good:

- **Nothing to configure.** With a Git provider token saved on the server, Cipi creates the webhook and its secret when it creates the app. You add `composer require cipi/agent` once.
- **No access for anyone.** No SSH key, no API token leaves the server. The provider only calls your app over HTTPS.
- **Fast feedback.** Push, and about a minute later it's live.

What it doesn't do: it deploys every push to the branch, **including a push with a failing test**. Cipi's [health check](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) can roll back a release that doesn't answer, but it can't know your tests failed.

## How a pipeline works 

```flow
git push | to main
> You push. The webhook is off for this app, so nothing deploys yet.
Tests | on CI machines
> Your CI installs the app and runs `php artisan test`. Red tests stop everything here.
Deploy | SSH or API
> The deploy job asks the server to deploy, over SSH or through the Cipi API, and waits for the result.
Check | health URL
> The job calls the app's health URL. If the new release doesn't answer, the job rolls back and turns red.
```

What makes it good:

- **A gate.** Only code that passes the tests reaches production.
- **More steps.** A backup before the release, an approval, a message to the team, a deploy to several servers in order.
- **Visible.** Every deploy is a green or red job in the tool your team already watches.

What it costs: a secret in CI, a workflow file to maintain, and slower releases (your tests run first).

## Side by side 

| | Push to deploy (agent) | CI pipeline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who starts the deploy | The Git provider | Your CI job |
| Time from push to live | About a minute | Test time + about a minute |
| Failing tests | Still deployed | Never deployed |
| Bad release that crashes | Rolled back by Cipi if [automatic rollback](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks#auto-rollback) is on | Rolled back by the pipeline's health check, or by Cipi |
| Secret outside the server | None | API token (`deploy-manage` only) or SSH key |
| Network | Provider → your app over HTTPS | CI → server over SSH (port 22) or the API |
| Works with | GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea, Forgejo, Azure DevOps | Any CI: GitHub Actions, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure, Jenkins, CircleCI, AWS CodeDeploy… |
| App requirement | `cipi/agent` (Laravel); built in for Node apps | None |
| Approvals before production | No | Yes, with your CI's environments |
| Several servers | One webhook per app on each server | One pipeline deploys them in order |
| Where you see the result | [Deploy notifications](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-notifications), panel, `cipi deploy --status` | The CI job, plus the same notifications |
| Audit ledger origin | `webhook`, with pusher and commit | `cipi-cli` (SSH) or `panel` (API), with the operator |

## When to choose push to deploy 

- A personal project, a prototype, an internal tool.
- A **staging** app where fast feedback matters more than a gate.
- A team that deploys many times a day and has good tests running elsewhere (pull request checks), so `main` is always green.
- You don't want any server secret stored in a third-party CI.

Set it up: [Auto-deploy on push](https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy).

## When to choose a pipeline 

- Production with paying users.
- More than one person pushes to the deploy branch.
- You need a backup, an approval or a compliance trail before every release.
- Your company already standardised on a CI: [GitHub Actions, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure, Forgejo, CircleCI](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines), [Jenkins](https://cipi.sh/docs/jenkins) or [AWS CodeDeploy](https://cipi.sh/docs/aws-codedeploy).

Set it up: [CI/CD for Laravel](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow).

## The hybrid most teams end up with 

Two Cipi apps from the same repository, one per environment, each with its own branch and its own mode.

| App | Branch | Mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `shop-staging` | `develop` | Push to deploy: every push is live on staging a minute later |
| `shop` | `main` | Pipeline: merge `develop` into `main`, tests run, then deploy |

```bash
# staging follows develop and keeps its webhook
$ cipi app create --user=shop-staging --domain=staging.shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=develop --env=staging
# production follows main; turn its webhook off and deploy from CI
$ cipi app edit shop --branch=main
```

Each app can read its own [`cipi-staging.yml`](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml) or `cipi.yml`, so workers, crons and limits can differ.

## Switching from one mode to the other 

### From push to deploy to a pipeline 

```flow
Add the pipeline | workflow file + secrets
> Add the workflow for your CI and its secrets. Don't push yet.
Turn the webhook off | in the Git provider
> GitHub: Settings → Webhooks → the `/cipi/webhook` hook → untick Active. Other providers: see the docs.
Push | first pipeline deploy
> Push a small change. Only the pipeline deploys now.
Verify | audit origin
> `cipi deploy shop --audit`: the newest entry should not say `webhook`.
```

Keep the agent installed: its health endpoint and MCP server are still useful.

### From a pipeline back to push to deploy 

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent          # if the app doesn't have it yet; commit and push
$ sudo cipi deploy shop                # once, so the /cipi/webhook route exists
$ sudo cipi app webhook recreate shop  # re-create the webhook in the Git provider
```

Then remove the deploy job from your pipeline (keep the tests: they still protect pull requests).

## Mistakes to avoid 

| Mistake | What happens | Instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Webhook and pipeline both on | Two deploys per push; the second hits the lock and fails | One mode per app |
| Rolling back whenever the deploy command fails | A failed build publishes nothing; the rollback takes you to older code | Roll back only when the new release is live and unhealthy ([why](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#deploy-step)) |
| Giving CI a personal SSH key | Leaks your access with the CI | A dedicated key, or an API token with `deploy-manage` |
| Calling the agent webhook from CI and expecting a result | CI turns green before the deploy even starts | Use SSH or the API when CI must wait |
| No health URL | A release that returns 500 counts as deployed | Set `cipi health set shop --url=https://shop.example.com/up` |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Push doesn't deploy (agent mode) | Wrong branch, or no webhook: `cipi git status`, then `cipi app webhook recreate shop` |
| 404 on `/cipi/webhook` | The agent isn't deployed yet: `sudo cipi deploy shop` once after adding it |
| Two deploys per push | Turn the webhook off for the app that uses a pipeline |
| *A deploy of 'shop' is running* in CI | Limit your CI to one deploy at a time and keep one trigger per app; a stale lock is removed by the next deploy (Cipi 5.13.0+) |
| Pipeline green, site broken | Add the health check step from the [recipes](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines#recipes) |


## A Laravel API with a Next.js or Nuxt front end on one server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-api-nextjs-nuxt

Two apps, one server: `api.acme.app` (Laravel) and `acme.app` (Next.js or Nuxt in SSR mode). Both deploy from Git with zero downtime; the Node app restarts blue/green.

```stack
acme.app | Node app, SSR, blue/green restarts
api.acme.app | Laravel app, FPM or Octane
Server | one Cipi install
```

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **API** | The Laravel app answers JSON, no HTML |
| **SSR** | Server-side rendering: Next.js or Nuxt runs as a Node process that builds HTML per request |
| **Sanctum** | Laravel's auth for SPAs (cookies) and mobile apps (tokens) |
| **CORS** | Browser rules for calling an API on another domain |

## 1. The API

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=api --domain=api.acme.app \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/api.git --php=8.6
$ sudo cipi deploy api && sudo cipi ssl install api
```

For cookie-based auth from the front end, configure Sanctum: `SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS=acme.app`, `SESSION_DOMAIN=.acme.app`, and CORS for `https://acme.app`:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env api --set=SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS=acme.app
$ sudo cipi app env api --set=SESSION_DOMAIN=.acme.app
```

## 2. The front end

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=web --domain=acme.app \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/web.git --node=ssr --framework=next --node-version=24
$ sudo cipi deploy web && sudo cipi ssl install web
```

Use `--framework=nuxt` for Nuxt. Each deploy installs from your lockfile, builds, starts the new process, checks the health path and only then switches traffic.

| Mode | For |
| --- | --- |
| `ssr` | Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix, Astro SSR |
| `static` | Pre-rendered sites (Astro, `nuxt generate`) |
| `spa` | Vite single-page apps |

## 3. Point the front end at the API

Build-time variables go in the Node app's `shared/.env`, read at build:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env web --set=NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.acme.app
$ sudo cipi deploy web
```

## 4. Keep both in their repositories

Each repository can carry its own `cipi.yml`: workers, schedule and health for the API, `node:` settings for the front end. Examples in [cipi.yml recipes](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-recipes).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| CORS error in the browser | Add the front end's origin in `config/cors.php`, `supports_credentials` true for cookies |
| 419 CSRF on login | Call `/sanctum/csrf-cookie` first; check `SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS` and `SESSION_DOMAIN` |
| 401 after login | Cookie on the wrong domain: `SESSION_DOMAIN=.acme.app` |
| Front end calls the old API URL | `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is baked at build: redeploy the front end |


## Deploy Laravel with AWS CodeDeploy and Cipi

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-aws-codedeploy

AWS CodeDeploy is good at deciding **when** and **where** a release goes: after an approval, to one server at a time, stopping if one fails. Cipi is good at **how**: pulling the app from Git, building a release, migrating and switching with zero downtime. This guide plugs them together, so CodeDeploy orchestrates and Cipi deploys.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **CodeDeploy agent** | A small program on the server that asks AWS "anything to deploy?" and runs your scripts |
| **Application / deployment group** | CodeDeploy's names for "what" (`shop`) and "where" (the servers tagged `app=shop`) |
| **Revision / bundle** | The files CodeDeploy sends: here only `appspec.yml` and two scripts |
| **Hook** | A moment of the deployment where CodeDeploy runs one of your scripts (`ApplicationStart`, `ValidateService`…) |
| **On-premises instance** | Any server outside EC2 (Hetzner, OVHcloud, your own hardware) registered with CodeDeploy |

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app already running on a Cipi server ([15-minute guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps)).
- An AWS account, the AWS CLI on your laptop, and an S3 bucket for the bundles (or a GitHub connection in CodeDeploy).
- A health URL, such as Laravel's `/up`.

```flow
Agent | on the Cipi server
> Install the CodeDeploy agent on the server. It only makes outgoing HTTPS calls.
Permissions | instance profile or registration
> Let the server talk to CodeDeploy: an IAM instance profile on EC2, or an on-premises registration elsewhere.
Application | deployment group, rollback off
> Create the CodeDeploy application and the group of servers. Turn CodeDeploy's own rollback off.
Bundle | appspec.yml + two scripts
> Add a `codedeploy/` folder to the repository: one script deploys with Cipi, one checks the app.
First release | from your laptop
> Push a bundle and create a deployment from the AWS CLI.
CI | GitHub Actions after the tests
> Let CI create the deployment when the tests pass, without long-lived AWS keys.
```

## 1. Install the CodeDeploy agent on the Cipi server

Log in to the server and install the agent 2.x for your Region (here `eu-central-1`):

```bash
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y wget
$ cd /tmp
$ wget https://aws-codedeploy-eu-central-1.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/latestv2/install
$ chmod +x ./install && sudo ./install auto
$ systemctl status codedeploy-agent
```

You should read *The AWS CodeDeploy agent is running*. The bucket name changes with the Region: AWS lists them in its [install guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/codedeploy-agent-operations-install-ubuntu.html). Nothing to change in Cipi's firewall: the agent only talks out, over HTTPS.

## 2. Let the server talk to CodeDeploy

| Server | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| **EC2** | Attach an IAM instance profile that can read the bundles from your S3 bucket (AWS provides a managed policy for CodeDeploy EC2 instances). Tag the instance `app=shop` |
| **Outside AWS** | Register it as an on-premises instance with an IAM role session (recommended) or an IAM user, following [Working with on-premises instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/instances-on-premises.html), and tag it `app=shop` |

On-premises updates are billed per instance update; deployments to EC2 have no CodeDeploy charge. Check the [current pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/pricing/).

## 3. Create the application and the deployment group

In the CodeDeploy console:

1. **Applications → Create application**: name `shop`, compute platform **EC2/On-premises**.
2. **Create deployment group**: name `production`, service role with the CodeDeploy permissions, environment = the instances tagged `app=shop`.
3. **Deployment settings**: `CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce` for one server, `CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime` for several.
4. **Load balancer**: off. Cipi already switches without downtime on each server.
5. **Rollbacks**: **untick** "Roll back when a deployment fails".

> [!warning] Step 5 matters. CodeDeploy rolls back by deploying the previous bundle again. With Cipi that would run `cipi deploy` again, which always takes the newest commit of the branch: you'd get the broken code a second time. The validate script in the next step rolls back with Cipi instead.

## 4. Add the bundle to the repository

```tree
shop/
└── codedeploy/
    ├── appspec.yml
    └── scripts/
        ├── deploy.sh
        └── validate.sh
```

```yaml
# codedeploy/appspec.yml
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /
    destination: /opt/codedeploy-cipi/shop
hooks:
  ApplicationStart:
    - location: scripts/deploy.sh
      timeout: 1800
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/validate.sh
      timeout: 300
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# codedeploy/scripts/deploy.sh: run by CodeDeploy as root
set -euo pipefail
/usr/local/bin/cipi deploy shop
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# codedeploy/scripts/validate.sh: is the new release answering?
set -uo pipefail
APP=shop
HEALTH_URL=https://shop.example.com/up

if ! curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null; then
  echo "Unhealthy: rolling back with Cipi"
  /usr/local/bin/cipi deploy "$APP" --rollback
  exit 1
fi

if [ -n "${BUNDLE_COMMIT:-}" ]; then     # set by CodeDeploy for GitHub revisions
  live=$(sudo -u "$APP" git -C "/home/$APP/current" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || true)
  [ "$live" = "$BUNDLE_COMMIT" ] || echo "Note: live commit $live, requested $BUNDLE_COMMIT"
fi
echo "Healthy"
```

```bash
$ chmod +x codedeploy/scripts/*.sh
$ git add codedeploy && git commit -m "CodeDeploy bundle for Cipi" && git push
```

What happens at each hook:

| Hook | Script | If it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ApplicationStart` | `cipi deploy shop`: pull, build, migrate, switch | Nothing was published; the deployment stops here, and the old release keeps serving |
| `ValidateService` | Health check; Cipi rollback if the app doesn't answer | The release is rolled back and the deployment is marked failed, so CodeDeploy doesn't touch the next server |

If the app also deploys on push, turn its webhook off now (GitHub: **Settings → Webhooks** → the `/cipi/webhook` hook → untick **Active**), otherwise every push would deploy before CodeDeploy does.

## 5. Run the first deployment from your laptop

```bash
$ aws deploy push --application-name shop \
    --s3-location s3://my-deploy-bundles/shop/first.zip --source codedeploy
$ aws deploy create-deployment --application-name shop --deployment-group-name production \
    --s3-location bucket=my-deploy-bundles,key=shop/first.zip,bundleType=zip
{ "deploymentId": "d-ABC123XYZ" }
$ aws deploy wait deployment-successful --deployment-id d-ABC123XYZ
```

Follow it in the CodeDeploy console (each hook shows its log) and on the server:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --status
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --audit
```

## 6. Deploy from GitHub Actions after the tests

Use GitHub's OpenID Connect so no long-lived AWS key sits in GitHub. Create an IAM role that GitHub can assume, allowed to upload to the bucket and to create and read CodeDeploy deployments for `shop`. Then:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Test and release with CodeDeploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
concurrency:
  group: codedeploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with:
          php-version: "8.4"     # the version your app uses
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
      - run: php artisan test

  release:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/github-codedeploy-shop
          aws-region: eu-central-1
      - name: Push the bundle and deploy
        run: |
          key="shop/${GITHUB_SHA}.zip"
          aws deploy push --application-name shop --s3-location "s3://my-deploy-bundles/$key" --source codedeploy
          id=$(aws deploy create-deployment --application-name shop --deployment-group-name production \
                 --s3-location bucket=my-deploy-bundles,key=$key,bundleType=zip \
                 --query deploymentId --output text)
          echo "Deployment $id"
          aws deploy wait deployment-successful --deployment-id "$id"
```

The job turns red if the deploy or the health check fails, and the CodeDeploy console shows which hook stopped it.

## 7. Roll out to several servers

Tag every Cipi server that runs `shop` with `app=shop` and set the deployment group to `CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime`. CodeDeploy then deploys the first server, waits for `ValidateService` to pass, and only then moves to the next. If one server fails its health check, Cipi rolls that server back and CodeDeploy stops before touching the others.

Each server must already have the app created with Cipi (same name, same branch). [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/docs/sync) can copy an app from one server to another.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deployment stays "Pending" | Agent not running, or no outgoing HTTPS | `systemctl status codedeploy-agent`; `sudo systemctl start codedeploy-agent` |
| "No instances found" | Tag mismatch | Same tag on the instance and in the deployment group |
| `ScriptFailed` at ApplicationStart | `cipi deploy` failed while building | `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=deploy`; nothing was published |
| `ScriptFailed` at ValidateService | The app didn't answer; Cipi rolled back | `sudo cipi deploy shop --log` for the failed release |
| "appspec.yml not found" | Bundle root is wrong | `--source codedeploy` with S3; `appspec.yml` at the repository root for GitHub revisions |
| Broken code deployed twice | CodeDeploy rollback is on | Turn it off in the deployment group |
| Permission denied on a script | Not executable in Git | `chmod +x codedeploy/scripts/*.sh`, commit, push |
| Deploy ran twice | The Cipi webhook is still on | Untick **Active** on the `/cipi/webhook` hook |


## CI/CD for Laravel with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow

Push-to-deploy is great until a broken test reaches production. A pipeline adds the gate: test, optionally back up, deploy, check that the app answers, and roll back only if it doesn't. For every other CI (Bitbucket, Azure, Forgejo, CircleCI, Jenkins, AWS CodeDeploy) see [CI/CD pipelines](https://cipi.sh/docs/ci-pipelines).

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **CI** | Continuous integration: tests run on every push |
| **CD** | Continuous delivery: a passing build deploys by itself |
| **Pipeline / workflow** | The list of steps GitHub Actions or GitLab CI runs |
| **Secret** | A value stored in the CI settings (a key, a token), never in the repository |

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app deployed with Cipi, with tests (`php artisan test`).
- Admin access to the repository settings to add secrets.

```flow
Push | to main
> You push to `main`. The webhook is off, so only the pipeline can deploy.
Test | php artisan test
> The pipeline runs `php artisan test`. Red tests stop it here.
Backup | optional
> Optional: take a backup on the server first.
Deploy | ssh → cipi deploy
> The pipeline connects with the CI key and runs `sudo cipi deploy shop`.
Check | health URL
> If the deploy succeeded, the pipeline calls `/up`. A deploy that failed while building published nothing, so there is nothing to undo: the job just turns red.
Roll back | only if unhealthy
> If the new release is live but doesn't answer, the pipeline runs `--rollback` and fails visibly.
```

## 1. A dedicated key for CI

```bash
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ci-deploy" -f ~/.ssh/ci_deploy -N ""
$ cat ~/.ssh/ci_deploy.pub     # on the server: sudo cipi ssh add ""
$ cat ~/.ssh/ci_deploy         # → CI secret SERVER_SSH_KEY
```

Save `SERVER_SSH_KEY` and `SERVER_HOST` as repository secrets. Never reuse a personal key or the app's deploy key.

## 2. Turn the webhook off

So only the pipeline deploys. Remove the webhook from the repository settings, or recreate the app's webhook only when you need it again with `sudo cipi app webhook recreate shop`.

## 3. GitHub Actions

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: "8.6" }
      - run: composer install --no-interaction && cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
      - run: php artisan test
  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: cipi
          key: ${{ secrets.SERVER_SSH_KEY }}
          script: "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

## 4. GitLab CI

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [test, deploy]
test:
  stage: test
  image: php:8.6-cli
  script: [composer install, php artisan test]
deploy:
  stage: deploy
  only: [main]
  before_script:
    - eval $(ssh-agent -s) && echo "$SERVER_SSH_KEY" | tr -d '\r' | ssh-add -
    - mkdir -p ~/.ssh && ssh-keyscan -H $SERVER_HOST >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts
  script:
    - ssh cipi@$SERVER_HOST "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

## 5. Add a safety net

| Add | How |
| --- | --- |
| Database snapshot before migrations | `sudo cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot` (every deploy) |
| Off-site backup step | `sudo cipi backup run --profile=shop-nightly` in a job before deploy |
| Validate `cipi.yml` | `php artisan cipi:yml validate --json` in the test job ([agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml)) |
| Automatic rollback when the app is down | A [health check](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) with `rollback_on_unhealthy: true` |
| Alerts | `sudo cipi notification add slack …` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts)) |

## Without SSH

Prefer HTTPS to SSH from CI? Use [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) with an API token that only has `deploy-manage`:

```bash
$ cipi-cli prod deploy shop
```

Next: a live URL for every branch with [preview environments](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` in CI | The CI public key isn't on the server: `sudo cipi ssh add "…"` |
| `Host key verification failed` | Add the server's host key to `known_hosts` in the workflow (`ssh-keyscan`) |
| Deploys twice per push | The webhook is still on: remove it from the repository |
| CI passes, site broken | Add a [health check](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) with `--rollback-on-unhealthy` |


## The self-hosted Laravel developer stack (2026)

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-developer-stack-2026

Every SaaS in a Laravel team's toolchain is reasonable on its own. Together they add up to a bill per developer, per server and per project, plus a pile of places where your data lives. Here's what's worth owning.

## What to own, what to buy

| Job | Self-hosted option | Bought option | Own it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Server management and deploys | [Cipi](https://cipi.sh/) (free) | Forge, Ploi | Almost always: it's the part you run every day |
| Backups | `cipi backup` to any S3-compatible bucket | Panel add-ons | Always: you need them anyway |
| Search | Meilisearch on the server | Algolia | Index fits in RAM |
| Object storage | [Johnny](https://johnny.web.ap.it/), MinIO | S3, R2 | You have a second VPS |
| Error tracking and uptime | [Boogle](https://boogle.web.ap.it/) | Sentry, Flare, Better Stack | Error payloads contain personal data |
| Analytics | [IndieStats](https://indiestats.web.ap.it/) | Google Analytics, Plausible | You don't want consent banners |
| Transactional e-mail | — | Postmark, SES, Mailgun | Buy: deliverability is a full-time job |
| CI | — | GitHub Actions, GitLab CI | Buy: free tiers are generous |

## The cost math

The pattern that matters is **per-server pricing**. A server panel charged per server per month costs more every time you add a staging or client server, while the servers themselves keep getting cheaper. Self-hosting the panel turns that line into zero; the VPS bill stays the same either way.

What you pay instead is attention: updates, backups and security. That's why the self-hosted tool has to do those by itself: nightly PHP and nginx patches, verified backups, alerts. If it doesn't, the saving is an illusion.

## When SaaS still wins

| Situation | Why |
| --- | --- |
| No one on the team is comfortable on a server | A managed platform hides it |
| Autoscaling to zero matters more than cost | Serverless platforms do it better |
| Compliance requires a vendor's certifications | Buying them is cheaper than earning them |

## A sensible default

Own the server, the deploys, the backups and the data. Buy e-mail delivery and CI. Add self-hosted error tracking and analytics once you have a second server for them. Start with [Deploy Laravel on an Ubuntu VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps).


## The Laravel ecosystem in 2026, mapped to production

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ecosystem-2026

Laravel is a framework plus a family of first-party and community tools. Choosing them is easy; running them in production is where projects stall. This map groups them by job and says what each needs from the server.

## Runtime

| Tool | Job | Needs on the server | On Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PHP-FPM | Classic request handling | A pool per app | Default |
| [Octane](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-octane-frankenphp) (FrankenPHP) | App kept in memory, much faster responses | A long-running process, a proxy | `--octane` |
| [Horizon](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues) | Queues with a dashboard | Redis, a supervised process | `cipi worker horizon enable` |
| Queue workers | Background jobs | Supervisor | One per app by default |
| Scheduler | Cron-like tasks | One cron line | Built in |
| [Reverb](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-reverb-websockets) | WebSockets | A process, a WebSocket proxy, open-file limits | `cipi app reverb enable` |

## Data and search

| Tool | Job | On Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MariaDB / MySQL | Default relational store | Default |
| [PostgreSQL](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-postgresql) | JSONB, extensions, analytics | `cipi db install pgsql` |
| Valkey (Redis) | Cache, sessions, queues for Horizon | Included |
| [Scout + Meilisearch](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scout-meilisearch) | Full-text search | `cipi search install` |

## UI

| Tool | Good for |
| --- | --- |
| Blade + Livewire | Full-stack reactive apps in PHP |
| Filament | Admin panels and back offices |
| Inertia (Vue, React, Svelte) | SPA feel with Laravel routing |
| Vite | Asset builds, run on deploy with `node_build` |

## Quality and observability

| Tool | Job |
| --- | --- |
| Pest / PHPUnit | Tests; run them in [CI before deploying](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow) |
| Larastan, Pint, Rector | Static analysis, style, upgrades |
| Pulse | Performance overview inside the app |
| Telescope | Local and staging debugging (off in production) |
| Health checks | `/up` and the [agent's `/cipi/health`](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring) |

## Hosting choices

You can rent all of this as a managed platform, rent a dashboard to manage your own VPS, or run it yourself for free. That trade-off is the subject of [our comparisons](https://cipi.sh/alternatives); the [developer stack guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-developer-stack-2026) does the cost math.
