## Laravel .env and secrets in production, done right

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-env-secrets

Every Laravel app reads its settings and secrets (database password, Stripe key, mail credentials) from a file called `.env`. Getting it right is mostly about **where it lives, who can read it and how you change it** without breaking a running app.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **`.env`** | A text file of `KEY=value` lines, read when Laravel boots |
| **Secret** | A value that grants access: passwords, API keys, tokens |
| **`config:cache`** | Laravel's compiled config: after it, `.env` isn't read again until the cache is rebuilt |
| **Rotation** | Replacing a secret with a new one and retiring the old |
| **Shared folder** | `/home//shared`: files that stay the same across releases |

```tree
/home/shop/
  shared/
    .env            ← the only copy, survives deploys
    storage/
  releases/
    20261122_101500/
      .env -> ../../shared/.env
  current -> releases/20261122_101500
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app on Cipi. Cipi wrote its `.env` at creation with the database, Valkey, app key and webhook values.

## 1. Read and change values 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --show            # secrets visible: careful when screen sharing
$ sudo cipi app env shop --get=APP_URL
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=STRIPE_SECRET=sk_live_…
$ sudo cipi app env shop --unset=OLD_KEY
$ sudo cipi app env shop                   # open in nano, as the app user
```

Every deploy caches Laravel's config, and a cached config doesn't read `.env` again. So after any change:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache     # web requests see the new value
$ sudo cipi worker restart shop               # workers, Horizon and Octane too
```

Or simply deploy: the deploy rebuilds the cache and restarts workers.

The same edit is available in the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/web-panel) (secrets masked, changes tracked), through the REST API (`PUT /api/apps/shop/env`) and through MCP.

In the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/web-panel), secrets are masked and every change is tracked:

## 2. Keep secrets out of Git 

```text
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
```

```text
# .env.example: the names, never the values
STRIPE_KEY=
STRIPE_SECRET=
MAIL_MAILER=smtp
```

If a secret was ever committed, **rotate it**: removing it from history doesn't un-leak it.

## 3. Rotate the database password 

```bash
$ sudo cipi db password shop
```

Cipi changes the password in the database and in `.env` together. Rebuild the config cache right after (`sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache`) so the app picks it up. Never change it by hand in one place only.

## 4. Rotate third-party keys 

```flow
Create new key | at the provider
> At the provider (Stripe, AWS, Mailgun…) create a second key. Most providers allow two valid keys at once.
Set it | cipi app env --set
> Save it on the server: `sudo cipi app env shop --set=STRIPE_SECRET=…`, then `sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache`.
Restart workers | if jobs use it
> If queued jobs use the key, `sudo cipi worker restart shop` so they reload it.
Check | logs, a test payment
> Check the logs and try the feature (a test payment, an e-mail) with the new key.
Revoke old key | at the provider
> Only then delete the old key at the provider. If something was missed, it fails now, while you're watching.
```

Most providers (Stripe, Mailgun, AWS) let two keys be valid at once, so there's no gap.

## 5. APP_KEY 

`APP_KEY` encrypts cookies, sessions and anything you store with `Crypt::`. Cipi generates it once. Rotating it:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=base64:OLDKEY…
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop key:generate --force
```

With `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS`, Laravel can still decrypt values made with the old key. Users are logged out once.

## 6. Different values per environment 

Staging and production are separate apps with separate `.env` files: a staging key can never reach production. `APP_ENV`/`CIPI_ENV` are set by `--env=staging` at creation ([staging guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production)).

## Keep secrets from leaking 

| Leak | Prevention |
| --- | --- |
| Error pages | `APP_DEBUG=false` in production, always |
| Logs | Don't log request bodies or headers with tokens |
| Screenshots, screen sharing | Use `--get` for one value instead of `--show` |
| AI assistants | Give them [anonymized data](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps); MCP tokens without `apps-env` can't read `.env` |
| Backups | [Encrypt them](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3); the server's own config is [encrypted at rest](https://cipi.sh/docs/vault) |
| `phpinfo()` routes | Remove them: they print the environment |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Change ignored | Cached config: `cipi app artisan shop config:cache`, then `cipi worker restart shop` |
| `env()` returns `null` in code | `env()` only works inside `config/` files once config is cached: read via `config('services.stripe.secret')` |
| `The MAC is invalid` | `APP_KEY` changed without `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` |
| `Access denied for user` | Password changed by hand: run `sudo cipi db password shop` |
| Value with spaces breaks | Quote it: `--set='MAIL_FROM_NAME="Acme Shop"'` |


## Laravel queues and Horizon in production

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues

A **queue** lets your app answer the visitor immediately and do slow work (e-mails, PDFs, imports, webhooks) a moment later, in the background. A **worker** is a long-running process that takes jobs from the queue and runs them. This guide sets both up for production, then switches to **Horizon** when you want a dashboard.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Job** | A class with a `handle()` method, dispatched with `SendInvoice::dispatch($order)` |
| **Queue** | A named line of jobs: `default`, `emails`, `exports` |
| **Connection** | Where jobs are stored: `database` (Cipi's default) or `redis` (Valkey) |
| **Worker** | `php artisan queue:work`, running forever, processing jobs |
| **Supervisor** | The Linux service that keeps workers running and restarts them if they crash |
| **Horizon** | Laravel's worker manager for Redis queues, with a dashboard |

```flow
Request | dispatch job, reply fast
> The controller calls `SendInvoice::dispatch($order)` and answers the visitor straight away.
Queue | database or Valkey
> The job is stored in the queue: the database by default, or Valkey with Horizon.
Worker | Supervisor keeps it alive
> A worker kept alive by Supervisor takes the next job.
Job runs | retries on failure
> The job runs. If it throws, it's retried according to `$tries` and `$backoff`.
failed_jobs | after the last try
> After the last failed attempt it lands in `failed_jobs`, where you can inspect and retry it.
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app deployed with Cipi: it already has **one worker on `default`**.
- Jobs implement `ShouldQueue`. Without it they run inline, in the request.

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker list shop
```

## 1. Add and scale queues 

Put slow or bursty work on its own queue, so a big export never delays password-reset e-mails:

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=3
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=exports --processes=1 --timeout=7200
$ sudo cipi worker edit shop --queue=default --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker list shop
```

| Flag | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--queue` | Queue to consume | `default` |
| `--processes` | Parallel processes | 1 |
| `--tries` | Attempts before a job goes to `failed_jobs` | 3 |
| `--timeout` | Seconds a worker process lives before it's recycled (`--max-time`), and how long a stop waits for the running job | 3600 |

Plain workers consume the **`database`** connection. To move queues to Valkey, use Horizon (step 4).

```php
SendInvoice::dispatch($order)->onQueue('emails');
ExportOrders::dispatch($user)->onQueue('exports');
```

## 2. Timeouts and retries, the part people get wrong 

```stack
$timeout on the job | the job is killed after N seconds (Laravel's default: 60)
retry_after | the queue hands the job to another worker after N seconds
--timeout of the worker | how long the process lives, and how long a stop waits for it
$tries / $backoff | per job: how many attempts, how long between
```

| Rule | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Long jobs declare their own limit | `public $timeout = 7000;` on `ExportOrders` |
| The worker waits at least that long | `cipi worker add shop --queue=exports --timeout=7200` |
| `retry_after` > the longest job | `'retry_after' => 7260` for that connection |
| Jobs that call APIs get a backoff | `public $backoff = [10, 60, 300];` |
| Limit attempts | `public $tries = 5;` or `retryUntil()` |
| Make jobs safe to run twice | Check state first: "already sent?" |

`retry_after` is set per connection in `config/queue.php`. If it's shorter than a job's runtime, the job runs twice.

## 3. Failed jobs 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop queue:failed
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop queue:retry all
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop queue:retry 5f1c…           # one job
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop queue:prune-failed --hours=168
```

Add a `failed()` method to the job to notify yourself, or alert on the count from the scheduler.

## 4. Switch to Horizon 

Horizon needs the queues on Redis. Each app has its own [Valkey](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-valkey-cache-sessions) ready.

```bash
# on your laptop
$ composer require laravel/horizon
$ php artisan horizon:install
$ git commit -am "Add Horizon" && git push
# on the server
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop
$ sudo cipi worker horizon status shop
```

Horizon replaces the app's `queue:work` workers: one or the other. Define supervisors in `config/horizon.php`:

```php
'environments' => [
    'production' => [
        'fast' => ['connection' => 'redis', 'queue' => ['default', 'emails'],
                   'balance' => 'auto', 'minProcesses' => 1, 'maxProcesses' => 6, 'tries' => 3],
        'slow' => ['connection' => 'redis', 'queue' => ['exports'],
                   'maxProcesses' => 1, 'timeout' => 7200, 'tries' => 1],
    ],
],
```

| The deploy finds | It does |
| --- | --- |
| Horizon, queues on Redis, no worker | Enables Horizon |
| Horizon plus existing workers | Explains how to switch; changes nothing |
| Horizon, queues not on Redis | Tells you which variable to set |

## 5. Protect the dashboard 

`/horizon` is closed in production until you open it:

```php
// app/Providers/HorizonServiceProvider.php
protected function gate(): void
{
    Gate::define('viewHorizon', fn ($user) => in_array($user->email, [
        'you@example.com',
    ]));
}
```

For extra safety, [basic auth](https://cipi.sh/docs/basic-auth) or [Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) in front of the app.

## 6. Deploys don't break jobs 

```flow
Build & migrate | workers keep running
> While the new release is built and migrated, workers keep processing jobs on the live code. The deploy never waits for a long job.
Swap release | atomic
> The new release goes live in one atomic switch.
Restart workers | after the job in hand
> Each worker (and Horizon) gets SIGTERM, finishes the job it is running and exits; Supervisor starts it again on the new code.
```

A job that was running when the deploy started finishes on the old code, after the migrations have run: keep migrations backward compatible for one release (add a column, deploy, use it in the next release). Jobs dispatched by the old code must still work with the new code, so don't rename a job class or change its constructor in the same deploy that removes the old one. Before Cipi 5.13.0 workers were stopped before the swap, and a long job could make the deploy fail after 300 seconds ([#536](https://github.com/cipi-sh/cipi/issues/536)).

## 7. Get alerted 

| Signal | How |
| --- | --- |
| Worker crashed repeatedly | Supervisor restarts it; [Cipi alerts](https://cipi.sh/guides/notifications-alerts) cover server events |
| Long waits | Horizon's `waits` config sends a notification when a queue waits too long |
| Failed jobs | `failed()` on the job, or a scheduled count check |
| Nothing processing at all | `sudo cipi pending` lists apps with Horizon installed but no worker |

## 8. In cipi.yml 

```yaml
workers:
  horizon: false
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: emails, processes: 3, tries: 5, timeout: 300 }
    - { queue: exports, processes: 1, timeout: 7200 }
```

Or `horizon: true` to hand everything to Horizon. [More on cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Jobs never run | No worker on that queue (`cipi worker list shop`), job not `ShouldQueue`, or `QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis` with plain workers: they read `database`, so enable Horizon or set it back |
| Job runs twice | `retry_after` shorter than the job's runtime |
| `MaxAttemptsExceededException` / job killed at 60 s | Set `$timeout` on the job and raise `retry_after` |
| Code change ignored by jobs | Workers not restarted: `sudo cipi worker restart shop` |
| Horizon shows "Inactive" | Not enabled: `cipi worker horizon enable shop`; or `QUEUE_CONNECTION` isn't `redis` |
| `/horizon` returns 403 | The `viewHorizon` gate doesn't include your user |
| Memory grows over time | A job leaks: `--max-jobs` / `maxJobs` in Horizon restarts processes regularly |


## Deploy Laravel from Jenkins to your own server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-jenkins-deploy

Your company already runs Jenkins, and you want Laravel releases to follow the same path as everything else: tests in Jenkins, then a zero-downtime deploy on your own server. With Cipi on the server, the Jenkins side is one short stage: Cipi does the deploy, Jenkins gives the order and reads the result.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Jenkinsfile** | A file in your repository that describes the pipeline: stages, steps, conditions |
| **Multibranch Pipeline** | A Jenkins job that finds every branch with a Jenkinsfile and builds it |
| **Credential** | A secret stored in Jenkins (a key, a token, a file), used by ID in the Jenkinsfile |
| **Health URL** | A page that answers 200 when the app works, like Laravel's `/up` |

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app already deployed with Cipi (follow the [15-minute guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps) first).
- Jenkins 2.x with the suggested plugins, plus **SSH Agent** (for the SSH way).
- A Jenkins agent with `ssh` and `curl`, and Docker or PHP + Composer for the tests.
- A health URL: Laravel 11+ serves `/up` when `health: '/up'` is set in `bootstrap/app.php`.

```flow
Choose | SSH or API
> Decide how Jenkins reaches the server. SSH is quicker to set up; the API gives Jenkins less power.
Secrets | on the server and in Jenkins
> Create a key or a token on the server side and store it as a Jenkins credential.
Job | Multibranch Pipeline
> Create the job that finds your Jenkinsfile.
Jenkinsfile | test → deploy → check
> Add the file to the repository.
Triggers | Git → Jenkins
> Make every push start the job; turn Cipi's own webhook off.
First deploy | push and verify
> Push a small change and check the result on both sides.
```

## 1. Choose SSH or the API

| | SSH | API |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jenkins runs | `ssh cipi@server "sudo cipi deploy shop"` | `cipi-cli prod deploy shop` |
| The secret can | Run any `cipi` command as root | Only deploy, roll back, unlock, read status |
| Server needs | Port 22 reachable from Jenkins | [`cipi api`](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) installed on a hostname |
| Jenkins agent needs | `ssh` | [`cipi-cli`](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) |

For production, prefer the API. For a first try, SSH works in five minutes. Both are shown below.

## 2. Create the secret

**SSH way.** On your laptop, make a key used only by Jenkins and authorize it on the server:

```bash
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "jenkins-deploy" -f ./jenkins_deploy -N ""
$ ssh cipi@your-server "sudo cipi ssh add '$(cat ./jenkins_deploy.pub)'"
$ ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 your-server > ./known_hosts     # the server's host key
```

Compare the fingerprint with the server's before trusting it: `ssh-keygen -lf ./known_hosts` on your laptop, `ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` on the server. They must match.

**API way.** On the server:

```bash
$ sudo cipi api token create --name=jenkins-shop --abilities=deploy-manage --expires=2027-12-31
```

Copy the token now: it's shown only once.

## 3. Store it in Jenkins

**Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials → Add credentials**:

| ID | Kind | What to paste |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cipi-ci-key` | SSH Username with private key | Username `cipi`; private key: the content of `./jenkins_deploy` |
| `cipi-known-hosts` | Secret file | Upload `./known_hosts` |
| `cipi-api-token` | Secret text | The API token (API way) |

Then delete the local copies: `rm ./jenkins_deploy ./jenkins_deploy.pub ./known_hosts`.

For the API way, install `cipi-cli` on the Jenkins agent once:

```bash
$ base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
$ curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
$ sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
$ sudo install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
```

## 4. Create the job

**New Item → Multibranch Pipeline**, name it `shop`. Under **Branch Sources**, add your Git server and the repository (with a read credential if it's private). **Build Configuration**: by Jenkinsfile. Save.

A Multibranch job builds every branch and pull request, so tests run everywhere, while the deploy stage below runs only on `main`.

## 5. Add the Jenkinsfile

At the root of the repository:

```groovy
pipeline {
    agent any

    options {
        disableConcurrentBuilds()            // never two builds of the same branch at once
        timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES')
    }

    environment {
        APP        = 'shop'
        SERVER     = 'cipi@203.0.113.10'
        HEALTH_URL = 'https://shop.example.com/up'
    }

    stages {
        stage('Test') {
            agent {
                docker {
                    image 'composer:2'      // or any image with PHP and Composer
                    reuseNode true
                }
            }
            steps {
                sh 'composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist'
                sh 'cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate'
                sh 'php artisan test'
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps {
                withCredentials([file(credentialsId: 'cipi-known-hosts', variable: 'KNOWN_HOSTS')]) {
                    sshagent(credentials: ['cipi-ci-key']) {
                        sh '''
                          ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile="$KNOWN_HOSTS" "$SERVER" \
                            "sudo cipi deploy $APP && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors $HEALTH_URL >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy $APP --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
                        '''
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The deploy line, piece by piece:

| Piece | Runs when | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sudo cipi deploy $APP` | Always | Builds and publishes the new release. If it fails, nothing was published: the build turns red here |
| `curl … $HEALTH_URL` | The deploy succeeded | Calls the app up to six times, five seconds apart |
| `sudo cipi deploy $APP --rollback; exit 1` | The app doesn't answer | Goes back to the previous release and turns the build red |

**API way:** replace the Deploy stage with this one.

```groovy
        stage('Deploy') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            environment {
                CIPI_API_URL   = 'https://api.example.com'
                CIPI_API_TOKEN = credentials('cipi-api-token')
            }
            steps {
                sh '''
                  export HOME="$(mktemp -d)"      # the cipi-cli profile lives only for this build
                  cipi-cli profiles add prod --endpoint "$CIPI_API_URL" --token "$CIPI_API_TOKEN"
                  cipi-cli prod deploy "$APP"
                  curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors "$HEALTH_URL" >/dev/null \
                    || { cipi-cli prod deploy rollback "$APP" -y; exit 1; }
                '''
            }
        }
```

> [!note] Keep the `'''` single quotes. The shell reads `$APP` and the secrets, not Groovy, so credentials never pass through Groovy string interpolation and Jenkins can mask them in the log.

## 6. Start it on every push and turn Cipi's webhook off

Make your Git server notify **Jenkins**:

| Git server | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub | GitHub plugin in Jenkins; repository webhook to `https://jenkins.example.com/github-webhook/`, event *push* |
| GitLab | GitLab plugin; project webhook to the URL shown in the job's triggers |
| Others | Their Jenkins plugin, or **Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers → Periodically** every 1–2 minutes |

Then turn **Cipi's** webhook off for this app, otherwise each push would also deploy directly. In GitHub: **Settings → Webhooks** → the hook ending in `/cipi/webhook` → untick **Active**. The Jenkins hook and the Cipi hook are two different entries: keep the first, turn off the second.

## 7. Run the first deploy

Push a small change to `main` and watch the build. On the server:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --status      # what's running now
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --audit       # the newest entry: origin cipi-cli (SSH) or panel (API)
$ sudo cipi app logs shop --type=deploy
```

To test the safety net, deploy a commit where `/up` returns 500 on purpose (on staging): the build should turn red and `--audit` should show the rollback.

## 8. Add approvals and a rollback button

**An approval before production.** Add this stage before Deploy:

```groovy
        stage('Approve') {
            when { branch 'main' }
            steps {
                timeout(time: 1, unit: 'HOURS') {
                    input message: 'Deploy shop to production?', ok: 'Deploy'
                }
            }
        }
```

**A rollback button.** Create a separate Pipeline job, "shop – rollback", with this script:

```groovy
pipeline {
    agent any
    stages {
        stage('Rollback') {
            steps {
                input message: 'Roll shop back to the previous release?', ok: 'Roll back'
                withCredentials([file(credentialsId: 'cipi-known-hosts', variable: 'KNOWN_HOSTS')]) {
                    sshagent(credentials: ['cipi-ci-key']) {
                        sh 'ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile="$KNOWN_HOSTS" cipi@203.0.113.10 "sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback"'
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

A rollback switches the code back in a second. Database migrations stay as they are, so write migrations that the previous release can live with, or turn on [pre-deploy snapshots](https://cipi.sh/docs/safe-deploy).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `No such DSL method 'sshagent'` | SSH Agent plugin missing | **Manage Jenkins → Plugins** → install SSH Agent |
| `Host key verification failed` | Known-hosts credential empty or from another server | Recreate it with `ssh-keyscan` and compare the fingerprint |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | Key not authorized | `sudo cipi ssh add ""` on the server |
| `sudo: a terminal is required` | Connected as a user other than `cipi` | Use `cipi@server` |
| Deploy stage always skipped | Classic Pipeline job, not Multibranch | Use a Multibranch Pipeline, or remove `when { branch 'main' }` |
| Two deploys per push | Cipi's webhook still active | Untick **Active** on the `/cipi/webhook` hook |
| *A deploy of 'shop' is running* | Two builds at once, or a webhook deploy in flight | Keep `disableConcurrentBuilds()`; a lock left by an interrupted deploy is removed by the next deploy (Cipi 5.13.0+) |
| `cipi-cli: command not found` | Not installed on that Jenkins agent | Install it (step 3) or pin the stage to an agent label that has it |
| 401 or 403 from the API | Token wrong, expired, or IP not allowed | `sudo cipi api token list`; `sudo cipi api ip-whitelist show` |


## Multi-tenant Laravel SaaS with wildcard subdomains

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-multi-tenant-wildcard

A multi-tenant app serves many customers from one codebase. A common shape gives each customer an address like `acme.yourapp.com`. Three things have to line up: **DNS** sends every subdomain to your server, **Nginx** sends them to your app, and a **certificate** covers all of them.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Tenant** | One customer (company, team, workspace) of your SaaS |
| **Wildcard DNS** | A record `*.yourapp.com` that points every subdomain at one IP |
| **Wildcard alias** | Tells Cipi's Nginx to send `*.yourapp.com` to your app |
| **Wildcard certificate** | One HTTPS certificate valid for every `*.yourapp.com` |
| **DNS-01** | How Let's Encrypt checks you own the domain for a wildcard: via a DNS record, not a web page |

```flow
acme.yourapp.com | browser
> A customer opens `acme.yourapp.com`.
DNS | * → 203.0.113.10
> The `*` DNS record sends every subdomain to your server's IP.
Nginx | alias *.yourapp.com → app saas
> Nginx sees the wildcard alias and hands the request to your app.
Laravel | Host header → tenant acme
> Your middleware reads the host, finds the tenant `acme` and loads its data.
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app on Cipi with its primary domain, e.g. `yourapp.com` ([first deploy](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps)).
- The domain's DNS on Cloudflare (free). Moving DNS doesn't move your traffic: you can keep records "DNS only" (grey cloud).

## 1. DNS records 

In Cloudflare, add:

| Type | Name | Content | Proxy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | `@` | your server IP | your choice |
| A | `*` | your server IP | same as above |

## 2. A Cloudflare API token 

Cloudflare → My Profile → API Tokens → Create token → template "Edit zone DNS", limited to this zone. That's the only permission needed (**Zone → DNS → Edit**).

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl dns set --token=YOUR_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN
```

## 3. Route every subdomain to the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi alias add saas '*.yourapp.com'      # the quotes matter
$ sudo cipi alias list saas
```

## 4. Issue the wildcard certificate 

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install saas --dns=cloudflare
$ sudo cipi ssl status
$ curl -sI https://acme.yourapp.com | head -1
HTTP/2 200
```

Takes about a minute. Renewals reuse the same token automatically. If the records are **proxied** (orange cloud), set Cloudflare SSL/TLS to **Full (strict)**.

Aliases and certificates are also visible in the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/web-panel):

## 5. Find the tenant in Laravel 

A middleware reads the subdomain and loads the tenant:

```php
// app/Http/Middleware/ResolveTenant.php
public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next)
{
    $host = $request->getHost();                       // acme.yourapp.com
    $sub  = Str::before($host, '.yourapp.com');

    $tenant = Tenant::where('slug', $sub)
        ->orWhere('custom_domain', $host)
        ->firstOrFail();

    app()->instance(Tenant::class, $tenant);
    URL::defaults(['tenant' => $tenant->slug]);

    return $next($request);
}
```

Or with route domains:

```php
Route::domain('{tenant}.yourapp.com')->middleware('tenant')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/', DashboardController::class);
});
```

| Concern | Tip |
| --- | --- |
| Data isolation | A global scope on `tenant_id`, or a package such as stancl/tenancy or spatie/laravel-multitenancy |
| Sessions | Leave `SESSION_DOMAIN` empty so each tenant has its own cookie; `.yourapp.com` only to share a login across tenants |
| Queued jobs | Pass the tenant id to the job; don't rely on the request |
| Cache keys | Prefix with the tenant: `"tenant:{$id}:stats"` |
| Reserved names | Block `www`, `api`, `admin`, `mail` as tenant slugs |

## 6. Customer custom domains 

A customer wants `portal.acme.com`. The routing part is easy: add it as an alias and save it as the tenant's `custom_domain`.

```bash
$ sudo cipi alias add saas portal.acme.com
```

The certificate needs a plan. An app has one certificate; with a wildcard issued over Cloudflare DNS, a name outside your Cloudflare zone can't join it over DNS, and a plain HTTP reissue would drop the wildcard.

| Approach | How | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cloudflare for SaaS** (recommended) | Customers CNAME to a hostname you proxy; Cloudflare issues each customer's certificate at the edge; your origin keeps its wildcard and Full (strict) | Many customers, self-service |
| **Separate app for custom domains** | A second Cipi app from the same repository, pointed at the same database, with the customer names as aliases and an HTTP-01 certificate (`cipi ssl install`) | A handful of customers, no Cloudflare |
| **No wildcard** | List every tenant subdomain and custom domain as aliases, HTTP-01, up to 100 names per certificate | Few, known tenants |

Automate whichever you pick from your app with the [Cipi API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) when a customer saves the domain (`POST /api/apps/{name}/aliases`, then `POST /api/apps/{name}/ssl`).

## 7. When to give a tenant its own app 

```flow
Shared app | one DB, tenant_id
> All tenants in one database, separated by a `tenant_id` column. Cheapest and simplest; start here.
Database per tenant | same app, many DBs
> One database per tenant, same code. Stronger separation and per-tenant restores, more to manage.
App per tenant | own user, PHP, DB, backups
> One Cipi app per tenant: its own user, PHP, database and backups. Created through the API at signup.
Server per tenant | enterprise contracts
> A dedicated server for a tenant who pays for it (enterprise contracts, data residency).
```

For the last two, create apps through the API from your signup flow (`POST /api/apps`), one per tenant, each with its own domain, database and backups.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` | Cloudflare SSL/TLS is Flexible: set Full (strict) |
| 525 SSL handshake failed | The name has no alias or certificate yet |
| 526 Invalid SSL certificate | Certificate doesn't cover the name: `cipi ssl status`, reissue |
| `a.b.yourapp.com` fails | One-level wildcard only: keep tenants one label deep |
| Every subdomain shows the same tenant | Middleware reads the wrong part of the host; log `$request->getHost()` |
| Unknown subdomain shows another site | It can't: unknown hosts are closed by Cipi's default server |


## Run Laravel on MySQL instead of MariaDB

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-mysql-instead-of-mariadb

MariaDB is Cipi's default and fits most Laravel apps without friction. Some teams need **MySQL itself**: a vendor that only certifies MySQL, parity with a managed MySQL in another environment, or a team standard. Since Cipi 5.13 one command puts MySQL on port 3306 instead, on a server that has no databases yet.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Port 3306** | Where Laravel's `mysql` driver connects. On a Cipi server it runs MariaDB *or* MySQL, never both |
| **Engine `mariadb`** | Cipi's name for "the server on port 3306". It keeps that name after a switch, so `--engine=mariadb`, `cipi.yml`, backups and the API don't change |
| **Switch** | MariaDB's packages removed, MySQL installed with the same root password and Cipi's tuning |
| **Empty server** | No database, no app and nothing in Cipi's registry on port 3306. The only place a switch runs |
| **Move** | A server already in use moves its apps to a new, switched server with `cipi sync` |

```flow
Decide | MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL | #decide
New server | Ubuntu 26.04, Cipi 5.13.1+ | #server
Switch | before the first app | #switch
Check | engines, client, tuning | #check
Create apps | as usual | #apps
Existing server | new box + cipi sync | #existing
Way back | while it's empty | #back
```

## 1. Decide: MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL 

The two servers grew from the same code and speak the same protocol, so most Laravel apps can't tell them apart. The differences show up in edge features and in operations.

| Stay on MariaDB if | Switch to MySQL if | Look at PostgreSQL if |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You have no specific reason to change: it's the default, tuned and tested on every Cipi server | A vendor, an auditor or a contract asks for MySQL by name | You need JSONB, rich indexes (GIN, GiST, partial), `pgvector` or PostGIS |
| Your app uses `RETURNING`, sequences, or the native `uuid` / `inet6` column types | Another environment runs managed MySQL (RDS, Aurora MySQL, Laravel MySQL) and you want the same engine everywhere | You want one engine for the app, analytics and BI tools |
| You want features such as the thread pool in the free community server (MySQL keeps its thread pool for the Enterprise edition) | Your team runs MySQL tooling (MySQL Shell, Percona Toolkit) and knows its behaviour | You're starting a new product and can choose freely ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-postgresql)) |

### Differences that matter for a Laravel app 

| Topic | MariaDB | MySQL 8.4 | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `json` columns | An alias of `LONGTEXT` with a `json_valid()` check | A binary JSON type | Nothing for casts and `where('meta->key', …)`: both work. See [moving data](#json) |
| UUID and IP types | Native `uuid` and `inet6` types | Not available | Laravel's `uuid()` on the `mysql` driver is `char(36)` on both. Only raw SQL or the `mariadb` driver uses the native types |
| `INSERT … RETURNING`, sequences | Supported | Not supported | Search the code for raw `RETURNING` and `NEXTVAL` before moving |
| Default `utf8mb4` collation | UCA 14 (`utf8mb4_uca1400_ai_ci`) | `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` | Laravel's `config/database.php` sets `utf8mb4_unicode_ci`, which both have. Cipi maps the server defaults on restore |
| Default authentication | `mysql_native_password` | `caching_sha2_password` | Nothing: PHP's `mysqlnd` supports both |
| Queue `SKIP LOCKED` | Yes | Yes | The database queue driver works on both |

## 2. Start from a new server 

A switch never converts data, so it belongs at the very beginning of a server's life.

| Choose | Because |
| --- | --- |
| **Ubuntu 26.04** | Its archive ships **MySQL 8.4 LTS**. On 24.04 you get 8.0, which Oracle stopped supporting on April 30, 2026; Ubuntu still publishes security updates for it, but a new server should start on the current LTS line |
| **Cipi 5.13.1 or later** | 5.13.0 could stop silently right after "Checking the MySQL packages…" (nothing was changed). `sudo cipi self-update` if in doubt |
| **A fresh VPS** | Same sizing as for MariaDB: 2 GB of RAM is comfortable for a few apps. Cipi sizes MySQL's buffer pool from the RAM |

Install Cipi as usual ([VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics)):

```bash
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

## 3. Switch before the first app 

Log in as the `cipi` user and look at what runs on port 3306:

```bash
$ sudo cipi db engines
$ sudo cipi db switch mysql
```

The command asks before it touches anything, then goes through these steps:

```flow
Checks | nothing changes if one fails
> Cipi verifies that the server has no databases on port 3306, that apt offers a `mysql-server` package, and — with a simulation — that removing MariaDB would remove nothing but its own packages and client libraries (a Perl driver or a monitoring agent that depends on them stops the switch). It also waits if a dump, such as a backup, is running.
Stop MariaDB | data kept aside
> MariaDB is stopped and its data directory is moved to `/var/lib/mysql.mariadb-`, not deleted. Its configuration is renamed, not removed.
Remove MariaDB | packages purged
> MariaDB's packages are purged (`libmariadb3` stays for anything that links it) and the MariaDB.org apt repository is removed, so it can't offer its own `mysql-common` next to MySQL.
Install MySQL | same root password
> MySQL is installed from the Ubuntu archive with the same root password, `caching_sha2_password`, and Cipi's tuning in `/etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/99-cipi.cnf` (buffer pool sized by RAM, redo log capacity, X protocol on localhost only). Like MariaDB, it is kept out of unattended upgrades.
Rollback on failure | MariaDB comes back
> If the removal or the install fails, Cipi puts MariaDB back with its data directory and tells you what failed.
Record + notify | db_switch
> The choice is recorded, the action logged, and a `db_switch` notification goes to your channels.
```

In a provisioning script there is no terminal to confirm on, so the switch refuses to run without `--yes`:

```bash
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | SSH_PUBKEY="ssh-ed25519 AAAA… ops" bash
$ cipi db switch mysql --yes
```

> [!warning] The switch is refused, on purpose, on a server that already has a database, an app or a registry entry on port 3306. The message lists what it found. Don't delete apps to get past it: use [step 6](#existing).

## 4. Check the result 

```bash
$ sudo cipi db engines           # "Port 3306 runs MySQL (engine id: mariadb)"
$ sudo cipi db engines --json    # "server": "mysql" for the engine "mariadb"
$ mysql --version
$ sudo cat /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/99-cipi.cnf
```

| Where | You should see |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi db engines` | `mariadb  installed  3306  *`, then *Port 3306 runs MySQL* |
| `cipi service list` | The MySQL unit, watched by the [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) |
| Web panel | *MySQL* on the server's databases tab |
| `/var/lib/mysql.mariadb-` | The old (empty) MariaDB data directory. Remove it once you're happy: `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/mysql.mariadb-*` |

## 5. Create apps as usual 

Nothing in the app workflow changes. The default engine is still `mariadb`, which now means MySQL:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.5
```

| Thing | Value on a MySQL server |
| --- | --- |
| `.env` | `DB_CONNECTION=mysql`, `DB_HOST=127.0.0.1`, `DB_PORT=3306`, its own user and password |
| TablePlus / DBeaver URL | `mysql+ssh://…` (printed at creation and by `cipi credentials`) |
| `cipi.yml` databases | `engine: mariadb`, or leave it out |
| Backups, `cipi db backup/restore`, `cipi db password` | Same commands; the MySQL client does the work |
| Patching | `cipi db upgrade` and the nightly [autoupdate](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades) follow MySQL's packages |
| Port | Localhost only. Connect over SSH; never open 3306 to the internet |

Run the test suite against MySQL in CI too, so you find engine differences before production does:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/tests.yml (excerpt)
services:
  mysql:
    image: mysql:8.4
    env: { MYSQL_DATABASE: testing, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: secret }
    ports: ["3306:3306"]
    options: --health-cmd="mysqladmin ping" --health-interval=10s --health-timeout=5s --health-retries=5
# then run the tests with DB_CONNECTION=mysql DB_HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_DATABASE=testing DB_USERNAME=root DB_PASSWORD=secret
```

## 6. Move a server that already runs apps 

The data is never converted in place: a dump can't carry everything (MariaDB's `uuid`/`inet6` types, sequences, SQL only one server understands), and what it drops would surface later, in your apps. So a server in use moves the way any app moves on Cipi: to a new server.

```flow
Test in CI | your app on MySQL 8.4
> Run the test suite against MySQL (the workflow above) and fix what fails. Search for raw `RETURNING`, `NEXTVAL`, `uuid`/`inet6` columns and MariaDB-only functions.
New server | 26.04, switched first
> Create a new VPS with Ubuntu 26.04, install Cipi, run `sudo cipi db switch mysql` and install the PHP versions your apps use (`sudo cipi php install 8.4`).
Trust | old → new
> On the new server: `sudo cipi sync trust`, pasting the key printed by `sudo cipi sync pubkey` on the old one.
Push | apps, data, storage
> On the old server: `sudo cipi sync push --host=NEW_IP --with-db --with-storage --import`. Dumps are adapted on the way in (see below).
Test | with your hosts file
> Point your domain at the new IP in `/etc/hosts` on your laptop only, and test logins, orders, queues and e-mails.
Cut over | DNS, then SSL
> Final sync, switch DNS, then `sudo cipi ssl install ` for each app. Keep the old server stopped but intact for a week: it's your way back.
```

```bash
# new server
$ sudo cipi db switch mysql
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4
$ sudo cipi sync trust                    # paste the key from the old server
# old server
$ sudo cipi sync pubkey
$ sudo cipi sync push --host=203.0.113.20 --with-db --with-storage --import
# new server, after DNS points to it
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop
```

### What happens to the dumps on the way in 

| In the dump | Restored into MySQL as |
| --- | --- |
| MariaDB's sandbox line (`/*M!999999\- enable the sandbox mode */`), which the MySQL client refuses | Dropped |
| UCA 14 collations (`utf8mb4_uca1400_*`) | The matching MySQL `0900` collations |
| Rows of data | Untouched |

The same filter works in the other direction: a MySQL dump restored into MariaDB gets its `0900` collations mapped to UCA 14. It applies to `cipi db restore`, `cipi sync` and restores from [backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3).

### JSON columns after the move 

A column created as `json` on MariaDB is a `LONGTEXT` with a check, and a dump carries it that way: on MySQL it stays a text column. Laravel's `json`/`array` casts and JSON `where` clauses keep working. If you want MySQL's binary JSON type, convert the column in a migration after the move, on a quiet moment and with a fresh backup:

```php
Schema::table('orders', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->json('meta')->nullable()->change();
});
```

## 7. The way back 

| Situation | How |
| --- | --- |
| Switched, no database created yet | `sudo cipi db switch mariadb`: same checks, same steps, the other way round |
| Apps already on MySQL | Move them to a MariaDB server with `cipi sync`, as in step 6 |
| Moved from an old server last week | Point DNS back at the old server you kept. Data written since the move has to be copied back |

## Troubleshooting 

| Message | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| *MariaDB → MySQL runs only on a server with no databases on port 3306* | The server is in use. Move the apps to a new, switched server ([step 6](#existing)) |
| *Replacing the database server is never implicit* | No terminal to confirm on: add `--yes` |
| *No mysql-server package available from apt* | Run `sudo apt-get update` and check `apt-cache policy mysql-server`: a source list is missing or broken. Nothing was changed |
| *Removing MariaDB would also remove: …* | Another package depends on MariaDB's client libraries. Remove it first, or stay on MariaDB. Nothing was changed |
| *A database dump is running* | A backup is in progress. Try again when `sudo cipi backup status` shows it finished |
| Stops after "Checking the MySQL packages…" with no message | Cipi 5.13.0: `sudo cipi self-update` to 5.13.1 or later and run it again |
| `cipi db install mysql` doesn't switch | By design: `install` never replaces a server. Use `cipi db switch mysql` |
| App says `Access denied` after a move | `sudo cipi db password ` sets a new password in the database and `.env` together |


## Laravel Octane with FrankenPHP on your own server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-octane-frankenphp

[Laravel Octane](https://laravel.com/docs/octane) boots your app once and keeps it in memory, so each request skips the framework bootstrap. With FrankenPHP as the server, a typical app answers several times faster on the same hardware. Cipi runs it natively, without containers, next to your PHP-FPM apps.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **PHP-FPM** | The classic way: PHP boots Laravel for **every** request |
| **Octane** | Boots Laravel **once** and keeps it in memory; requests reuse it |
| **FrankenPHP** | A modern PHP server (one binary with PHP inside) that Octane runs on |
| **Octane worker** | One long-lived process handling requests in turn |
| **State leak** | Data from one request still in memory during the next: the main thing to avoid |

```flow
PHP-FPM | boot, handle, forget: every request
> Classic PHP: for every request, Laravel boots (config, providers, routes), handles the request, then everything is thrown away.
Octane | boot once, handle many
> Octane: Laravel boots once per worker and stays in memory; each request skips the boot. Faster, but data you leave in memory carries over to the next request.
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app on Cipi ([first deploy](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps)) with a test suite.
- About 150 MB of free RAM per Octane worker you plan to run.

## 1. Prepare the project

```bash
$ composer require laravel/octane
$ php artisan octane:install --server=frankenphp
```

Commit both changes. Octane apps keep state between requests: avoid storing per-request data in static properties or singletons. The [Octane docs](https://laravel.com/docs/octane#dependency-injection-and-octane) list the patterns to watch.

## 2. Create the app as Octane, or convert one

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/shop.git --octane
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

An existing app moves over (and back) in one command; the certificate is kept:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app convert shop --to=octane
$ sudo cipi app convert shop --to=fpm
```

## 3. What runs on the server

```flow
Nginx | static files, TLS
> Nginx handles HTTPS and serves static files from `public/` itself.
Octane on 127.0.0.1 | a port in 8100–8999
> Other requests go to Octane on a local port (8100–8999), unreachable from outside.
FrankenPHP build | pinned for this app
> The app runs on its own pinned FrankenPHP build, so PHP never changes by surprise.
Supervisor | restarts, reloads on deploy
> Supervisor keeps Octane alive and reloads it on every deploy.
```

| Piece | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| Nginx | Serves `current/public` directly and proxies the rest to the app's local port |
| Process | Supervisor program `shop-octane`, next to the queue workers |
| `.env` | `OCTANE_SERVER=frankenphp`, `OCTANE_HTTPS=true` |
| Deploys | The pinned binary is linked into the new release, then Octane reloads |

## 4. Tune the workers

```bash
$ sudo cipi app limits shop --octane-workers=4
```

Start with one worker per CPU core and watch memory with `sudo cipi status`. Long jobs belong on [queues or Horizon](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues), WebSockets on [Reverb](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-reverb-websockets).

## 5. Keep FrankenPHP patched, safely

```bash
$ sudo cipi frankenphp              # each app's build and PHP, patched or not
$ sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade shop  # newest build on the same PHP minor
```

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Upgrades stay on the app's PHP minor | No surprise PHP jump |
| Octane must answer after an upgrade | Otherwise the previous build comes back |
| Nightly patches via `cipi autoupdate` | Security fixes without manual work |

To move to a new PHP minor: `sudo cipi app edit shop --php=8.6`, then `sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade shop`.

## In cipi.yml

The runtime is chosen at creation or with `convert`; worker counts can live in the repository:

```yaml
app:
  limits: { octane_workers: 4 }
```

## Avoid state leaks 

| Risky | Safer |
| --- | --- |
| `static $cache = []` in a service | Laravel's cache, or reset it per request |
| Injecting `Request` into a singleton's constructor | Resolve the request inside the method |
| Singletons holding the logged-in user | Bind as `scoped()` instead of `singleton()` |
| Growing arrays in long-lived objects | Octane recycles each worker after 500 requests by default, which limits the damage, not the cause |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| 502 Bad Gateway | Octane isn't running: `sudo cipi worker list shop`, then `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=worker` |
| One user sees another's data | A state leak: see the table above |
| `.env` change ignored | `cipi app artisan shop config:cache`, then `cipi worker restart shop` |
| Memory climbs until restart | A leak in a long-lived object: find it (static arrays, listeners added per request); lower the worker count meanwhile |
| `cipi php upgrade` lists the app | Its FrankenPHP build is behind: `sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade shop` |
| Uploads larger than a few MB fail | Raise `client_max_body_size` and `upload_max_filesize` with `cipi ini` |


## Laravel on PostgreSQL, on your own server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-postgresql

PostgreSQL is an open-source database known for being strict, predictable and extensible. Laravel supports it natively: same Eloquent, same migrations, `DB_CONNECTION=pgsql`. This guide sets it up on a Cipi server, explains what changes compared to MySQL, and covers the day-two tasks.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Engine** | The database server program: MariaDB (MySQL-compatible) or PostgreSQL |
| **Database** | One container of tables, e.g. `shop` |
| **Database user** | The login an app uses. On Cipi each app has its own, which owns its database |
| **Superuser** | `postgres`: can do anything. Cipi keeps its password in the encrypted vault |
| **SSH tunnel** | A way to reach the database from your laptop through SSH, without opening a port |

```stack
Your Laravel app | DB_CONNECTION=pgsql, own user
PostgreSQL | port 5432, localhost only
MariaDB | port 3306, localhost only, always installed
Ubuntu server | firewall: 22, 80, 443 open
```

## When PostgreSQL is the better choice 

| You need | PostgreSQL gives you |
| --- | --- |
| Rich JSON queries | `jsonb` columns with GIN indexes; Laravel's `whereJsonContains` uses them |
| Safe migrations | DDL runs inside transactions: a failing migration rolls back cleanly |
| Strict data | No silent truncation or invalid dates |
| Advanced indexes | Partial, expression and full-text indexes |
| Extensions | pgvector (AI embeddings), PostGIS (maps), pg_trgm (fuzzy search) |

## Before you start 

- A Cipi server ([install guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps)) and SSH access as `cipi`.
- A Laravel app in a Git repository. Nothing in your code needs to change unless you used MySQL-only SQL (see [differences](#differences)).

## 1. Install PostgreSQL 

```bash
$ sudo cipi db install pgsql
$ sudo cipi db engines
```

Cipi installs `postgresql` and `postgresql-contrib`, makes it listen on `localhost` only, sets a random superuser password in the vault and pins the package so unattended upgrades never restart it. MariaDB keeps running next to it.

Want every new app on PostgreSQL by default?

```bash
$ sudo cipi db default pgsql
```

## 2. Create a Laravel app on PostgreSQL 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --engine=pgsql
```

```flow
Linux user | shop
> Cipi creates a Linux user named after the app. Files and processes belong to it.
Database | shop, owned by user shop
> A PostgreSQL database with the same name, owned by a database user of the same name, with its own password.
.env | DB_CONNECTION=pgsql, port 5432
> The app's `.env` gets `DB_CONNECTION=pgsql`, port 5432 and the credentials.
First deploy | php artisan migrate --force
> The first deploy runs your migrations and builds the schema.
```

Cipi creates the database with `UTF8` encoding and gives the app user ownership of it and of the `public` schema, so migrations can create, alter and drop anything inside it, and nothing outside it.

Check the result:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --get=DB_CONNECTION
pgsql
$ sudo cipi db list
```

## 3. Extra databases 

An analytics database for the same app, or a database for a tool:

```bash
$ sudo cipi db create --name=analytics --engine=pgsql --app=shop
```

Add a second connection in `config/database.php` and the credentials Cipi prints to the app's `.env` (`sudo cipi app env shop`).

## 4. Connect from your laptop 

The database port is never exposed. TablePlus, DBeaver, DataGrip and Postico all support an SSH tunnel:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| SSH host / user | Server IP, `cipi` (your SSH key) |
| Database host / port | `127.0.0.1`, `5432` |
| Database, user, password | From `sudo cipi app env shop --show` |

Or from a terminal:

```bash
$ ssh -L 5433:127.0.0.1:5432 cipi@203.0.113.10
# in another terminal
$ psql "postgresql://shop:PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:5433/shop"
```

## 5. Backups and restores 

```bash
$ sudo cipi db backup shop                     # one-off pg_dump, gzipped
$ sudo cipi backup profile add hourly-db --scope=db --databases=shop --every=1h --keep=48 --dest=s3 --encrypt
$ sudo cipi db restore shop /var/log/cipi/backups/shop_20261123_101500.sql.gz
```

PostgreSQL restores run **in one transaction**: if the file is truncated or a statement fails, nothing changes and your data stays as it was. Full setup in the [backup guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3).

## 6. Upgrades 

```bash
$ sudo cipi db upgrade pgsql
```

Minor releases (security and bug fixes) install with a brief restart. Plan it outside peak hours, or schedule it with [stack upgrades](https://cipi.sh/docs/stack-upgrades).

The same databases, backups and password rotation in the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/web-panel):

## MySQL habits that change 

| MySQL / MariaDB | PostgreSQL |
| --- | --- |
| `LIKE` is case-insensitive | `LIKE` is case-sensitive: use `ILIKE` or `whereLike(..., caseSensitive: false)` |
| `GROUP BY` lets you select any column | Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated |
| Backticks `` `name` `` | Double quotes `"name"` (Laravel handles this for you) |
| `0000-00-00` dates accepted | Rejected: use `NULL` |
| Auto-increment | `bigserial` / identity, same `$table->id()` |
| `FIELD()`, `IF()` | `CASE WHEN … END` |

Raw SQL (`DB::raw`, `whereRaw`) is where problems hide: grep for it before switching.

## Move an existing app from MySQL 

There's no in-place switch. You create a PostgreSQL app and move the data once:

```flow
Test locally | run the suite on pgsql
> Run your test suite against PostgreSQL on your machine and fix raw SQL that only worked on MySQL.
New app | --engine=pgsql, same repo
> Create a second app with `--engine=pgsql` from the same repository and deploy it: migrations build the schema.
Copy data | pgloader or an export job
> Copy the data with pgloader (data only) into the tables your migrations created.
Check | counts, a few pages
> Compare row counts and click through the important pages.
Switch DNS | or swap the domain
> Move the domain to the new app (or switch DNS). Keep the old app until you're sure.
```

1. Run your test suite against PostgreSQL locally (`DB_CONNECTION=pgsql` in `.env.testing`) and fix raw queries.
2. Create `shop-pg` with `--engine=pgsql` and deploy: migrations build the schema.
3. Copy the data. [pgloader](https://pgloader.io) reads MySQL and writes PostgreSQL directly; install it on the server (`sudo apt install pgloader`) and run it against both local databases with `--with "data only"` so it fills the tables your migrations created.
4. Reset sequences (pgloader does it; for a hand-made import run `SELECT setval(...)` per table).
5. Compare row counts, click through the app, then move the domain (`sudo cipi app edit shop-pg --domain=shop.example.com` after removing it from the old app).

Do a dry run with a copy first, ideally an [anonymized one](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps).

## pgvector and other extensions 

App users own their database but aren't superusers, so they can't create most extensions themselves. As `cipi`:

```bash
$ psql --version                                # e.g. 16 on Ubuntu 24.04
$ sudo apt install postgresql-16-pgvector        # postgresql--pgvector
$ sudo -u postgres psql -d shop -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;"
```

After that, migrations can use the `vector` column type.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `could not find driver` | Rare: Cipi installs `php-pgsql` with every PHP version. Check `php -m` as the app user and reinstall the version if it's missing |
| `permission denied to create extension` | Create it as `postgres` (see above) |
| `column must appear in the GROUP BY clause` | Add the column to `groupBy()` or aggregate it |
| Search stopped matching uppercase | `LIKE` is case-sensitive: use `ILIKE` |
| Duplicate key on insert after an import | Sequences weren't reset |
| `--engine=pgsql` refused | PostgreSQL isn't installed yet: `sudo cipi db install pgsql` |


## Preview environments for every Laravel pull request

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments

Reviewers click a link instead of pulling a branch. Each pull request gets a complete, isolated Cipi app at an address like `feature-cart-3a1f9c2e4b.preview.example.com`, updated on every push and removed when the pull request closes. This guide sets it up end to end; the reference with every recipe is in the [preview environments docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments).

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Preview environment** | A temporary copy of the app for one branch or pull request |
| **Wildcard DNS** | One DNS record, `*.preview.example.com`, that sends every subdomain to the preview server |
| **App name** | The Linux user of the preview: `pv` + 10 characters computed from repository and branch |
| **Webhook mode** | Each preview has its own Git webhook, so pushes update it without CI |

```flow
Server | DNS, Git token, API
> Prepare a server for previews: a wildcard DNS record, a Git token and the Cipi API with a token for previews.
Script | .cipi/preview.sh
> Commit the script that creates, updates and deletes the preview of a branch.
Laptop | first preview by hand
> Run it once from your laptop to see it work.
CI | open and close
> Call it from GitHub Actions or GitLab when a pull request opens and closes.
Polish | data, privacy, cleanup
> Seed useful data, keep previews private, and sweep the ones nobody closed.
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, already deployed with Cipi somewhere.
- [`cipi/agent`](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-install) in the app, so each preview updates through its own webhook.
- A domain where you can add a DNS record.
- A Cipi server for previews: a small separate one is best (4 GB of RAM is a good start).

## 1. Prepare the preview server

On the preview server:

```bash
$ sudo cipi git github-token ghp_xxx                 # or gitlab-token, bitbucket-token…
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4                          # the PHP version of your app
$ sudo cipi api api.preview.example.com              # the API, with its own certificate
$ sudo cipi api token create --name=previews \
    --abilities=apps-view,apps-create,apps-delete,apps-env,apps-artisan,deploy-manage,ssl-manage,yml-manage \
    --expires=2027-12-31
```

At your DNS provider, add `A *.preview.example.com → preview server IP` (and an `A` record for `api.preview.example.com` before running `cipi api`).

| Why each piece | |
| --- | --- |
| Git token | Cipi adds a read-only deploy key and a webhook for each preview, and removes them when the preview is deleted |
| API + token | The script and CI talk to the server over HTTPS with a token that can only manage apps, deploys and certificates |
| Separate server | Reviews never slow production, and the token can't touch production apps |

## 2. Add the script to the repository

Copy [`.cipi/preview.sh`](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments#script) from the docs into your repository and make it executable:

```bash
$ mkdir -p .cipi && $EDITOR .cipi/preview.sh      # paste the script
$ chmod +x .cipi/preview.sh
$ git add .cipi/preview.sh && git commit -m "Preview environments" && git push
```

What it does, in one table:

| Command | First time | Next times |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `up` | Creates the app on the branch (label `preview`), sets `MAIL_MAILER=log`, issues the certificate, turns on `cipi-preview.yml`, deploys, seeds | Nothing in webhook mode (the webhook deploys); deploys with `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` |
| `down` | Deletes the app, its database, certificate, deploy key and webhook | Says there's nothing to delete |
| `url` | Prints the address | Same |

## 3. Create the first preview from your laptop

```bash
$ cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint https://api.preview.example.com --token "1|…"
$ git switch -c feature/cart && git push -u origin feature/cart
$ PREVIEW_DOMAIN=preview.example.com .cipi/preview.sh up
…
https://feature-cart-3a1f9c2e4b.preview.example.com
```

Open the address: the app is there, with HTTPS and seeded data. Push a commit to `feature/cart`, wait a minute, reload: the change is live. Then delete it:

```bash
$ PREVIEW_DOMAIN=preview.example.com .cipi/preview.sh down
```

## 4. Automate it in CI

**GitHub:** add the two secrets `CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL` and `CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN`, then copy the [GitHub Actions recipe](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments#github) to `.github/workflows/preview.yml`. Each pull request shows a **View deployment** button; closing or merging it deletes the preview.

**GitLab:** add the same two CI/CD variables (masked), then copy the [GitLab recipe](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments#gitlab). Merge requests show the review app link and a **Stop** button; deleting the branch stops it too.

**Bitbucket, Gitea, Forgejo, Jenkins:** see the [other recipes](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments#recipes).

Pull requests from forks don't get previews in these recipes: they don't receive your secrets, and code from outside your team shouldn't run on your server.

## 5. Make previews worth opening

| Add | How |
| --- | --- |
| Lighter previews | A `cipi-preview.yml` with one worker and no scheduler ([example](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments#yml)) |
| Realistic data without personal data | An [anonymized dump](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps), restored with `sudo cipi db restore pv… dump.sql.gz` |
| A login in front | [Cloudflare Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust) (keeps the webhook working), or basic auth with `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` |
| No side effects | Sandbox keys for payments and webhooks, set once with `cipi-cli preview apps env set` |
| End-to-end tests | Point Playwright or Cypress at the preview URL in a CI job after `up` ([how](https://cipi.sh/guides/preview-environments-for-teams#e2e)) |

## 6. Clean up what nobody closed

Branches get deleted without a pull request, and some CIs have no "closed" event. Schedule [`.cipi/preview-cleanup.sh`](https://cipi.sh/docs/preview-environments#cleanup) nightly: it deletes every preview of this repository whose branch no longer exists, and nothing else.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/preview-cleanup.yml (GitHub example)
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: "30 3 * * *" }]
jobs:
  cleanup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      PREVIEW_REPOSITORY: git@github.com:${{ github.repository }}.git
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: |
          base=https://github.com/cipi-sh/cli/releases/latest/download
          curl -fsSLO "$base/cipi-cli-linux-amd64" && curl -fsSLO "$base/checksums.txt"
          sha256sum --check --ignore-missing checksums.txt
          sudo install -m 0755 cipi-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cipi-cli
          cipi-cli profiles add preview --endpoint "${{ secrets.CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL }}" --token "${{ secrets.CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN }}"
          .cipi/preview-cleanup.sh
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Invalid username` | Don't build names by hand: the script makes `pv` + 10 lowercase hex characters |
| Preview doesn't update on push | The app has no `cipi/agent`, or basic auth is on: add the agent, or set `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` |
| No HTTPS | Wildcard DNS missing (`dig +short test.preview.example.com`), or the Let's Encrypt weekly limit: use a separate domain for previews |
| "Could not add the webhook" | GitHub allows 20 push webhooks per repository: close stale pull requests, or use `PREVIEW_MODE=deploy` |
| `403` from the API | The token lacks an ability: recreate it with the list in step 1 |
| Previews send real e-mails | The script sets `MAIL_MAILER=log`; check that your app doesn't override it in config |
| Leftover previews | Run `.cipi/preview-cleanup.sh`, or list them with `cipi-cli preview apps list` |


## Real-time Laravel with Reverb, on your own domain

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-reverb-websockets

[Laravel Reverb](https://reverb.laravel.com) is Laravel's own WebSocket server. Here you'll add live notifications to an app and run Reverb in production on the same domain and certificate as the app: no Pusher account, no extra port to open, no credentials to invent.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **WebSocket** | A connection the browser keeps open, so the server can push messages |
| **Broadcasting** | Laravel sending an event to connected browsers |
| **Channel** | A named stream: public, private (logged-in users) or presence (who's online) |
| **Echo** | The JavaScript client that listens on channels |
| **Reverb** | The WebSocket server, a long-running process on your server |

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app on Cipi with a queue worker running (broadcasts are queued).
- A domain with HTTPS, so browsers connect over `wss://`.

## 1. Add broadcasting to the project

```bash
$ composer require laravel/reverb
$ php artisan install:broadcasting
```

That installs Echo and writes `resources/js/echo.js`. Broadcast an event:

```php
class OrderShipped implements ShouldBroadcast
{
    public function __construct(public Order $order) {}

    public function broadcastOn(): array
    {
        return [new PrivateChannel('orders.'.$this->order->user_id)];
    }
}
```

```js
Echo.private(`orders.${userId}`).listen('OrderShipped', (e) => {
    toast(`Order ${e.order.number} shipped`);
});
```

Commit and push.

## 2. Turn Reverb on for the app

```bash
$ sudo cipi app reverb enable shop
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop       # wss:// instead of ws://
$ sudo cipi deploy shop             # Vite bakes VITE_REVERB_* into the bundle
```

```flow
Browser | wss://shop.example.com/app/{key}
> The browser connects to `wss://shop.example.com/app/{key}`, on the app's own domain.
Nginx | same domain, same certificate
> Nginx proxies only the WebSocket paths, with the app's certificate.
Reverb on 127.0.0.1 | a port in 9000–9099
> Reverb listens locally, on a port between 9000 and 9099.
Supervisor | shop-reverb, as the app user
> Supervisor runs it as the app's user and restarts it when needed.
```

Cipi generates the `REVERB_*` credentials once, writes the `VITE_REVERB_*` copies for the front end, and proxies only the WebSocket paths. The stock `echo.js` reads exactly those variables.

## 3. Check it

```bash
$ sudo cipi app reverb status shop
 Reverb: enabled 127.0.0.1:9000
 shop-reverb RUNNING pid 21847, uptime 3 days
 Clients dial: wss://shop.example.com:443/app/3f9c1ab27de40518b6c4
```

Events are broadcast from queued jobs, so keep a [worker or Horizon](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues) running.

| Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Clients use `ws://` after adding a certificate | Redeploy, so Vite rebuilds the bundle with `wss://` |
| `Missing in .env` in status | Run `enable` again: it fills in missing keys, keeps port and credentials |
| Domain changed | Redeploy so the bundle picks up the new host |

## 4. Keep it in the repository

```yaml
# cipi.yml
workers:
  reverb: true
```

A clone or staging copy gets its own port, credentials and host, never production's.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Console: WebSocket connection failed | Reverb not running: `sudo cipi app reverb status shop` |
| Connects, but no events | No queue worker, or the event isn't `ShouldBroadcast`; check `queue:failed` |
| 403 on `/broadcasting/auth` | User not logged in, or the channel rule in `routes/channels.php` returns false |
| Mixed content blocked | Page on HTTPS, socket on `ws://`: install the certificate, redeploy |
| Works locally, not on the server | `VITE_REVERB_*` baked in at build time: redeploy after changing them |


## Laravel scheduler and cron jobs in production

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scheduler-cron

Most apps need things to happen on their own: send a daily report, clear old records, renew subscriptions. Laravel's **scheduler** lets you list those tasks in code. A single cron line runs the scheduler every minute, and it decides what's due.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **cron** | The Linux service that runs commands at fixed times |
| **crontab** | A user's list of cron jobs, one per line |
| **Scheduler** | Laravel's list of tasks in `routes/console.php`, checked once a minute |
| **`schedule:run`** | The Artisan command cron calls every minute; it runs what's due and exits |
| **Overlap** | A task still running when its next run starts |

```flow
cron, every minute | as user shop
> Linux's cron starts one command every minute, as the app's user.
schedule:run | reads routes/console.php
> That command is `php artisan schedule:run`, which reads the tasks you defined in `routes/console.php`.
Due tasks | run or dispatch to the queue
> Tasks that are due right now run (or dispatch a job to the queue).
Exit | until the next minute
> `schedule:run` exits. A minute later cron calls it again.
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app deployed with Cipi ([first deploy](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps)).
- Nothing to configure: the cron line already exists.

## 1. See what Cipi set up 

```bash
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop
$ sudo crontab -u shop -l
* * * * * /usr/bin/php8.6 /home/shop/current/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1
```

It runs as `shop`, so tasks have the app's permissions and nothing more, with **the app's** PHP version, against `current/`, which always points at the live release.

## 2. Write your first tasks 

In `routes/console.php`:

```php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

Schedule::command('reports:daily')
    ->dailyAt('06:00')
    ->timezone('Europe/Rome')
    ->withoutOverlapping()
    ->onFailure(fn () => logger()->error('Daily report failed'));

Schedule::command('model:prune')->daily();
Schedule::job(new SyncStock)->everyFifteenMinutes();     // queued, runs on a worker
Schedule::command('backup:clean')->weekly()->sundays()->at('03:00');
```

Commit and deploy. Then list them as the server sees them:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop schedule:list
```

| Option | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| `->withoutOverlapping()` | A run can take longer than the interval |
| `->onOneServer()` | The app runs on more than one server (needs a shared cache) |
| `->runInBackground()` | Several long commands are due at the same minute |
| `->evenInMaintenanceMode()` | It must run during `artisan down` |
| `Schedule::job(...)` | The work is heavy: the scheduler only dispatches it |

## 3. Keep the scheduler light 

`schedule:run` runs due tasks one after another. A ten-minute command at 06:00 delays every other task due at 06:00.

```flow
Scheduler | small, fast commands
> Keep scheduled commands short: they run one after another in the same minute.
Queue | heavy work, retries, timeouts
> Put heavy work in a job: the queue retries it and enforces timeouts.
Worker | Supervisor, restarted on deploy
> A worker under Supervisor runs it, and restarts on every deploy.
```

Schedule a job instead of the work itself, and give long queues their own worker ([queues guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues)):

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=reports --processes=1 --timeout=1800
```

## 4. Get told when a task fails 

Inside Laravel, `->onFailure()` and `->emailOutputOnFailure('ops@example.com')` (which needs working Laravel mail). On the server side, wrap a root cron job with `cipi-cron-notify` and it alerts the [channels you configured](https://cipi.sh/guides/notifications-alerts) when the command exits non-zero:

```text
# /etc/cron.d/shop-reports
0 4 * * * root /usr/local/bin/cipi-cron-notify daily-report sudo -u shop php /home/shop/current/artisan report:daily
```

For "did it run at all?", schedule a heartbeat to an external monitor:

```php
Schedule::command('reports:daily')->dailyAt('06:00')
    ->pingOnSuccess('https://hc-ping.com/your-uuid');
```

## 5. Extra cron jobs 

Prefer the scheduler: tasks stay in code, versioned and deployed. When you really need a plain cron job (a shell script, a non-PHP tool), add it to the app user's crontab:

```bash
$ sudo su - shop
$ crontab -e
# keep the schedule:run line, add yours below
*/15 * * * * /home/shop/current/scripts/sync.sh >> /home/shop/logs/sync.log 2>&1
```

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Keep the `schedule:run` line | `cipi schedule on shop` puts it back if it goes |
| Use absolute paths | Cron has a minimal `PATH` |
| Log to a file | Otherwise output disappears |
| Root jobs in `/etc/cron.d/` | Never give an app more rights than it needs |

## 6. Pause and resume 

```bash
$ sudo cipi schedule off shop        # e.g. during a data migration
$ sudo cipi schedule on shop
```

## Debug a task that never ran 

```flow
Is it listed? | schedule:list
> `cipi app artisan shop schedule:list` shows every task and when it's next due. Missing? It isn't in the deployed code.
Is cron calling? | grep CRON syslog
> `grep CRON /var/log/syslog | grep shop` shows whether cron is calling `schedule:run` every minute.
Did it fail? | laravel.log
> `cipi app logs shop --type=laravel` shows the exception if the task crashed.
Run it by hand | artisan command
> Run the command by hand with `cipi app artisan shop ` to see the error directly.
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop schedule:list
$ grep CRON /var/log/syslog | grep shop | tail -5
$ sudo cipi app logs shop --type=laravel          # Laravel log
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop reports:daily        # run it now, see the error
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop schedule:clear-cache # stuck overlap lock
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Task listed but never runs | `schedule status` says off: `cipi schedule on shop` |
| Runs at the wrong hour | Server time is UTC: set `->timezone()` per task or `timezone` in `config/app.php` |
| Skipped forever after a crash | Overlap lock left behind: `schedule:clear-cache` |
| Runs twice | Two servers without `->onOneServer()`, or a duplicate line in the crontab |
| Works by hand, fails from cron | Missing env or relative path: use absolute paths, check the log |
| Skipped while the app is down | You ran `artisan down`: add `->evenInMaintenanceMode()` only to tasks that are safe then |


## Laravel Scout with Meilisearch, self-hosted

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scout-meilisearch

Here you'll add instant, typo-tolerant product search to a Laravel shop with [Scout](https://laravel.com/docs/scout) and [Meilisearch](https://www.meilisearch.com), running on the same server. Each app gets a key that can only touch its own indexes.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Scout** | Laravel's search layer: `Product::search('shoes')->get()` |
| **Meilisearch** | An open-source search engine, typo-tolerant and fast |
| **Index** | Meilisearch's copy of the searchable fields of your models |
| **Filterable / sortable attributes** | Fields you can filter or sort on; they must be declared |

## 1. Install Meilisearch on the server

```bash
$ sudo cipi search install
```

A single binary under systemd, listening on localhost, with a hardened unit and a health check. The master key lives in a root-only file.

## 2. Prepare the model

```bash
$ composer require laravel/scout meilisearch/meilisearch-php http-interop/http-factory-guzzle
$ php artisan vendor:publish --provider="Laravel\Scout\ScoutServiceProvider"
```

```php
use Laravel\Scout\Searchable;

class Product extends Model
{
    use Searchable;

    public function toSearchableArray(): array
    {
        return [
            'id' => $this->id,
            'name' => $this->name,
            'brand' => $this->brand,
            'price' => $this->price,
        ];
    }
}
```

Filterable and sortable attributes go in `config/scout.php` under `meilisearch.index-settings`. Commit and deploy.

## 3. Enable search for the app

```bash
$ sudo cipi search enable shop
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop scout:sync-index-settings
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop scout:import "App\Models\Product"
```

Cipi writes `SCOUT_DRIVER=meilisearch`, the host, a key scoped to `shop-*` indexes and the prefix into the app's `.env`.

```flow
App shop | SCOUT_PREFIX=shop-
> Cipi writes `SCOUT_PREFIX=shop-` to the app's `.env`, so its indexes are named `shop-products`, `shop-users`…
Scoped key | shop-* indexes only
> The app's key works only on `shop-*` indexes. Another app's indexes answer 403.
Meilisearch | 127.0.0.1, no public port
> Meilisearch listens on localhost only, never on a public port.
```

## 4. Search

```php
$results = Product::search($request->q)
    ->where('brand', 'Acme')
    ->paginate(20);
```

Add `scout:sync-index-settings` to your deploy steps so settings follow the code:

```yaml
# cipi.yml
search: true
deploy:
  post:
    - artisan scout:sync-index-settings
```

## Operations

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Status and keys | `sudo cipi search status --check`, `sudo cipi search list` |
| Rotate the app key | `sudo cipi search key rotate shop` (`.env` updated) |
| Upgrade | `sudo cipi search upgrade` (old binary returns if the store is refused) |
| Turn off for an app | `sudo cipi search disable shop --purge-indexes` |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| No results | Not imported yet: `scout:import "App\Models\Product"` |
| `Attribute is not filterable` | Declare it in `scout.meilisearch.index-settings`, then `scout:sync-index-settings` |
| Changes don't show up | `SCOUT_QUEUE=true` and no worker running, or `searchable()` not called |
| `invalid_api_key` | Key rotated: check `MEILISEARCH_KEY` in `.env`, `cipi search status --check` |


## Laravel cache, sessions and queues on Valkey (Redis)

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-valkey-cache-sessions

Laravel can keep **cache**, **sessions** and **queues** in several places. New apps on Cipi keep them in the database, which works fine at the start. As traffic grows, moving them to **Valkey**, an in-memory store, makes them much faster and lighter on the database.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Cache** | Saved results (`Cache::remember`) so you don't compute them again |
| **Session** | What the app remembers about a logged-in visitor between requests |
| **Queue** | Jobs waiting for a worker to process them |
| **Valkey / Redis** | An in-memory key-value store: very fast, data mostly in RAM |
| **Eviction** | What Valkey does when it's full: e.g. drop the least recently used keys |

```stack
Laravel app shop | CACHE_STORE, SESSION_DRIVER, QUEUE_CONNECTION
Valkey for shop | 127.0.0.1:64xx, own password, user shop
```
