Valkey for blog | another port, another password
Ubuntu server | nothing exposed to the internet
```

## When to switch 

| Sign | Move |
| --- | --- |
| Heavy `Cache::` use, slow pages under load | `CACHE_STORE=redis` |
| Many logged-in users, the `sessions` table grows | `SESSION_DRIVER=redis` |
| You want Horizon, or many jobs per minute | `QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis` with Horizon |
| Rate limiting, `Cache::lock()`, Reverb scaling | Already covered by `CACHE_STORE=redis` |

You can switch one at a time.

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app on Cipi. `phpredis` is installed with every PHP version, and the `.env` already holds `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT` and `REDIS_PASSWORD` for the app's own instance.

```bash
$ sudo cipi valkey list
$ sudo cipi app env shop --get=REDIS_PORT
```

## 1. Switch the drivers 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=CACHE_STORE=redis
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=SESSION_DRIVER=redis
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache  # deploys cache the config: rebuild it
$ sudo cipi worker restart shop            # workers re-read the config
```

Queues on Valkey run under **Horizon** (plain workers read the `database` connection):

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop     # needs laravel/horizon in the app
```

[Horizon guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues).

| What happens | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Cache | Starts empty: the first requests rebuild it |
| Sessions | Logged-in users are logged out once (old sessions were in the database) |
| Queue (with Horizon) | Jobs already in the `jobs` table stay there: drain them once with `queue:work database --stop-when-empty` |

Switch sessions at a quiet time, or tell users they'll need to log in again.

## 2. Check it works 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop tinker --execute="Cache::put('ping','pong',60); echo Cache::get('ping');"
pong
$ sudo cipi valkey list                    # shop: its own instance, running
```

## 3. Cap memory and pick an eviction policy 

Without a cap, an instance grows with your data. For an app that still uses the shared instance, set the cap while you isolate it (step 4):

```bash
$ sudo cipi valkey isolate shop --maxmemory=256mb --policy=allkeys-lru
```

For an app that already has its own instance (every new app), add the two lines to its config and restart it:

```bash
$ echo -e "maxmemory 256mb\nmaxmemory-policy allkeys-lru" | sudo tee -a /etc/cipi-valkey/shop.conf
$ sudo cipi valkey restart shop
```

| Policy | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `allkeys-lru` | Mostly cache: drops the least used keys when full |
| `volatile-lru` | Cache plus data without expiry (sessions with TTL, queue): drops only keys with an expiry |
| `noeviction` | Queues only: refuses writes when full, so jobs are never dropped silently |

If you keep queues and cache in the same instance, `volatile-lru` is the safe middle: cache keys have a TTL, queued jobs don't.

## 4. Apps still on the shared instance 

Older servers started with one Valkey for everybody. Move each app to its own:

```bash
$ sudo cipi pending                          # lists apps still on the shared instance
$ sudo cipi valkey isolate shop              # or --all
```

```flow
Maintenance on | app returns 503 for seconds
> The app returns 503 for a few seconds so nothing writes during the move.
Workers stop | nothing writes
> Its workers stop.
Copy keys | with their expiry
> Every key is copied to the app's own instance, with its expiry.
Switch .env | config cache rebuilt
> `.env` points at the new instance and the config cache is rebuilt.
Back online | on its own instance
> The app is back online on its own instance. If anything failed, it stays where it was.
```

If the copy fails, the app stays exactly where it was. Once nobody uses the shared instance, `sudo cipi valkey flush-shared` empties it and changes its password.

## 5. Look inside 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --get=REDIS_PORT
$ valkey-cli -p 6401 -a "$(sudo cipi app env shop --get=REDIS_PASSWORD)" info memory
$ valkey-cli -p 6401 -a "…" --scan --pattern '*cache*' | head
```

Avoid `KEYS *` on a big instance: it blocks it. `--scan` doesn't.

## Good habits 

| Habit | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Always set a TTL on cache keys | Lets eviction work and memory stay flat |
| Don't treat cache as storage | Anything in it may disappear |
| Separate queue and cache Redis databases (`REDIS_CACHE_DB`) | `cache:clear` won't touch queued jobs |
| Restart workers after driver changes | They keep the old config in memory |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Connection refused` | Instance stopped: `sudo cipi valkey restart shop` |
| `NOAUTH` / `WRONGPASS` | `.env` and instance disagree: compare `REDIS_PASSWORD` with `requirepass` in `/etc/cipi-valkey/shop.conf` |
| Everyone logged out | Expected once after switching `SESSION_DRIVER` |
| Jobs stuck in the database | Drain the old `jobs` table (see step 1) |
| `OOM command not allowed` | Memory cap reached with `noeviction`: raise `--maxmemory` or change policy |
| `Class "Redis" not found` | Very rare: the app's PHP lacks `phpredis`; reinstall that PHP version |


## Zero-downtime Laravel deploys with safe migrations

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-zero-downtime-migrations

Zero downtime is two problems: switching code without a gap, and changing the database without breaking the code that's still live. Cipi solves the first. This guide shows how to handle the second.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Atomic release** | The new code goes live in one instant switch |
| **Expand / contract** | First add (columns, tables) so old and new code both work; remove later |
| **Snapshot** | A database dump taken right before migrations |
| **Auto-rollback** | Cipi restores the previous release if the health check fails |

## How a release goes live

```flow
Clone | new folder in releases/
> The code is cloned into a brand new folder under `releases/`. Visitors still use the old one.
Build | composer, npm, link .env and storage
> Dependencies and assets are built there; `.env` and `storage` are linked from `shared/`.
Migrate | against the live database
> Migrations run against the **live** database while the **old** code is still serving. That's why migrations must not break the old code.
Swap | one atomic symlink
> `current` switches to the new folder in one atomic step.
Restart | workers, Octane, FPM reload
> Workers and Octane restart, PHP-FPM reloads: everything runs the new code.
```

The old release keeps serving until the swap. The previous five releases stay on disk for an instant `sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback`.

## The catch: migrations run before the swap

For a few seconds the **old code runs against the new schema**. Migrations must be backward compatible with the release that's still live.

| Change | Safe way |
| --- | --- |
| Add a column | Nullable or with a default. Safe in one deploy |
| Rename a column | Add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads, drop the old one in a later deploy |
| Drop a column | First deploy code that no longer uses it, then drop it in the next deploy |
| Add an index on a big table | Use the engine's online method (`ALGORITHM=INPLACE` on MariaDB, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on PostgreSQL) |
| Make a column NOT NULL | Backfill first, constrain later |

This "expand, then contract" rhythm is what lets you deploy many times a day.

## Take a snapshot first

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --snapshot             # dump first, continue if the dump fails
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --snapshot-required    # abort the deploy if the dump fails
$ sudo cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot # every deploy, whatever triggered it
```

Dumps land in `/var/log/cipi/backups/`. To undo a bad migration:

```bash
$ sudo cipi db restore shop /var/log/cipi/backups/shop_20261123_143012.sql.gz
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback
```

## Roll back automatically

```yaml
# cipi.yml
health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  expect: 200
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true
deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
```

After every deploy Cipi calls the health URL. If the new release doesn't answer as expected, the previous release goes back live and you get notified.

## Know who deployed what

Every deploy, from any trigger, is recorded in a hash-chained [audit trail](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit):

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --audit
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --history
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Old release errors during deploy | A migration removed something it uses: split into expand and contract |
| Deploy stuck on a migration | A table lock: check running queries, use online DDL |
| Rolled back code, data still new | Expected: restore the snapshot if needed |
| No snapshot was taken | `--snapshot` continues if the dump fails; use `--snapshot-required` |


## What preview environments can do for your team

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/preview-environments-for-teams

Without previews, a change lives on one developer's laptop until it's merged. Everyone else reviews a diff, imagines the result, and finds out what it really does on staging, where three other changes are already waiting. A preview environment fixes that: **every pull request gets a real, running copy of the app at its own address**, created when the pull request opens and gone when it closes.

With Cipi a preview is just another isolated app on a server you own, so you get the idea without a platform bill per environment. Setup is in the [how-to guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments); this one is about what to do with them.

## In 30 seconds 

| Before | With previews |
| --- | --- |
| Review the diff, imagine the result | Click the link, use the feature |
| One shared staging, changes queue up and overwrite each other | One environment per pull request, nobody waits |
| "Works on my machine" | Works on a server built exactly like production |
| Client feedback after release | Client approval before merge |
| Migrations tried for the first time in production | Migrations run on every push, on their own database |

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Preview** | A temporary, complete copy of the app for one branch |
| **Ephemeral** | It lives as long as the pull request, then it's deleted with its data |
| **Staging** | One shared, long-lived environment where merged changes meet |
| **E2E test** | A test that drives a real browser against a real URL |

## Who gains what 

| Person | What changes for them |
| --- | --- |
| Developer | Shares a link instead of screenshots; sees the branch on production-like PHP, Nginx and database |
| Reviewer | Tests the behaviour, not only the code |
| Product manager, designer | Approves the real thing before it's merged |
| QA | Tests each change alone, with its own data, without stepping on others |
| Client (agencies) | Signs off on a URL, not on a call |
| Support, sales | Gets a working demo of an upcoming feature |
| Ops | Sees every branch deploy with the same pipeline as production, long before release day |

## Ten things teams do with previews 

### 1. Review the change, not the diff 

The pull request shows a **View deployment** button (GitHub) or a review app link (GitLab). The reviewer clicks it, tries the new checkout flow, and comments on what it does. Bugs that are invisible in a diff (a broken redirect, a slow page, a missing translation) show up in seconds.

### 2. Sign-off from product and design 

Paste the preview link in the ticket. The product manager checks the flow, the designer checks spacing and states, both approve in the pull request. Nothing reaches `main` that the owner of the feature hasn't seen.

### 3. Client approval, for agencies 

Send the client a link that's protected with a login ([Cloudflare Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/docs/zero-trust), or basic auth). They see their feature on a real server, with their content seeded, and approve before you merge. No more "it's on staging, but ignore the other things you see".

### 4. QA without collisions 

On a shared staging, one tester's data resets another's test. Each preview has **its own database**, seeded the same way every time, so a tester can break things freely. When the pull request closes, the data goes with it.

### 5. Try migrations before production does 

Every push runs the branch's migrations on the preview's database. A migration that fails, locks a table or loses a column fails there first. With an [anonymized dump](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) restored into the preview, you test against data shaped like production's, without anyone's personal data.

### 6. End-to-end tests against a real URL 

Run Playwright or Cypress against the preview instead of a test server you maintain. The preview deploys through its own webhook, so the job first waits for the deploy of the latest push to finish:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .cipi/preview-wait.sh : wait until the latest push is deployed on the preview
set -euo pipefail
APP=${1:?app name, from .cipi/preview.sh name}
H="Authorization: Bearer ${CIPI_PREVIEW_API_TOKEN:?}"
sleep 75                                    # the webhook queues the deploy; it starts within a minute
for i in $(seq 1 60); do
  s=$(curl -fsS "${CIPI_PREVIEW_API_URL:?}/api/apps/$APP/deploy/status" -H "$H" -H "Accept: application/json")
  if [ "$(jq -r .data.state  Set up the preview server and run `.cipi/preview.sh up` from a laptop for a couple of branches. Check memory, seeders and e-mail settings.
Week 2 | CI on one repository
> Add the GitHub or GitLab recipe to one repository. Every pull request gets a link; closing it deletes the preview.
Week 3 | reviews use the link
> Agree that reviews start from the preview link, and that product sign-off happens there.
Week 4 | E2E and cleanup
> Add the end-to-end job and the nightly cleanup. Watch the server's memory as the number of open pull requests grows.
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| E2E tests run against old code | Use `.cipi/preview-wait.sh` before the tests; it waits for the latest deploy to finish |
| Reviewers see stale data | The seeders run once, when the preview is created: `.cipi/preview.sh down` and `up` to start fresh |
| Server runs out of memory | Lighter `cipi-preview.yml`, close stale pull requests, or a bigger preview server |
| Client sees a login error | Zero Trust: add their e-mail to the access policy; basic auth: send them the user and password |
| A preview has no link in the pull request | Pull requests from forks are skipped on purpose |

## How to use a recipe 

```flow
Copy | into cipi.yml at the repo root
> Pick the recipe closest to your app and paste it into `cipi.yml` at the root of the repository.
Adapt | names, domains, sizes
> Replace `shop` with your app's name everywhere, and adjust domains, process counts and schedules.
Validate | php artisan cipi:yml validate
> Run `php artisan cipi:yml validate` (Cipi Agent) locally or in CI. It uses the same rules as the server.
Deploy | the release carries the file
> Commit and deploy. The file travels inside the release.
Plan, apply | cipi yml plan / apply
> On the server, `cipi yml plan shop` shows the changes; `cipi yml apply shop` makes them, all or nothing.
```

Names inside the file (databases, backup profiles) must start with the app's name, so replace `shop` with yours. New to the file? Start with [the cipi.yml guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml).

Find a recipe

## A first, simple Laravel app 

**When to use it.** Your first `cipi.yml`: one queue worker, the scheduler, a health check and nightly backups. Good for a blog, a small business site or an internal tool.

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 1 }
schedule: true
health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [local] }
```

- `health.url` must be one of the app's own domains. Laravel 11+ answers `/up` out of the box.
- `destinations: [local]` keeps backups on the server; add `s3` once you have a bucket ([backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3)).

## SaaS: Horizon, Reverb, search, backups 

**When to use it.** A product with paying users: Horizon for queues, Reverb for live updates, Meilisearch for search, frequent database backups and automatic rollback if a release breaks.

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
  aliases: ["www.acme.app"]
  www: to-root
workers:
  horizon: true
  reverb: true
schedule: true
search: true
health:
  url: "https://acme.app/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true
deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
  post:
    - artisan scout:sync-index-settings
env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET, POSTMARK_TOKEN] }
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: acme-db, scope: db, every: 30m, keep: 48, destinations: [local] }
    - { name: acme-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 30, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

- The app is called `acme`, so backup profiles are `acme-…`.
- `search: true` needs `sudo cipi search install` once on the server.
- Horizon needs `laravel/horizon` in the app and `QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues)).

## API on Octane with a reporting database 

**When to use it.** A JSON API served by Octane, a separate PostgreSQL database for reports, a busy webhook queue and a cleanup task.

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
  limits: { octane_workers: 4 }
databases:
  - name: api_reporting
    engine: pgsql
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: webhooks, processes: 4, tries: 10, timeout: 120 }
schedule: true
crons:
  - { every: 30m, run: artisan queue:prune-batches }
```

- The app itself must be created with `--octane`; the file sets how many Octane workers it runs.
- `engine: pgsql` needs `sudo cipi db install pgsql` first ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-postgresql)). Credentials go to `shared/cipi-databases.env`.

## Online shop: busy queues, big uploads, frequent backups 

**When to use it.** A Laravel shop (Bagisto, Lunar or your own): order e-mails on their own queue, larger product image uploads, a database snapshot before every deploy and a backup every 30 minutes.

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 32M, post_max_size: 40M, memory_limit: 512M }
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: orders, processes: 2, tries: 5, timeout: 300 }
    - { queue: mail, processes: 1, tries: 5 }
schedule: true
health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true
deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-db, scope: db, every: 30m, keep: 48, destinations: [local, s3], encrypt: true }
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 3 * * *", keep_days: 30, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

- With a 30-minute database backup, the most orders you can lose is half an hour's worth.
- More in [self-host PHP e-commerce](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-ecommerce-vps).

## Multi-tenant SaaS on a wildcard domain 

**When to use it.** Every customer on their own subdomain (`acme.yourapp.com`), one app, one certificate.

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  aliases: ["*.yourapp.com"]          # covers www and every tenant
ssl: { force_https: true }
health:
  url: "https://www.yourapp.com/up"
```

- The wildcard certificate is issued over DNS: run `sudo cipi ssl install saas --dns=cloudflare` once ([multi-tenant guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-multi-tenant-wildcard)).
- `app.aliases` replaces the whole list: write every alias you want to keep.

## Moving to a new domain 

**When to use it.** You renamed the product. The old app keeps its domain only to send visitors (and search engines) to the new one, keeping the path.

```yaml
version: 1
redirect: { to: "https://newbrand.com", code: 301, keep_path: true }
```

- `keep_path: true` sends `/pricing` to `https://newbrand.com/pricing`, which keeps your SEO.
- Use 301 for a permanent move.

## Marketing site: redirects and a proxied blog 

**When to use it.** Old URLs redirected after a redesign, docs moved to their own subdomain, and a blog served from another local service under `/blog/`.

```yaml
version: 1
redirects:
  - { from: /pricing-old, to: /pricing }
  - { from: /docs/, to: "https://docs.acme.app/", code: 308 }
proxies:
  - { prefix: /blog/, upstream: "http://127.0.0.1:3000", strip_prefix: true }
```

- Proxies to Cipi's own ports, link-local or cloud metadata addresses are refused on purpose.

## Staging next to production 

**When to use it.** The staging app reads `cipi-staging.yml` instead of `cipi.yml`: fewer workers, a password, the `develop` branch.

```yaml
# cipi-staging.yml
version: 1
app:
  basic_auth: { users: [preview] }
workers:
  queues: [{ queue: default, processes: 1 }]
deploy: { branch: develop, predeploy_snapshot: false }
```

- The staging app must be created (or cloned) with `--env=staging`.
- Step by step: [staging and production](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production).

## Internal tool behind a password 

**When to use it.** A back-office tool only your team should reach, with HTTPS forced and two named users.

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  basic_auth:
    users:
      - admin
      - { name: ops, password_hash: "$2y$12$replace.with.a.real.bcrypt.hash" }
ssl: { force_https: true }
```

- `admin` keeps the password already set on the server; `ops` uses a bcrypt hash. Never write plain passwords in the file.
- Create a hash with `htpasswd -nbB ops 'your-password'`.

## Next.js front end (SSR) 

**When to use it.** A server-rendered Next.js app as a Node app, on Node 24.

```yaml
version: 1
node:
  framework: next
  mode: ssr
  version: 24
deploy:
  branch: main
```

- The `node:` section is applied by the deploy itself and needs `sudo cipi yml auto web on`.

## Nuxt front end (SSR) with a health path 

**When to use it.** Nuxt in SSR mode, started from its build output, with a health path checked before traffic switches.

```yaml
version: 1
node:
  framework: nuxt
  mode: ssr
  version: 24
  start: node .output/server/index.mjs
  health_path: /health
```

- The new release must answer the health path before Nginx switches to it.

## Static site or SPA (Vite, Astro) 

**When to use it.** A built site served by Nginx, with no Node process running in production.

```yaml
version: 1
node:
  framework: vite
  mode: static
  output: dist
```

- The deploy fails if `dist/` has no `index.html`, so a broken build never goes live.

## Long-running jobs (imports, exports, video) 

**When to use it.** Exports and imports that run for minutes on their own queue, so they never delay e-mails.

```yaml
version: 1
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: exports, processes: 1, tries: 1, timeout: 7200 }
```

- Also set `public $timeout` on the job class, and `retry_after` above it in `config/queue.php` ([why](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-horizon-queues#timeouts)).
- Video work needs `sudo cipi package install ffmpeg` once.

## AI app with embeddings on PostgreSQL 

**When to use it.** An app that embeds documents in the background and stores vectors in a PostgreSQL database.

```yaml
version: 1
databases:
  - name: rag_vectors
    engine: pgsql
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
    - { queue: embeddings, processes: 3, tries: 5, timeout: 600 }
env: { required: [OPENAI_API_KEY] }
```

- The app is called `rag`. pgvector must be created once by the database superuser ([PostgreSQL guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-postgresql#extensions)).

## Custom steps after every deploy 

**When to use it.** Commands to run after each successful deploy, plus extra Artisan caches during the build.

```yaml
version: 1
deploy:
  keep_releases: 10
  extra_artisan: [event:cache, icons:cache]
  post:
    - artisan scout:sync-index-settings
    - node scripts/warm-cache.mjs
  post_on_failure: warn
```

- Only allowlisted runners are accepted (`artisan`, `composer`, `npm`, `npx`, `yarn`, `pnpm`, `php`/`node` with a script in the release). No shells, no pipes.
- `post_on_failure: abort` makes the deploy fail if a step fails.

## Extra scheduled commands without touching code 

**When to use it.** Commands on a timer, declared in the file instead of `routes/console.php`.

```yaml
version: 1
crons:
  - { every: 30m, run: artisan queue:prune-batches }
  - { cron: "15 4 * * *", run: artisan model:prune }
```

- Up to 20 entries. Your own crontab lines are left untouched. Most apps should prefer Laravel's scheduler ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-scheduler-cron)).

## Backups for a database that grows 

**When to use it.** Frequent database backups that skip noisy tables, plus weekly full backups kept for months.

```yaml
version: 1
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-db, scope: db, every: 1h, keep: 72, exclude_tables: ["*.telescope_*", "*.jobs"], destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
    - { name: shop-weekly, scope: all, cron: "0 4 * * 0", keep_weeks: 12, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

- `exclude_tables` keeps debug and queue tables out of the archive.
- Restore and verify: [backups to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3).

## A busy PHP-FPM app, tuned 

**When to use it.** More PHP processes and memory for an app with a lot of traffic.

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  ini: { memory_limit: 512M, max_execution_time: 60 }
  limits: { fpm_max_children: 30, worker_procs: 6 }
```

- Bounds are enforced: `fpm_max_children` 1–50, `worker_procs` 1–20, `octane_workers` 1–16. Out-of-range values block the plan.
- Each PHP process can use up to `memory_limit`: 30 × 512M must fit in RAM.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `search: true` blocked | Meilisearch isn't installed on the server: `sudo cipi search install` |
| Wildcard alias works, HTTPS doesn't | The wildcard certificate needs DNS-01: [wildcard guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-multi-tenant-wildcard) |
| `horizon: true` and queues both set | Horizon replaces the queues: keep one |
| Engine `pgsql` blocked | PostgreSQL isn't installed: `sudo cipi db install pgsql` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-postgresql)) |


## Staging and production from one repository with cipi.yml

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production

Most teams want two copies of the same app: **production**, which your customers use, and **staging**, where you try changes first. This guide sets that up on Cipi from scratch, explaining each idea along the way. No previous Cipi experience needed.

## What you'll build

```stack
Git repository | one codebase, two branches
shop (production) | branch main → reads cipi.yml
shop-stg (staging) | branch develop → reads cipi-staging.yml
```

| | Production | Staging |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App name (Linux user) | `shop` | `shop-stg` |
| Domain | `shop.example.com` | `staging.shop.example.com` |
| Branch that deploys | `main` | `develop` |
| Settings file | `cipi.yml` | `cipi-staging.yml` |
| Database | `shop` | `shop-stg` (separate) |
| Who can see it | everyone | only your team (password) |

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **App** | One running copy of your code on the server: its own user, folder, PHP pool, database and domain |
| **Environment** | A label on an app (`production`, `staging`…). Laravel sees it as `APP_ENV`, Cipi uses it to pick a settings file |
| **Branch** | The Git branch an app deploys. Push to it and that app updates |
| **`cipi.yml`** | A file in your repository that describes how the server should run the app: PHP version, workers, backups… ([what it is](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml)) |
| **Plan / apply** | Cipi first shows what the file would change (plan), then does it (apply) |

## Before you start 

- A server with Cipi and your production app already running ([Deploy Laravel on a VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps)).
- A `develop` branch in your repository: `git checkout -b develop && git push -u origin develop`.
- A DNS record for `staging.shop.example.com` pointing at the server (same IP as production).

## 1. Create the staging app as a clone 

A **clone** copies the app's configuration (PHP version, repository, workers, deploy settings) into a new, fully separate app:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app clone shop --domain=staging.shop.example.com --name=shop-stg \
    --branch=develop --env=staging --with-db
```

| Flag | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `--domain` | The address of the new app |
| `--name` | Its Linux user and app name |
| `--branch=develop` | Staging deploys the `develop` branch |
| `--env=staging` | Marks it as staging: it will read `cipi-staging.yml` and get `APP_ENV=staging` |
| `--with-db` | Creates a fresh, **empty** database for it |

The clone gets new database credentials, its own deploy key, its own Reverb credentials and search key. **Nothing points back to production.** Save the summary it prints.

Then deploy it once and add HTTPS:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop-stg
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop-stg
```

## 2. Keep strangers out of staging 

Staging often contains unfinished features. Put a password in front of it:

```bash
$ sudo cipi basicauth enable shop-stg --user=preview --password='a-long-random-passphrase'
```

Pick a long password and share it with your team (without `--user` and `--password`, Cipi generates both and shows them once). Search engines and visitors now get a login prompt.

## 3. Write the two settings files 

In your repository root, production keeps its `cipi.yml`. Add a second file, `cipi-staging.yml`, with what staging needs. The staging file **does not inherit** from `cipi.yml`: write everything staging needs.

```yaml
# cipi.yml — production
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
  aliases: ["www.shop.example.com"]
  www: to-root
workers:
  horizon: true
schedule: true
health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true
deploy:
  branch: main
  predeploy_snapshot: true
env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, MAIL_HOST] }
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

```yaml
# cipi-staging.yml — staging
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.6"
  basic_auth:
    users: [preview]           # the user created above; keeps its password
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 1 }
schedule: true
deploy:
  branch: develop
env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY] }   # test keys, set on the staging server
```

| Difference | Why |
| --- | --- |
| No aliases or www redirect | Staging has one domain |
| One queue worker instead of Horizon | Less memory; enough for testing |
| No backup profile | Staging data is disposable |
| `basic_auth` in the file | The password protection can't be removed by accident |
| `deploy.branch: develop` | Pushes to `develop` deploy staging |

Validate both before you commit (with the [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml) installed in the app):

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:yml validate
$ CIPI_ENV=staging php artisan cipi:yml validate
```

Commit and push to **both** branches (merge `develop` into `main` later, or cherry-pick the files).

## 4. Plan, then apply on staging 

After the next deploy of `shop-stg` the file is on the server. See what it would change:

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml plan shop-stg
$ sudo cipi yml apply shop-stg
$ sudo cipi yml auto shop-stg on      # apply after every deploy from now on
```

Do the same for production with `shop`. From now on, the files are the source of truth: change them in a pull request, merge, and each app applies its own file on the next deploy.

## 5. Push-to-deploy for each branch 

Each app has its own webhook and only deploys its own branch:

```flow
git push develop | GitHub webhook
> You push to `develop`. GitHub calls the webhook of the staging app.
shop-stg | deploys develop
> The staging app `shop-stg` deploys `develop` and reads `cipi-staging.yml`.
git push main | GitHub webhook
> You push (or merge) to `main`. GitHub calls the production app's webhook.
shop | deploys main
> The production app `shop` deploys `main` and reads `cipi.yml`. One repository, two apps, never mixed.
```

Get each app's webhook URL and secret with `sudo cipi deploy shop-stg --webhook` and add it to the repository ([auto-deploy](https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy)). Pushes to other branches answer `skipped`.

## 6. Get realistic data into staging 

An empty database isn't much of a test. Never copy production as is: personal data ends up in a less protected place. Use an **anonymized dump**:

```bash
$ cipi-cli prod db anonymize shop --email you@example.com
$ cipi-cli db anonymize download "" -o shop-anon.sql
# copy it to the server, then:
$ sudo cipi db restore shop-stg /home/cipi/shop-anon.sql
```

Step by step: [GDPR-safe production data](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps).

## The daily workflow 

```flow
Branch | feature/x from develop
> Create a feature branch from `develop` and work there.
Merge to develop | staging deploys
> Merge it into `develop`: staging deploys it automatically.
Test on staging | behind the password
> Test on the staging URL, behind its password, with anonymized data.
Merge to main | production deploys
> When it's good, merge `develop` into `main`: production deploys.
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi yml plan shop-stg` says it reads `cipi.yml` | The app's env isn't `staging`: `sudo cipi app edit shop-stg --env=staging` |
| Plan says "blocked: STRIPE_KEY missing" | Set it on the staging app: `sudo cipi app env shop-stg --set=STRIPE_KEY=sk_test_…` |
| Staging deploys `main` | `deploy.branch` is applied from the **next** deploy, or set it now: `sudo cipi app edit shop-stg --branch=develop` |
| Invalid `cipi-staging.yml` | The error names the file; validate locally with `CIPI_ENV=staging php artisan cipi:yml validate` |
| Staging sends real e-mails | Use a mail catcher or a sandbox SMTP in the staging `.env` |


## cipi.yml: keep your server settings in the repository

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml

Most panels keep an app's server settings in a database you can't review. Cipi lets you put them in **`cipi.yml`**, a file at the root of your repository. It travels with each release: you review it in a pull request, see exactly what it would change, and apply it in one step.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **YAML** | A plain-text format of `key: value` lines, indented to nest |
| **Desired state** | The file says how the app *should* be; Cipi works out the steps |
| **Plan** | The list of changes Cipi would make, shown before anything happens |
| **Apply** | Making those changes, all of them or none |
| **Blocker** | A problem that stops the plan: an invalid value, a missing variable |

```flow
Edit cipi.yml | in a branch
> Change the file in a branch, like any code change.
Review | pull request
> Open a pull request: teammates see exactly which server setting changes.
Merge, deploy | the file ships with the release
> Merge and deploy. The file arrives with the release.
Plan | what would change
> `cipi yml plan shop` lists what would change. Nothing happens yet.
Apply | all or nothing
> `cipi yml apply shop` (or the automatic mode) applies everything, or nothing if one change fails.
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel (or Node) app deployed with Cipi.
- Shell access as `cipi` for the first `generate` and `plan`.

```flow
Generate | from what the app has | #generate
Describe | PHP, workers, backups… | #describe
Validate | before you push | #validate
Plan & apply | all or nothing | #plan
Automatic | after every deploy | #auto
```

## 1. Start from what the app already has 
```bash
$ sudo cipi yml generate shop --save
$ cat /home/shop/cipi.yml
```

Commit that file at the root of the repository. After the next deploy, `cipi yml plan shop` should say there's nothing to do: the file describes the server as it is.

## 2. Describe the app 
A typical Laravel app:

```yaml
version: 1

app:
  php: "8.6"
  aliases: ["www.shop.example.com"]
  www: to-root
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 50M }

workers:
  horizon: true
  reverb: true

schedule: true
search: true

health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true

deploy:
  branch: main
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
  post:
    - artisan cache:clear

env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET, MAIL_HOST] }

backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

| Block | Replaces |
| --- | --- |
| `app` | `cipi php`, `cipi alias`, `cipi www`, `cipi ini`, `cipi app limits` |
| `workers`, `schedule` | `cipi worker`, `cipi app reverb`, the scheduler cron |
| `search` | `cipi search enable` |
| `health` | `cipi health set` |
| `deploy` | `cipi deploy-config` |
| `backup.profiles` | `cipi backup profile` |

The full list, with routes, proxies, crons and Node apps, is in the [cipi.yml reference](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml).

## 3. Validate before you push 
Install the [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent) in the app and validate with the same rules as the server, locally or in CI:

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ php artisan cipi:yml validate
```

Add `# yaml-language-server: $schema=./cipi.schema.json` at the top of the file (after `php artisan cipi:yml schema --write`) for autocompletion in VS Code or PhpStorm.

## 4. Plan and apply 
After deploying the release that contains the file:

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml plan shop
Plan for 'shop' (/home/shop/current/cipi.yml)
  Would change
    → workers: add queue 'emails' (3 processes)
    → backup profile 'shop-nightly': cron 0 2 * * * to s3, keep 14 days
$ sudo cipi yml apply shop
✓ Applied 2 change(s) from cipi.yml
```

`plan` lists every change and every blocker. `apply` performs them as one transaction: if anything fails, nothing is left half done.

## 5. Apply on every deploy 
```bash
$ sudo cipi yml auto shop on
```

From now on each successful deploy (CLI, webhook or panel) applies the file. **Anyone who can push can now change this app's server settings**, which is the point: protect the branch and review the file like code.

## Why it's safe

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Plan before apply | You see every change; blockers stop everything |
| Namespaced resources | Databases must be `shop` or `shop_*`, backup profiles `shop` or `shop-*`: a file can't touch another app |
| No secrets | Required variables are names; credentials are written to `shared/`, never to the repo |
| Allowlisted commands | `deploy.post` and `crons` accept known runners only (`artisan`, `php`, `composer`, `npm`…) |
| Server picks the file | The app's environment decides between `cipi.yml` and `cipi-staging.yml`; a commit can't redirect production |

Next: one repository, two servers or two apps, with [staging and production files](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `plan` says nothing to do after an edit | The release with the edit isn't deployed yet: deploy first |
| Blocked: required variable missing | Add it to the server's `.env` with `cipi app env shop --set=…` |
| Blocked: database name | Extra databases must be named `shop` or `shop_*` |
| Blocked: command not allowed | `deploy.post` and `crons` accept known runners only (`artisan`, `php`, `composer`, `npm`…) |
| Validation passes locally, fails on server | Different Cipi Agent version: update `cipi/agent` |


## Anonymize a Laravel database with Cipi Agent, step by step

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps

Debugging with seed data misses the bugs real data causes. Copying production to laptops spreads personal data where it's least protected. The **anonymizer** in [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-laravel-mcp) gives you the middle ground: production's structure, volume and relations, with every name, e-mail, phone, address and note replaced by realistic fake values.

## What you'll build

```flow
You ask | cipi-cli, HTTP or Artisan
> You (or a script, or your AI assistant) ask for a dump. The most comfortable way is `cipi-cli prod db anonymize shop --email you@example.com` from your laptop: no SSH, no token typed by hand.
> The request only *asks*: it returns at once with `{"status":"queued"}`. Nothing heavy happens inside a web request.
Queue job | in your Laravel app
> The agent puts a job on the app's queue. A queue worker (Cipi creates one with every Laravel app) picks it up within seconds.
> No worker running? Then nothing happens: check with `sudo cipi worker list shop`.
Dump | mysqldump / pg_dump
> The job reads the production database with the standard tool for your engine. It only **reads**: production is never modified.
Rewrite | only the columns you listed
> While the dump streams, every column listed in `anonymization.json` is replaced (fake name, fake e-mail, masked phone…). Tables in `truncate` are emptied. Everything else (ids, prices, dates) is kept, so relations still work.
> The raw dump is deleted as soon as the anonymized file is written.
Signed link | by e-mail, valid 15 minutes
> You receive an e-mail with a download link. It works for 15 minutes and only through that signed URL: the API never returns it, so a stolen token alone can't download data.
Your laptop | import into a local DB
> Download with `cipi-cli db anonymize download "" -o shop.sql` and import it into a local database (step 5). Then grep for a real e-mail to be sure it's gone (step 6).
```

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Anonymization** | Replacing personal values with fake ones, so the data no longer identifies people |
| **Transformation** | The rule for one column: `fakeEmail`, `fakeName`, `mask:3,2`, `null`… |
| **Consistent** | The same original value always becomes the same fake value, across tables and runs |
| **Seed** | A private value that makes `consistent` reproducible and not guessable |
| **Truncate** | Keep the table, drop its rows (sessions, tokens, jobs) |

## Before you start 

- A Laravel app (12 or 13) deployed with Cipi, on MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL.
- A queue worker running (Cipi creates one with every Laravel app).
- Working Laravel mail (`MAIL_*` in the app's `.env`): the download link is sent by e-mail.

## 1. Install the agent and turn the anonymizer on 

On your laptop:

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ git commit -am "Add Cipi Agent" && git push       # deploys
```

On the server, as the app user (or remotely with `cipi-cli apps artisan shop …`):

```bash
$ ssh shop@203.0.113.10
$ cd ~/current
$ php artisan cipi:service anonymize --enable
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token anonymize
```

The service answers **404** until it's enabled, and every feature of the agent has its own token.

## 2. Let it propose the rules 

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:init-anonymize --scan
```

The agent reads your schema and proposes a transformation for each column that looks personal, plus tables to empty. It writes `~/.db/anonymization.json`, **outside the repository** (mode `0640`): the file maps your schema and never ships with your code.

## 3. Review the rules 

Open the file and check it. A typical result:

```json
{
  "transformations": {
    "users": {
      "name": "fakeName",
      "email": { "type": "fakeEmail", "consistent": true },
      "password": "password",
      "remember_token": "null",
      "phone": "mask:3,2",
      "date_of_birth": "fakeDate"
    },
    "orders": {
      "customer_email": { "type": "fakeEmail", "consistent": true },
      "shipping_address": "fakeAddress",
      "notes": "fakeParagraph",
      "ip_address": "fakeIpv4"
    },
    "invoices": { "vat_number": "fakeIdentifier" }
  },
  "truncate": ["sessions", "jobs", "failed_jobs", "password_reset_tokens", "personal_access_tokens"],
  "options": { "faker_locale": "it_IT", "consistent": true, "seed": "a-private-random-string" }
}
```

| Rule | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `fakeName`, `fakeEmail`, `fakeAddress`, `fakePhoneNumber` | Realistic values in the chosen locale |
| `consistent: true` | `users.email` and `orders.customer_email` stay joinable |
| `password` | Every password becomes the hash of `options.password` (default `password`), so developers can log in as any user |
| `mask:3,2` | Keeps the first 3 and last 2 characters: `+39*******56` |
| `null`, `redact`, `fixed:value` | Remove or replace entirely |
| `truncate` | Empties tables with tokens and sessions |
| Columns not listed | **Copied unchanged**: ids, prices, statuses, timestamps |

Then check the rules against the real database (`php artisan cipi:anonymize --check` does the same plus validation, without dumping):

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:anonymize-audit
```

The audit fails on tables or columns that don't exist and lists personal-looking columns you haven't covered, with a suggestion. **Run it after every migration** that adds a column.

## 4. Request a dump from your laptop 

With [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) and an API token (abilities `apps-view` and `apps-env`), no SSH and no token in your shell history:

```bash
$ cipi-cli prod db anonymize shop --email you@example.com
→ Requesting anonymized dump of 'shop' via https://shop.example.com/cipi/db
✓ Anonymization job queued for 'shop'
```

Within minutes you get an e-mail with a link valid for 15 minutes.

| Other ways to request | When |
| --- | --- |
| `POST https://shop.example.com/cipi/db` with the anonymizer token | From a script or CI |
| `php artisan cipi:anonymize` on the server | No e-mail; writes the file to `storage/cipi/` |
| The MCP `anonymizer` tool | From Claude, Cursor or VS Code |

## 5. Import it locally 

```bash
$ cipi-cli db anonymize download "" -o shop.sql
$ mysql -u root -e "CREATE DATABASE shop_local"
$ mysql -u root shop_local " -o - | mysql -u root shop_local`.

## 6. Check it 

```bash
$ grep -c "real.customer@gmail.com" shop.sql        # must print 0
$ mysql shop_local -e "SELECT name, email FROM users LIMIT 5"
```

## Keep it safe 

| Practice | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Private `seed`, never committed | Fakes can't be mapped back to people |
| Audit after every migration | New personal columns are copied verbatim until listed |
| Rotate the token when people leave | `php artisan cipi:generate-token anonymize` |
| Disable when unused | `php artisan cipi:service anonymize --disable` (endpoints answer 404) |
| Tell people the shared password | Every user's password is `options.password` |
| Document the rules | For your records of processing and DPA |

## Common uses 

| Use | How |
| --- | --- |
| Staging with realistic data | Restore the dump into the staging app ([staging guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production)) |
| Reproduce a customer's bug | Find the user id first with `POST /cipi/db/user` (ids survive anonymization), then look it up in the dump |
| AI assistants | Let them query the anonymized copy, not production ([MCP guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents)) |
| Contractors | Share a file instead of production access |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `queued` but no e-mail | Laravel mail isn't working: test with `php artisan tinker --execute="Mail::raw('t', fn(\$m)=>\$m->to('you@example.com')->subject('t'));"`; the file may already be in `storage/cipi/` |
| 404 from `/cipi/db` | Service disabled or no config: `cipi:service anonymize --enable`, `cipi:init-anonymize` |
| 400 with a list of errors | Fix `anonymization.json`; `cipi:anonymize-audit` prints the same list |
| 410 on download | The 15-minute link expired: request a new dump |
| Job never runs | No queue worker: `sudo cipi worker list shop` |


## Monitor a Laravel app's health with the Cipi Agent and any uptime service

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring

Laravel's `/up` route says the app boots. The agent's `/cipi/health` says whether the app actually works: database, cache, queue, storage and the deploy.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Health check** | A URL that answers "OK" only when the app really works |
| **Uptime monitor** | An outside service that calls it every minute and alerts you |
| **Degraded** | Up, but one dependency (queue, cache) has a problem |

## 1. Enable the endpoint

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:service health --enable
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token health
$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CIPI_HEALTH_TOKEN" https://shop.example.com/cipi/health
```

```json
{
  "status": "healthy",
  "checks": {
    "database": { "ok": true, "driver": "mysql" },
    "cache": { "ok": true, "driver": "database" },
    "queue": { "ok": true, "pending_jobs": 0, "failed_jobs": 0 },
    "storage": { "ok": true, "disk_free_gb": 31.2, "disk_used_percent": 41 },
    "deploy": { "ok": true, "short_commit": "0123456", "in_progress": false }
  }
}
```

If the database, cache, queue or storage fails, `status` becomes `degraded` with **HTTP 503**, which is what uptime services watch.

## 2. Connect an uptime service

| Service | Set up |
| --- | --- |
| Better Stack, UptimeRobot, Pingdom | HTTP monitor on `/cipi/health`, header `Authorization: Bearer `, alert on non-200 |
| Grafana / Prometheus | Blackbox exporter with the header; parse `checks.*.ok` with a JSON exporter |
| Plain cron | `curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer …" https://…/cipi/health >/dev/null || notify` |

## 3. Combine with the server checks

| Layer | Watches | Alerts via |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cipi monitor` | CPU, memory, disk, services, certificates | Your [Cipi channels](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts) |
| `cipi health` | One URL per app, every 5 minutes and after deploys; can roll back | Your Cipi channels |
| `/cipi/health` | Inside the app: DB, cache, queue, storage, deploy | Your uptime service, from outside |

The outside view catches what the server can't see about itself: DNS, network, a down server.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Always 401 | Missing `Authorization: Bearer` header in the monitor |
| `queue` not ok | Failed or pending jobs above threshold: check workers and `queue:failed` |
| `storage` not ok | Disk full or permissions: `cipi app fix-permissions shop`, check disk |
| Monitor flaps | Increase its timeout; the check queries the database each time |


## Cipi Agent: connect your Laravel app to its server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-laravel-mcp

`cipi/agent` is a Laravel package that lets your app talk to the server it runs on. One `composer require` and the app gains five features, each behind its own token and each off until you want it.

| Feature | Endpoint / command | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push-to-deploy | `POST /cipi/webhook` | [Webhook deploys](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-webhook-deploy) |
| Health | `GET /cipi/health` | [Uptime monitoring](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring) |
| MCP for AI assistants | `/cipi/mcp` | [Claude, Cursor and the Cipi MCP](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents) |
| `cipi.yml` tooling | `php artisan cipi:yml` | [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml) |
| Anonymized dumps | `php artisan cipi:anonymize`, `/cipi/db` | [Safe data for developers](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) |

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Agent** | A Composer package inside your app that talks to the server it runs on |
| **Service** | One feature of the agent (health, MCP, anonymizer…), each off by default |
| **Token** | One secret per service, in the app's `.env` |

## 1. Install

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ git commit -am "Add Cipi Agent" && git push
```

On a Cipi server, `cipi app create` already wrote the `.env` variables; the service provider auto-discovers. Laravel 12 or 13, PHP 8.3+.

## 2. Check it after the deploy

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop cipi:status
```

`cipi:status` shows configuration, environment, live release and commit, enabled features, `cipi.yml` validity and database connectivity.

## 3. Turn on what you need

```bash
$ php artisan cipi:service health --enable && php artisan cipi:generate-token health
$ php artisan cipi:service mcp --enable && php artisan cipi:generate-token mcp
$ php artisan cipi:service anonymize --enable && php artisan cipi:generate-token anonymize
```

Run them as the app user (`ssh shop@server`) or through `sudo cipi app artisan shop …`. Each feature has its own token; a disabled feature answers **404**, so it's invisible.

## 4. Use it in CI

```yaml
- run: php artisan cipi:yml validate --json --app=shop
```

The agent ships the same `cipi.yml` validator as the server, so a broken file fails the pipeline instead of the deploy.

## Agent or API?

The agent works **inside one app**, on its domain. The [Cipi API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) runs on its own domain and manages the **whole server**. Install the [PHP SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk) next to the agent and the app's MCP gains server-side tools: rollback, database backup, job status.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi:status` says not configured | The `.env` lacks the `CIPI_*` keys Cipi writes at creation: compare with a fresh app and add the missing ones |
| An endpoint answers 404 | The service is disabled: `cipi:service  --enable` |
| 403 with a valid-looking token | Token from another service: each has its own |
| Package refuses to install | Laravel 12 or 13 and PHP 8.3+ are required |


## Push-to-deploy Laravel from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Gitea

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-webhook-deploy

With a token, Cipi sets up the webhook on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps by itself. This guide shows what happens behind it, and how to wire Gitea or Forgejo by hand.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Webhook** | An HTTP call your Git provider makes on each push |
| **Signature** | A hash of the request made with a shared secret, proving it came from your provider |
| **Trigger** | A small file the webhook leaves; a cron starts the deploy from it |

```flow
git push | to the deploy branch
> You push to the app's deploy branch. Other branches are ignored.
Webhook | POST /cipi/webhook, signed
> Your Git provider sends a signed `POST` to the app's webhook URL.
Verify | signature, branch
> Cipi checks the signature (only someone with the secret can trigger a deploy) and the branch.
Trigger file | instant HTTP answer
> It writes a small trigger file and answers immediately, so the provider never sees a timeout, however long the build.
Deploy | within a minute, as the app user
> Within a minute a cron job picks up the trigger and deploys as the app's own user, with zero downtime.
```

The request never runs the deploy itself: it verifies the push and drops a trigger. A cron picks it up and deploys with zero downtime. A slow build can't time out a webhook, and a forged request can't start anything.

## 1. Get the URL and token

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --webhook
```

## 2. Add the webhook

| Provider | Payload URL | Secret / token | Events |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | `https://shop.example.com/cipi/webhook` | Secret = token (HMAC-SHA256), content type JSON | Just the push event |
| GitLab | same | Secret token | Push events |
| Bitbucket Cloud | same | Secret (HMAC) | Repository push |
| Gitea / Forgejo | same | Secret (HMAC) | Push events |

Only pushes to the app's branch (`CIPI_DEPLOY_BRANCH`) deploy; others answer `skipped`. GitHub's ping answers `pong`.

## 3. Push and watch

```bash
$ git push origin main
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --status      # running, queued or idle
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --log
```

## 4. Know who pushed

Each trigger records what the push claimed (provider, pusher, commit, delivery ID, IP) in the [deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit). It's recorded as a claim, not a fact: the ledger is hash-chained, so it can't be quietly edited later.

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --audit
```

## Rotate the secret

```bash
$ sudo cipi app webhook recreate shop --rotate-secret
```

Need tests before deploying? Turn the webhook off and use [a pipeline](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Provider shows 401/403 | Secret or token mismatch: copy it again from `cipi deploy shop --webhook` |
| 200 but no deploy | Push to a branch that isn't the deploy branch |
| Deploy starts a minute later | Normal: the cron picks the trigger up within a minute |
| Nothing at all reaches the server | Webhook URL wrong, or the app is behind Zero Trust without a bypass rule for `/cipi/webhook` |


## Manage Laravel in production with Claude, Cursor and the Cipi MCP

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents

MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets an AI assistant call tools. Cipi ships two MCP servers, so you can ask *"is production healthy, what failed last night, deploy main"* and get answers from the real app, not guesses.

| | Agent MCP | Server MCP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Endpoint | `https://shop.example.com/cipi/mcp` | `https://api.example.com/mcp` |
| Scope | One app: health, logs, database, Artisan, deploy, `cipi.yml` | The server: apps, domains, SSL, databases, backups, PHP |
| Installed with | `composer require cipi/agent` | `cipi api api.example.com` |

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **MCP** | Model Context Protocol: a standard way for an AI assistant to call tools |
| **Tool** | One action the assistant can take: read logs, run a query, deploy |
| **Token** | The secret your assistant sends with every call; scoped and revocable |
| **Guard** | A rule that blocks dangerous calls whatever the assistant asks |

```flow
You ask | in Claude, Cursor, VS Code
> You type a question in plain words in Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or VS Code: "is production healthy?"
Assistant | picks a tool
> The assistant chooses which tool to call (`health`, `logs`, `deploy`…) and with which arguments.
MCP server | checks token and guards
> The MCP server checks the token, then the guards: blocked SQL, blocked Artisan commands, read-only mode.
App or server | runs it, output redacted
> The tool runs against the real app or server. Secrets are masked in the output before the assistant sees it.
```

## 1. Turn on the agent's MCP server

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent        # commit, push, deploy
# as the app user on the server (or: sudo cipi app artisan shop …)
$ php artisan cipi:service mcp --enable
$ php artisan cipi:generate-token mcp
$ php artisan cipi:mcp               # endpoint + ready-to-paste config
```

## 2. Connect your assistant

```bash
# Claude Code
$ claude mcp add --transport http cipi-shop https://shop.example.com/cipi/mcp \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_CIPI_MCP_TOKEN"
```

```json
// Cursor: ~/.cursor/mcp.json
{ "mcpServers": { "cipi-shop": {
    "type": "http", "url": "https://shop.example.com/cipi/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_CIPI_MCP_TOKEN" } } } }
```

VS Code and Claude Desktop configs are in the [MCP docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp#clients). VS Code can prompt for the token so it's never committed.

## 3. Ask real questions

```text
You:    Is production healthy, and what commit is live?
Claude: [health, deploy_status] Healthy. Release 20261109103000, commit 0123456 (webhook, 42 s).
You:    Show the last errors and tell me which job fails.
Claude: [logs level=error] InvoiceJob: column invoices.paid_at not found.
        [artisan migrate:status] 2026_11_08_add_paid_at is pending.
You:    Deploy main and note that Jane asked.
Claude: [deploy actor=jane@example.com] Queued; it runs within a minute.
```

| Tool | What it's good for |
| --- | --- |
| `health`, `deploy_status` | "Is it up? What's live? Is a deploy running?" |
| `logs` | Laravel, Nginx, PHP, worker, Horizon, Reverb and deploy logs with level and keyword filters |
| `db_schema`, `db_query` | Understand data; reads capped at 100 rows |
| `artisan` | `migrate:status`, `queue:retry`, cache commands; dangerous ones blocked |
| `env_check`, `cipi_yml` | Missing variables; validate a `cipi.yml` draft before you commit it |
| `deploy` | Queue a zero-downtime deploy, recorded in the audit with who asked |

## 4. Add the server MCP

For server work ("create a staging app", "issue the certificate", "back up the database"), install the API on its own domain and create a token with `mcp-access`:

```bash
$ sudo cipi api api.example.com
$ sudo cipi api token create --name=claude --abilities=mcp-access
$ claude mcp add --transport http cipi-server https://api.example.com/mcp \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer "
```

Destructive host operations (dropping databases, removing PHP versions, installing software outside the [closed package catalog](https://cipi.sh/docs/packages)) are kept off the API on purpose, and the server MCP doesn't install or remove even those packages: it lists them.

## Guardrails in one table

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| One token per feature | Rotate with `php artisan cipi:generate-token mcp`; disabled routes answer 404 |
| SQL and Artisan guards | No DDL, no `GRANT`, no `migrate:fresh`, no `tinker` |
| Redaction | Secrets masked in every output |
| Origin check | Browser requests from other hosts refused |
| Tool annotations | Clients know which tools are read-only and ask before acting |
| Audit | Deploys record the actor in the [hash-chained ledger](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit) |

> [!tip] For production, start with `CIPI_MCP_DB_WRITE=false`. Need realistic data for the assistant to experiment on? Give it an [anonymized dump](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) instead of production.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| 401 Unauthorized | Wrong or old token: generate a new one, update the client config |
| 404 on `/cipi/mcp` | Service disabled: `php artisan cipi:service mcp --enable` |
| Tool refused: blocked command | By design (DDL, `migrate:fresh`, `tinker`): run it yourself if you really need it |
| Query returns 100 rows only | Reads are capped: ask for a narrower query or an aggregate |
| Client can't connect | The client needs HTTP transport support; update it |


## Spec-driven development with AI agents in Laravel

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/spec-driven-development-ai-laravel

AI coding agents are good at implementing a clear, testable specification and bad at guessing what you meant. The teams getting value write the spec first, keep the agent inside guardrails, and give it eyes on production through MCP.

```flow
Spec | what and why, acceptance criteria | #spec
Tests | written from the spec | #tests
Agent | implements until tests pass
Review | a human, on a preview URL | #review
Production | deploy, then observe through MCP | #production
```

## 1. Write the spec, not the prompt 
| A good spec has | Example |
| --- | --- |
| The user and the problem | "Accountants can't find unpaid invoices quickly" |
| Acceptance criteria | "Filter by status and due date; overdue rows highlighted" |
| Constraints | "No new tables; reuse `invoices.paid_at`" |
| Out of scope | "No export in this iteration" |

Tools like [Larapilot](https://larapilot.web.ap.it/) structure this with personas and review steps on top of Laravel Boost.

## 2. Tests before code 
Ask the agent to write Pest tests from the acceptance criteria first, review them, then let it implement until they pass. The tests are the contract.

## 3. Review on a real URL 
Push the branch and get a [preview environment](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments). Reviewers click instead of pulling code; seed it with an [anonymized dump](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) so edge cases from real data show up.

## 4. Close the loop on production 
After the deploy, the same assistant can check the result through the [Cipi MCP](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents):

```text
You:    Did the invoices release go out cleanly? Any new errors since?
Claude: [deploy_status] Release 134 live, 58 s, from the pipeline.
        [logs level=error since=deploy] None.
```

## Guardrails that matter

| Risk | Guardrail |
| --- | --- |
| Agent runs destructive SQL | MCP SQL guard blocks DDL and multi-statements; `CIPI_MCP_DB_WRITE=false` |
| Agent sees personal data | Redaction in outputs; anonymized dumps for experiments |
| Agent deploys untested code | Deploy only through CI with tests; the MCP `deploy` tool records who asked |
| Server config drifts | `cipi.yml` changes go through pull requests like code |


## Add Laravel security checks (SAST) to CI with Checkpoint

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/checkpoint-laravel-sast-ci

Most security bugs in Laravel apps are small and repeated: a `whereRaw` with a variable, `$guarded = []`, `{!! $input !!}` in a view, a forgotten `dd()`, a dependency with a known CVE. [Checkpoint](https://checkpoint.web.ap.it) finds them in seconds, on your laptop and in CI, so they never reach the server.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **SAST** | Static analysis: reading code (not running it) to find risky patterns |
| **CVE** | A publicly known vulnerability in a package or program |
| **CI** | The pipeline that runs on every push (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) |
| **Gate** | A step that stops the pipeline when something is wrong |
| **Suppression** | Accepting one specific finding on purpose, by its hash |

```flow
Write code | on your laptop
> You run `php artisan checkpoint:scan` before committing, like a test.
Push | to GitHub or GitLab
> The pipeline starts.
Checkpoint | in CI
> The same scan runs in CI. A FAIL exits with code 1 and the pipeline stops: nothing is deployed.
Deploy | only if clean
> If the scan (and your tests) pass, the pipeline deploys with Cipi ([CI/CD guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow)).
```

## Before you start 

- A Laravel project (8 to 13) on PHP 8.1 or newer.
- For the CI part: a repository on GitHub or GitLab, deployed with Cipi.

## 1. Install 

```bash
$ composer require --dev andreapollastri/checkpoint
```

`--dev` because it's a development tool: it's not installed on production (Cipi deploys with `--no-dev`).

## 2. Run it 

```bash
$ php artisan checkpoint:scan
```

Each check prints **PASS**, **WARN** or **FAIL**, with the file and line and a short hash in brackets.

| Result | Meaning | Do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PASS | Nothing found | Nothing |
| WARN | Possibly risky, needs a human look | Review; fix or suppress |
| FAIL | Likely a real problem | Fix before deploying |

Useful options:

```bash
$ php artisan checkpoint:scan --only="SQL Injection Risks,CSRF Protection"
$ php artisan checkpoint:scan --skip="NPM CVE Audit"
$ php artisan checkpoint:scan --fail-on-warn
$ php artisan checkpoint:scan --json | tee checkpoint-report.json
```

## 3. What it checks 

| Area | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| Dependencies | Composer CVE audit, npm CVE audit, PHP CVE audit, outdated and abandoned packages, package freshness (supply chain), supply-chain tooling, Composer configuration, suspicious vendor autoload |
| Configuration | Environment (`APP_DEBUG`, `APP_KEY`…), `.gitignore` for sensitive files, file permissions, CORS, session and cookie security, PHP `php.ini`, EOL versions, public directory exposure |
| Code | SQL injection, mass assignment, XSS, CSRF, open redirect, command injection, insecure deserialization, SSRF, TLS verification turned off, path traversal, weak cryptography, insecure random numbers, XXE, hardcoded secrets, debug functions, sensitive data exposure |

## 4. Fix the classic ones 

| Finding | Risky | Safer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQL injection | `->whereRaw("total > $min")` | `->whereRaw('total > ?', [$min])` or `->where('total', '>', $min)` |
| Mass assignment | `protected $guarded = [];` | `protected $fillable = ['name', 'email'];` |
| XSS | `{!! $comment->body !!}` | `{{ $comment->body }}`, or sanitize HTML first |
| Open redirect | `redirect($request->input('next'))` | `redirect()->intended('/dashboard')` or an allowlist |
| SSRF | `Http::get($request->url)` | Validate the host against an allowlist |
| TLS off | `Http::withoutVerifying()` | Remove it; fix the certificate instead |
| Debug left | `dd($order)` in a controller | Remove it; use logs |

## 5. Accept a finding on purpose 

Sometimes a pattern is fine (a `whereRaw` with a constant, for example). Publish the config and add the finding's hash:

```bash
$ php artisan vendor:publish --tag=checkpoint-config
```

```php
// config/checkpoint.php
'suppressed' => [
    '7d02be', // ReportController: whereRaw with a constant, reviewed 2026-11
],
'exclude_paths' => ['legacy/'],
```

Leave a comment with each hash so the next person knows why.

## 6. Block risky code in CI 

GitHub Actions, generated for you:

```bash
$ php artisan checkpoint:github       # writes .github/workflows/checkpoint.yml
```

It runs on pushes to `main`/`master` and on pull requests, installs dependencies, runs the scan and uploads `checkpoint-report.json` as an artifact. GitLab: `php artisan checkpoint:gitlab`.

To make it a **gate** before your Cipi deploy, put the scan in the same workflow, before the deploy job:

```yaml
jobs:
  checkpoint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.5', coverage: none }
      - run: composer install --prefer-dist --no-progress --no-interaction
      - run: php artisan checkpoint:scan
  deploy:
    needs: checkpoint                  # runs only if the scan passed
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SERVER_HOST }}
          username: cipi
          key: ${{ secrets.CI_SSH_KEY }}
          script: "sudo cipi deploy shop && { curl -fsS --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 --retry-all-errors https://shop.example.com/up >/dev/null || { sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback; exit 1; }; }"
```

Turn off the app's push webhook so only the pipeline deploys ([CI/CD guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-ci-cd-git-workflow)).

## 7. Also on every composer install (optional) 

```bash
$ php artisan checkpoint:install-hooks       # adds the scan to post-install/post-update
$ php artisan checkpoint:install-hooks --remove
```

## Checkpoint, Hackly and Cipi together 

| Layer | Tool | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your code, before deploy | Checkpoint | Every push |
| Your running sites and repositories | [Hackly](https://cipi.sh/guides/hackly-security-scanning) | Weekly, before releases |
| The server | Cipi | Every night: PHP patches, services, firewall, integrity scans |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Composer/npm audit says it can't run | Install the tool in CI, or skip that check with `--skip` |
| Environment check fails in CI | It reads CI's environment: set `APP_DEBUG=false` there, or skip it in CI |
| Too many WARNs on old code | Fix FAILs first; suppress reviewed WARNs by hash; tighten with `--fail-on-warn` later |
| Package freshness FAIL | A dependency was released in the last 3 days: wait, or whitelist it in `package_freshness` |
| Pipeline passes but deploys anyway on push | The webhook is still on: remove it from the repository |


## Put a Laravel server behind Cloudflare Zero Trust, step by step

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel

Normally a server waits for visitors on open ports (80, 443 for websites, 22 for SSH), and anyone on the internet can knock. With a **Cloudflare Tunnel**, your server dials out to Cloudflare instead, and visitors reach it **through** Cloudflare. Once every app goes through the tunnel you can close the ports completely: nothing left to attack directly. Cipi does it in small, reversible steps, and nothing closes until you ask.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Tunnel** | A connection your server opens *to* Cloudflare; visitor traffic comes back through it |
| **cloudflared** | The small program on the server that keeps the tunnel open |
| **Access** | Cloudflare's login wall: only people you allow get through |
| **Policy** | Who is allowed: e-mail addresses, a domain (`@acme.com`), a group |
| **Locking** | Closing ports 80/443 and 22 once the tunnel carries everything |

```stack
Visitors and you | browser, ssh
Cloudflare | CDN, WAF, Access login
Tunnel | outbound from your server
Your server | ports 80, 443, 22 closed
```

```flow
Token & enable | tunnel; ports still open | #token
Route | apps, staging, panel | #route
SSH | through Access | #ssh
Certificates | DNS-01 or Origin CA | #certificates
Test | everything, from outside | #test
Lock | close the ports | #lock
```

## Before you start 

- Your domain's DNS on Cloudflare (free plan is fine). See [Cloudflare in front of Laravel](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-proxy-ssl-wildcard) if it isn't yet.
- A Cloudflare **Zero Trust** organisation: open **Zero Trust** in the Cloudflare dashboard once and choose a team name (free plan). Under **Settings → Authentication** keep **One-time PIN** (login codes by e-mail) or add Google/GitHub.
- Your **Account ID**: Cloudflare dashboard → your domain → right column, *Account ID*.
- Access to your VPS provider's **web console**, in case you lock yourself out.
- `cloudflared` on your laptop for SSH later (`brew install cloudflared`, or the package from Cloudflare's site).

## 1. Create the token and enable the tunnel 

In Cloudflare: **My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token → Custom token**, with these permissions:

| Scope | Permission | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account · Cloudflare Tunnel | Edit | Creating the tunnel |
| Account · Access: Apps and Policies | Edit | Login walls |
| Zone · DNS | Edit | Pointing hostnames at the tunnel |
| Zone · SSL and Certificates | Edit (optional) | Origin CA certificates |

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt token set --token=CF_API_TOKEN --account=ACCOUNT_ID
$ sudo cipi zt enable
$ sudo cipi zt status
```

`enable` installs `cloudflared`, creates the tunnel, and teaches Nginx, Fail2ban and CrowdSec Cloudflare's IP ranges so apps see real visitor IPs. **No port is closed**: if anything goes wrong, your sites keep working as before.

## 2. Route the apps through the tunnel 

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt hostname add shop          # public site, through CDN and WAF
$ sudo cipi zt hostname add shop-stg      # staging
$ sudo cipi zt hostname add --gui         # the web panel, if installed
```

Each command points the app's hostname at the tunnel (a DNS record in Cloudflare). Now add a login wall where only your team should enter:

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt access enable shop-stg
$ sudo cipi zt access enable --gui
```

```flow
Visitor opens staging | shop-stg.example.com
> The request reaches Cloudflare, not your server.
Access asks who they are | e-mail code, Google, SSO
> Cloudflare shows its login page. With One-time PIN, the visitor types their e-mail and receives a code.
Policy decides | allowed or not
> Only addresses (or domains) in the Access policy get in. Edit the policy in Zero Trust → Access → Applications.
Request goes through the tunnel | to your server
> Allowed visitors reach the app. Everyone else never touches your server. `/cipi/webhook` is bypassed so Git pushes still deploy.
```

## 3. SSH through the tunnel 

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt ssh enable --hostname=ssh.example.com
```

On your laptop, add to `~/.ssh/config` (Cipi prints this block for you):

```text
Host ssh.example.com
  ProxyCommand cloudflared access ssh --hostname %h
  User cipi
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

Then `ssh ssh.example.com`. The first time, a browser window asks you to log in to Access; after that, SSH works as usual, with your key.

## 4. Certificates that keep renewing 

Once port 80 is closed, Let's Encrypt can't check your server over HTTP. Switch each app to DNS validation, or use a long-lived Cloudflare Origin CA certificate:

| Option | Command | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Let's Encrypt over DNS | `sudo cipi ssl dns set --token=…` then `sudo cipi ssl install shop --dns=cloudflare` | Renews automatically; also works without the tunnel |
| Cloudflare Origin CA | `sudo cipi zt origin-cert shop` | 15 years; trusted only by Cloudflare, fine behind the proxy |

`cipi zt lock http` refuses to run while any app still renews over HTTP, so you can't forget one.

## 5. Test everything from outside 

From your laptop (not from the server):

| Check | Expected |
| --- | --- |
| `https://shop.example.com` | The site, through Cloudflare |
| `https://shop-stg.example.com` | Cloudflare's login page first |
| `ssh ssh.example.com` | A shell, after the Access login |
| A `git push` to the deploy branch | A deploy (check `sudo cipi deploy shop --status`) |
| `sudo cipi zt status` | Tunnel healthy, every hostname listed |

Don't go on until all five pass.

## 6. Close the ports 

```bash
$ sudo cipi zt lock http --yes     # 80/443 closed (or Cloudflare-only if something isn't on the tunnel)
$ sudo cipi zt lock ssh --yes      # 22 closed: SSH only through Access
$ sudo cipi zt status
```

> [!warning] Lock SSH last, only after `ssh ssh.example.com` works from your machine, and keep your provider's web console open in another tab. Cipi refuses to close 22 if the tunnel doesn't carry SSH yet.

## Undo any step 

| Step | Undo |
| --- | --- |
| `lock ssh` | `sudo cipi zt ssh unlock` |
| `lock http` | `sudo cipi zt unlock http` |
| `access enable` | `sudo cipi zt access disable ` |
| `hostname add` | `sudo cipi zt hostname remove ` |
| `ssh enable` | `sudo cipi zt ssh disable` |
| Everything | `sudo cipi zt disable` (reopens 22/80/443, removes what Cipi created in Cloudflare) |

Locked out? Log in through your provider's web console as `cipi` and run the unlock commands.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| 502 / 1033 from Cloudflare | Tunnel down: `sudo cipi zt status`; check `cloudflared` is running |
| Access login loops | Clear cookies for the team domain; check the policy includes your e-mail |
| SSH: `websocket: bad handshake` | `cloudflared` missing or old on your laptop; update it |
| `lock http` refused | An app still renews over HTTP: move it to `--dns=cloudflare` or `origin-cert` |
| Webhook deploys stopped | Bot Fight Mode or a WAF rule challenges `/cipi/webhook`: add a skip rule |
| Visitors' IPs all the same | Run `sudo cipi zt enable` again to refresh the real-IP setup; Laravel must trust proxies ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-proxy-ssl-wildcard#real-ip)) |
| Locked out completely | Provider web console → `sudo cipi zt ssh unlock` |


## Block attackers automatically with CrowdSec on a Laravel server

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/crowdsec-laravel-server

Every public server is probed all day: bots looking for `/wp-login.php`, `.env` files, old admin panels, known exploits. They rarely get in, but they fill your logs and waste resources, and the occasional one finds something. **CrowdSec** spots that behaviour in your logs and blocks the source at the firewall, helped by a blocklist shared by its whole community. On Cipi it's one command, with guards so it can't lock you out.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Engine** | The CrowdSec service that reads logs and decides |
| **Scenario** | A pattern of bad behaviour, e.g. "many 404s on admin paths" |
