| **Decision** | A ban on an IP, for a duration |
| **Bouncer** | The part that enforces decisions; here, the firewall |
| **Community blocklist** | IPs reported as attacking by many CrowdSec users |
| **Allowlist** | Addresses that must never be banned |

```flow
A bot probes your site | /.env, /wp-login.php, exploits
> Requests hit Nginx like any visitor and are written to each app's access log (`/home/*/logs/nginx-*.log`).
CrowdSec reads the logs | nginx, sshd, linux scenarios
> The engine matches the behaviour against scenarios from the nginx, sshd and linux collections.
A decision is made | ban the IP for a while
> When a scenario triggers, CrowdSec creates a decision: this IP is banned for a period.
The firewall bouncer drops it | before it reaches Nginx
> The firewall bouncer drops traffic from that IP at the network level: your apps never see it again.
The community learns | shared blocklist
> Known attackers reported by others are blocked on your server too, often before they try.
```

## Before you start 

- A Cipi server with at least **512 MB of free RAM**.
- If the server is behind Cloudflare's proxy (orange cloud): run `sudo cipi zt enable` first. It configures the real visitor IP (and closes no ports). Without it, Cipi refuses to enable CrowdSec, to avoid banning Cloudflare.
- Note your own public IP (`curl -s ifconfig.me` from your laptop) and any office or CI addresses.

## 1. Enable it 

```bash
$ ssh cipi@YOUR_SERVER
$ sudo cipi crowdsec enable
$ sudo cipi crowdsec status
```

| What `enable` does | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Installs the engine and the firewall bouncer | Detection plus enforcement |
| Allowlists your current SSH session's IP first | You can't ban yourself while enabling |
| Allowlists Let's Encrypt, localhost, private ranges | Certificates keep renewing |
| Allowlists GitHub, Bitbucket and GitLab webhook ranges (refreshed weekly) | Push-to-deploy keeps working |
| Starts a small rescue listener | A way back in if you're ever banned (step 4) |
| Installs the nginx, sshd and linux collections | The scenarios that matter on a web server |

## 2. Allow the addresses you trust 

```bash
$ sudo cipi crowdsec allow 203.0.113.42      # office
$ sudo cipi crowdsec allow 198.51.100.7      # CI runner, uptime monitor
```

Remove one with `sudo cipi crowdsec unallow `. Allowlist monitors and CI that hit the site often, or run security scans against it (for example [Hackly](https://cipi.sh/guides/hackly-security-scanning)'s scanner IP).

## 3. See what it blocks 

```bash
$ sudo cipi crowdsec status        # engine, bouncer, rescue, active decisions
$ sudo cipi ban list               # banned IPs, CrowdSec and Fail2ban together
$ sudo cipi ban unban 192.0.2.10   # lift a ban everywhere at once
```

Within a day you'll usually see bans for scanners that probed paths your apps don't have. With the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/firewall#panel) (Cipi 5.14.0+), the server's Firewall tab shows the same list, CrowdSec's decisions and Fail2ban's bans together, each with *Unban*, and edits the allowlist.

## 4. If you ban yourself: the rescue 

Changed network and can't reach the server any more? Cipi prepared a way back:

```bash
# print it now, store it OFF the server (password manager)
$ sudo cipi crowdsec rescue token
```

```flow
You're banned | SSH and site unreachable
> Your new IP triggered a ban (or a typo'd password did, in Fail2ban).
Run the saved curl | from where you are
> The command calls a small TLS listener on a high port that stays open even while you're banned.
Your IP is allowlisted | bans lifted
> It allowlists the IP the request comes from (never a header), and lifts its bans in CrowdSec and Fail2ban.
A new token is mailed | old one dies
> Each token works once. A fresh one is e-mailed to you, so print and store it again.
```

The rescue grants nothing except the ability to connect again; wrong tokens are throttled. `sudo cipi crowdsec rescue rotate` makes a new token at any time. The provider's web console is always the last resort.

## 5. Remove it 

```bash
$ sudo cipi crowdsec disable
```

Firewall rules are flushed **before** the packages are removed, so nothing stays blocking.

## Your defence layers 

| Layer | Stops | On Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Firewall (UFW) | Everything except 22, 80, 443 | Always on |
| Fail2ban | SSH password guessing | Always on |
| CrowdSec | Scanners, probes, known attackers on the web | `cipi crowdsec enable` |
| Cloudflare proxy / Zero Trust | Bad requests before they reach you; closed ports | [Zero Trust guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) |
| Patching | Known vulnerabilities in PHP and Nginx | Nightly ([CVE case study](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching)) |
| Your code | App-level bugs | [Checkpoint](https://cipi.sh/guides/checkpoint-laravel-sast-ci), [Hackly](https://cipi.sh/guides/hackly-security-scanning) |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `enable` refused: proxy without real IP | `sudo cipi zt enable` first (it closes nothing) |
| `enable` refused: not enough RAM | Free memory or keep Fail2ban only |
| A colleague is banned | `sudo cipi ban unban `, then `sudo cipi crowdsec allow ` |
| Uptime monitor shows outages | Allowlist the monitor's IPs |
| Git pushes stopped deploying | Run `sudo cipi crowdsec refresh` to update webhook ranges; check `cipi ban list` |
| You're locked out | Rescue curl (step 4), or the provider's web console |


## Security-test your Laravel apps with Hackly, self-hosted

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/hackly-security-scanning

Patching servers (which Cipi does for you) is half of security. The other half is checking **your own** sites and code for weaknesses: exposed paths, weak TLS, missing headers, vulnerable dependencies, leaked secrets. [Hackly](https://hackly.web.ap.it) runs the industry's open-source scanners for you, safely, from one panel.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Target** | A domain you own and want to scan, e.g. `shop.example.com` |
| **DAST** | Dynamic testing: probing the running site from outside, like an attacker would |
| **SAST** | Static testing: reading the source code for dangerous patterns |
| **SCA** | Checking your dependencies (Composer, npm) for known vulnerabilities |
| **Finding** | One problem found, ranked High, Medium or Low |
| **Ownership check** | A DNS TXT record proving you control the domain, required before scanning |

```flow
Add target | your domain
> You register `shop.example.com` in Hackly. Nothing is scanned yet.
Prove ownership | DNS TXT record
> Hackly shows a TXT record. You publish it at your DNS provider and click **Check DNS**. No proof, no scan: Hackly can't be used against sites you don't control.
Scan | quick, standard or deep
> Scanners run in the background on Hackly's queue: DNS and TLS, ports, path discovery, Nuclei templates, OWASP ZAP; plus Semgrep, Trivy, Gitleaks, Checkov and Composer audits on linked repositories.
Triage | High to Low
> You go through findings by severity and mark each one Acknowledged, Fixed or False positive (with a note).
Report | PDF or Markdown
> Export a report for your team or your client, or share one finding through a link you can revoke.
```

## Before you start 

- A **separate** server for scanning, with Cipi installed: 2 vCPU and 4 GB RAM is a comfortable minimum (OWASP ZAP is Java and memory-hungry).
- A subdomain such as `hackly.example.com` pointing at it.
- Working e-mail (weekly digest, e-mail two-factor codes).
- A GitHub account to fork Hackly, and (optional) a read-only GitHub token for repository scans.
- Written permission for every domain you scan that isn't yours.

## 1. Fork and create the app 

Fork [github.com/andreapollastri/hackly](https://github.com/andreapollastri/hackly), then:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@SCANNER_IP
$ sudo cipi app create --user=hackly --domain=hackly.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:YOU/hackly.git --branch=main \
    --node-build='npm ci && npm run build'
```

Add the deploy key to your fork, then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy hackly
$ sudo cipi ssl install hackly
$ sudo cipi app artisan hackly db:seed --force
```

The seeded admin is `admin@hackly.test` / `password`: **change it immediately** and enable two-factor authentication.

## 2. Install the scanners 

The scanners are system programs, installed once as root with Hackly's own scripts. On a Cipi server, become root from the `cipi` user (`su root`), then:

```bash
# cd /home/hackly/current
# bash scripts/install-scanner-binaries-ubuntu.sh     # dig, whois, nmap, nuclei, nikto, wpscan, ZAP
# bash scripts/install-repo-scanners.sh               # semgrep, trivy, gitleaks, checkov
# exit
$ sudo cipi app artisan hackly hackly:check-binaries
```

Missing tools aren't fatal: tasks that need them are skipped and **Settings → Scanner health** tells you what's missing and how to fix it.

## 3. Production settings 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env hackly      # then set:
```

```text
HACKLY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_TARGETS=false      # never scan internal addresses
HACKLY_ALLOWLIST_ONLY=true              # only domains you list…
HACKLY_ALLOWLIST=example.com            # …here
HACKLY_JOB_TIMEOUT=960                  # longer than the slowest scanner (ZAP)
MAIL_MAILER=smtp                        # plus MAIL_HOST, MAIL_USERNAME…
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan hackly config:cache
$ sudo cipi worker restart hackly
```

Cipi already runs what Hackly needs: a queue worker (scans run there) and the scheduler (Sunday digest, daily scanner database updates, self-updates).

## 4. Add a target and prove you own it 

**Targets → New**: enter the domain. Hackly shows the TXT record to publish:

Add it at your DNS provider (Cloudflare: **DNS → Add record → TXT**). Existing TXT records (SPF and others) stay. Then **Check DNS**. You can delete the record afterwards.

> [!tip] The scanner's IP is shown on that screen. If the site sits behind a WAF, CrowdSec or Cloudflare rules, allowlist that IP for the duration of the scans, or results will be blocked and incomplete.

## 5. Run a scan 

| Profile | What it adds | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quick | DNS, mail security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), TLS, fingerprint | First look, any time |
| Standard | Ports, path discovery, Nuclei templates | Weekly |
| Deep | OWASP ZAP baseline | Before releases, off-peak |

From the CLI: `sudo cipi app artisan hackly hackly:scan shop.example.com --profile=standard`.

## 6. Scan your repositories too 

**Settings → GitHub tokens**: add a fine-grained token with **read-only** access to the repositories. Then **Repositories → New** `you/shop`, and link it to the `shop.example.com` target. A linked pair is scanned together, and the routes found in the code feed the site scan.

| Scanner | Finds |
| --- | --- |
| Semgrep | Dangerous PHP and Laravel patterns |
| Trivy, Composer audit, OSV | Vulnerable dependencies |
| Gitleaks | Secrets committed to Git |
| Checkov | Risky infrastructure files |
| Checkpoint | Laravel-specific checks ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/checkpoint-laravel-sast-ci)) |

## 7. Triage and report 

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Open | Needs a look |
| Acknowledged | Real, planned |
| Fixed | Resolved; reopens if detected again |
| False positive | Not a problem (a note is required) |

Export a scan as **PDF or Markdown**, copy a finding as Markdown or as an AI prompt for your assistant, or share a read-only link you can turn off.

## A routine that works 

```flow
Every push | Checkpoint in CI
> Code-level checks before anything deploys ([Checkpoint guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/checkpoint-laravel-sast-ci)).
Weekly | standard scan + repos
> Hackly scans production and the linked repository; the Sunday digest summarises what changed.
Before big releases | deep scan on staging
> ZAP against staging, where heavy traffic doesn't bother anyone.
Every night | Cipi patches the server
> PHP and services patched by Cipi; Hackly covers what's yours: code, config, dependencies.
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Scan stays queued | Hackly's queue worker isn't running: `sudo cipi worker list hackly` |
| Tasks skipped | Scanner missing: Settings → Scanner health, re-run the install scripts as root |
| Check DNS fails | The TXT record isn't visible yet (wait), or it was added to the wrong name |
| Few or no web findings | A WAF blocked the scanner: allowlist its IP during the scan |
| Scan killed after ~15 minutes | Raise `HACKLY_JOB_TIMEOUT` and the queue's `retry_after` (`DB_QUEUE_RETRY_AFTER`) |
| No digest e-mail | Mail settings, or the scheduler is off: `sudo cipi schedule status hackly` |


## Laravel production security checklist

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-security-checklist

Security on your own server is a list of boring things done every time. Here's the list, split between what's yours (the app) and what the server should do for you.

## The app

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| `APP_DEBUG=false`, `APP_ENV=production` | `sudo cipi app env shop --get=APP_DEBUG` |
| Dependencies without known CVEs | `composer audit` in CI; [Checkpoint](https://checkpoint.web.ap.it/) for a broader Laravel audit |
| Secrets only in `.env`, never committed | `cipi.yml` lists required names (`env.required`), never values |
| Rate limiting on login, API and forms | `RateLimiter::for(...)` and the `throttle` middleware |
| Authorization on every route | Policies and gates; test them |
| Mass-assignment guarded | `$fillable` on models |
| Uploads validated and stored outside `public/` | `mimes:` rules, `Storage::disk('local')` |
| Admin tools (Horizon, Telescope, Pulse) gated | `viewHorizon` gate; Telescope off in production |
| Security headers | CSP, HSTS (after HTTPS works everywhere), `X-Frame-Options` |

## The server

| Check | Cipi does it with |
| --- | --- |
| Each app isolated from the others | Own Linux user, PHP pool with `open_basedir`, database user |
| SSH by key only, no root login | Installer default; `sudo cipi ssh list` |
| Firewall with only 22, 80, 443 | UFW by default; `sudo cipi firewall status`, or the panel's [Firewall tab](https://cipi.sh/docs/firewall#panel) |
| Brute-force bans | fail2ban; `sudo cipi firewall attempts 3`; optional [CrowdSec](https://cipi.sh/docs/crowdsec) |
| PHP patched the day fixes ship | Nightly at 03:30; `sudo cipi php upgrade` ([case study](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching)) |
| nginx patched | `sudo cipi nginx security`, `sudo cipi autoupdate on nginx` |
| Credentials encrypted at rest | The vault (AES-256) for configs, tokens and keys |
| HTTPS everywhere | `sudo cipi ssl install shop` and `sudo cipi ssl force shop` |
| Malware and integrity checks | `sudo cipi scan`, nightly integrity checks |
| Compliance report | `sudo cipi compliance` |

## Access

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| Per-person SSH keys, removed when people leave | `sudo cipi ssh add`, `sudo cipi ssh remove` |
| Panel with 2FA or SSO, least-privilege roles | [Web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-sso) |
| API tokens scoped and expiring | `cipi api token create --abilities=… --expires=…` |
| Staging and admin behind a login | [Cloudflare Access](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) or basic auth |

## Data

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| Encrypted off-site backups, restored at least once | [Backups to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) with `encrypt: true` and `cipi backup verify` |
| No production data on laptops | [Anonymized dumps](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps) |
| Logs that expire | [Log retention](https://cipi.sh/docs/log-retention) |

## Monitoring

| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| Alerts where you look | Telegram, Slack, e-mail or webhooks ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts)) |
| Health check with automatic rollback | `health.rollback_on_unhealthy: true` in `cipi.yml` |
| Who deployed what | The [deploy audit](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-audit) |

## Quick self-check 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --get=APP_DEBUG       # false
$ composer audit                               # no known CVEs
$ sudo cipi php list                           # every version patched
$ curl -sI https://shop.example.com | grep -i strict-transport
$ sudo cipi status                             # firewall, fail2ban, updates
```

Related: [.env and secrets](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-env-secrets), [anonymized data](https://cipi.sh/guides/anonymized-database-dumps), [Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel).


## How Cipi handled the November 2026 PHP and nginx CVEs

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching

Two security releases landed within a day of each other in November 2026: **nginx 1.31.9** (18 November, ten CVEs) and a **PHP security release** for every supported branch (19 November). This is what reached a server running Cipi, what didn't, and why.

## nginx 1.31.9

| CVE | What | On a Cipi server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2026-118899 | Endless loop reading a request body over TLS 1.3: one request pins a worker at 100% CPU | **Reachable** on every HTTPS vhost. Fixed by the upgrade |
| CVE-2026-125283 | Buffer overflow with `try_files` under an `alias` | The panel API vhost had that pattern for `/api-docs`; the line is removed by the migration |
| CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633 | Memory corruption in HTTP/2 | **Not reachable**: Cipi writes `listen 443 ssl;` and never enables HTTP/2 |
| Six more | Resolver, HTTP/3, mail, stream, PROXY protocol v2 | Not used by Cipi |

What `cipi self-update` did:

```flow
Check | nginx -t passes on the current config
> Before touching anything, `nginx -t` must pass on the current configuration. If it doesn't, nothing happens and you get a warning naming the file.
Simulate | one apt transaction, all or nothing
> The whole package change is simulated first as one apt transaction. If apt can't do all of it, nothing is removed.
Upgrade | nginx.org mainline 1.31.9
> Nginx is upgraded to the fixed version from nginx.org.
Verify | the running binary is the new one
> Cipi checks that the running binary is the new one, so the fix is really live.
```

Servers installed between June and November 2026 were found on Ubuntu's archive nginx, which wasn't receiving these fixes. The migration moved them to nginx.org's mainline repository in one simulated transaction: if apt couldn't do all of it, nothing changed. When a long-lived WebSocket kept a worker on the old binary, Cipi restarted nginx instead of reloading (well under a second).

```bash
$ sudo cipi nginx security      # version vs fixes, running binary, any HTTP/2 config
$ dpkg-query -W nginx           # 1.31.9-1~noble = nginx.org
```

## PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and 8.6.0

| CVE | What | On a Cipi server before the update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CVE-2026-129289 | Request smuggling in PHP-FPM | Needs `fastcgi_keep_conn`, which Cipi vhosts never set |
| CVE-2026-129291 | Use-after-free in the FPM master | Needs `catch_workers_output`, set only in the panel's own pools, plus code already running as that user |
| CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-115560 | Code execution through session files | Upload progress is off in every pool (admin flag): the upload path is closed |
| CVE-2026-129474 | Use-after-free in fatal-error backtraces (8.5+) | `fatal_error_backtraces` off in every pool |
| CVE-2026-129496 | Use-after-free of the timezone cache | **No setting closes it**: needs the update |

Hardening Cipi had already applied, as admin flags `.user.ini` and `ini_set()` can't undo:

```ini
php_admin_flag[session.upload_progress.enabled] = off
php_admin_flag[fatal_error_backtraces] = off
```

The fix itself:

```bash
$ sudo cipi php upgrade
```

Cipi installs PHP from packages.sury.org first, the fastest source for security releases, and patches **every night at 03:30**. While a version is `VULNERABLE`, the command exits 1 and the nightly job alerts until it's fixed. Only the affected FPM services restart.

## Octane apps

An Octane app runs the PHP compiled into its FrankenPHP binary. `cipi php upgrade` lists it as vulnerable until it runs a build with a fixed PHP:

```bash
$ sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade --all
```

If Octane doesn't answer after the upgrade, the previous build returns automatically.

## Lessons for any PHP server

| Practice | Why it mattered here |
| --- | --- |
| Don't enable features you don't need (HTTP/2 on a plain app vhost, keep-alive to FPM, upload progress) | Five CVEs needed one of them |
| Patch PHP from a source that ships fixes the same day | One CVE had no workaround |
| Alert while a known-vulnerable build is installed | Nobody has to remember to check |
| Treat embedded runtimes (FrankenPHP, Docker images) as separate patch targets | apt doesn't see them |

Follow security notes as they ship on the [Telegram channel](https://t.me/cipicloud).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi php list` shows `VULNERABLE` | Run `sudo cipi php upgrade` now; the nightly job will also retry |
| Octane app still on an old PHP | `sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade shop` |
| Nginx didn't move to nginx.org | A file uses a headers-more directive or `nginx -t` fails: the warning names it, fix and re-run `cipi self-update` |


## Back up Laravel apps and databases to S3, and restore them

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3

A backup you haven't restored is a hope. This guide sets up encrypted backups to S3-compatible storage, checks them automatically and walks through a restore.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Destination** | Where archives go: the server's disk, or an S3-compatible bucket |
| **Profile** | What to back up, how often and how long to keep it |
| **Retention** | How many runs or days are kept before old ones are deleted |
| **Off-site** | In another place than the server, so one disaster can't take both |
| **3-2-1** | Three copies, two kinds of storage, one off-site |

```flow
Destination | S3-compatible bucket | #destination
Profiles | what, how often, how long | #profiles
In cipi.yml | the app declares its own | #in-cipi-yml
Verify | archives readable | #verify
Restore | one app or everything | #restore
```

## 1. Add a destination 
Create a bucket and an access key limited to it, at any S3-compatible provider. Then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup configure                 # interactive: endpoint, bucket, keys
$ sudo cipi backup destination test
```

Secret keys are entered on the server and never travel through the panel or the API.

## 2. Create profiles 
```bash
$ sudo cipi backup profile add nightly --scope=all --cron='0 2 * * *' --keep-days=14 \
    --dest=s3 --encrypt
$ sudo cipi backup profile add hourly-db --scope=db --databases='shop,tenant_*' \
    --exclude-tables='*.jobs,*.telescope_*' --every=30m --keep=48 --dest=local
$ sudo cipi backup status
```

| Scope | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| `db` | Database dumps |
| `files` | Each app's `shared/` (`.env`, `storage`, uploads) |
| `all` | Both |

`cipi backup status` flags apps and databases that **no enabled profile covers**, so a new app can't silently go unprotected.

A very large uploads folder (hundreds of GB) is better copied with `rsync` than archived every night. Leave it out of a profile (Cipi 5.13.0+):

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup profile edit nightly --exclude-paths='storage/app/uploads,*.mp4'
$ sudo cipi backup run --profile=nightly --dry-run     # says what each app leaves out
```

Paths are relative to the app (`shop:storage/app/uploads` for one app only); the archive's `meta.json` lists what was left out, so a restore knows which folders come back from elsewhere.

## 3. Let the app declare its own backups 
```yaml
# cipi.yml
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-db, scope: db, every: 30m, keep: 48, destinations: [local] }
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

Profile names must start with the app's name, so a repository can't touch another app's backups.

## 4. Verify 
```bash
$ sudo cipi backup verify           # archives present and readable
$ sudo cipi backup verify --deep    # also decrypts and checks contents
```

Failures go to your [notification channels](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts).

## 5. Restore 
```bash
$ sudo cipi backup list --profile=nightly
$ sudo cipi backup fetch nightly 2026-11-22_020000 --dest=/root/restore
$ sudo cipi db restore shop /root/restore/shop.sql.gz
```

For a whole server, restoring backups works, but moving with [`cipi sync`](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync) is faster when the old server is still alive.

## Before risky deploys

A local snapshot before migrations is cheap: `sudo cipi app edit shop --predeploy-snapshot`. See [safe migrations](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-zero-downtime-migrations).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `destination test` fails | Key lacks bucket permissions, wrong region or endpoint |
| Backups overdue | `cipi backup status` names the profile; check disk space and the log |
| Can't open an archive | Wrong key: use the one from `cipi backup key show` at that time |
| Restore refuses an empty dump | By design: an empty backup never wipes a database |


## Monitor Laravel errors and uptime with Boogle, self-hosted

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/boogle-laravel-monitoring

When a Laravel app throws an exception in production, you want to know **before** your users tell you. [Boogle](https://boogle.web.ap.it) is a free, self-hosted exception tracker and uptime monitor for Laravel. This guide installs it as a Cipi app on its own small server, connects your apps, and sets up alerts.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Exception** | An error your code didn't handle: a 500 page for the user |
| **Exception tracker** | A service that collects exceptions from your apps, groups them and shows the details |
| **Issue** | A group of identical exceptions, with a code like `#BUG42` |
| **Uptime check** | A request every minute to see if the site answers; failing means an outage (`#OUT`) |
| **Client package** | `boogle-client`, installed in each app you monitor; it sends exceptions to Boogle |

```flow
Exception | in one of your apps
> Something breaks in production. Laravel's exception handler catches it as usual.
Client | boogle-client
> The client package sends the exception, with the stack trace, request and logged-in user, to your Boogle's `/api/log`, authenticated with the project's keys.
Boogle | groups it into an issue
> Boogle stores it and processes it on its queue: identical exceptions become one issue with a code (`#BUG42`).
You | e-mail, triage, fix
> You get it in the digest e-mail, open it in the panel, read the trace with your own code highlighted, and mark it Read, Fixed or Done.
```

## Before you start 

- A **separate** small server for Boogle (1–2 GB RAM is enough), with Cipi installed. A monitor on the same server as the apps can't warn you when that server is down.
- A subdomain such as `boogle.example.com` pointing at it.
- Working e-mail for Boogle (an SMTP service): alerts and digests are e-mails.
- GitHub (or GitLab) account to fork the Boogle repository.

## 1. Fork Boogle 

Cipi deploys from a Git repository you control, with a read-only deploy key. Open [github.com/andreapollastri/boogle](https://github.com/andreapollastri/boogle) and click **Fork**. Your copy is `git@github.com:YOU/boogle.git`.

## 2. Create the app on Cipi 

```bash
$ ssh cipi@MONITOR_IP
$ sudo cipi app create --user=boogle --domain=boogle.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:YOU/boogle.git --branch=main \
    --node-build='npm ci && npm run build'
```

Add the deploy key from the summary to your fork (**Settings → Deploy keys**, read-only), then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi git check boogle
$ sudo cipi deploy boogle
$ sudo cipi ssl install boogle
```

What you get for free on Cipi, which Boogle's README asks you to set up by hand:

| Boogle needs | On Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| A queue worker under Supervisor | Created with the app |
| The scheduler every minute (uptime checks, digests) | Already in the app user's crontab |
| A database | Created, credentials in `.env` |
| HTTPS | `cipi ssl install` |

## 3. Configure it 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env boogle --set=APP_URL=https://boogle.example.com
$ sudo cipi app env boogle --set=MAIL_MAILER=smtp
$ sudo cipi app env boogle      # add MAIL_HOST, MAIL_PORT, MAIL_USERNAME, MAIL_PASSWORD, MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS
$ sudo cipi app artisan boogle db:seed --force
$ sudo cipi app artisan boogle config:cache
$ sudo cipi worker restart boogle
```

The seeder creates the admin `admin@users.test` / `password`. **Log in at once and change it** (Profile), and turn on two-factor authentication.

## 4. Create a project 

In Boogle, **Projects → New**: name, URL (`https://shop.example.com`) and, optionally, a group (its prefix becomes the issue code, e.g. `BUG`). Open the project's **Installation** tab: it shows the exact commands and the three keys for that app.

## 5. Connect your Laravel app 

In the app you want to monitor (on your laptop):

```bash
$ composer require andreapollastri/boogle-client
$ php artisan boogle:install
```

Register the reporter. Laravel 11 and newer, in `bootstrap/app.php`:

```php
use Boogle\Facade as Boogle;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Configuration\Exceptions;

->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions): void {
    Boogle::registerExceptionHandler($exceptions);
})
```

(Laravel 9 or 10: call `Boogle::handle($e);` in a `reportable` callback in `app/Exceptions/Handler.php`.)

Commit and deploy. Then put the keys **on the server** (never in Git):

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=BOOGLE_KEY=…
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=BOOGLE_PROJECT_KEY=…
$ sudo cipi app env shop --set=BOOGLE_SERVER=https://boogle.example.com/api/log
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop boogle:test
```

Within seconds the test exception appears in the project.

> [!note] The client reports only from the environments listed in `config/boogle.php` (`production` by default). On staging, add `staging` there if you want staging errors too.

## 6. Turn on uptime checks 

In the project's settings, enable **uptime** and, if you want a specific page, set the uptime URL (for example the app's `/up`). Boogle pings it every minute. When it fails, an outage issue (`#OUT`) opens and you get an e-mail; when it's back, the issue closes and you get a recovery e-mail.

## 7. Triage like a team 

| Status | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| Open | New, nobody looked yet |
| Read | Seen, being investigated |
| Fixed | A fix is deployed |
| Done | Closed for good |

Keyboard shortcuts move through the list; bulk actions handle noisy days. Share a read-only link with a client when needed.

## How it fits with Cipi's own monitoring 

| Tool | Watches | Alerts on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Cipi monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) | The server: disk, memory, services, backups, certificates | Server problems |
| [Cipi health checks](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) | Each app's health URL, also right after a deploy | Broken releases (with auto-rollback) |
| **Boogle** | Exceptions inside the code, and uptime from outside | Bugs and outages |

Use all three: they answer different questions. Cipi's alerts go to Telegram, Slack and more ([notifications](https://cipi.sh/guides/notifications-alerts)); Boogle's go by e-mail.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `boogle:test` fails | Check `BOOGLE_SERVER` ends with `/api/log`, the keys match the Installation tab, and run `config:cache` |
| Test sent but nothing appears | Boogle's queue worker isn't running: `sudo cipi worker list boogle` |
| No e-mails | `MAIL_*` wrong in Boogle's `.env`; e-mails also go through the queue |
| Uptime never checks | The scheduler is off: `sudo cipi schedule status boogle` |
| Nothing reported from staging | Add `staging` to `environments` in `config/boogle.php` of the monitored app |
| 419 or login loop on the panel | `APP_URL` doesn't match the domain: fix it and `config:cache` |


## The Cipi web panel and REST API

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-gui-and-api

Cipi is CLI-first, but not CLI-only. Two optional pieces, each on its own subdomain, open it up: the **API** (for automation, the panel, the CLI client and AI assistants) and the **web panel** (for people).

```stack
Browser, cipi-cli, SDK, MCP | clients
Cipi API | api.example.com, token per client
cipi CLI | same code path as SSH
```

## 1. Install the API

```bash
$ sudo cipi api api.example.com
$ sudo cipi api token create --name=panel --full-access
```

The API checks DNS, issues its certificate and runs as `www-data`, calling an allowlist of `cipi` commands. Dropping data, and installing anything outside the [closed package catalog](https://cipi.sh/docs/packages), stays on the CLI.

## 2. Install the panel

```bash
$ sudo cipi gui panel.example.com
```

Log in with the admin account it asks for, then **Connections → add server** with the API URL and token. Add more servers the same way: the panel shows them as one fleet.

## 3. Invite the team

| Role | Sees |
| --- | --- |
| Admin | Everything |
| User | Only granted servers (View or Manage) or apps (View, Deploy, Edit, Environment, Logs, Commands, Delete) |

Invites are copyable links that work once and expire after seven days. Turn on TOTP 2FA per user, [require it for every account](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-install#two-factor-required) (Team → Two-factor authentication), or use [single sign-on](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-sso) with Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta or any OIDC provider.

## 4. Automate with the API

```bash
$ cipi-cli api token add prod      # on your laptop
$ cipi-cli prod apps list
$ cipi-cli prod deploy shop
```

Or from PHP with the [SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk), from WHMCS with the [module](https://cipi.sh/docs/whmcs), or from an assistant with the [MCP server](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents).

## 5. Lock it down

| Step | How |
| --- | --- |
| IP allowlist for the API | `sudo cipi api ip-whitelist set --ips=203.0.113.0/24` |
| Panel behind Cloudflare Access | `sudo cipi zt access enable --gui` ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel)) |
| Small tokens | One per client, only the abilities it needs, with an expiry |
| Keep it current | `sudo cipi gui update`, `sudo cipi api update` (the API also updates nightly) |

See [Web panel](https://cipi.sh/web-panel), [API](https://cipi.sh/api) and [MCP](https://cipi.sh/mcp) for the full picture.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| API install fails on DNS | The API's hostname must point at the server first |
| 403 from the API | Token lacks the ability: create one with the right `--abilities` |
| Panel can't reach the API | Check `cipi api status`; tokens and URL in the panel settings |


## Cipi metrics explained: server, application and uptime

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-metrics-server-app-uptime

Cipi watches a server at three levels. The **server**: is the machine healthy? Each **application**: is this app healthy, and is it the one causing trouble? **Uptime**: can its URL be reached, and how fast does it answer? On top sits a timeline of **events**: deploys, incidents, alerts. This article explains what each number means, how it's measured, and how to use them together.

## Three layers, one timeline 

| Layer | Question | Recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Server** | Is the machine healthy? | CPU, load, memory, swap, disk, network |
| **Application** | Is this app healthy, and is it the noisy neighbour? | CPU and memory of its processes, PHP-FPM pool usage, requests, 5xx, queue workers |
| **Uptime** | Can it be reached, and how fast? | Status code and response time of its health URL, every minute |
| **Events** | What changed, and when? | Releases with their health verdict, monitor alerts and recoveries, incidents, heartbeat failures |

```flow
How | one cron | #how
Server | the machine | #server
Apps | each app | #app
Uptime | every minute | #uptime
Events | what changed | #events
Playbook | read together | #playbook
Outside | Prometheus, API | #outside
```

Metrics and alerts are separate on purpose. The [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor) and the [health checks](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) decide when to wake you up; metrics only record. Every state change of a monitor check is also written as an event, so the history explains the alert.

## How it's collected 

```stack
Cron, every minute | /etc/cron.d/cipi-metrics
Read | /proc, one ps, new access-log lines, supervisorctl
Probe | each app's health URL
Write | one SQLite transaction
Store | /var/lib/cipi-metrics/metrics.db (root, 0600)
```

About 0.2 seconds of CPU per minute. Nothing listens on a port, nothing leaves the server. Compared with a Prometheus server and exporters on every VPS, that's hundreds of megabytes of RAM saved on the small machines most Cipi servers are; if you already run Prometheus, [scrape Cipi](#prometheus) instead.

```bash
$ sudo cipi metrics status        # collector, database size, retention
$ sudo cipi metrics               # now, last hour, uptime per app
```

## Server metrics 

| Metric | What it means | Worry when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **CPU %** | Share of all cores busy | Sustained near 100%: requests queue behind each other |
| **Load (1 min)** | Processes running or waiting for CPU or disk | Above the number of cores for long; the monitor alerts at 4× the cores for two runs in a row |
| **Memory % and MB** | RAM in use, without cache | High *and* swap rising |
| **Swap %** | Memory pushed to disk | Any steady growth on a PHP server: too many FPM children or workers for the RAM |
| **Disk % of `/`** | The root filesystem | The monitor warns at 80% and goes critical at 90%; `cipi disk` says who uses it |
| **Network in / out** | Bytes per second | Sudden outbound spikes: a crawler, a big export, or something that shouldn't be there |

Load and CPU together tell a story: high load with low CPU usually means processes are **waiting for disk**, not computing. On a database-heavy app, look at the slow queries before buying a bigger server.

## Application metrics 

| Metric | How it's measured | Read it as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **CPU** | CPU time of the app user's processes between two minutes, as % of **one core** | 100% = one core fully busy. FPM masters run as root and aren't counted; Octane and Node processes are |
| **Memory** | Sum of the resident memory of its processes | An upper bound: pages PHP-FPM children share are counted once per child. Watch the trend |
| **PHP-FPM children** / `pm.max_children` | Workers of the app's pool, against its cap | Close to the cap at peak is fine; at the cap is not |
| **Hit `max_children`** | How many times the pool reached its cap in the minute | **The most useful number for "the site is slow"**: requests waited for a free worker |
| **Requests / min** | New lines in the app's Nginx access log | Traffic, per minute |
| **5xx / min** | Responses 500–599 in the same lines | Errors your users saw |
| **Queue workers** | Programs running, against programs configured | Running  [!info] The probe runs **on the server**. It sees a broken release, a dead database or an expired certificate, but not a DNS mistake or a network outage between your users and the server. For that, the [heartbeat](#heartbeat) and an external monitor complete the picture.

## Events 

| Event | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Release live, with its post-deploy health verdict | Every deploy, from the CLI, the panel, a webhook or CI |
| Monitor state change | `ok → warn/critical`, escalations, recoveries |
| Healthcheck incident | Opened and closed |
| Heartbeat failure | A call to your heartbeat URL that didn't go through |

```bash
$ sudo cipi metrics events --range=7d
$ sudo cipi metrics events --source=deploy
```

In the panel, events are the dotted vertical lines on every chart: blue for releases, red for incidents, green for recoveries. Most investigations start by asking "what was the last marker before the line went up?".

## Read them together: a playbook 

| Symptom | Look at | Likely cause | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5xx jump right after a release marker | App 5xx, events | The release | `sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback`, then read `cipi app logs shop --type=laravel` |
| Site slow, app CPU high, pool at the cap | App CPU, `max_children` hits | CPU-bound code or a traffic spike | Compare requests/min with last week; profile; resize if it's real traffic |
| Site slow, app CPU low, pool at the cap | `max_children` hits, server load | Workers waiting on the database or an API | Slow query log, timeouts on outgoing calls |
| Memory climbs for days, swap grows | App memory, server swap | Too many workers for the RAM, or a leaking worker | Fewer workers (`cipi app limits --worker-procs`); let leaking workers restart (`maxJobs` / `maxTime` in Horizon, `--max-jobs` / `--max-time` on `queue:work`) |
| Queue workers below configured | Queue workers | A worker crashing on start | `cipi app logs shop --type=worker` |
| Uptime red, server and app metrics normal | Healthcheck status code | A dependency the health URL checks, or the certificate | Open the URL; `cipi health check shop` |
| One app's CPU high, others slow | Every app's CPU on the server tab | A noisy neighbour | Limits: `cipi app limits` ([docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/limits)), or move it with `cipi sync` |
| Gap in every chart | Nothing recorded | The server was down or rebooting | Check the heartbeat service's history and `uptime` |
| Disk % climbing steadily | Server disk | Logs, local backups, uploads | `sudo cipi disk`, then [exclude big folders](https://cipi.sh/guides/exclude-files-from-backups) from local backups |

## Retention and size 

| Data | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every minute | 7 days | `--raw=1d` … `90d` |
| Average and peak per 15 minutes | 30 days | `--rollup=` up to `400d` (never shorter than raw), `--resolution=5m` … `60m` |
| Events | 90 days | `--events=7d` … `730d` |

```bash
$ sudo cipi metrics retention
$ sudo cipi metrics retention --raw=14d --rollup=180d --resolution=30m
```

About 2 MB per app per week of minutes, and a third of that per month of rollups: 20–30 MB for ten apps on the defaults. Charts always ask for about 240 points, whatever the range: minutes inside the raw window, rollups beyond it. That's why a 30-day chart shows averages **and** peaks: a one-minute spike stays visible.

## Outside the server 

### Heartbeat: for the day the server goes quiet 

A server that's down can't send an alert. The heartbeat calls a URL of yours every N minutes; when the calls stop, the service on the other end alerts you.

```bash
$ sudo cipi metrics heartbeat set https://hc-ping.com/ --every=1
$ sudo cipi metrics heartbeat test
```

Works with Healthchecks.io, Uptime Kuma (push monitor), Better Stack heartbeats, Cronitor or your own endpoint. Set the receiver's period to the interval plus a few minutes of grace.

### Prometheus and Grafana 

If you already run Prometheus, turn on OpenMetrics: the latest values on their own port, behind an IP allowlist and a bearer token.

```bash
$ sudo cipi metrics openmetrics on --allow=203.0.113.50 --port=9273
$ sudo cipi metrics openmetrics token --show
```

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
- job_name: cipi-production
  scrape_interval: 60s
  authorization: { credentials:  }
  static_configs: [{ targets: ['203.0.113.10:9273'] }]
```

| Server | Each app (`{app="shop"}`) |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi_host_cpu_percent`, `cipi_host_load1` | `cipi_app_cpu_percent`, `cipi_app_memory_rss_megabytes`, `cipi_app_processes` |
| `cipi_host_memory_percent`, `cipi_host_memory_used_megabytes`, `cipi_host_swap_percent` | `cipi_app_fpm_children`, `cipi_app_fpm_max_children`, `cipi_app_fpm_max_children_reached` |
| `cipi_host_disk_percent` | `cipi_app_requests_per_minute`, `cipi_app_http_5xx_per_minute` |
| `cipi_host_network_receive_bytes_per_second`, `cipi_host_network_transmit_bytes_per_second` | `cipi_app_healthcheck_up`, `cipi_app_healthcheck_status_code`, `cipi_app_healthcheck_duration_milliseconds` |
| `cipi_metrics_collected_timestamp_seconds` | `cipi_app_workers_up`, `cipi_app_workers_total` |

Example alert rules built on them:

```yaml
groups:
  - name: cipi
    rules:
      - alert: AppDown
        expr: cipi_app_healthcheck_up == 0
        for: 3m
      - alert: PoolSaturated
        expr: cipi_app_fpm_max_children_reached > 0
        for: 10m
      - alert: Many5xx
        expr: cipi_app_http_5xx_per_minute > 20
        for: 5m
      - alert: WorkerMissing
        expr: cipi_app_workers_up  300
```

> [!warning] The endpoint is plain HTTP: keep it on a private network or a tunnel (WireGuard, Tailscale). `0.0.0.0/0` is refused, and the panel API can't turn it on, because it opens a port.

### The panel, the API, the SDK and AI assistants 

| Interface | What |
| --- | --- |
| [Web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui-overview) 4.3+ | A Metrics tab per server and per app: charts from 1 hour to 30 days with markers, hover details, 30-day uptime bars, the events timeline, retention and heartbeat settings. Refreshes every 30 seconds while open |
| [REST API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) | `GET /api/metrics`, `/api/metrics/series`, `/api/apps/{name}/metrics`, `/api/metrics/uptime`, `/api/metrics/events`; abilities `metrics-view`, `metrics-manage` |
| [PHP SDK](https://cipi.sh/docs/php-sdk) | `$cipi->metrics()->series('shop', ['req', 'http_5xx'], '7d')` |
| [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client) | `cipi-cli metrics`, `metrics show --app shop`, `metrics uptime` |
| [MCP](https://cipi.sh/docs/mcp) | Ask your assistant *"when did the 5xx on shop start, and what was deployed just before?"* |

## What metrics don't do 

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Alerts | The [monitor](https://cipi.sh/docs/monitor), [health checks](https://cipi.sh/docs/health-checks) and [notifications](https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts) |
| Slow routes, queries and jobs inside the app | Laravel Pulse or Telescope |
| Exceptions with stack traces | An error tracker such as [Boogle](https://cipi.sh/guides/boogle-laravel-monitoring) |
| Uptime seen from the internet | An external monitor, plus the heartbeat |
| Long-term history across a fleet | Prometheus or Grafana, scraping OpenMetrics |

```bash
$ sudo cipi metrics probe off     # stop the per-minute probe (the 5-minute check stays)
$ sudo cipi metrics disable       # stop collecting, keep the history
```


## Cloudflare in front of Laravel, explained: DNS, proxy, SSL modes and wildcards

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-proxy-ssl-wildcard

Cloudflare sits between your visitors and your server. Used well, it adds a CDN, DDoS protection and a firewall for free. Used wrong, it causes the two classic problems: **redirect loops** and **certificate errors**. This guide sets it up correctly for an app on Cipi, and explains every setting so you know why.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **DNS only (grey cloud)** | Cloudflare only answers DNS; visitors connect to your server directly |
| **Proxied (orange cloud)** | Visitors connect to Cloudflare; Cloudflare connects to your server |
| **Edge certificate** | The certificate visitors see, from Cloudflare (when proxied) |
| **Origin certificate** | The certificate on your server, for Cloudflare-to-server traffic |
| **SSL/TLS mode** | How Cloudflare talks to your server: not at all, HTTP, or HTTPS (checked or not) |
| **DNS-01** | Proving domain ownership with a DNS record: needed for wildcard certificates |

```flow
Visitor | https://shop.example.com
> The browser connects to Cloudflare (orange cloud) and gets Cloudflare's edge certificate.
Cloudflare | CDN, WAF, DDoS
> Cloudflare filters the request, serves cached static files if it can, and otherwise forwards it.
Your server | Nginx, Cipi's certificate
> With Full (strict), Cloudflare connects to your server over HTTPS and checks your certificate is valid. Cipi's Let's Encrypt certificate is.
Laravel | your app
> The app answers; Cloudflare passes the response back. With real-IP configured, Laravel sees the visitor's IP, not Cloudflare's.
```

## Before you start 

- A domain whose DNS is (or will be) on Cloudflare. Moving DNS to Cloudflare is free and doesn't move your website: you copy the records, then change the nameservers at your registrar.
- An app on Cipi ([first deploy](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-laravel-ubuntu-vps)).

## 1. DNS records 

In Cloudflare, **DNS → Records**:

| Type | Name | Content | Proxy status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | `@` | your server IPv4 | Orange or grey |
| A | `www` | your server IPv4 | Same as `@` |
| AAAA | `@`, `www` | your server IPv6 (if any) | Same |
| A | `*` | your server IPv4 | Only for [wildcards](#wildcard) |

**Start grey** (DNS only) until the site works over HTTPS, then switch to orange. That way you test one thing at a time.

## 2. Choose the SSL/TLS mode: Full (strict) 

**SSL/TLS → Overview**. This is the setting that breaks most sites:

| Mode | Cloudflare → your server | With Cipi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Off | No HTTPS at all | Don't |
| Flexible | **HTTP** | **Redirect loop**: Cipi sends HTTP to HTTPS, forever |
| Full | HTTPS, certificate **not** checked | Works, but an attacker in between wouldn't be noticed |
| **Full (strict)** | HTTPS, certificate **checked** | **Use this** |

Full (strict) needs a valid certificate on your server. Cipi gives you one:

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop                      # Let's Encrypt over HTTP
# or, if the record is already orange or you need wildcards:
$ sudo cipi ssl dns set --token=YOUR_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop --dns=cloudflare     # Let's Encrypt over DNS
```

> [!tip] DNS validation (`--dns=cloudflare`) works whatever the proxy status and even with port 80 closed. If you're behind Cloudflare, prefer it: renewals never depend on Cloudflare rules.

## 3. Create the API token (for DNS validation) 

**My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token → Edit zone DNS** template. Limit it to your zone. That's the only permission needed (**Zone → DNS → Edit**). Save it once on the server:

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl dns set --token=YOUR_CLOUDFLARE_TOKEN
$ sudo cipi ssl dns list
```

Several Cloudflare accounts (one per client)? Name them: `--name=client-a`, then `--account=client-a` when issuing ([SSL docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl#accounts)).

## 4. Switch on the proxy 

When `https://shop.example.com` works with the grey cloud, click the cloud to make it orange, for `@` and `www`. Then, in **SSL/TLS → Edge Certificates**:

| Setting | Set to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Always Use HTTPS | On | Cloudflare redirects HTTP itself |
| Minimum TLS Version | 1.2 | Old clients only |
| Automatic HTTPS Rewrites | On | Fixes mixed `http://` links |
| HSTS | On, **only after** everything works over HTTPS | Browsers refuse HTTP for months: hard to undo |

## 5. Wildcards: every subdomain, one certificate 

For multi-tenant apps (`acme.example.com`, `globex.example.com`…):

```bash
$ sudo cipi alias add saas '*.example.com'        # quotes matter
$ sudo cipi ssl install saas --dns=cloudflare     # ~1 minute
$ curl -sI https://test.example.com | head -1
```

| Fact | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Let's Encrypt issues wildcards only via DNS-01 | Cipi needs the Cloudflare token (step 3) |
| Cloudflare's free edge certificate covers `example.com` and `*.example.com` | Keep tenants one level deep |
| Exact names beat the wildcard | `api.example.com` can still be another app |
| `@` and `*` must have the same proxy status | Otherwise the apex and the tenants get different certificates and IPs |
| Any name with its own DNS record skips `*` | A stray record silently takes a tenant name away |

Every Cloudflare setting for wildcards, with checks and errors: [Wildcard domains](https://cipi.sh/docs/wildcard-domains). Full walkthrough with Laravel tenant resolution: [Multi-tenant SaaS on wildcard subdomains](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-multi-tenant-wildcard).

## 6. Real visitor IPs 

Behind the orange cloud, every request comes from a Cloudflare IP. Two layers must know that:

1. **Nginx** must take the visitor's IP from Cloudflare's header. `sudo cipi zt enable` configures exactly that (Cloudflare's ranges, refreshed daily) and teaches Fail2ban and CrowdSec the same ranges. It closes no port: it's the first step of [Zero Trust](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel), safe to run alone.
2. **Laravel** must trust the proxy, so `$request->ip()`, rate limiting and HTTPS detection work. In `bootstrap/app.php`:

```php
->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
    $middleware->trustProxies(at: '*');
})
```

Trusting all proxies is safe **only** when the server can't be reached except through Cloudflare or Nginx on localhost. With ports still open to the world, list Cloudflare's ranges instead.

## 7. Caching without surprises 

By default Cloudflare caches static files (CSS, JS, images) and **not** HTML. Keep it that way for Laravel: HTML pages carry sessions and CSRF tokens.

| Rule (Caching → Cache Rules) | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Bypass cache for `/admin*`, `/horizon*`, `/livewire*`, `/broadcasting*` | Dynamic, per-user |
| Cache `/build/*` for a long time | Vite file names change on every build |
| Never "Cache Everything" on HTML | Users would see each other's pages |

After a deploy, Vite's hashed file names make purging unnecessary.

## 8. Firewall basics (free plan) 

| Setting | Suggestion |
| --- | --- |
| Security → Bots → Bot Fight Mode | On, unless it blocks your API clients or webhooks |
| WAF → Custom rule | Challenge `/login` from countries you never serve |
| Rate limiting | Protect `/login` and `/api` (Laravel's `throttle` too) |
| Skip rule | Let your CI and uptime monitors through, if challenged |

Git webhooks hit `/cipi/webhook` on your domain: don't challenge that path.

## Troubleshooting 

| You see | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` | SSL/TLS on Flexible | Full (strict) |
| 525 SSL handshake failed | No certificate on the server for that name | `cipi ssl install` (or add the alias first) |
| 526 Invalid SSL certificate | Certificate doesn't cover the name, or expired | `sudo cipi ssl status`, reissue |
| 521 Web server is down | Nginx unreachable, or ports closed without a tunnel | `sudo cipi status`, firewall |
| 522 Connection timed out | Provider firewall blocks Cloudflare | Allow 80/443 |
| 413 on large uploads | Plan's request size limit | Direct-to-S3 uploads or a grey subdomain |
| Login loops, 419 errors | Laravel thinks it's on HTTP | `trustProxies`, `APP_URL=https://…`, `config:cache` |
| Every visitor has the same IP | Real IP not configured | Step 6 |
| Webhook deploys fail | Bot protection challenges `/cipi/webhook` | Skip rule for that path |


## Exclude files and folders from backups

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/exclude-files-from-backups

A nightly backup should take minutes, not hours. When one app keeps hundreds of gigabytes of uploads or videos, archiving them every night makes runs slow, buckets expensive and restores painful. Since Cipi 5.13 a backup profile can **leave paths out** of the app archives, from the CLI, from `cipi.yml`, from your laptop or from the panel.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **App archive** | `files.tar.gz` per app per run. A Laravel app's `shared/` folder (`.env`, `storage/`, uploads); a custom app's `htdocs/` |
| **Profile** | What to back up, how often, where and for how long. Exclusions belong to a profile |
| **Exclude pattern** | A path relative to the app, or a wildcard: `storage/app/uploads`, `*.mp4` |
| **Per-app pattern** | `shop:storage/app/uploads`: only for the apps named (or matched by a glob) before the colon |
| **`meta.json`** | Travels with each archive and lists `excluded_paths`, so a restore knows what is missing |

```flow
Find | what's heavy | #find
Patterns | what matches | #choose
CLI | --exclude-paths | #cli
Dry run | see it first | #dry-run
cipi.yml | per app | #in-cipi-yml
Keep safe | rsync, S3 | #keep-safe
Restore | and check | #restore
```

## 1. Find what makes the archives heavy 

```bash
$ sudo cipi disk                                   # apps, largest first
$ sudo du -sh /home/shop/shared/storage/app/* | sort -h | tail
$ sudo cipi backup list --profile=nightly          # the runs a profile has kept
```

`cipi disk` shows files and database per app; `du` tells you which folder inside `shared/` is the big one. Usual suspects:

| Folder | Typical content | Exclude? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `storage/app/uploads`, `storage/app/public` | User uploads, media library | Yes, **if** they're copied elsewhere ([step 7](#keep-safe)) |
| `*.mp4`, `*.mov`, `*.zip` | Videos, exports, archives | Yes, if they're kept elsewhere or can be produced again |
| `storage/framework/cache` | File cache | Yes: rebuilt on demand |
| `storage/logs` | `laravel.log` | Usually yes: logs are rotated on the server and better shipped to a log service |
| `storage/app/livewire-tmp` | Livewire temporary uploads | Yes |
| `storage/debugbar`, `storage/clockwork` | Debug data | Yes |
| `wp-content/cache`, `wp-content/ai1wm-backups`, `wp-content/updraft` | WordPress caches and *plugins' own* backups | Yes |
| `.env` | Configuration and `APP_KEY` | **Never** |

## 2. Write patterns that match what you mean 

Patterns are matched against the names **inside the archive**, which start with `shared/` (Laravel and Node apps) or `htdocs/` (custom apps). You write them relative to the app; Cipi takes care of the rest.

| Rule | Example | Leaves out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relative to the app | `storage/app/uploads` | `shared/storage/app/uploads` and everything in it |
| Custom apps too | `wp-content/uploads` | `htdocs/wp-content/uploads` |
| Matched after any `/` | `storage/logs` | Any `…/storage/logs`, at any depth |
| Wildcards cross `/` | `*.mp4` | Every `.mp4`, in every folder |
| Wildcards inside a path | `storage/app/*/cache` | `storage/app/tenant1/cache`, `storage/app/tenant2/cache`… |
| Some apps only (CLI) | `shop:storage/app/uploads`, `api-*:*.csv` | Only in `shop`; only in apps whose name starts with `api-` |
| Refused | `/home/shop/shared/…`, `*`, `shared`, `htdocs` | Absolute paths match nothing; the last three would leave the whole app out |

> [!warning] Short, generic names catch more than you think. `cache` leaves out **every** folder called `cache`, including one your users upload into. Prefer the full path: `storage/framework/cache`. Patterns are case-sensitive.

Allowed characters: letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`, `/`, `@`, `+`, spaces, `*`, `?` and `[ ]`. At most 255 characters per pattern.

## 3. Exclude in a server-wide profile 

Server profiles are yours, the operator's. Set exclusions when you create a profile or edit it later:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup profile add nightly --scope=all --cron='0 2 * * *' --keep-days=14 \
    --dest=s3 --encrypt --exclude-paths='storage/framework/cache,storage/logs'
$ sudo cipi backup profile edit nightly \
    --exclude-paths='storage/framework/cache,storage/logs,shop:storage/app/uploads,*.mp4'
$ sudo cipi backup profile show nightly
```

> [!tip] `--exclude-paths` **replaces** the list. To add one pattern, pass the old ones again; to take everything again, empty it: `--exclude-paths=`.

A common layout keeps databases frequent and complete, and files lighter:

```bash
# every 30 minutes, databases only: nothing to exclude
$ sudo cipi backup profile add db-30m --scope=db --every=30m --keep=48 --dest=local,s3 --encrypt \
    --exclude-tables='*.jobs,*.failed_jobs,*.telescope_*'
# nightly files, without the heavy media kept elsewhere
$ sudo cipi backup profile add files-nightly --scope=files --cron='30 2 * * *' --keep-days=30 \
    --dest=s3 --encrypt --exclude-paths='storage/app/uploads,storage/framework/cache,storage/logs,*.mp4'
# weekly full copy, uploads included, kept longer
$ sudo cipi backup profile add weekly-full --scope=all --cron='0 4 * * 0' --keep-weeks=8 --dest=offsite --encrypt
```

The weekly full copy is the safety net: even if your uploads sync breaks silently, there is a recent archive with everything.

## 4. Check with a dry run 

Before the next scheduled run, ask the profile what it would do:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup run --profile=nightly --dry-run
```

```text
Backup profile 'nightly' (all, 2026-11-24_101500)
  Would archive files for 3 app(s):
    shop (shared; leaving out storage/framework/cache,storage/logs,storage/app/uploads,*.mp4)
    blog (htdocs; leaving out storage/framework/cache,storage/logs,*.mp4)
    api (shared; leaving out storage/framework/cache,storage/logs,*.mp4)
  Would dump 3 database(s):
    shop (mariadb)
    blog (mariadb)
    api (pgsql)
  Destinations: s3 (encrypted)
```

The real run prints the same "leaving out" list for each app, in the terminal and in the backup log. Then confirm that nothing is left unprotected:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup run --profile=nightly
$ sudo cipi backup status        # also flags apps and databases no profile covers
$ sudo cipi backup verify --deep
```

## 5. Let the app declare its exclusions in cipi.yml 

An app can own its backup profiles in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml), next to its workers and schedule. `exclude_paths` is a list:

```yaml
# cipi.yml (app "shop")
backup:
  profiles:
    # frequent, cheap: databases only
    - name: shop-db
      scope: db
      every: 30m
      keep: 48
      exclude_tables: ["*.jobs", "*.failed_jobs", "*.telescope_*"]
      destinations: [local, s3]
      encrypt: true

    # nightly: .env and storage, without what is kept elsewhere
    - name: shop-nightly
      scope: all
      cron: "0 2 * * *"
      keep_days: 14
      exclude_paths: ["storage/app/uploads", "storage/framework/cache", "storage/logs", "*.mp4"]
      destinations: [s3]
      encrypt: true
```

A WordPress site deployed as a custom app writes paths relative to `htdocs/`:

```yaml
# cipi.yml (custom app "blog")
backup:
  profiles:
    - name: blog-nightly
      scope: all
      cron: "15 2 * * *"
      keep_days: 30
      exclude_paths: ["wp-content/cache", "wp-content/ai1wm-backups", "wp-content/updraft", "*.log"]
      destinations: [s3]
      encrypt: true
```

Per environment, a staging copy rarely needs the uploads at all ([staging and production](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production)):

```yaml
# cipi-staging.yml (app "shop-stg"; this file doesn't inherit from cipi.yml)
backup:
  profiles:
    - name: shop-stg-nightly
      scope: all
      every: 1d
      keep: 3
      exclude_paths: ["storage/app", "storage/logs"]
      destinations: [local]
```

Then plan and apply, as with any `cipi.yml` change:

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml validate shop   # parse and check, change nothing
$ sudo cipi yml plan shop       # what would change
$ sudo cipi yml apply shop
$ sudo cipi yml generate shop   # the app's current setup as a file, exclude_paths included
```

| cipi.yml rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Profile names are `` or `-*` | A repository can't change another app's backups |
| No `app:` prefix in patterns | The file already belongs to one app |
| `*`, `shared`, `htdocs` and absolute paths refused | *"would leave the whole app out of its backup"* / *"invalid pattern"*: the plan stops before applying |
| At most 10 profiles per app | Keeps the schedule readable |

## 6. From your laptop, the API or the panel 

Same field, same validation, wherever you edit it:

```bash
$ cipi-cli backup profile edit nightly --exclude-paths storage/app/uploads,*.mp4
$ cipi-cli backup profile edit nightly --exclude-paths ""     # take everything again
$ cipi-cli backup status
```

| Interface | Where |
| --- | --- |
| [cipi-cli](https://cipi.sh/docs/cli-client#backup) | `backup profile add|edit --exclude-paths` |
| [REST API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) | Backup profile fields, ability `backups-manage` |
| [Web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) | Server → Backups → profile form (cipi/gui 4.5+) |

S3 secrets are never set this way: destinations are added on the server.

## 7. Keep the excluded folders safe 

Excluding a folder from the archive is not the same as not protecting it. Pick one of these for every excluded folder that holds data you can't recreate:

| Option | Good for | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Object storage from the start** | New apps, media libraries | Store uploads on an S3 disk (`FILESYSTEM_DISK=s3`) with bucket versioning; the server keeps no copy. Your own bucket: [Johnny](https://cipi.sh/guides/johnny-s3-storage) |
| **rsync to another server** | Large folders that change a little every day | Only changes travel; see below |
| **rclone to a bucket** | Off-site copies without a second server | `rclone sync` to any S3-compatible bucket with versioning on |
| **The weekly full profile** | A safety net for all of the above | [Step 3](#cli) |

An hourly `rsync` of the uploads folder to a backup host, as root on the Cipi server:

```bash
# /etc/cron.d/shop-uploads
15 * * * * root rsync -aH --partial -e "ssh -i /root/.ssh/uploads_backup" \
  /home/shop/shared/storage/app/uploads/ backup@203.0.113.30:shop/uploads/ >> /var/log/shop-uploads-rsync.log 2>&1
```

Leave `--delete` out unless the target keeps snapshots: without it, a file deleted by mistake on the server survives on the backup host. With `rclone`, turn on versioning on the bucket and use `rclone sync … --backup-dir` for the same reason.

> [!info] Whatever you choose, test it: download one file from the copy and open it. A copy that has stopped working looks exactly like one that works until the day you need it.

## 8. Restore, knowing what is missing 

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup list --profile=nightly
$ sudo cipi backup fetch nightly 2026-11-24_020000 --dest=/root/restore
$ jq .excluded_paths /root/restore/apps/shop/meta.json
[
  "storage/app/uploads",
  "storage/framework/cache",
  "storage/logs",
  "*.mp4"
]
$ sudo cipi db restore shop /root/restore/databases/mariadb/shop.sql.gz
$ tar -xzf /root/restore/apps/shop/files.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore-files
```

Then bring the excluded folders back from where you keep them (`rsync` from the backup host, `rclone copy` from the bucket) and fix ownership with `sudo cipi app fix-permissions shop`. Caches and logs need nothing: they are written again as the app runs.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| *Invalid --exclude-paths entry* | An absolute path, a character outside the allowed set, or a pattern that would leave the whole app out. Write it relative to the app |
| Nothing is left out | The pattern doesn't match a name in the archive. Check case and spelling, then `--dry-run` |
| Too much is left out | A short name (`cache`, `tmp`) matched folders you wanted. Use the full path |
| I added a pattern and lost the others | `--exclude-paths` replaces the list: pass all of them |
| `cipi.yml` plan refuses `shop:…` | The prefix is CLI-only; in `cipi.yml` write the bare pattern |
| `cipi yml plan` says the profile name is invalid | It must be the app's name or start with it: `shop`, `shop-nightly` |
| Archives are still big | Check the database side too: `--exclude-tables` for logs, jobs and Telescope tables |


## Free, privacy-friendly website analytics with IndieStats

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/indiestats-privacy-analytics

Most websites send every visitor to Google Analytics, with cookies, a consent banner and data leaving the EU. [IndieStats](https://indiestats.web.ap.it) gives you the numbers that matter (visitors, pages, sources, campaigns, conversions) from **your own server**, without cookies or third parties. On Cipi it's one Laravel app.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Pageview** | One page opened by one visitor |
| **Visitor ID** | A random identifier kept in the browser's `localStorage`, not a cookie |
| **Snippet** | A one-line `` you paste in your site's layout |
| **Event** | Something a visitor does that you want to count: `signup`, `purchase` |
| **Goal** | An event you follow over time, to measure conversions |
| **Retention** | How long raw data is kept before it's deleted |

```flow
Visitor opens a page | your website
> The browser loads the IndieStats snippet from your stats domain, asynchronously, so your page doesn't wait.
Snippet sends a pageview | to stats.example.com
> Path, title, referrer, UTM tags, language, timezone and device type. A random visitor ID lives in `localStorage`; no cookies.
IndieStats checks the origin | domain allowlist
> Only domains you listed for that site are accepted, so nobody can pollute your numbers from elsewhere.
Data stays on your server | until retention deletes it
> Raw data is pruned after the retention window you choose. Nothing is sent to third parties.
```

## Before you start 

- A server with Cipi (it can share a server with other apps, or live on the same one as your [Boogle](https://cipi.sh/guides/boogle-laravel-monitoring)).
- A subdomain such as `stats.example.com` pointing at it.
- A GitHub account to fork IndieStats.

## 1. Create the app 

Fork [github.com/andreapollastri/indiestats](https://github.com/andreapollastri/indiestats), then:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@YOUR_SERVER
$ sudo cipi app create --user=stats --domain=stats.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:YOU/indiestats.git --branch=main --php=8.5
```

Add the deploy key to your fork, then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy stats
$ sudo cipi ssl install stats
$ sudo cipi app artisan stats db:seed --force
```

IndieStats needs PHP 8.4 or newer. Its built front-end assets are committed to the repository, so no Node build is needed on the server. The seeder creates `admin@users.test` / `password`: **log in and change it right away**.

| IndieStats needs | On Cipi |
| --- | --- |
| The scheduler every minute (pruning, GeoIP updates) | Already on |
| A queue worker (Excel exports) | Created with the app |
| HTTPS | `cipi ssl install` (needed: an HTTP script on an HTTPS site is blocked) |

## 2. Add your site 

**Sites → New site**: name, and the **allowed domains** (`example.com, www.example.com`). IndieStats shows the snippet to copy:

## 3. Paste the snippet 

In a Laravel app, put it in your main layout, before ``, only in production:

```blade
@production

@endproduction
```

WordPress: paste it in the theme's footer (or a "header and footer scripts" plugin). Static sites: the shared layout. Deploy, open a page, and the visit appears in **Real-time** within seconds.

## 4. Track events and goals 

```js
indiestats.track('signup');
indiestats.track('purchase', { plan: 'pro', price: 29.99, currency: 'EUR' });
```

Up to 20 properties per event. On the site's **Events** tab, add a goal to follow an event over time (for example `signup` per day).

## 5. Make it as private as you can 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env stats --set=ANALYTICS_RETENTION_DAYS=180
$ sudo cipi app artisan stats config:cache
```

| Setting | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Shorter retention | Less personal data kept (IPs are deleted with their pageviews) |
| Country only, or no GeoIP | The GeoIP and ASN databases are optional: skip them if you don't need location |
| Domain allowlist on every site | Only your sites can send data |
| Privacy policy | Say what you measure, why, and for how long |
| Real visitor IPs behind Cloudflare | IndieStats reads `CF-Connecting-IP`; behind other proxies configure Laravel's trusted proxies |

> [!note] This guide isn't legal advice. Cookieless, first-party, self-hosted analytics with short retention is the privacy-friendliest setup, but whether you need consent depends on your jurisdiction. Ask your DPO.

## What you'll see 

| Tab | Answers |
| --- | --- |
| Summary | How many visitors, pageviews, time on page |
| Content | Which pages, which on-site searches |
| Traffic | Where visitors come from |
| UTM | Which campaigns work |
| Technology | Devices, browsers, systems |
| Geography | Countries and networks (optional databases) |
| Events | Conversions and goals |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| No visits arrive | The site's domain isn't in the allowlist, or the snippet isn't on the page |
| Browser blocks the script | Mixed content: IndieStats must be on HTTPS (`cipi ssl install stats`) |
| Every visitor from one country/network | Behind a proxy without real IP: see [Cloudflare guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-proxy-ssl-wildcard#real-ip) |
| Excel export never finishes | Queue worker not running: `sudo cipi worker list stats` |
| Old data not deleted | Scheduler off: `sudo cipi schedule status stats` |
| Ad blockers hide some visits | Expected for any analytics; a first-party subdomain helps |


## Your own S3 storage for Laravel with Johnny

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/johnny-s3-storage

Laravel apps store uploads, exports and backups in **object storage**: S3 and its compatibles. [Johnny](https://johnny.web.ap.it) gives you that on your own VPS, with a clean panel. Your Cipi apps then use it exactly like AWS S3.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Object storage** | Storage for files ("objects") reached over HTTP, not a disk you mount |
| **S3** | Amazon's object storage API, now a standard many products speak |
| **Bucket** | A named container of files, e.g. `shop-uploads` |
| **Access key** | An ID and a secret an app uses to read or write buckets |
| **Endpoint** | The URL of the storage server, e.g. `https://s3.example.com` |
| **Path style** | Bucket in the path (`/shop-uploads/…`), as Johnny expects |

```stack
Cipi server | your Laravel apps, Storage::disk('s3')
HTTPS | path-style S3 requests
Johnny VPS | Caddy + Garage + panel
SFTP target | nightly copy of every bucket
```

## Before you start 

- A **separate** VPS with **Ubuntu 24.04**, with enough disk for your files (storage-optimised plans are cheap at Hetzner, OVHcloud and others).
- Two subdomains pointing at it **before** installing: one for S3 (`s3.example.com`), one for the panel (`panel.storage.example.com`).
- Optional but recommended: an SFTP destination for nightly backups (a storage box, another server).

## 1. Install Johnny 

```bash
$ ssh root@STORAGE_IP
$ mkdir -p /opt && git clone https://github.com/andreapollastri/johnny /opt/johnny
$ cd /opt/johnny
$ bash scripts/autoinstall.sh
```

The wizard installs Garage and Caddy, issues HTTPS for your S3 domain, creates a `default` bucket and keys, sets up the nightly jobs and, if you say yes, the panel. Check it:

```bash
$ source /etc/johnny/credentials/default-s3.env
$ aws s3 ls --endpoint-url "$AWS_ENDPOINT_URL"
```

Create your panel login:

```bash
$ sudo -u www-data php /opt/johnny/panel/artisan johnny:admin you@example.com 'a-strong-password'
```

Open the panel, sign in, and turn on two-factor authentication in **Settings**.

## 2. Create a bucket and a key per app 

**Buckets → New**: `shop-uploads`. Then **Access keys → New**: name it after the app, give it **read and write** on `shop-uploads` only.

Copy the key ID and secret now. In the bucket's **Connect** tab, Johnny shows ready-made configuration snippets.

## 3. Connect a Laravel app 

In the app (on your laptop):

```bash
$ composer require league/flysystem-aws-s3-v3 "^3.0" --with-all-dependencies
```

Commit and deploy. Then set the variables on the Cipi server:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app env shop        # add these lines:
```

```text
FILESYSTEM_DISK=s3
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=GK…
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=…
AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=johnny
AWS_BUCKET=shop-uploads
AWS_ENDPOINT=https://s3.example.com
AWS_USE_PATH_STYLE_ENDPOINT=true
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop config:cache
$ sudo cipi worker restart shop
$ sudo cipi app artisan shop tinker --execute="Storage::disk('s3')->put('hello.txt','hi'); echo Storage::disk('s3')->exists('hello.txt') ? 'ok' : 'fail';"
```

`ok` means the app writes to Johnny. The file appears in the panel's object browser.

## 4. Send Cipi backups to Johnny 

Create a `cipi-backups` bucket and a key for it, then on each Cipi server:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup destination add johnny --bucket=cipi-backups \
    --key=GK… --secret=… --region=johnny --endpoint=https://s3.example.com
$ sudo cipi backup destination test
$ sudo cipi backup profile add shop-nightly --scope=all --cron='0 2 * * *' \
    --keep-days=14 --dest=johnny --encrypt
```

Backups are encrypted on the Cipi server before they leave it, so Johnny only ever stores encrypted archives. [More on backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3).

## 5. Bring your files from AWS, Spaces or R2 

**Transfers → New connection**: enter the provider's endpoint and keys. Johnny lists its buckets: import them once, or set a scheduled sync (copy or mirror, with a dry run first).

When the copy is complete, switch the app's `AWS_*` variables to Johnny and run `config:cache`.

## 6. Keep a copy elsewhere 

Every night at 03:00 Johnny copies every bucket to the SFTP targets in `/etc/johnny/backup.json`, in dated folders, and deletes folders older than the retention (90 days by default). Add at least one target: a single storage server is a single point of failure. Logs: `/var/log/johnny-nightly.log`.

## Security checklist 

| Do | Why |
| --- | --- |
| One key per app, scoped to its bucket | Limits the damage of a leaked key |
| Keys only in the server's `.env` | Never in Git ([secrets guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-env-secrets)) |
| Two-factor on the panel | The panel can create keys |
| An SFTP backup target in another place | Disk or server failure |
| Expiring share links | Links to private files expire in an hour, a day or a week |

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Could not resolve host shop-uploads.s3.example.com` | Path style is off: `AWS_USE_PATH_STYLE_ENDPOINT=true`, then `config:cache` |
| `AccessDenied` | The key isn't allowed on that bucket, or is read-only |
| `Class "League\Flysystem\AwsS3V3\…" not found` | Install `league/flysystem-aws-s3-v3` and deploy |
| Certificate error at install | DNS didn't point at the VPS before installing: fix DNS, run the installer again |
| `destination test` fails from Cipi | Check endpoint, region `johnny`, and that the key can write to the bucket |
| Uploads work, browser can't load files | Bucket is private (good): serve files through signed URLs (`Storage::temporaryUrl`) |


## Move Laravel apps to a new server with cipi sync

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-server-cipi-sync

`cipi sync` copies whole apps between Cipi servers: configuration, deploy keys, workers, crontab, PHP version and, if you want, database and storage. Archives are encrypted with AES-256. The old server keeps serving until you switch DNS.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Sync** | Copying apps (settings, keys, workers, optionally data) between Cipi servers |
| **Trust** | The new server accepts pushes from the old one's key only |
| **Cut-over** | Switching DNS to the new server |

## 1. Prepare the new server

Install Cipi on it ([providers](https://cipi.sh/guides/#providers)) and install the same PHP versions your apps use (`sudo cipi php install 8.5`).

## 2. Trust between the two servers

```bash
# old server
$ sudo cipi sync pubkey
# new server: paste it
$ sudo cipi sync trust
```

## 3. Push the apps

```bash
$ sudo cipi sync push --host=203.0.113.20 --with-db --with-storage --import
```

Or one app at a time: `sudo cipi sync push shop --host=…`.

| Travels | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| `.env`, `auth.json`, `deploy.php` | Always |
