| Deploy key and SSH config | The same key keeps working on GitHub |
| Workers, crontab, PHP version, limits | Always |
| Database | With `--with-db`; new database password on a new app |
| `shared/storage` | With `--with-storage` |
| Certificates | Never: issued on the new server after DNS moves |

## 4. Test before switching

Point your laptop's `/etc/hosts` at the new IP and browse the app. Then deploy once on the new server to check the Git path end to end:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

## 5. Switch DNS, then certificates

Lower the TTL a day before. Change the `A` records, wait for propagation, then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop
```

Run a last `sync push --with-db --update` just before the switch if the database changed in the meantime.

## Keep a warm standby

The same command on a schedule replicates apps to a second server. Combined with [backups](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3), it covers both "restore yesterday" and "this server is gone".

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Push refused: not trusted | Run `cipi sync trust` on the new server with the old one's key |
| App fails on the new server | Its PHP version isn't installed there: `cipi php install` |
| Site still served by the old server | DNS TTL: wait, check `dig +short` |
| Duplicate jobs during the move | Stop workers on the old server after the final sync |


## Server notifications: Telegram, Slack, e-mail and webhooks done right

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/notifications-alerts

A server that fails quietly is the worst kind. Cipi can tell you when something needs your attention (a failed deploy, a backup that didn't run, a full disk, an SSH login) on the channels you already use. This guide explains how notifications work and how to set them up so they help instead of becoming noise.

## How it works

```flow
Something happens | deploy, backup, monitor, login…
> An event happens on the server: a deploy finishes, a backup fails, disk fills up, someone logs in.
Trigger | is this event enabled?
> Cipi checks whether that event type (trigger) is enabled. You can turn each one off.
Event log | always written, kept a year
> Every event is written to the event log anyway, kept for a year, even if no alert goes out.
Channels | every enabled channel, in parallel
> The alert is sent to every enabled channel at once: e-mail, Telegram, Slack, webhooks…
You | e-mail, chat or phone
> You get it where you are. A broken channel never blocks the others or the deploy.
```

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Event** | Something that happened on the server: `deploy_fail`, `backup_stale`, `ssh_login`… |
| **Trigger** | An on/off switch per event type. All are on by default |
| **Channel** | A destination: an e-mail address, a Telegram chat, a Slack channel, a webhook URL |
| **Event log** | `/var/log/cipi/events.log`, written for every event, muted or not |

## 1. Choose your channels 

| Channel | Good for | You need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `smtp`, `resend`, `ses` | A searchable record of everything | SMTP credentials, a Resend key, or SES keys |
| `telegram` | Alerts on your phone, free | A bot token and a chat id |
| `slack`, `mattermost`, `googlechat`, `discord` | Team channels | An incoming webhook URL |
| `ntfy`, `pushover` | Push notifications with priorities | A topic URL, or Pushover keys |
| `webhook` | Your own automation (PagerDuty, n8n, a Laravel route) | A URL and a shared secret |

A sensible start: **e-mail for the record, Telegram or Slack for action**.

## 2. Add e-mail 

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification add smtp --host=smtp.example.com --port=587 \
    --user=alerts@example.com --password=… --from=alerts@example.com --to=ops@example.com --tls=on
```

Use a transactional provider (Postmark, Mailgun, Brevo, SES): mail sent directly from a VPS usually lands in spam.

## 3. Add Telegram 

```flow
@BotFather | /newbot → bot token
> In Telegram, open @BotFather, send `/newbot`, choose a name. It answers with the bot token.
Your chat | send /start to the bot
> Open a chat with your new bot (or add it to a group) and send `/start`. Bots can't write to you first.
getUpdates | read the chat id
> Open `https://api.telegram.org/bot/getUpdates` in a browser and copy `chat.id`. Group ids are negative.
cipi notification add | token + chat id
> On the server: `sudo cipi notification add telegram oncall --token= --chat-id=`, then `sudo cipi notification test oncall`.
```

1. In Telegram, open **@BotFather**, send `/newbot`, pick a name. Copy the **token**.
2. Send `/start` to your new bot (or add it to a group and write something there).
3. Open `https://api.telegram.org/bot/getUpdates` in a browser and copy `chat.id` (groups have negative ids).
4. Add the channel:

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification add telegram oncall --token= --chat-id=
```

## 4. Add Slack (or Mattermost, Google Chat, Discord) 

Create an **incoming webhook** for the channel (Slack: Apps → Incoming Webhooks), then:

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification add slack ops --url=https://hooks.slack.com/services/…
```

## 5. Test everything 

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification              # channels and triggers, no secrets shown
$ sudo cipi notification test all
```

## 6. Decide what's worth an alert 

Everything is on by default. Mute what you don't act on:

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification triggers
$ sudo cipi notification triggers disable monitor_load
$ sudo cipi notification triggers disable deploy_success
```

| Category | Events | Keep on? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deploy | `deploy_fail`, `deploy_rollback`, `deploy_health_fail`, `deploy_snapshot_fail` | **Yes** |
| | `deploy_success` | Optional: noisy with many pushes |
| Health & monitor | `health_fail`, `monitor_disk`, `monitor_ssl`, `monitor_services`, `monitor_workers`, `monitor_http_5xx` | **Yes** |
| | `monitor_load`, `monitor_ok` | Optional |
| Backups & cron | `backup_fail`, `backup_stale`, `cron_fail` | **Yes** |
| Security | `ssh_login`, `sudo`, `su`, `ssh_key_*` | **Yes** if few people log in |
| Apps & config | `app_create`, `alias_*`, `yml_apply`, `yml_fail` | Useful for teams |
| Updates | `php_upgrade`, `nginx_upgrade`, `pending_report` | Useful as a weekly record |

> [!tip] A good rule: if nobody would do anything after reading it, mute it. Alerts you ignore train you to ignore the ones that matter.

## 7. Signed webhooks for your own automation 

A webhook channel posts JSON (`server`, `trigger`, `subject`, `body`, `ts`). With a secret, each request carries `X-Cipi-Signature: sha256=…`. Verify it before trusting the payload, for example in a Laravel route:

```php
Route::post('/hooks/cipi', function (Request $request) {
    $expected = 'sha256='.hash_hmac('sha256', $request->getContent(), config('services.cipi.secret'));
    abort_unless(hash_equals($expected, (string) $request->header('X-Cipi-Signature')), 401);

    $event = $request->json()->all();       // server, trigger, subject, body, ts
    if (in_array($event['trigger'], ['deploy_fail', 'backup_fail', 'health_fail'])) {
        // page the on-call person, open a ticket…
    }
    return response()->noContent();
});
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification add webhook router --url=https://ops.example.com/hooks/cipi --secret=…
```

This is also how you route: urgent triggers to a phone, the rest to a channel.

## 8. Alerts for your own cron jobs 

Wrap a job in a root cron file with `cipi-cron-notify  `:

```text
# /etc/cron.d/shop-reports
0 4 * * * root /usr/local/bin/cipi-cron-notify daily-report sudo -u shop php /home/shop/current/artisan report:daily
```

A non-zero exit sends `cron_fail` with the label and the output, through the same channels. Cipi wraps its own nightly jobs the same way.

## A setup that works for small teams 

```stack
E-mail | everything, searchable record
Telegram group "ops" | deploy_fail, backup_*, health/monitor, security
Muted | deploy_success, monitor_load, monitor_ok
Weekly | read pending_report and update notes
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Telegram test doesn't arrive | Wrong chat id (groups are negative), or you never sent `/start` to the bot |
| E-mail in spam | Use a provider; add SPF and DKIM for the `--from` domain |
| Slack 404 | The webhook was revoked: create a new one and `cipi notification add` again |
| Too many messages | Disable noisy triggers (step 6) |
| Need history | `sudo tail -f /var/log/cipi/events.log` |


## Upgrade PHP for a Laravel app without downtime

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/php-version-upgrade

PHP has a new minor version every year (8.4, 8.5, 8.6…), each supported with security fixes for a few years. Moving apps forward keeps them fast and patched. On a Cipi server you can do it **one app at a time**, test it, and move back in seconds if needed.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Minor version** | 8.5, 8.6: new features, small breaking changes |
| **Patch version** | 8.5.3 → 8.5.4: bug and security fixes only |
| **PHP-FPM pool** | The PHP processes that serve one app's web requests |
| **Server default** | The version for `php` on the command line and new apps |
| **End of life (EOL)** | No more security fixes from PHP: move off it |

```stack
shop | PHP 8.6 pool
blog | PHP 8.4 pool
legacy | PHP 8.3 pool
Nginx | routes each domain to its app's pool
```

## Before you start 

- Know your app's current version: `sudo cipi app show shop`.
- Read the PHP migration notes for the target version (php.net has one per minor).
- Have a [backup](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3) or a [pre-deploy snapshot](https://cipi.sh/docs/safe-deploy).

## 1. Check your code locally 

```bash
$ php -v                                    # run the target version on your laptop
$ composer why-not php 8.6                  # which dependencies block it
$ composer update                           # within your constraints
$ php artisan test
```

Update `composer.json`'s `"php"` constraint (e.g. `"^8.3"`) only if you want to drop old versions. Commit the updated `composer.lock`.

## 2. Install the version on the server 

```bash
$ sudo cipi php list
$ sudo cipi php install 8.6
```

The install adds the version next to the others. Nothing changes for running apps.

## 3. Try it on a copy first 

With a staging app (or a clone):

```bash
$ sudo cipi app clone shop --domain=shop-86.example.com --name=shop-86
$ sudo cipi app edit shop-86 --php=8.6
$ sudo cipi deploy shop-86
```

Click through, run the queue, check `sudo cipi app logs shop-86 --type=laravel` for deprecations.

## 4. Move the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app edit shop --php=8.6
```

```flow
New pool | PHP 8.6 for shop
> A PHP-FPM pool for the app is created on the new version.
Vhost | points to the new pool
> The app's Nginx vhost is pointed at the new pool.
Nginx reload | no dropped requests
> Nginx reloads gracefully: requests in flight finish, new ones use the new PHP.
Workers, cron | restarted on 8.6
> Workers and cron lines switch to the new PHP binary and restart.
Old pool | removed for this app
> The app's pool on the old version is removed. The old version itself stays installed for other apps.
```

Then deploy once, so Composer installs dependencies under the new version:

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy shop
```

If the lock file rejects the new version, the deploy fails and **the live release keeps running**: update the dependency, commit, deploy again.

## 5. Roll back if needed 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app edit shop --php=8.5
$ sudo cipi deploy shop --rollback          # if a deploy changed the vendor folder
```

## 6. Change the server default and clean up 

```bash
$ sudo cipi php switch 8.6                  # CLI `php`, panel, new apps
$ sudo cipi php remove 8.3                  # refused while any app uses it
```

## Patches happen on their own 

| What | When | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PHP security releases | Every night at 03:30 | Only affected pools restart |
| Check now | Any time | `sudo cipi php upgrade` |
| Octane apps | With FrankenPHP | `sudo cipi frankenphp upgrade` |

`cipi php list` shows the state of each version: `patched`, `VULNERABLE` (a fix exists, not installed yet), `distro`, `END OF LIFE`, `prerelease`. [How CVEs are handled](https://cipi.sh/guides/php-nginx-cve-patching).

## php.ini settings survive 

Settings set with `cipi ini` move with the app. Check them after the switch:

```bash
$ sudo cipi ini list --app=shop
```

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `Your lock file does not contain a compatible set of packages` | A dependency doesn't support the version yet: `composer why-not php 8.6`, update or wait |
| Assigning is refused: missing extensions | The extension isn't published for that version yet; `--force` only if the app doesn't use it |
| Deprecation warnings flood the log | Set `LOG_DEPRECATIONS_CHANNEL=null` while you fix them |
| `php -v` shows the old version | That's the server default: `cipi php switch` (apps use their own anyway) |
| Worker still on the old version | `sudo cipi worker restart shop` |


## Server monitoring and alerts on Telegram, Slack and e-mail

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/server-monitoring-alerts

Cipi checks the server every five minutes with a cron job and a few state files: no agent, no metrics database, no external service. You choose where the alerts go.

## 1. Add a channel

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification add telegram oncall --token= --chat-id=
$ sudo cipi notification add slack ops --url=https://hooks.slack.com/services/…
$ sudo cipi notification add webhook pager --url=https://example.com/hooks/cipi --secret=…
$ sudo cipi notification test all
```

For Telegram: create a bot with @BotFather, send it `/start`, and read the chat id from `getUpdates`. Group chats have negative ids.

## 2. Pick what notifies

```bash
$ sudo cipi notification triggers
$ sudo cipi notification triggers disable monitor_load
```

Deploy failures, backups, health checks, monitor alerts, security events and SSO changes are separate triggers.

## 3. Tune the monitor

```bash
$ sudo cipi monitor list
$ sudo cipi monitor set disk --warn=85 --crit=95
$ sudo cipi monitor test
```

| Check | Alerts on |
| --- | --- |
| CPU, load, memory, swap | Sustained high usage |
| Disk | Thresholds per filesystem; [`cipi disk`](https://cipi.sh/docs/disk) shows which app is filling it |
| Services | nginx, databases, Valkey, Supervisor, PHP-FPM down |
| Certificates | Expiring soon |
| App disk | An app over its soft limit |

## 4. Watch each app from outside

```bash
$ sudo cipi health set shop --url=https://shop.example.com/up --expect=200
$ sudo cipi health check shop
```

The same check runs after every deploy and can [roll back automatically](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-zero-downtime-migrations). For a richer per-app status (database, cache, queue, storage, deploy), use the [agent's health endpoint](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-agent-health-monitoring) with an external uptime service.

More channels and webhook signatures: [notifications and alerts](https://cipi.sh/guides/notifications-alerts).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| No alerts at all | No channel configured: add one with `cipi notification add`, then `cipi notification test all` |
| Telegram silent | Bot never received `/start`, or wrong chat id (groups are negative) |
| Too many disk alerts | Clean logs and releases; lower `--keep-releases` |


## Deploy a Symfony app on an Ubuntu VPS with Cipi

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-symfony

Cipi is Laravel-first, but any PHP framework runs as a **custom app**: Nginx serves the document root you pick, PHP-FPM runs in the app's own pool, and Git deploys pull into `~/htdocs`. Here's a Symfony app end to end.

## 1. Create the app and the database

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=billing --domain=billing.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/billing.git --branch=main --docroot=public --php=8.4
$ sudo cipi db create --name=billing                 # or --engine=pgsql
```

Add the deploy key from the summary to the repository (read-only).

## 2. Configure the environment

As the app user, create `~/htdocs/.env.local` (never committed):

```bash
APP_ENV=prod
APP_SECRET=change-me
DATABASE_URL="mysql://billing:PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:3306/billing?serverVersion=mariadb-11.4.0"
```

## 3. Build after every deploy

Custom apps pull the code; `cipi.yml` runs the build steps from the live folder:

```yaml
# cipi.yml
version: 1
deploy:
  post:
    - composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader --no-interaction
    - php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction
    - php bin/console cache:clear
  post_on_failure: abort
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy billing
```

> [!note] Custom apps deploy in place (a pull into `htdocs`), not as atomic releases like Laravel apps. Keep migrations backward compatible and deploy at quiet times, or put the app behind [Cloudflare](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel) with a maintenance page.

## 4. Messenger and scheduled tasks

As the app user (`crontab -e`):

```text
* * * * * php ~/htdocs/bin/console messenger:consume async --time-limit=55 --quiet
```

Each run consumes for 55 seconds and exits, so a deploy never leaves an old worker running for long.

## 5. HTTPS, backups, alerts

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install billing
$ sudo cipi backup profile add billing-nightly --scope=all --cron='0 2 * * *' --keep-days=14 --dest=s3 --encrypt
$ sudo cipi health set billing --url=https://billing.example.com/ --expect=200
```

Everything else (firewall, PHP patches, monitoring) is server-wide and already on.

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| 500 with no details | Check `var/log/prod.log`; `APP_ENV=prod` hides errors on screen |
| Database connection refused | Wrong `DATABASE_URL`; MariaDB on 3306 or PostgreSQL on 5432, both localhost |
| Cache permission errors | `var/` must belong to the app user: `cipi app fix-permissions billing` |


## Host WordPress on your own VPS next to Laravel apps

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app

WordPress isn't Laravel, but it's PHP, and Cipi hosts it as a **custom app**: its own user, PHP pool, Nginx vhost and certificate, isolated from everything else on the server.

| | Laravel app | Custom app (WordPress) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code | Zero-downtime releases | `~/htdocs`, from Git or SFTP |
| Database | Created | One command |
| Workers, scheduler | Yes | Use the app user's crontab |

## 1. Create the app and its database

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=blog --domain=blog.example.com
$ sudo cipi db create --name=blog
```

Save the database password from the output. For a site in Git (a theme or Bedrock), add `--repository=git@github.com:acme/blog.git` and, with Bedrock, `--docroot=web`.

## 2. Upload WordPress

SFTP as the app user to `~/htdocs` (the credentials are in the create summary), or from SSH:

```bash
$ ssh blog@203.0.113.10
$ cd ~/htdocs && rm -f index.html
$ curl -sO https://wordpress.org/latest.tar.gz && tar xzf latest.tar.gz --strip-components=1 && rm latest.tar.gz
```

Open `https://blog.example.com` (after step 3) and run the installer with database `blog`, user `blog` and the saved password, host `127.0.0.1`.

## 3. HTTPS

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install blog
$ sudo cipi ssl force blog
```

Set both URLs to `https://` in **Settings → General**.

## 4. Real cron instead of WP-Cron

In `wp-config.php`: `define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true);` then, as the app user (`crontab -e`):

```text
*/5 * * * * php ~/htdocs/wp-cron.php >/dev/null 2>&1
```

## 5. PHP settings and limits

```yaml
# cipi.yml in htdocs (vhosts never serve it)
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.4"
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 64M, post_max_size: 64M, memory_limit: 256M }
```

Or from the CLI: `sudo cipi app edit blog --php=8.4`. Check plugin compatibility before moving to a newer PHP.

## 6. Back it up

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup profile add blog-nightly --scope=all --cron='0 3 * * *' --keep-days=14 --dest=s3 --encrypt
```

`all` covers the database and the files. More in [backups to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3). Running a shop? See [WooCommerce on a VPS](https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps).

## Troubleshooting 

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| "Error establishing a database connection" | Credentials in `wp-config.php` don't match `cipi db create` output |
| Upload size limit | `sudo cipi ini set upload_max_filesize=64M --app=blog` and `post_max_size` |
| Permalinks 404 | Cipi's vhost already routes to `index.php`; resave permalinks |
| Mixed content after HTTPS | Update `siteurl`/`home` to `https://` |


## Self-host PHP e-commerce on a VPS: Bagisto, Lunar, Sylius, PrestaShop and more

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/php-ecommerce-vps

PHP runs a large share of the world's online shops. There's no single "right" platform: some are full shops you configure from an admin panel, others are toolkits developers build on. This guide explains the options and shows how to run each on your own server with Cipi, starting from zero.

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Laravel app** on Cipi | Deploys as atomic releases with zero downtime and rollback; gets queue workers, the scheduler and `cipi.yml` |
| **Custom app** on Cipi | Any other PHP software: code in `~/htdocs`, deployed from Git (in place) or by SFTP |
| **Document root** | The folder the web server exposes: `public/` for Laravel and Symfony, `pub/` for Magento, the root for PrestaShop |
| **Queue / workers** | Background processes for e-mails, payments callbacks, imports |
| **Headless** | A shop engine with an API; you build the storefront separately (for example with Next.js or Nuxt) |

## Which platform runs how 

| Platform | Built on | Runs on Cipi as | Document root | Background tasks | Search |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Bagisto** | Laravel | Laravel app | managed | Workers + scheduler, built in | Database or Meilisearch |
| **Lunar** | Laravel (package) | Laravel app | managed | Workers + scheduler | Scout + Meilisearch |
| **Aimeos** | Laravel (package) | Laravel app | managed | Workers + scheduler | Database |
| **Sylius** | Symfony | Custom app | `public` | Messenger via cron | Plugins |
| **PrestaShop** | Symfony + legacy | Custom app | root | Module crons | Built in |
| **WooCommerce** | WordPress | Custom app | root | Real cron ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps)) | Built in |
| **Magento 2** | Laminas/Symfony | Possible as custom app | `pub` | Cron | Needs OpenSearch, hosted elsewhere |

```flow
Laravel-based? | yes → Laravel app, full automation
> Bagisto, Lunar, Aimeos: create them as Laravel apps and get workers, scheduler, atomic deploys and `cipi.yml`.
Symfony or other PHP? | custom app + cipi.yml post-deploy steps
> Sylius, PrestaShop or other PHP: create a custom app; add the build steps in `deploy.post` of `cipi.yml`.
Needs OpenSearch/Varnish? | host those services separately
> Platforms that require OpenSearch or Varnish (e.g. Magento) need those services elsewhere: Cipi doesn't install them.
```

## Example 1: Bagisto, a Laravel shop 

Because Bagisto is a Laravel app, it gets everything: zero-downtime deploys, queue workers, the scheduler and Meilisearch.

**1. Create the project** (on your laptop), commit it to Git:

```bash
$ composer create-project bagisto/bagisto store
$ cd store && git init && git add . && git commit -m "Bagisto" && git push
```

**2. Create the app and deploy** (on the server):

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=store --domain=store.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/store.git --branch=main --php=8.4
$ sudo cipi deploy store
$ sudo cipi ssl install store
```

Cipi writes the `.env` with database credentials, creates the database, a queue worker and the scheduler cron. Run Bagisto's installer once:

```bash
$ sudo cipi app artisan store bagisto:install
```

**3. Describe the shop in `cipi.yml`** and commit it:

```yaml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.4"
  aliases: ["www.store.example.com"]
  www: to-root
  ini: { memory_limit: 512M, upload_max_filesize: 64M, post_max_size: 64M }
workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }
schedule: true
health:
  url: "https://store.example.com/"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true
deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: store-db, scope: db, every: 30m, keep: 48, destinations: [local] }
    - { name: store-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 3 * * *", keep_days: 30, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy store && sudo cipi yml plan store && sudo cipi yml apply store
```

From now on, every push deploys with a database snapshot first, and rolls back by itself if the shop stops answering.

## Example 2: Sylius, a Symfony shop 

Sylius is Symfony, so it runs as a **custom app** with `public/` as document root. Build steps run after each pull through `cipi.yml`.

**1. Create the app and the database:**

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=sylius --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:acme/sylius-shop.git --branch=main --docroot=public --php=8.4
$ sudo cipi db create --name=sylius --app=sylius
$ sudo cipi ssl install sylius
```

**2. Configure the environment** as the app user, in `~/htdocs/.env.local` (never committed):

```bash
APP_ENV=prod
APP_SECRET=change-me-to-a-random-string
DATABASE_URL="mysql://sylius:PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:3306/sylius?serverVersion=mariadb-11.4.0"
MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN=doctrine://default
```

**3. Build steps after each deploy** in `htdocs/cipi.yml`:

```yaml
version: 1
deploy:
  post:
    - composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader --no-interaction
    - php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction
    - php bin/console sylius:install:assets
    - php bin/console cache:clear
  post_on_failure: abort
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi deploy sylius
```

**4. Background messages:** as the app user (`crontab -e`):

```text
* * * * * php ~/htdocs/bin/console messenger:consume async --time-limit=55 --quiet
```

> [!note] Custom apps deploy in place (a `git pull` into `htdocs`), not as atomic releases. Keep migrations backward compatible and deploy at quiet times. Full Symfony walkthrough: [Deploy Symfony](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-symfony).

## Example 3: PrestaShop 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=presta --domain=presta.example.com --php=8.3
$ sudo cipi db create --name=presta --app=presta
$ sudo cipi ssl install presta
```

Upload the PrestaShop release to `~/htdocs` by SFTP, open the domain and run the installer (database host `127.0.0.1`). Delete the `install` folder afterwards and rename the `admin` folder as the installer asks. Add the cron URLs of the modules you use to the app user's crontab.

## What every shop needs 

| Need | How |
| --- | --- |
| HTTPS, forced | `sudo cipi ssl install  && sudo cipi ssl force ` |
| Database every 30 minutes | `--every=30m --keep=48` profile, local |
| Everything nightly, off-site | `--cron='0 3 * * *' --dest=s3 --encrypt` profile ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3)) |
| Verified backups | `sudo cipi backup verify` (alerts on failure) |
| Enough PHP workers | `sudo cipi app limits  --fpm-max-children=12` |
| A staging copy | Laravel shops: `cipi app clone`; others: a second custom app with a restored dump |
| Alerts | [Telegram, Slack or e-mail](https://cipi.sh/guides/notifications-alerts) |
| Transactional e-mail | An SMTP or API provider, never direct from the VPS |

## Troubleshooting 

| Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| 404 on every page but the home (Symfony, PrestaShop) | Wrong document root: recreate with `--docroot=public`, or check the platform's Nginx rules |
| 500 after deploy (custom app) | Read `sudo cipi app logs  --type=php`; a `deploy.post` step may have failed |
| Assets missing after deploy | Run the asset build in `deploy.post` (Symfony) or `node_build` (Laravel) |
| Slow admin | Raise `memory_limit` and `fpm_max_children`; check slow queries |


## WooCommerce on your own VPS, step by step

URL: https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps

WooCommerce turns WordPress into a shop. A shop is more demanding than a blog: orders arrive all day, payment webhooks must never be missed, and losing a day of data means losing orders. This guide sets up a WooCommerce shop on your own server with Cipi, from an empty VPS to a protected, backed-up store, explaining each step.

## What you'll build

```stack
Visitors | https://shop.example.com
Nginx + PHP-FPM | isolated app "shop", its own PHP pool
WordPress + WooCommerce | files in /home/shop/htdocs
MariaDB | database "shop", its own user
Cron every minute | Action Scheduler: orders, e-mails, webhooks
Backups | DB every 30 min, everything nightly to S3
```

## Key ideas, in plain words 

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Custom app** | How Cipi hosts any PHP software that isn't Laravel: code in `~/htdocs`, served by Nginx and PHP-FPM ([docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/custom-apps)) |
| **PHP-FPM pool** | The PHP processes that run your shop. Each app has its own, with its own limits |
| **Action Scheduler** | The queue WooCommerce uses for background tasks (e-mails, stock, webhooks, subscriptions) |
| **WP-Cron** | WordPress' built-in scheduler, triggered by visits. Not reliable for a shop |
| **Staging** | A private copy of the shop where you try updates first |

## Before you start 

- A VPS with Cipi installed ([quickstart](https://cipi.sh/docs/quickstart)): 2 GB RAM or more.
- A domain, with an `A` record for `shop.example.com` pointing at the server.
- An account at an e-mail provider for order e-mails (SMTP credentials).

## 1. Create the app and its database 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com --php=8.4
$ sudo cipi db create --name=shop --app=shop
```

The first command creates a Linux user `shop`, the folder `/home/shop/htdocs`, a PHP pool and the Nginx site. The second creates the database `shop` with its own user and links it to the app. **Save the database password** from the output: it's shown once.

> [!tip] Check your plugins' PHP support before choosing the version. You can change it later with `sudo cipi app edit shop --php=8.5`.

## 2. Install WordPress 

Log in as the app user and download WordPress into the web folder:

```bash
$ ssh shop@203.0.113.10          # password and key from the create summary
$ cd ~/htdocs && rm -f index.html
$ curl -sO https://wordpress.org/latest.tar.gz
$ tar xzf latest.tar.gz --strip-components=1 && rm latest.tar.gz
```

Prefer a graphical tool? Connect with SFTP (FileZilla, Transmit, Cyberduck) as `shop` and upload the files to `htdocs`.

## 3. HTTPS before anything else 

```bash
$ sudo cipi ssl install shop
$ sudo cipi ssl force shop
```

The certificate is free (Let's Encrypt), covers every alias and renews itself. `force` redirects every `http://` request to `https://`, which payment providers require.

Now open `https://shop.example.com`, run the WordPress installer (database `shop`, user `shop`, the saved password, host `127.0.0.1`), then install **WooCommerce** from Plugins.

## 4. PHP limits for a shop 

Product imports, big carts and payment callbacks need more than WordPress' defaults. Put the settings in a `cipi.yml` at the root of `htdocs` (Nginx never serves it):

```yaml
# /home/shop/htdocs/cipi.yml
version: 1
app:
  php: "8.4"
  ini:
    memory_limit: 512M
    max_execution_time: 120
    upload_max_filesize: 64M
    post_max_size: 64M
```

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml plan shop && sudo cipi yml apply shop
$ sudo cipi app limits shop --fpm-max-children=12     # parallel PHP workers
```

| Setting | Why a shop needs it |
| --- | --- |
| `memory_limit` | WooCommerce with a page builder and a few plugins easily exceeds 256 MB |
| `max_execution_time` | CSV imports and report generation take time |
| Upload sizes | Product images and import files |
| `fpm_max_children` | How many shoppers PHP serves at once. Each child uses ~60–120 MB: 12 children ≈ 1.5 GB |

## 5. A real cron for Action Scheduler 

Tell WordPress to stop running cron on page views. In `wp-config.php`, above "That's all, stop editing":

```php
define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true);
```

Then add a real cron as the app user (`crontab -e`):

```text
* * * * * php ~/htdocs/wp-cron.php >/dev/null 2>&1
```

Check it: WooCommerce → Status → Scheduled Actions should show past-due actions going to zero.

## 6. Order e-mails that arrive 

Install an SMTP plugin (WP Mail SMTP, FluentSMTP…) and enter your provider's SMTP host, port 587 and credentials. Send a test e-mail from the plugin. Add your provider's SPF and DKIM records to your DNS.

## 7. Speed 

| Layer | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| PHP | OPcache is on by default. Keep PHP current: Cipi patches it every night |
| Page cache | A plugin that writes static HTML (cart, checkout and account pages excluded) |
| Images | Serve WebP; the optional `image-optimizers` host package adds `cwebp`, `jpegoptim`, `pngquant` (`sudo cipi package install image-optimizers`) |
| CDN | Cloudflare in front (orange cloud) with SSL mode **Full (strict)** |
| Database | Keep `wp_options` autoload small; delete old transients |

## 8. Backups that match your orders 

A shop changes every few minutes, so back up the database often and everything nightly, to another place:

```bash
$ sudo cipi backup configure          # once: your S3-compatible bucket
$ sudo cipi backup profile add shop-db --scope=db --databases=shop --every=30m --keep=48 --dest=local
$ sudo cipi backup profile add shop-nightly --scope=all --cron='0 3 * * *' --keep-days=30 --dest=s3 --encrypt
$ sudo cipi backup verify
```

```flow
Every 30 min | database dump, kept 24 h
> A database-only backup every 30 minutes, kept for 24 hours: orders placed in the last half hour are the most you can lose.
Every night | files + database, encrypted
> Every night, files and database together, encrypted.
Off-site | S3-compatible bucket
> Archives go to an S3-compatible bucket at another provider or region.
Verify | archives checked automatically
> Cipi checks the archives can be opened and alerts you if a profile stops producing backups.
```

At worst you lose 30 minutes of orders. Full guide: [backups to S3](https://cipi.sh/guides/backup-vps-s3).

## 9. A staging copy for updates 

Never update WooCommerce, the theme or payment plugins straight on the live shop.

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --custom --user=shopstg --domain=staging.shop.example.com --php=8.4
$ sudo cipi db create --name=shopstg --app=shopstg
$ sudo cipi basicauth enable shopstg
$ sudo cipi ssl install shopstg
```

Copy the files (`rsync -a /home/shop/htdocs/ /home/shopstg/htdocs/` as root, then `sudo cipi app fix-permissions shopstg`), restore last night's dump into `shopstg`, change the database name, user and password in `wp-config.php`, and set `WP_HOME` and `WP_SITEURL` to the staging URL. Then **turn off** payment gateways (or switch them to test mode) and outgoing e-mail on staging.

## 10. Security 

| Item | How |
| --- | --- |
| HTTPS everywhere | Done in step 3 |
| Brute-force on `/wp-login.php` | fail2ban is on; add Cloudflare Access on `/wp-admin` for the team ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/cloudflare-zero-trust-laravel)) |
| File changes | `sudo cipi scan shop` finds known malware; run it after installing plugins |
| Isolation | Other apps on the server can't read `/home/shop` |
| Updates | PHP patched nightly by Cipi; WordPress, themes and plugins by you, after staging |
| Alerts | Backup failures and server problems on Telegram or Slack ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/notifications-alerts)) |

## Troubleshooting 

| Symptom | Likely cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| "Error establishing a database connection" | Wrong DB credentials in `wp-config.php`, or host `localhost` instead of `127.0.0.1` |
| White page or 502 after a plugin install | PHP memory: raise `memory_limit`, check `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=php` |
| Uploads fail above 2 MB | `upload_max_filesize` and `post_max_size` not applied: `sudo cipi yml plan shop` |
| Orders stuck "pending payment" | Payment webhook blocked: the shop must be reachable over HTTPS; check the gateway's webhook log |
| Scheduled actions past due | Real cron missing: `crontab -l` as `shop` |
| Mixed-content warnings | Site URLs still `http://`: update them in Settings → General |

# Comparisons


## Cipi vs 20i

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-20i

## In 30 seconds 

20i is a UK hosting company: you buy a plan and they run the servers, with their own panel, e-mail and backups. Cipi is software: you rent a VPS anywhere and Cipi runs it for your apps, with full root access, queues, Octane and Git releases. Choose 20i if you want hosting with nothing to manage and mail included; choose Cipi for full control of Laravel apps and predictable server pricing.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | 20i |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you buy | Nothing: Cipi is free; you rent a VPS anywhere | A hosting plan from 20i |
| Root access | Yes | No on shared plans |
| Laravel queues, Horizon, Octane, Reverb | Built in | Limited by the plan |
| E-mail hosting | Not included | Included |
| Where it runs | Any provider | 20i's infrastructure |

Prices as published by 20i in November 2026; check [their site](https://www.20i.com) for the current ones.

## What 20i is 

20i is a hosting provider offering shared, WordPress, reseller and cloud server hosting managed through its own control panel, with e-mail, DNS and backups included.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where 20i is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing to manage | They run the servers. |
| Mail and DNS included | One bill for web, mail and domains. |
| Reseller tools | For agencies selling hosting. |

**Where 20i falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Shared-hosting limits | Long-running workers, Supervisor and custom services are restricted on shared plans. |
| Less control | No root on shared plans. |
| Tied to one provider | Moving means a migration like this one. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**Real Laravel.** Queue workers, Horizon, Reverb, Octane and the scheduler every minute.

**Root access.** Install what you need with [packages](https://cipi.sh/docs/packages).

**Any provider.** Pick price and region freely.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every 20i feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In 20i | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Website | `cipi app create` | [Create an app](https://cipi.sh/docs/create-app) |
| Databases (phpMyAdmin) | `cipi db`, SSH tunnel tools | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| SSL | `cipi ssl install` | [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl) |
| Backups | `cipi backup` | [Backups](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) |
| Email | Not included | Mail provider |
| DNS | Not included | Your registrar or Cloudflare |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Export the site's database and files from 20i, rebuild on Cipi, switch DNS and MX.

**Before you start**

- Access to 20i's control panel for the site.
- A plan for e-mail if 20i hosts your mailboxes.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | sites, databases, mail | #inventory
Make a backup | download everything | #backup
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Recreate each site | Laravel or custom app | #create
Import the databases | from the .sql files | #data
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, mail | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

List every site in 20i: domain, document root, PHP version, databases, cron jobs. Note what isn't a website: **e-mail accounts, DNS zones, FTP users**. Cipi hosts apps, not mailboxes or DNS, so those need a new home (see *What doesn't move* below).

### 2. Make a backup 

From 20i's control panel, export each database with **phpMyAdmin** (Export → SQL) and download the website files over SFTP or the File Manager. 20i also offers backups you can download.

### 3. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and install Cipi:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Then log in as `cipi` (`ssh cipi@NEW_IP`). New to this? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 4. Recreate each site 

Pick the right kind of app for each site:

| Site | Create it as | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laravel app in Git | Laravel app | `sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.com --repository=git@…` |
| WordPress, PrestaShop, plain PHP | Custom app | `sudo cipi app create --custom --user=blog --domain=blog.com` |
| Static HTML | Custom app | same, then upload the files |

For custom apps, upload the site's files into `~/htdocs` as the app user (SFTP, or `rsync` from the extracted backup), then create its database with `sudo cipi db create --name=blog --app=blog`. Step by step: [WordPress](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app), [WooCommerce](https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps).

### 5. Import the databases 

Copy each `.sql` file from the backup to the server and restore it:

```bash
$ scp blog.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore blog /tmp/blog.sql"
```

Then update the site's config with the new database name, user and password Cipi printed (`wp-config.php` for WordPress, `.env` for Laravel). Database names usually change: hosting panels prefix them with the account name (`acct_blog`), Cipi doesn't.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

If the old panel also handled your **e-mail**, move the MX records to your new mail provider at the same time, and keep the old mailboxes until every message has been copied.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| E-mail accounts and mailboxes | Move mail to a mail provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Fastmail, Zoho, Migadu…) and change the MX records. Cipi sends app e-mail through any SMTP service. |
| DNS zones | Keep DNS at your registrar or move it to Cloudflare (free). |
| FTP accounts | SFTP as each app's own user, with keys or a password. |
| Reseller accounts and hosting packages | Not a Cipi feature: it hosts your apps. Hosting providers can automate Cipi apps with the [WHMCS module](https://cipi.sh/docs/whmcs). |
| Softaculous / one-click installers | Install the CMS yourself (WordPress: [guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app)). |


## The best Laravel Forge alternatives in 2026

URL: https://cipi.sh/best-laravel-forge-alternatives

Forge made deploying Laravel to your own server easy. It's also a subscription, and the control plane lives on someone else's servers. Here are the alternatives, grouped by how they work.

| Tool | Model | Price | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cipi** | Self-hosted, CLI + optional panel | Free (MIT) | Laravel teams that want everything on their own server, configuration in Git and AI tooling |
| Vito Deploy | Self-hosted dashboard | Free | Teams that want a central, plugin-friendly GUI |
| Ploi | SaaS panel | Free tier, then €8–30/month by server count | A Forge-like hosted panel based in the EU |
| RunCloud, Cleavr | SaaS panels | Paid plans | Hosted GUI, PHP and WordPress-friendly |
| Laravel Cloud | Managed platform | From $5/month plus usage | No servers, autoscaling |
| Coolify | Self-hosted Docker platform | Free | Containers for many stacks |
| Kamal | Deploy tool | Free | Docker teams that provision servers themselves |

## 1. Cipi

Free and open source. One command turns an Ubuntu VPS into a hardened Laravel platform: zero-downtime releases, workers, scheduler, Octane, Horizon, Reverb, Meilisearch, backups to S3, monitoring and nightly security patches. Server settings can live in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml); the [web panel](https://cipi.sh/docs/gui) and [API](https://cipi.sh/docs/api) are optional and self-hosted; [MCP servers](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents) let AI assistants help safely. [Cipi vs Forge](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-forge).

## 2. Vito Deploy

Free, open-source dashboard built with Laravel, with provider integrations, plugins and workflows. Runs as its own app that manages your servers. [Cipi vs Vito Deploy](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-vito-deploy).

## 3. Ploi

The closest SaaS to Forge, from the Netherlands, with plans by server count and an MCP server. [Cipi vs Ploi](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-ploi).

## 4. RunCloud and Cleavr

Hosted panels with PHP and WordPress strengths. [RunCloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-runcloud), [Cleavr](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cleavr).

## 5. Laravel Cloud

No servers: you push code and pay usage, with autoscaling and scale-to-zero. [Cipi vs Laravel Cloud](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-cloud).

## 6. Coolify

A self-hosted Docker platform for any stack. [Cipi vs Coolify](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify).

## 7. Kamal

Container deploys over SSH to servers you prepare. [Cipi vs Kamal](https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-kamal).

## How to choose

```flow
Want to own the server? | no → Laravel Cloud
Laravel or PHP? | many stacks → Coolify
Want a subscription? | yes → Ploi or Forge
Otherwise | Cipi or Vito Deploy
```

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Build a Cipi server, recreate each site, copy env and data, test privately, switch DNS.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Workers and scheduled jobs | daemons, scheduled jobs | #workers

```

### 1. Take inventory 

Open Cleavr's dashboard and write down, for each site you move:

| What | Where to find it in Cleavr | You'll need it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domain and aliases | the site's domain settings | `cipi app create --domain`, `cipi alias add` |
| Repository and branch | the site's Git / deployment settings | `--repository`, `--branch` |
| PHP version | the site's PHP settings | `--php` (Cipi offers 8.3–8.6) |
| Environment (`.env`) | the site's environment or `.env` file | your own keys and `APP_KEY` |
| Daemons | the server's daemons / Supervisor section | `cipi worker add` or Horizon |
| Scheduled jobs | the server's cron section | the scheduler (automatic) or `crons:` in cipi.yml |
| Deploy script | the site's deploy script or hooks | Cipi's deploy options or `deploy.post` |
| Databases | the server's databases section | `cipi db restore` |

Replace `SITE_PATH` below with the folder Cleavr shows for the site (with releases, use its `current` folder for `.env` and `storage`).

On the old server, the site's files are usually in `SITE_PATH`. You'll log in with `ssh cleavr@OLD_IP`.

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 (don't install Cipi on the old server: it configures Nginx, PHP and users its own way). Then:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4          # the version the app uses today, if not the default
```

New to servers? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.4
```

The summary shows a **deploy key**: add it to the repository as a read-only deploy key (or save a Git token in Cipi and it's done for you). Check with `sudo cipi git check shop`. Then add the other domains with `sudo cipi alias add shop www.shop.example.com`.

### 4. Copy the .env 

Print the old file: `ssh cleavr@OLD_IP "cat SITE_PATH/.env"`. Copy your own keys (mail, payments, storage, APIs) into the new app with `sudo cipi app env shop` (opens an editor). **Keep Cipi's database and Redis values**: they point at the new server.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

Then deploy once: `sudo cipi deploy shop`. Migrations create an empty schema; the data comes next.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database, from the old server:

```bash
$ ssh cleavr@OLD_IP
$ mysqldump --single-transaction --quick -u DB_USER -p shop | gzip > /tmp/shop.sql.gz
$ exit
$ scp cleavr@OLD_IP:/tmp/shop.sql.gz . && scp shop.sql.gz cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql.gz"
```

Uploaded files (skip if they're on S3):

```bash
$ rsync -az cleavr@OLD_IP:SITE_PATH/storage/app/ ./shop-storage/
$ rsync -az ./shop-storage/ cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/shop-storage/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo rsync -a /tmp/shop-storage/ /home/shop/shared/storage/app/ && sudo chown -R shop:shop /home/shop/shared/storage/app"
```

Cipi's restore stops at the first error and refuses empty dumps, so a broken file never wipes the database.

### 6. Workers and scheduled jobs 

For every queue Cleavr ran, add a worker. The Laravel scheduler is already on for every app.

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop     # if you used Horizon
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop
```

Or put it all in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) so it lives with your code. Extra commands from the old deploy script go in `sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --extra-artisan=…` or in `deploy.post`.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

Also stop the old server's daemons and scheduled jobs, so jobs don't run twice against the old database.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Server provisioning from the dashboard | Create the VPS at your provider, then install Cipi. |


## Cipi vs CloudPanel

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cloudpanel

## In 30 seconds 

CloudPanel is a free GUI panel for PHP, Node, Python and static sites on one server, with per-site users and nightly database dumps. It leaves deployment to you. Cipi automates the Laravel lifecycle (Git releases, rollback, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Octane), adds `cipi.yml` and MCP, and is also free. Choose CloudPanel for a GUI over mixed stacks; choose Cipi when your apps are Laravel and PHP and you want deploys automated.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | CloudPanel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free, MIT | Free |
| Interface | CLI first, optional panel | Web GUI |
| Git push-to-deploy, releases, rollback | Built in | Do it yourself |
| Queues and scheduler | Built in | Configure by hand |
| Stacks | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends, static | PHP, Node, Python, static, reverse proxy |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | No |

Prices as published by CloudPanel in November 2026; check [their site](https://www.cloudpanel.io) for the current ones.

## What CloudPanel is 

CloudPanel is a free control panel you install on a server. Each site gets a site user, with files in `/home//htdocs/`. It manages Nginx vhosts, PHP versions, databases (with nightly dumps kept 7 days), SSL and cron jobs, and has a CLI (`clpctl`).

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where CloudPanel is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free, fast GUI | Easy for mixed sites. |
| Multi-stack | PHP, Node, Python, static. |
| Nightly database dumps | Kept for 7 days. |

**Where CloudPanel falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| No deployment pipeline | Git deploys, releases and rollback are up to you. |
| Laravel workers by hand | Supervisor and scheduler configuration are manual. |
| No config as code | Settings live in the GUI, not in your repository. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**Deploys done for you.** Push, release, rollback, workers restarted.

**Laravel runtime wired in.** Horizon, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, Valkey per app.

**Same price: free.** No licence on either side, so the choice is about features.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every CloudPanel feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In CloudPanel | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Site | `cipi app create` (Laravel) or `--custom` | [Create an app](https://cipi.sh/docs/create-app) |
| Site user | The app's Linux user | [App SSH](https://cipi.sh/docs/app-ssh) |
| Databases | `cipi db` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| clpctl db:export / import | `cipi db backup` / `cipi db restore` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |

| Let's Encrypt | `cipi ssl install` | [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl) |

## Cipi vs Coolify

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-coolify

## In 30 seconds 

Coolify is an open-source, self-hostable PaaS: it builds and runs Docker containers for almost any stack, with one-click services and a web dashboard. Cipi skips containers for PHP and runs Laravel natively, with the Laravel lifecycle built in, configuration as code and MCP. Choose Coolify if you host many different stacks; choose Cipi if your apps are Laravel and PHP and you want them lean and Laravel-aware.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Coolify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free (MIT) | Free self-hosted (Apache 2.0); paid cloud-hosted dashboard |
| Model | Native Nginx, PHP-FPM or Octane, databases on Ubuntu | Docker containers behind a proxy |
| Interface | CLI first, optional panel | Web dashboard |
| Laravel lifecycle | Releases, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb built in | Generic app containers you configure |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Compose files and dashboard settings |
| One-click services | Meilisearch, PostgreSQL, Valkey | Large catalogue |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |

Prices as published by Coolify in November 2026; check [their site](https://coolify.io) for the current ones.

## What Coolify is 

Coolify is an open-source, self-hostable platform (often described as a self-hosted Heroku or Vercel). It deploys apps from Git with Nixpacks, Dockerfiles or Docker Compose, runs databases and one-click services in containers, handles certificates through its proxy, and schedules database backups to S3.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Coolify is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Any stack | Node, Python, Go, PHP, static, compose files. |
| One-click services | Hundreds of templates. |
| Free and open source | Self-host it at no cost. |
| Database backups to S3 | Scheduled from the dashboard. |

**Where Coolify falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Containers for everything | Extra layer, memory and complexity for a PHP app. |
| Laravel is generic | Workers, scheduler and Horizon are containers you wire yourself. |
| A dashboard to run and update | Coolify itself is an app to keep healthy. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Not for every stack | Cipi runs Laravel, PHP and Node front ends natively. Go, Python, Rails or arbitrary Docker images aren't its job. |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**No container layer for PHP.** Nginx and PHP-FPM (or Octane) run directly on the server: less memory, simpler debugging, logs where you expect them.

**Laravel's lifecycle built in.** Releases with rollback, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane and health checks without writing Dockerfiles or compose files.

**Server care included.** Firewall, Fail2ban, nightly PHP patches, encrypted backups to S3 and monitoring.

**Config as code and AI.** `cipi.yml` and MCP out of the box.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every Coolify feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In Coolify | In Cipi | Docs |

| Services catalogue | Meilisearch, Valkey, PostgreSQL, packages | [Services](https://cipi.sh/docs/services) |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Rebuild each Laravel app natively on a Cipi server, copy env and data, then switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- Access to the Coolify dashboard and SSH to its server.
- Your app's repository.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | apps, env, volumes | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | natively, not in a container | #create
Copy the environment | variables → .env | #env
Copy the data | dump and volumes | #data
Workers and schedules | Supervisor, cron | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

For each app on Coolify, note: the Git repository and branch, the build or Dockerfile, environment variables (the resource's **Environment Variables** tab), attached databases, persistent volumes (uploads), workers and scheduled commands, domains. 

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a new VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and run `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash`. Cipi runs PHP, Nginx and databases natively: no Docker needed. For PostgreSQL apps add `sudo cipi db install pgsql`.

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.5
```

What the Dockerfile did, Cipi already does: PHP extensions, Composer, `npm run build` (`--node-build`), migrations. Commands specific to your image go in `deploy.post` of [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml). Node front ends become [Node apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/node-apps).

### 4. Copy the environment 

Copy your variables from the resource's **Environment Variables** tab into the app's `.env` with `sudo cipi app env shop`. Keep Cipi's `DB_*` and `REDIS_*` values: the database is now local.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database:

```bash
# on the Coolify server: find the database container, then dump it
$ docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -i postgres     # or mysql / mariadb
$ docker exec CONTAINER pg_dump -U USER --no-owner --no-acl DBNAME > shop.sql
# MySQL/MariaDB: docker exec CONTAINER mariadb-dump -u root -pPASSWORD DBNAME > shop.sql
$ scp shop.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/ && ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql"
```

Files: uploads stored on a volume can be copied with `docker cp CONTAINER:/path/to/storage/app ./storage-app` (the path depends on your image), then `rsync` to `/home/shop/shared/storage/app/` on Cipi. If you used Coolify's scheduled backups, you can also download the latest dump from S3.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Workers and schedules 

Worker containers become Supervisor workers (`sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=…`), a Horizon container becomes `sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop`, and the scheduler container isn't needed: Cipi runs `schedule:run` every minute for every Laravel app.

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Non-PHP apps and arbitrary images | Keep them on Coolify or another container platform. |
| One-click services Cipi doesn't run | Host them separately and connect over the network. |


## Cipi vs cPanel

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-cpanel

## In 30 seconds 

cPanel & WHM is built for hosting companies: accounts, mailboxes, DNS, FTP, resellers. It's licensed per server by the number of accounts. If you run your own Laravel or PHP apps, most of that is weight you pay for. Cipi hosts apps only, isolated and deployed from Git, for free. Choose cPanel if you sell hosting with e-mail; choose Cipi to run your own apps.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | cPanel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free, MIT | Solo $29.99 (1 account), Admin $35.99 (5), Pro $53.99 (30), Premier $69.99 (100) per month, cloud licences |
| Built for | Deploying your apps | Shared and reseller hosting |
| E-mail, DNS, FTP | Not included (use specialised providers) | Included |
| Zero-downtime Git deploys | Yes | No (Git Version Control without releases) |
| Laravel queues and scheduler | Built in | Cron jobs by hand |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 | AlmaLinux, Rocky, CloudLinux, Ubuntu |

Prices as published by cPanel in November 2026; check [their site](https://cpanel.net) for the current ones.

## What cPanel is 

cPanel & WHM is a commercial control panel for web hosting. WHM manages the server and hosting accounts; each account gets cPanel to manage its websites, e-mail, databases, DNS and files. It's licensed per server, with tiers based on how many accounts the server hosts.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where cPanel is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| All-in-one hosting | Web, mail, DNS, FTP, resellers in one product. |
| Familiar | Most shared-hosting users know it. |
| Full backups | One tarball per account with files, mail and databases. |

**Where cPanel falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Built for hosting businesses | Mail, DNS, FTP and reseller features you pay for even if you only deploy apps. |
| No Laravel lifecycle | No Git releases with rollback, queue workers or scheduler management. |
| Licence costs | A monthly licence per server, on top of the server. |
| Rising prices | Licences have gone up year after year; the jump from one account to two moves you to a higher tier. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**Made for apps, not hosting accounts.** Each app is isolated with its own user, PHP pool and database, deployed from Git with zero downtime.

**No licence.** Free and open source, on any number of servers.

**Less running on the server.** No mail, DNS or FTP daemons to patch: a smaller attack surface.

**Laravel included.** Workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane, health checks and rollback.

| Up to 30 sites, 3 years (Pro) | $53.99 × 36 ≈ $1,944 | $0 |

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every cPanel feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| MySQL databases | `cipi db create`, `cipi db restore` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| phpMyAdmin | TablePlus/DBeaver over SSH (`mariadb+ssh://`) | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| Cron jobs | Laravel scheduler; app user's crontab |  |
| SSL/TLS (AutoSSL) | `cipi ssl install` | [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl) |
| Backup Wizard | `cipi backup` to S3 | [Backups](https://cipi.sh/docs/backups) |
| Git Version Control | Webhook deploys with releases | [Auto-deploy](https://cipi.sh/docs/auto-deploy) |
| MultiPHP Manager | `--php`, `cipi php` | [PHP](https://cipi.sh/docs/php) |
| Email accounts | Not included | Use a mail provider |
| Zone editor | Not included | Use your DNS provider |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Download a full backup of each cPanel account, rebuild each site as a Cipi app, import the databases, then switch DNS (and MX for mail).

**Before you start**

- Access to cPanel for each account (or WHM as root).
- A plan for e-mail if cPanel hosts your mailboxes.
- Enough disk on your laptop for the backups.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | sites, databases, mail | #inventory
Make a backup | download everything | #backup
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Recreate each site | Laravel or custom app | #create
Import the databases | from the .sql files | #data
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, mail | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

List every site in cPanel: domain, document root, PHP version, databases, cron jobs. Note what isn't a website: **e-mail accounts, DNS zones, FTP users**. Cipi hosts apps, not mailboxes or DNS, so those need a new home (see *What doesn't move* below).

### 2. Make a backup 

In cPanel, open **Files → Backup** (or Backup Wizard) and generate a **full account backup**, then download it. From WHM, root can also create account backups.

The file is named like `backup-_.tar.gz`. Inside, `homedir/public_html` holds the main site's files and the `mysql/` folder holds one `.sql` dump per database:

```bash
$ tar -xzf backup-*_acct.tar.gz
$ ls backup-*/homedir/public_html backup-*/mysql
```

### 3. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and install Cipi:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Then log in as `cipi` (`ssh cipi@NEW_IP`). New to this? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 4. Recreate each site 

Pick the right kind of app for each site:

| Site | Create it as | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laravel app in Git | Laravel app | `sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.com --repository=git@…` |
| WordPress, PrestaShop, plain PHP | Custom app | `sudo cipi app create --custom --user=blog --domain=blog.com` |
| Static HTML | Custom app | same, then upload the files |

For custom apps, upload the site's files into `~/htdocs` as the app user (SFTP, or `rsync` from the extracted backup), then create its database with `sudo cipi db create --name=blog --app=blog`. Step by step: [WordPress](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app), [WooCommerce](https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps).

### 5. Import the databases 

Copy each `.sql` file from the backup to the server and restore it:

```bash
$ scp blog.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore blog /tmp/blog.sql"
```

Then update the site's config with the new database name, user and password Cipi printed (`wp-config.php` for WordPress, `.env` for Laravel). Database names usually change: hosting panels prefix them with the account name (`acct_blog`), Cipi doesn't.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

If the old panel also handled your **e-mail**, move the MX records to your new mail provider at the same time, and keep the old mailboxes until every message has been copied.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| E-mail accounts and mailboxes | Move mail to a mail provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Fastmail, Zoho, Migadu…) and change the MX records. Cipi sends app e-mail through any SMTP service. |
| DNS zones | Keep DNS at your registrar or move it to Cloudflare (free). |
| FTP accounts | SFTP as each app's own user, with keys or a password. |
| Reseller accounts and hosting packages | Not a Cipi feature: it hosts your apps. Hosting providers can automate Cipi apps with the [WHMCS module](https://cipi.sh/docs/whmcs). |
| Softaculous / one-click installers | Install the CMS yourself (WordPress: [guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app)). |
