## Cipi vs Dokku

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-dokku

## In 30 seconds 

Dokku is a tiny, battle-tested Heroku-style PaaS: `git push dokku main` builds a container with buildpacks or a Dockerfile, and plugins add databases and certificates. Cipi manages the whole server for Laravel and PHP natively, with releases, workers, patching, backups and MCP. Choose Dokku for Heroku-style workflows across languages; choose Cipi for Laravel with less container plumbing and more built in.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Dokku |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free (MIT) | Free (MIT) |
| Model | Native stack | Containers via git push |
| Server management | Firewall, patching, backups, monitoring | PaaS-focused, plugins |
| Laravel lifecycle | Built in | Buildpacks or Dockerfile + Procfile |
| Databases | MariaDB, PostgreSQL native | Plugins (containers) |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |

Prices as published by Dokku in November 2026; check [their site](https://dokku.com) for the current ones.

## What Dokku is 

Dokku is an open-source, single-server PaaS. You push code with Git, it builds a container (Heroku buildpacks, Cloud Native Buildpacks or a Dockerfile) and runs processes from a `Procfile`. Plugins add PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, Let's Encrypt and more.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Dokku is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Heroku workflow | `git push` to deploy. |
| Any language | Buildpacks and Dockerfiles. |
| Small and stable | Minimal moving parts. |

**Where Dokku falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You assemble Laravel | Procfile entries for workers and scheduler, buildpack tweaks for PHP extensions. |
| Server care is up to you | Patching, backups and monitoring are separate tasks. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Not for every stack | Cipi runs Laravel, PHP and Node front ends natively. Go, Python, Rails or arbitrary Docker images aren't its job. |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**No container layer for PHP.** Nginx and PHP-FPM (or Octane) run directly on the server: less memory, simpler debugging, logs where you expect them.

**Laravel's lifecycle built in.** Releases with rollback, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane and health checks without writing Dockerfiles or compose files.

**Server care included.** Firewall, Fail2ban, nightly PHP patches, encrypted backups to S3 and monitoring.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every Dokku feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In Dokku | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App | `cipi app create` | [Create an app](https://cipi.sh/docs/create-app) |
| `dokku config:set` | `cipi app env` | [Environment](https://cipi.sh/docs/environment) |
| Procfile `worker:` | `cipi worker add`, Horizon | [Workers](https://cipi.sh/docs/workers) |
| Procfile scheduler / cron | Scheduler built in | [Scheduler](https://cipi.sh/docs/scheduler) |
| postgres / mysql plugin | `cipi db` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| letsencrypt plugin | `cipi ssl install` | [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl) |
| Storage mounts | `/home//shared/storage` |  |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Rebuild each app natively on Cipi, export config and databases with Dokku's commands, switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- SSH access to the Dokku server.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | apps, env, volumes | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | natively, not in a container | #create
Copy the environment | variables → .env | #env
Copy the data | dump and volumes | #data
Workers and schedules | Supervisor, cron | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

For each app on Dokku, note: the Git repository and branch, the build or Dockerfile, environment variables (`dokku config:export shop` on the Dokku server), attached databases, persistent volumes (uploads), workers and scheduled commands, domains. 

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a new VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and run `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash`. Cipi runs PHP, Nginx and databases natively: no Docker needed. For PostgreSQL apps add `sudo cipi db install pgsql`.

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.5
```

What the Dockerfile did, Cipi already does: PHP extensions, Composer, `npm run build` (`--node-build`), migrations. Commands specific to your image go in `deploy.post` of [cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml). Node front ends become [Node apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/node-apps).

### 4. Copy the environment 

Copy your variables from `dokku config:export shop` on the Dokku server into the app's `.env` with `sudo cipi app env shop`. Keep Cipi's `DB_*` and `REDIS_*` values: the database is now local.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database:

```bash
# on the Dokku server
$ dokku postgres:export shop-db > shop.sql      # or: dokku mysql:export shop-db > shop.sql
$ scp shop.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/ && ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql"
```

Files: for apps with persistent storage, find the host folder with `dokku storage:report shop` and `rsync` it to `/home/shop/shared/storage/app/` on Cipi.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Workers and schedules 

Worker containers become Supervisor workers (`sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=…`), a Horizon container becomes `sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop`, and the scheduler container isn't needed: Cipi runs `schedule:run` every minute for every Laravel app.

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Non-PHP apps | Keep them on Dokku or another container platform. |


## Cipi vs Easypanel

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-easypanel

## In 30 seconds 

Easypanel is a modern dashboard for running Docker apps and databases on your server, with templates and a free tier. Cipi runs Laravel and PHP natively with the lifecycle built in. Choose Easypanel for a GUI over containers; choose Cipi for Laravel without containers, with `cipi.yml` and MCP.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Easypanel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free, MIT | Free tier, paid plans |
| Model | Native stack | Docker containers |
| Interface | CLI, optional panel, API | Web dashboard |
| Laravel lifecycle | Built in | Generic containers |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Dashboard |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |

Prices as published by Easypanel in November 2026; check [their site](https://easypanel.io) for the current ones.

## What Easypanel is 

Easypanel is a server control panel built on Docker: you create projects with app services (from Git, images or Dockerfiles) and database services, with automatic HTTPS through its proxy.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Easypanel is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Clean dashboard | Easy to use for people who prefer a GUI. |
| Templates | Many apps in a few clicks. |
| Any stack | Through containers. |

**Where Easypanel falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Containers for PHP | Extra layer and wiring for workers and scheduler. |
| Paid features | Some features need a paid plan. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Not for every stack | Cipi runs Laravel, PHP and Node front ends natively. Go, Python, Rails or arbitrary Docker images aren't its job. |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**No container layer for PHP.** Nginx and PHP-FPM (or Octane) run directly on the server: less memory, simpler debugging, logs where you expect them.

**Laravel's lifecycle built in.** Releases with rollback, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Reverb, Octane and health checks without writing Dockerfiles or compose files.

**Server care included.** Firewall, Fail2ban, nightly PHP patches, encrypted backups to S3 and monitoring.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every Easypanel feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In Easypanel | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App service | `cipi app create` | [Create an app](https://cipi.sh/docs/create-app) |
| Environment | `cipi app env` | [Environment](https://cipi.sh/docs/environment) |
| Database service | `cipi db` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| Mounts / volumes | `/home//shared/storage` |  |
| Domains and HTTPS | `cipi alias add`, `cipi ssl install` | [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl) |

## Cipi vs fortrabbit

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-fortrabbit

## In 30 seconds 

fortrabbit is a European managed hosting platform for PHP apps (Laravel, Craft and others), with Git deploys and managed MySQL. Cipi gives you the same workflow on your own VPS with full root, Octane, Horizon and Reverb. Choose fortrabbit to stay hands-off on a PHP-specialist host; choose Cipi for root, full Laravel features and any provider.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | fortrabbit |

Prices as published by fortrabbit in November 2026; check [their site](https://www.fortrabbit.com) for the current ones.

## What fortrabbit is 

fortrabbit is a managed PHP hosting platform in Europe: you deploy with Git, it runs your PHP app with managed MySQL, and you access it over SSH/SFTP.

## Pros and cons, honestly

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| No autoscaling | You size the server; to grow, resize it or add servers. |

| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**A fixed, predictable bill.** One VPS price, whatever the traffic spikes; no per-request or per-GB surprises.

**Root access.** Install what you need, read any log, tune PHP and Nginx.

**No lock-in.** A standard Ubuntu stack on any provider; move with `cipi sync`.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every fortrabbit feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Create the app on Cipi, copy variables, dump MySQL, copy files, switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- fortrabbit's database access details (via SSH tunnel) and SSH/SFTP access.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | app, env, database, storage | #inventory
Install Cipi | on your own server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the environment | variables → .env | #env
Copy the data | database and files | #data
Workers and schedules | queues, cron | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

In fortrabbit's dashboard, note for each app: the repository and branch, build and start commands, environment variables (the app's ENV vars settings), the database and its engine/version, file storage (local disk or a bucket), workers, scheduled jobs and domains. 

### 2. Install Cipi 

Rent a VPS (2–4 GB RAM is plenty for most apps that ran on a PaaS) with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and run `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash`. For PostgreSQL apps: `sudo cipi db install pgsql`. Guide: [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --engine=pgsql
```

Use `--engine=pgsql` if the app used PostgreSQL, `--octane` if it ran on Octane, `--node-build='npm ci && npm run build'` for assets. Add the deploy key to the repository.

### 4. Copy the environment 

Export or copy the variables from the app's ENV vars settings into `sudo cipi app env shop`. Keep Cipi's `DB_*`/`REDIS_*` values.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

### 5. Copy the data 

Dump MySQL with the access details fortrabbit gives you (usually through an SSH tunnel) using `mysqldump`, then `sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql` on Cipi.

Files: copy uploaded files over SFTP, or keep your object storage bucket.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Workers and schedules 

Add a worker per queue (`sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=…`) or enable Horizon. The scheduler is already on. Then deploy once more and check `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=laravel`.

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install

Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
```

## Cipi vs Kamal

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-kamal

## In 30 seconds 

Kamal (from 37signals) deploys Docker images to servers you prepare, with zero-downtime switches through its proxy. Everything else (images, databases, backups, patching, monitoring) is yours to build. Cipi provisions and runs the whole Laravel stack natively, then deploys it. Choose Kamal if your team lives in Docker images; choose Cipi if you want the server taken care of too.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Kamal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free (MIT) | Free (MIT) |
| Provisioning | Full stack: web server, PHP, databases, firewall, SSL | Docker on your hosts; the rest is yours |
| Model | Native | Docker containers |
| Backups, monitoring, patching | Built in | Not included |
| Laravel lifecycle | Built in | Through your image and config |

Prices as published by Kamal in November 2026; check [their site](https://kamal-deploy.org) for the current ones.

## What Kamal is 

Kamal is an open-source deploy tool: from `config/deploy.yml` it builds or pulls an image, pushes it to a registry, and starts it on your hosts behind kamal-proxy, with accessories (databases, Redis) as extra containers.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Kamal is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |

| Simple, image-based deploys | One config file, one command. |

**Where Kamal falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You build the platform | Dockerfile, registry, accessories, backups, patching. |
| Laravel by hand | Workers and scheduler as extra roles. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |

**Where Cipi falls short**

```bash
# on the host running the database accessory
$ docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep -i db
$ docker exec CONTAINER pg_dump -U USER --no-owner --no-acl DBNAME > shop.sql
$ scp shop.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/ && ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql"
```

Files: copy files from the volume or directory mounted into your app container (see `volumes:` in `deploy.yml`).

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Workers and schedules 

Worker containers become Supervisor workers (`sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=…`), a Horizon container becomes `sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop`, and the scheduler container isn't needed: Cipi runs `schedule:run` every minute for every Laravel app.

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Multi-host image deploys | Each Cipi server runs its own apps; use several servers behind a load balancer if needed. |


## Cipi vs Laravel Cloud

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-cloud

## In 30 seconds 

Laravel Cloud is the Laravel team's fully managed platform: no servers, autoscaling, scale-to-zero, managed Postgres, MySQL and Valkey, preview environments. You pay plans plus usage. Cipi gives you the same Laravel features on a VPS you control, for the price of the VPS. Choose Laravel Cloud to never think about servers and to scale automatically; choose Cipi for predictable cost, root access and portability.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Laravel Cloud |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing | Free tool; fixed VPS price | Plans plus usage |
| Servers | Your VPS, full root | None to manage, no root |
| Autoscaling, scale-to-zero | No: size the VPS | Yes |
| Managed databases and cache | On your VPS (MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Valkey) | Managed (Serverless Postgres, MySQL, Valkey) |
| Preview environments | Via CI ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments)) | Built in on higher plans |
| Octane, queues, Reverb | Yes | Yes |
| Portability | Standard Ubuntu stack, any provider | Tied to the platform |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Environment settings in the platform |

Prices as published by Laravel Cloud in November 2026; check [their site](https://cloud.laravel.com) for the current ones.

## What Laravel Cloud is 

Laravel Cloud is a fully managed platform from the Laravel team. You connect a repository, pick compute and attach managed databases, caches and object storage; it builds, deploys and scales the app, with preview environments and scale-to-zero options.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Laravel Cloud is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing to manage | No OS, no patches, no SSH. |
| Autoscaling | Handles spikes and scales to zero. |
| Laravel-native | Built by the framework's team. |

**Where Laravel Cloud falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Usage-based bill | Harder to predict; grows with traffic and resources. |
| No root | You can't install or tune system software. |
| Platform lock-in | Databases and storage are platform resources. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| No autoscaling | You size the server; to grow, resize it or add servers. |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**A fixed, predictable bill.** One VPS price, whatever the traffic spikes; no per-request or per-GB surprises.

**Root access.** Install what you need, read any log, tune PHP and Nginx.

**No lock-in.** A standard Ubuntu stack on any provider; move with `cipi sync`.

**Same Laravel features.** Octane, Horizon, Reverb, Meilisearch, scheduler, health checks and rollback.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every Laravel Cloud feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In Laravel Cloud | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application / environment | `cipi app create` (one app per environment) | [Create an app](https://cipi.sh/docs/create-app) |
| Environment variables | `cipi app env` | [Environment](https://cipi.sh/docs/environment) |
| Serverless Postgres / MySQL | `cipi db` (PostgreSQL or MariaDB) on the server | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| Valkey cache | Per-app Valkey | [Valkey](https://cipi.sh/docs/valkey) |
| Object storage | Keep your S3 bucket, or any S3-compatible provider |  |
| Workers | `cipi worker add`, Horizon | [Workers](https://cipi.sh/docs/workers) |
| Scheduler | On by default |  |
| Preview environments | CI + wildcard domain | [Guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments) |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Create the app on Cipi, copy variables, dump the managed database through its connection details, switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- Access to the Laravel Cloud dashboard (database connection details, environment variables).
- `pg_dump` or `mysqldump` on your laptop.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | app, env, database, storage | #inventory
Install Cipi | on your own server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the environment | variables → .env | #env
Copy the data | database and files | #data
Workers and schedules | queues, cron | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

In Laravel Cloud's dashboard, note for each app: the repository and branch, build and start commands, environment variables (the environment's **Settings → Environment variables**), the database and its engine/version, file storage (local disk or a bucket), workers, scheduled jobs and domains. 

### 2. Install Cipi 

Rent a VPS (2–4 GB RAM is plenty for most apps that ran on a PaaS) with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and run `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash`. For PostgreSQL apps: `sudo cipi db install pgsql`. Guide: [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --engine=pgsql
```

Use `--engine=pgsql` if the app used PostgreSQL, `--octane` if it ran on Octane, `--node-build='npm ci && npm run build'` for assets. Add the deploy key to the repository.

### 4. Copy the environment 

Export or copy the variables from the environment's **Settings → Environment variables** into `sudo cipi app env shop`. Keep Cipi's `DB_*`/`REDIS_*` values.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

### 5. Copy the data 

Get the database's host, user and password from the database's connection details in the dashboard, then dump from your laptop:

```bash
# PostgreSQL
$ pg_dump "postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@HOST/DB?sslmode=require" --no-owner --no-acl > shop.sql
# MySQL
$ mysqldump -h HOST -u USER -p --single-transaction DB > shop.sql
$ scp shop.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/ && ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql"
```

Files: if the app stores files in object storage (S3/R2), keep using the same bucket: copy its `AWS_*` variables. Nothing to move.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Workers and schedules 

Add a worker per queue (`sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=…`) or enable Horizon. The scheduler is already on. Then deploy once more and check `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=laravel`.

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Autoscaling and scale-to-zero | Size the VPS for your peak; resize later if needed. |
| Managed database features (branching, point-in-time restore) | Cipi backups every 30 minutes and pre-deploy snapshots. |


## Cipi vs Laravel Forge

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-laravel-forge

## In 30 seconds 

Forge is a hosted dashboard that provisions and manages servers on your cloud accounts, for a monthly account fee. Cipi does the same job for Laravel and PHP from **inside** your server, for free, with configuration in Git (`cipi.yml`), built-in AI tooling (MCP) and nightly security patching. Pick Forge if you want servers created for you from a dashboard and commercial support from the Laravel team; pick Cipi if you'd rather own the whole stack and stop paying for the control plane.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Laravel Forge |

Prices as published by Laravel Forge in November 2026; check [their site](https://forge.laravel.com) for the current ones.

## What Laravel Forge is 

Laravel Forge is the Laravel team's hosted server-management service. It's billed per account, not per server.

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**Stop paying for the control plane.** Cipi does deploys, workers, SSL, databases, backups and monitoring for free; you keep paying only the VPS.

**Review infrastructure like code.** A pull request that changes PHP, adds a worker or a backup profile shows the exact plan before anything is applied ([cipi.yml](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml)).

**Safer by default.** Per-app users, nightly PHP patches, malware integrity scans, health-check rollback and a hash-chained deploy ledger come out of the box.

**Ready for AI.** Let Claude, Cursor or VS Code read logs, check migrations and deploy, through [MCP](https://cipi.sh/mcp) servers with guards and redaction.

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

The plan: build a Cipi server next to the Forge one, copy each app, test it privately, then switch DNS. The Forge server keeps running until the last step, so you can stop at any point. Full walkthrough with extra detail: [Move from Forge to Cipi](https://cipi.sh/guides/migrate-from-laravel-forge).

**Before you start**

- SSH access to the Forge server (`ssh forge@OLD_IP`) and to your DNS.
- The app's repository, and a moment to add a deploy key to it.
- About an hour per app the first time, less after.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | what the app uses | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the .env | your keys, the old APP_KEY | #env
Copy the data | database and uploads | #data
Workers and scheduled jobs | daemons, scheduled jobs | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

Open Forge's dashboard and write down, for each site you move:

| What | Where to find it in Forge | You'll need it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domain and aliases | Site → Domains | `cipi app create --domain`, `cipi alias add` |
| Repository and branch | Site → Repository | `--repository`, `--branch` |
| PHP version | Site → Settings (PHP version) | `--php` (Cipi offers 8.3–8.6) |
| Environment (`.env`) | Site → Environment | your own keys and `APP_KEY` |
| Daemons | Server → Daemons / Background processes | `cipi worker add` or Horizon |
| Scheduled jobs | Server → Scheduler | the scheduler (automatic) or `crons:` in cipi.yml |
| Deploy script | Site → Deployments → Deploy script | Cipi's deploy options or `deploy.post` |
| Databases | Server → Databases | `cipi db restore` |

On the old server, the site's files are usually in `/home/forge/shop.example.com`. You'll log in with `ssh forge@OLD_IP`.

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 (don't install Cipi on the old server: it configures Nginx, PHP and users its own way). Then:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4          # the version the app uses today, if not the default
```

If the site used PostgreSQL on Forge: `sudo cipi db install pgsql` and add `--engine=pgsql` when creating the app.

New to servers? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.4
```

The summary shows a **deploy key**: add it to the repository as a read-only deploy key (or save a Git token in Cipi and it's done for you). Check with `sudo cipi git check shop`. Then add the other domains with `sudo cipi alias add shop www.shop.example.com`.

### 4. Copy the .env 

Print the old file: `ssh forge@OLD_IP "cat /home/forge/shop.example.com/.env"`. Copy your own keys (mail, payments, storage, APIs) into the new app with `sudo cipi app env shop` (opens an editor). **Keep Cipi's database and Redis values**: they point at the new server.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

Then deploy once: `sudo cipi deploy shop`. Migrations create an empty schema; the data comes next.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database, from the old server:

```bash
$ ssh forge@OLD_IP
$ mysqldump --single-transaction --quick -u forge -p shop | gzip > /tmp/shop.sql.gz
$ exit
$ scp forge@OLD_IP:/tmp/shop.sql.gz . && scp shop.sql.gz cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql.gz"
```

Uploaded files (skip if they're on S3):

```bash
$ rsync -az forge@OLD_IP:/home/forge/shop.example.com/storage/app/ ./shop-storage/
$ rsync -az ./shop-storage/ cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/shop-storage/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo rsync -a /tmp/shop-storage/ /home/shop/shared/storage/app/ && sudo chown -R shop:shop /home/shop/shared/storage/app"
```

Cipi's restore stops at the first error and refuses empty dumps, so a broken file never wipes the database.

### 6. Workers and scheduled jobs 

For every queue Forge ran, add a worker. The Laravel scheduler is already on for every app.

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop     # if you used Horizon
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop
```

Or put it all in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) so it lives with your code. Extra commands from the old deploy script go in `sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --extra-artisan=…` or in `deploy.post`.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

Also stop the old server's daemons and scheduled jobs, so jobs don't run twice against the old database.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Server creation on cloud accounts | Create the VPS in your provider's console (two minutes), then install Cipi. |
| Forge's hosted dashboard | Use the CLI, or install Cipi's [self-hosted web panel](https://cipi.sh/web-panel). |
| Forge circles and billing | Panel users with roles; API tokens with scoped abilities. |


## Cipi vs moss.sh

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-moss

## In 30 seconds 

moss.sh manages servers and deploys several stacks from a hosted dashboard, with a free tier and paid plans. Cipi is free, Laravel-first and lives on your server, with no deploy quotas. Choose moss.sh for a hosted multi-stack GUI for an agency; choose Cipi to automate Laravel end to end without a subscription.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | moss.sh |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free, MIT | Free tier, then paid plans |
| Control plane | On your server | SaaS |
| Laravel lifecycle | Built in | Generic |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Dashboard |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |

Prices as published by moss.sh in November 2026; check [their site](https://moss.sh) for the current ones.

## What moss.sh is 

moss.sh is a hosted service that connects to your servers to deploy and manage PHP, Node and other web apps, aimed at freelancers and agencies.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where moss.sh is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Multi-stack | PHP, Node and more. |
| Hosted GUI | For agencies managing client sites. |
| Free tier | To start small. |

**Where moss.sh falls short**

**Where Cipi is strong**

**No quotas.** Unlimited apps, deploys and servers.

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Build a Cipi server, recreate each site, copy env and data, test, switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- SSH access to the server moss.sh manages, and the site's folder from moss.sh's site settings.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | what the app uses | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the .env | your keys, the old APP_KEY | #env
Copy the data | database and uploads | #data
Workers and scheduled jobs | background workers, scheduled tasks | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

Open moss.sh's dashboard and write down, for each site you move:

| What | Where to find it in moss.sh | You'll need it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domain and aliases | the site's domain settings | `cipi app create --domain`, `cipi alias add` |
| Repository and branch | the site's Git / deployment settings | `--repository`, `--branch` |
| PHP version | the site's PHP settings | `--php` (Cipi offers 8.3–8.6) |
| Environment (`.env`) | the site's environment or `.env` file | your own keys and `APP_KEY` |
| Background workers | the server's daemons / Supervisor section | `cipi worker add` or Horizon |
| Scheduled tasks | the server's cron section | the scheduler (automatic) or `crons:` in cipi.yml |
| Deploy script | the site's deploy script or hooks | Cipi's deploy options or `deploy.post` |
| Databases | the server's databases section | `cipi db restore` |

Replace `SITE_USER` and `SITE_PATH` with the system user and folder moss.sh shows for the site.

On the old server, the site's files are usually in `SITE_PATH`. You'll log in with `ssh SITE_USER@OLD_IP`.

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 (don't install Cipi on the old server: it configures Nginx, PHP and users its own way). Then:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4          # the version the app uses today, if not the default
```

New to servers? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.4
```

The summary shows a **deploy key**: add it to the repository as a read-only deploy key (or save a Git token in Cipi and it's done for you). Check with `sudo cipi git check shop`. Then add the other domains with `sudo cipi alias add shop www.shop.example.com`.

### 4. Copy the .env 

Print the old file: `ssh SITE_USER@OLD_IP "cat SITE_PATH/.env"`. Copy your own keys (mail, payments, storage, APIs) into the new app with `sudo cipi app env shop` (opens an editor). **Keep Cipi's database and Redis values**: they point at the new server.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

Then deploy once: `sudo cipi deploy shop`. Migrations create an empty schema; the data comes next.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database, from the old server:

```bash
$ ssh SITE_USER@OLD_IP
$ mysqldump --single-transaction --quick -u DB_USER -p shop | gzip > /tmp/shop.sql.gz
$ exit
$ scp SITE_USER@OLD_IP:/tmp/shop.sql.gz . && scp shop.sql.gz cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql.gz"
```

Uploaded files (skip if they're on S3):

```bash
$ rsync -az SITE_USER@OLD_IP:SITE_PATH/storage/app/ ./shop-storage/
$ rsync -az ./shop-storage/ cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/shop-storage/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo rsync -a /tmp/shop-storage/ /home/shop/shared/storage/app/ && sudo chown -R shop:shop /home/shop/shared/storage/app"
```

Cipi's restore stops at the first error and refuses empty dumps, so a broken file never wipes the database.

### 6. Workers and scheduled jobs 

For every queue moss.sh ran, add a worker. The Laravel scheduler is already on for every app.

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop     # if you used Horizon
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop
```

Or put it all in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) so it lives with your code. Extra commands from the old deploy script go in `sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --extra-artisan=…` or in `deploy.post`.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

Also stop the old server's background workers and scheduled tasks, so jobs don't run twice against the old database.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Hosted dashboard | Cipi CLI or the self-hosted [web panel](https://cipi.sh/web-panel). |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Export each site's files and databases from Plesk, rebuild each site as a Cipi app, import, switch DNS and MX.

**Before you start**

- Access to Plesk for each subscription.
- A plan for e-mail.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | sites, databases, mail | #inventory
Make a backup | download everything | #backup
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Recreate each site | Laravel or custom app | #create
Import the databases | from the .sql files | #data
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, mail | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

List every site in Plesk: domain, document root, PHP version, databases, cron jobs. Note what isn't a website: **e-mail accounts, DNS zones, FTP users**. Cipi hosts apps, not mailboxes or DNS, so those need a new home (see *What doesn't move* below).

### 2. Make a backup 

For each subscription, export the database from **Databases → Export Dump** and download the site files (File Manager, FTP/SFTP, or `rsync` over SSH). Plesk's **Backup Manager** can also create and download a full backup.

On Linux, a site's files usually live in `/var/www/vhosts//httpdocs`.

### 3. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and install Cipi:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
```

Then log in as `cipi` (`ssh cipi@NEW_IP`). New to this? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 4. Recreate each site 

Pick the right kind of app for each site:

| Site | Create it as | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laravel app in Git | Laravel app | `sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.com --repository=git@…` |
| WordPress, PrestaShop, plain PHP | Custom app | `sudo cipi app create --custom --user=blog --domain=blog.com` |
| Static HTML | Custom app | same, then upload the files |

For custom apps, upload the site's files into `~/htdocs` as the app user (SFTP, or `rsync` from the extracted backup), then create its database with `sudo cipi db create --name=blog --app=blog`. Step by step: [WordPress](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app), [WooCommerce](https://cipi.sh/guides/woocommerce-vps).

### 5. Import the databases 

Copy each `.sql` file from the backup to the server and restore it:

```bash
$ scp blog.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore blog /tmp/blog.sql"
```

Then update the site's config with the new database name, user and password Cipi printed (`wp-config.php` for WordPress, `.env` for Laravel). Database names usually change: hosting panels prefix them with the account name (`acct_blog`), Cipi doesn't.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

If the old panel also handled your **e-mail**, move the MX records to your new mail provider at the same time, and keep the old mailboxes until every message has been copied.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| E-mail accounts and mailboxes | Move mail to a mail provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Fastmail, Zoho, Migadu…) and change the MX records. Cipi sends app e-mail through any SMTP service. |
| DNS zones | Keep DNS at your registrar or move it to Cloudflare (free). |
| FTP accounts | SFTP as each app's own user, with keys or a password. |
| Reseller accounts and hosting packages | Not a Cipi feature: it hosts your apps. Hosting providers can automate Cipi apps with the [WHMCS module](https://cipi.sh/docs/whmcs). |
| Softaculous / one-click installers | Install the CMS yourself (WordPress: [guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app)). |
| Windows / IIS sites | Cipi is Linux-only: keep .NET sites on Windows hosting. |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Create the app on Cipi, copy variables, dump the database with its connection details, switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- Access to Ploi Cloud's dashboard and the database connection details.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | app, env, database, storage | #inventory
Install Cipi | on your own server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the environment | variables → .env | #env
Copy the data | database and files | #data
Workers and schedules | queues, cron | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

In Ploi Cloud's dashboard, note for each app: the repository and branch, build and start commands, environment variables (the app's environment settings), the database and its engine/version, file storage (local disk or a bucket), workers, scheduled jobs and domains. 

### 2. Install Cipi 

Rent a VPS (2–4 GB RAM is plenty for most apps that ran on a PaaS) with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and run `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash`. For PostgreSQL apps: `sudo cipi db install pgsql`. Guide: [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --engine=pgsql
```

Use `--engine=pgsql` if the app used PostgreSQL, `--octane` if it ran on Octane, `--node-build='npm ci && npm run build'` for assets. Add the deploy key to the repository.

### 4. Copy the environment 

Export or copy the variables from the app's environment settings into `sudo cipi app env shop`. Keep Cipi's `DB_*`/`REDIS_*` values.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

### 5. Copy the data 

Dump the database with the connection details shown for it (`pg_dump` or `mysqldump` from your laptop), copy the file to the server and run `sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql`.

Files: keep using your S3 bucket by copying its variables, or download the files and upload them to `/home/shop/shared/storage/app/`.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Workers and schedules 

Add a worker per queue (`sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=…`) or enable Horizon. The scheduler is already on. Then deploy once more and check `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=laravel`.

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```


## Cipi vs Ploi

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-ploi

## In 30 seconds 

Ploi manages servers from a hosted dashboard, with a free tier for one server and paid plans by server count. Cipi gives you the same Laravel workflow (zero-downtime deploys, queues, scheduler, SSL, backups) without any subscription, plus `cipi.yml`, MCP for AI assistants and nightly security patching. Pick Ploi for a hosted dashboard with team features and status pages; pick Cipi to own the stack and stop paying per server.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Ploi |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free, MIT licence | Free (1 server, 1 site, 5 deploys/month); Basic €8, Pro €13, Unlimited €30 per month |
| Where the control plane runs | On your server | ploi.io (SaaS, EU) |
| Creates servers on clouds | No | Yes, several providers |
| Zero-downtime deploys | Yes, always | Yes (Pro and up) |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Dashboard |
| Web dashboard | Optional, self-hosted | Hosted, plus mobile app |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Two built-in MCP servers | MCP server for the Ploi API |
| Backups | Built in, S3, encrypted, verified | Pro and up |
| Team management | Panel roles, scoped tokens | Unlimited plan |
| Cancel the subscription | Nothing to cancel | Servers keep running; management stops |

Prices as published by Ploi in November 2026; check [their site](https://ploi.io) for the current ones.

## What Ploi is 

Ploi is a hosted server-management panel run by a Dutch company. It provisions servers on your cloud accounts, deploys PHP (and Node) sites, manages databases, queues, cron jobs, SSL and backups, and offers extras such as status pages and a mobile app. Plans are priced by how many servers you manage.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Ploi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Generous feature set | Load balancers, database and worker servers, status pages, file explorer, mobile app. |
| EU company | Data stays with an EU provider. |
| Free tier | One server and one site to try it. |
| Servers keep working if you cancel | Ploi doesn't touch your servers when the subscription ends. |

**Where Ploi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Pricing grows with servers | More servers means a higher plan. |
| Key features behind higher plans | Backups and zero-downtime deploys from Pro; team management on Unlimited. |
| Configuration in a dashboard | Not reviewed in pull requests. |
| External control plane | Inventory and credentials stored with a third party. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**No per-server pricing.** Ten servers or a hundred: Cipi costs nothing.

**Every feature on every server.** Zero-downtime deploys, backups, health-check rollback and monitoring aren't plan-gated.

**Settings in pull requests.** `cipi.yml` makes server changes reviewable and repeatable.

**AI with guardrails.** Built-in MCP inside each app and for the whole server.

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Build the Cipi server next to the Ploi one, copy each site, test privately, then switch DNS. The Ploi server stays untouched until you're done.

**Before you start**

- SSH access to the Ploi server (`ssh ploi@OLD_IP`).
- Access to your DNS and to the repository settings.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | what the app uses | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the .env | your keys, the old APP_KEY | #env
Copy the data | database and uploads | #data
Workers and scheduled jobs | daemons, cronjobs | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

Open Ploi's dashboard and write down, for each site you move:

| What | Where to find it in Ploi | You'll need it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domain and aliases | Site → Settings / Aliases | `cipi app create --domain`, `cipi alias add` |
| Repository and branch | Site → Repository | `--repository`, `--branch` |
| PHP version | Site → PHP version | `--php` (Cipi offers 8.3–8.6) |
| Environment (`.env`) | Site → Environment | your own keys and `APP_KEY` |
| Daemons | Server → Daemons | `cipi worker add` or Horizon |
| Cronjobs | Server → Cronjobs | the scheduler (automatic) or `crons:` in cipi.yml |
| Deploy script | Site → Deploy script | Cipi's deploy options or `deploy.post` |
| Databases | Server → Databases | `cipi db restore` |

On the old server, the site's files are usually in `/home/ploi/shop.example.com`. You'll log in with `ssh ploi@OLD_IP`.

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 (don't install Cipi on the old server: it configures Nginx, PHP and users its own way). Then:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4          # the version the app uses today, if not the default
```

New to servers? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.4
```

The summary shows a **deploy key**: add it to the repository as a read-only deploy key (or save a Git token in Cipi and it's done for you). Check with `sudo cipi git check shop`. Then add the other domains with `sudo cipi alias add shop www.shop.example.com`.

### 4. Copy the .env 

Print the old file: `ssh ploi@OLD_IP "cat /home/ploi/shop.example.com/.env"`. Copy your own keys (mail, payments, storage, APIs) into the new app with `sudo cipi app env shop` (opens an editor). **Keep Cipi's database and Redis values**: they point at the new server.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

Then deploy once: `sudo cipi deploy shop`. Migrations create an empty schema; the data comes next.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database, from the old server:

```bash
$ ssh ploi@OLD_IP
$ mysqldump --single-transaction --quick -u ploi -p shop | gzip > /tmp/shop.sql.gz
$ exit
$ scp ploi@OLD_IP:/tmp/shop.sql.gz . && scp shop.sql.gz cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql.gz"
```

Uploaded files (skip if they're on S3):

```bash
$ rsync -az ploi@OLD_IP:/home/ploi/shop.example.com/storage/app/ ./shop-storage/
$ rsync -az ./shop-storage/ cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/shop-storage/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo rsync -a /tmp/shop-storage/ /home/shop/shared/storage/app/ && sudo chown -R shop:shop /home/shop/shared/storage/app"
```

Cipi's restore stops at the first error and refuses empty dumps, so a broken file never wipes the database.

### 6. Workers and scheduled jobs 

For every queue Ploi ran, add a worker. The Laravel scheduler is already on for every app.

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop     # if you used Horizon
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop
```

Or put it all in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) so it lives with your code. Extra commands from the old deploy script go in `sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --extra-artisan=…` or in `deploy.post`.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

Also stop the old server's daemons and cronjobs, so jobs don't run twice against the old database.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Status pages | Use an uptime service pointed at the app's health endpoint. |
| Load-balancer and dedicated database servers | Cipi manages each server on its own; put several behind your provider's load balancer if needed. |
| Mobile app | Web panel (responsive) or cipi-cli. |


## Cipi vs Render

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-render

## In 30 seconds 

Render hosts web services, workers, cron jobs and managed Postgres for many languages, billed by instance size and usage. Laravel runs there through Docker. Cipi runs Laravel natively on your VPS with the lifecycle built in, for a fixed price. Choose Render for managed multi-language services with previews; choose Cipi for Laravel with root and predictable cost.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Render |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing | Free tool; fixed VPS price | Usage-based instances |
| Stack | Native Nginx, PHP-FPM or Octane, MariaDB/PostgreSQL | Containers and managed services |
| Preview environments | Via CI ([guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/laravel-preview-environments)) | Built in |
| Autoscaling | No | Yes |
| Root access | Yes | No |

Prices as published by Render in November 2026; check [their site](https://render.com) for the current ones.

## What Render is 

Render is a managed cloud platform for web services, background workers, cron jobs, static sites and managed PostgreSQL and key-value stores. PHP apps typically run from a Dockerfile.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Render is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Managed and multi-language | Many runtimes without servers to run. |

| Autoscaling | Instances added under load. |

**Where Render falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| PHP through Docker | You maintain the image. |
| Usage billing | Each service and database is a separate line. |
| No root | You can't install or tune system software. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| No autoscaling | You size the server; to grow, resize it or add servers. |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**A fixed, predictable bill.** One VPS price, whatever the traffic spikes; no per-request or per-GB surprises.

**Root access.** Install what you need, read any log, tune PHP and Nginx.

**No lock-in.** A standard Ubuntu stack on any provider; move with `cipi sync`.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every Render feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In Render | In Cipi | Docs |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Create the app on Cipi, copy variables, dump Postgres via its external URL, switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- The database's **External Database URL** from Render's dashboard.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | app, env, database, storage | #inventory
Install Cipi | on your own server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the environment | variables → .env | #env
Copy the data | database and files | #data
Workers and schedules | queues, cron | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

In Render's dashboard, note for each app: the repository and branch, build and start commands, environment variables (the service's **Environment** tab and environment groups), the database and its engine/version, file storage (local disk or a bucket), workers, scheduled jobs and domains. 

### 2. Install Cipi 

Rent a VPS (2–4 GB RAM is plenty for most apps that ran on a PaaS) with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 and run `wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash`. For PostgreSQL apps: `sudo cipi db install pgsql`. Guide: [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --engine=pgsql
```

Use `--engine=pgsql` if the app used PostgreSQL, `--octane` if it ran on Octane, `--node-build='npm ci && npm run build'` for assets. Add the deploy key to the repository.

### 4. Copy the environment 

Export or copy the variables from the service's **Environment** tab and environment groups into `sudo cipi app env shop`. Keep Cipi's `DB_*`/`REDIS_*` values.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

### 5. Copy the data 

```bash
$ pg_dump "EXTERNAL_DATABASE_URL" --no-owner --no-acl > shop.sql
$ scp shop.sql cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/ && ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql"
```

Create the Cipi app with `--engine=pgsql` (after `sudo cipi db install pgsql`).

Files: files on a persistent disk can be copied with Render's shell or `scp`; files in S3 stay where they are.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 6. Workers and schedules 

Add a worker per queue (`sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=…`) or enable Horizon. The scheduler is already on. Then deploy once more and check `sudo cipi app logs shop --type=laravel`.

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files

Switch DNS | A record → new IP

HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```
