## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Build a Cipi server, recreate each web application, copy files and databases, then switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- SSH access to the RunCloud server as the web app's system user (by default `runcloud`).
- For WordPress sites, read the [WordPress guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app) first.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | what the app uses | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the .env | your keys, the old APP_KEY | #env
Copy the data | database and uploads | #data
Workers and scheduled jobs | supervisor programs, cron jobs | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

Open RunCloud's dashboard and write down, for each site you move:

| What | Where to find it in RunCloud | You'll need it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domain and aliases | Web Application → Domain Name | `cipi app create --domain`, `cipi alias add` |
| Repository and branch | Web Application → Git | `--repository`, `--branch` |
| PHP version | Web Application → Settings (PHP version) | `--php` (Cipi offers 8.3–8.6) |
| Environment (`.env`) | Web Application → File Manager (`.env`) | your own keys and `APP_KEY` |
| Supervisor programs | Server → Supervisor | `cipi worker add` or Horizon |
| Cron jobs | Server → Cron Jobs | the scheduler (automatic) or `crons:` in cipi.yml |
| Deploy script | Web Application → Git → Deployment script | Cipi's deploy options or `deploy.post` |
| Databases | Server → Databases | `cipi db restore` |

RunCloud shows each web app's root path in its settings; it's under `/home//webapps/`. WordPress and plain PHP sites become Cipi **custom apps**.

On the old server, the site's files are usually in `/home/runcloud/webapps/shop`. You'll log in with `ssh runcloud@OLD_IP`.

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 (don't install Cipi on the old server: it configures Nginx, PHP and users its own way). Then:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4          # the version the app uses today, if not the default
```

New to servers? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.4
```

The summary shows a **deploy key**: add it to the repository as a read-only deploy key (or save a Git token in Cipi and it's done for you). Check with `sudo cipi git check shop`. Then add the other domains with `sudo cipi alias add shop www.shop.example.com`.

### 4. Copy the .env 

Print the old file: `ssh runcloud@OLD_IP "cat /home/runcloud/webapps/shop/.env"`. Copy your own keys (mail, payments, storage, APIs) into the new app with `sudo cipi app env shop` (opens an editor). **Keep Cipi's database and Redis values**: they point at the new server.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

Then deploy once: `sudo cipi deploy shop`. Migrations create an empty schema; the data comes next.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database, from the old server:

```bash
$ ssh runcloud@OLD_IP
$ mysqldump --single-transaction --quick -u DB_USER -p shop | gzip > /tmp/shop.sql.gz
$ exit
$ scp runcloud@OLD_IP:/tmp/shop.sql.gz . && scp shop.sql.gz cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql.gz"
```

Uploaded files (skip if they're on S3):

```bash
$ rsync -az runcloud@OLD_IP:/home/runcloud/webapps/shop/storage/app/ ./shop-storage/
$ rsync -az ./shop-storage/ cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/shop-storage/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo rsync -a /tmp/shop-storage/ /home/shop/shared/storage/app/ && sudo chown -R shop:shop /home/shop/shared/storage/app"
```

Cipi's restore stops at the first error and refuses empty dumps, so a broken file never wipes the database.

### 6. Workers and scheduled jobs 

For every queue RunCloud ran, add a worker. The Laravel scheduler is already on for every app.

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop     # if you used Horizon
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop
```

Or put it all in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) so it lives with your code. Extra commands from the old deploy script go in `sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --extra-artisan=…` or in `deploy.post`.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

Also stop the old server's supervisor programs and cron jobs, so jobs don't run twice against the old database.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| WordPress staging and cloning tools | Create a second custom app and restore a dump into it. |
| Apache `.htaccess` rules | Rewrite them as Nginx rules or [redirects](https://cipi.sh/docs/redirects-proxies). |


## Cipi vs ServerPilot

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-serverpilot

## In 30 seconds 

ServerPilot sets up Nginx, PHP and MySQL on your server and manages PHP apps and WordPress from a hosted dashboard; files usually arrive by SFTP. Cipi adds what Laravel needs (Git releases, rollback, workers, scheduler, Horizon, Octane) and costs nothing. Choose ServerPilot for simple hosted management of WordPress and PHP sites; choose Cipi for Laravel and Git-based deploys.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | ServerPilot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free, MIT | Paid plans per server |
| Focus | Laravel and PHP apps | PHP and WordPress |
| Git releases with rollback | Yes | Not built in |
| Queue workers, scheduler | Built in | Set up yourself |
| PHP patching | Nightly, with alerts | Managed by ServerPilot |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Dashboard |

Prices as published by ServerPilot in November 2026; check [their site](https://serverpilot.io) for the current ones.

## What ServerPilot is 

ServerPilot is a hosted panel that connects to your Ubuntu server and manages a PHP stack (Nginx, PHP-FPM, MySQL) for you. Each app runs as a system user, with its files under `/srv/users//apps//public`. It's aimed at WordPress and PHP sites updated over SFTP.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where ServerPilot is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Simple | Few settings, good defaults for PHP sites. |
| Hands-off PHP updates | PHP versions maintained by the service. |
| App isolation by system user | Apps can run as separate users. |

**Where ServerPilot falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| No Laravel lifecycle | No releases, rollback, queues or scheduler management. |
| Subscription per server | Costs scale with servers. |
| Deploys over SFTP | No Git push-to-deploy pipeline out of the box. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**Git deploys with rollback.** Push and the new release goes live atomically; one command goes back.

**Queues and scheduler included.** Every Laravel app gets a worker and the scheduler.

**Still hosts WordPress.** As isolated [custom apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/custom-apps).

**No subscription.** Free, open source.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every ServerPilot feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In ServerPilot | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App | `cipi app create` (Laravel) or `--custom` | [Create an app](https://cipi.sh/docs/create-app) |
| SFTP uploads | SFTP as the app user into `~/htdocs` (custom apps) | [Custom apps](https://cipi.sh/docs/custom-apps) |
| PHP version | `--php`, `cipi app edit --php` | [PHP](https://cipi.sh/docs/php) |
| SSL | `cipi ssl install` | [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl) |
| Databases | `cipi db` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |

**Before you start**

- For WordPress sites, the [WordPress guide](https://cipi.sh/guides/deploy-wordpress-custom-app).

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | what the app uses | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the .env | your keys, the old APP_KEY | #env
Copy the data | database and uploads | #data
Workers and scheduled jobs | background processes, cron jobs | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

## Cipi vs Sevalla

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-sevalla

## In 30 seconds 

Sevalla (by Kinsta) hosts applications, databases, static sites and object storage on managed infrastructure, billed by resources. Cipi runs Laravel and PHP on your own VPS with root and a fixed bill. Choose Sevalla for a managed platform with a polished dashboard; choose Cipi for control and predictable cost.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Sevalla |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing | Free tool; fixed VPS price | Resource-based |
| Servers | Your VPS, full root | Managed |
| Octane, Horizon, Reverb | One command each | Via your build or image |
| Regions | Any provider | The platform's data centres |

Prices as published by Sevalla in November 2026; check [their site](https://sevalla.com) for the current ones.

## What Sevalla is 

Sevalla is a managed platform from Kinsta for applications (built from Git or images), databases, static sites and object storage.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Sevalla is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Managed | No servers to patch. |
| Polished dashboard | Easy for non-technical teammates. |
| Global data centres | Many regions to choose from. |

**Where Sevalla falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Resource billing | Costs follow usage. |
| No root | You can't install or tune system software. |
| Laravel extras by hand | Workers and Octane through your build. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| No autoscaling | You size the server; to grow, resize it or add servers. |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**A fixed, predictable bill.** One VPS price, whatever the traffic spikes; no per-request or per-GB surprises.

**Root access.** Install what you need, read any log, tune PHP and Nginx.

**No lock-in.** A standard Ubuntu stack on any provider; move with `cipi sync`.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every Sevalla feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In Sevalla | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |

| Database | `cipi db` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| Object storage | Keep the bucket, or any S3-compatible provider |  |
| Processes | `cipi worker add` | [Workers](https://cipi.sh/docs/workers) |

Create the app on Cipi, copy variables, dump the database through its external connection, switch DNS.

### 1. Take inventory

### 6. Workers and schedules

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow

Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP

HTTPS | cipi ssl install
```

## Cipi vs Vito Deploy

URL: https://cipi.sh/alternative-to-vito-deploy

## In 30 seconds 

Vito and Cipi share the same values: free, open source, no SaaS. Vito is a central dashboard (a Laravel app you host) that provisions and manages servers over SSH, with plugins. Cipi is installed on every server and runs it by itself; its optional panel talks to each server's API. Cipi goes deeper on running Laravel in production (health-checked rollback, `cipi.yml`, MCP, nightly patching); Vito shines as a visual, extensible dashboard.

## At a glance 

|  | Cipi | Vito Deploy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Price | Free, MIT | Free, open source (AGPL) |
| Architecture | Each server manages itself; optional panel | Central dashboard managing servers over SSH |
| Dashboard needed | No | Yes (you host it) |
| Zero-downtime deploys | Always | "Modern deployment" option |
| Per-site isolation | Always | Per-site system user |
| Server settings in Git | `cipi.yml` | Dashboard |
| AI assistants (MCP) | Built in | Not advertised |
| Plugins | No plugin system | Yes |

Prices as published by Vito Deploy in November 2026; check [their site](https://vitodeploy.com) for the current ones.

## What Vito Deploy is 

Vito Deploy is a free, open-source, self-hosted server-management panel built with Laravel. You install it on its own server (or Docker), connect your servers, and from its dashboard you create sites, run deployments, manage databases, workers, cron jobs, firewall and SSL. Sites live under the site user's home, e.g. `/home//`.

## Pros and cons, honestly 

**Where Vito Deploy is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | Like Cipi. |
| Visual dashboard | Everything in one place. |
| Plugins | Extend site types and features. |

**Where Vito Deploy falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| A dashboard server to run | One more Laravel app to host, back up and patch. |
| Zero downtime is opt-in | "Modern deployment" must be enabled per site. |
| Fewer production guardrails | No health-check rollback, anonymizer or MCP built in. |

**Where Cipi is strong**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| Free and open source | MIT licence, no subscription, no per-server or per-site fees. You pay only the server. |
| Lives on your server | No external control plane: nothing stops working if a vendor changes plans, prices or goes down. |
| Laravel built in | Zero-downtime releases, rollback, queues, Horizon, scheduler, Reverb, Octane, Meilisearch, health checks with auto-rollback. |
| Isolation by default | Every app has its own Linux user, PHP pool, database user and Valkey instance. |
| Configuration as code | `cipi.yml` keeps PHP, workers, domains, backups and deploy steps in the repository, planned and applied all or nothing. |
| Security on autopilot | PHP patched nightly, Nginx and services via autoupdate, firewall, Fail2ban, optional CrowdSec, malware integrity scans, encrypted secrets. |
| Built for automation and AI | Full CLI, REST API, PHP SDK, cipi-cli and two MCP servers for AI assistants, with guardrails and an audit trail. |

**Where Cipi falls short**

| Point | What it means for you |
| --- | --- |
| You create the server yourself | Cipi installs on a VPS you rent (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, AWS…). It doesn't create servers on cloud accounts for you. |
| Ubuntu LTS only | Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, on a full virtual machine. No other distributions, no containers. |
| Focused on apps | Laravel, PHP, Node front ends and static sites. No e-mail hosting, DNS server or reseller accounts. |
| No paid support desk | Help comes from the docs, GitHub and the Telegram channel. You (or your team) own the server. |

## Why teams choose Cipi instead 

**Nothing extra to host.** Each server is self-sufficient; the panel is optional.

**Production depth.** Health-checked rollback, deploy audit ledger, malware integrity scans, nightly PHP patching.

**Config as code and AI.** `cipi.yml` and MCP out of the box.

## Where everything goes in Cipi 

Every Vito Deploy feature you use today, and its place in Cipi. Use it as your migration checklist.

| In Vito Deploy | In Cipi | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server | VPS + Cipi installer | [Installation](https://cipi.sh/docs/installation) |
| Site | `cipi app create` | [Create an app](https://cipi.sh/docs/create-app) |
| Modern deployment | Always on | [How deploys work](https://cipi.sh/docs/how-deploys-work) |
| Deployment script | Deploy options, `deploy.post` | [Deploy options](https://cipi.sh/docs/deploy-script) |
| Workers | `cipi worker add`, Horizon | [Workers](https://cipi.sh/docs/workers) |
| Cronjobs | Scheduler, crontab | [Scheduler](https://cipi.sh/docs/scheduler) |
| Databases | `cipi db` | [Databases](https://cipi.sh/docs/databases) |
| SSL | `cipi ssl install` | [SSL](https://cipi.sh/docs/ssl) |
| Firewall | `cipi firewall` | [Firewall](https://cipi.sh/docs/firewall) |

## Moving to Cipi, step by step 

Build a Cipi server, recreate each site, copy env and data, test, switch DNS.

**Before you start**

- SSH access to the server Vito manages, as the site user.

Click a step to jump to it; the map follows you down the page.

```flow
Take inventory | what the app uses | #inventory
Install Cipi | on a new server | #install
Create the app | same repo, same domain | #create
Copy the .env | your keys, the old APP_KEY | #env
Copy the data | database and uploads | #data
Workers and scheduled jobs | workers, cronjobs | #workers
Cut-over day | DNS, HTTPS, done | #cutover
```

### 1. Take inventory 

Open Vito's dashboard and write down, for each site you move:

| What | Where to find it in Vito | You'll need it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domain and aliases | Site → Settings / Aliases | `cipi app create --domain`, `cipi alias add` |
| Repository and branch | Site → Application (repository, branch) | `--repository`, `--branch` |
| PHP version | Site → Settings (PHP version) | `--php` (Cipi offers 8.3–8.6) |
| Environment (`.env`) | Site → Application → Update .env | your own keys and `APP_KEY` |
| Workers | Server → Workers | `cipi worker add` or Horizon |
| Cronjobs | Server → Cronjobs | the scheduler (automatic) or `crons:` in cipi.yml |
| Deploy script | Site → Application → Deployment script | Cipi's deploy options or `deploy.post` |
| Databases | Server → Databases | `cipi db restore` |

With modern deployment on, `.env` and `storage` are in the site folder's shared area and the code in `current/`.

On the old server, the site's files are usually in `/home/SITE_USER/shop.example.com`. You'll log in with `ssh SITE_USER@OLD_IP`.

### 2. Install Cipi 

Create a **new** VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 (don't install Cipi on the old server: it configures Nginx, PHP and users its own way). Then:

```bash
$ ssh root@NEW_IP
$ wget -O - https://cipi.sh/setup.sh | bash
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP
$ sudo cipi php install 8.4          # the version the app uses today, if not the default
```

New to servers? [VPS, SSH and DNS basics](https://cipi.sh/guides/vps-ssh-dns-basics).

### 3. Create the app 

```bash
$ sudo cipi app create --user=shop --domain=shop.example.com \
    --repository=git@github.com:you/shop.git --branch=main --php=8.4
```

The summary shows a **deploy key**: add it to the repository as a read-only deploy key (or save a Git token in Cipi and it's done for you). Check with `sudo cipi git check shop`. Then add the other domains with `sudo cipi alias add shop www.shop.example.com`.

### 4. Copy the .env 

Print the old file: `ssh SITE_USER@OLD_IP "cat /home/SITE_USER/shop.example.com/.env"`. Copy your own keys (mail, payments, storage, APIs) into the new app with `sudo cipi app env shop` (opens an editor). **Keep Cipi's database and Redis values**: they point at the new server.

> [!warning] Copy the **old `APP_KEY`** into the new app (`sudo cipi app env  --set=APP_KEY=base64:…`). With a different key, everyone is logged out and anything encrypted with `Crypt` (tokens, settings) can't be read any more.

Then deploy once: `sudo cipi deploy shop`. Migrations create an empty schema; the data comes next.

### 5. Copy the data 

Database, from the old server:

```bash
$ ssh SITE_USER@OLD_IP
$ mysqldump --single-transaction --quick -u DB_USER -p shop | gzip > /tmp/shop.sql.gz
$ exit
$ scp SITE_USER@OLD_IP:/tmp/shop.sql.gz . && scp shop.sql.gz cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo cipi db restore shop /tmp/shop.sql.gz"
```

Uploaded files (skip if they're on S3):

```bash
$ rsync -az SITE_USER@OLD_IP:/home/SITE_USER/shop.example.com/storage/app/ ./shop-storage/
$ rsync -az ./shop-storage/ cipi@NEW_IP:/tmp/shop-storage/
$ ssh cipi@NEW_IP "sudo rsync -a /tmp/shop-storage/ /home/shop/shared/storage/app/ && sudo chown -R shop:shop /home/shop/shared/storage/app"
```

Cipi's restore stops at the first error and refuses empty dumps, so a broken file never wipes the database.

### 6. Workers and scheduled jobs 

For every queue Vito ran, add a worker. The Laravel scheduler is already on for every app.

```bash
$ sudo cipi worker add shop --queue=emails --processes=2
$ sudo cipi worker horizon enable shop     # if you used Horizon
$ sudo cipi schedule status shop
```

Or put it all in [`cipi.yml`](https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml) so it lives with your code. Extra commands from the old deploy script go in `sudo cipi app deploy-config shop --extra-artisan=…` or in `deploy.post`.

### Test before anyone sees it 

You can open the new copy with your real domain **only on your computer**, before changing DNS. Add one line to your hosts file (`/etc/hosts` on macOS and Linux, `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on Windows):

```text
203.0.113.20   shop.example.com
```

Browse the site, log in, place a test order, check e-mails and queued jobs. Remove the line when you're done. (HTTPS will warn until the certificate is issued after the DNS switch; that's expected.)

### 7. Cut-over day 

```flow
Lower the DNS TTL | a day before
> At your DNS provider, set the TTL of the domain's records to 300 seconds a day before the move. When you switch, the world follows within minutes instead of hours.
Freeze the old app | maintenance mode
> Put the old site in maintenance mode (`php artisan down` for Laravel) so nobody writes to the old database during the final copy.
Final data copy | last dump + files
> Dump the database again, copy it over and restore it with `sudo cipi db restore  `. Re-run the files sync (`rsync`): only changes are copied, so it's quick.
Switch DNS | A record → new IP
> Point the domain's `A` (and `AAAA`) records at the Cipi server. Check with `dig +short yourdomain.com`.
HTTPS | cipi ssl install
> As soon as DNS answers with the new IP, run `sudo cipi ssl install `. The certificate is issued in seconds and renews by itself.
Keep the old one | a week, then cancel
> Leave the old server stopped but intact for a week: going back is one DNS change. Then cancel the subscription and delete it.
```

Also stop the old server's workers and cronjobs, so jobs don't run twice against the old database.

### What doesn't move to Cipi 

| Thing | What to do instead |
| --- | --- |
| Vito plugins | No plugin system in Cipi; most needs are covered by `deploy.post`, packages and the API. |


---

# cipi.yml: your server settings, in your repository

URL: https://cipi.sh/cipi-yml

## What it is, in one minute 

Without `cipi.yml`, an app's server settings (PHP version, queue workers, domains, backups…) live only on the server: you change them with commands, and nobody else sees what changed or why. With `cipi.yml`, they live in a file **at the root of your repository**, next to `composer.json`. You change the file, a teammate reviews it, you deploy, and Cipi makes the server match it.

| Without cipi.yml | With cipi.yml |
| --- | --- |
| Settings scattered across commands you ran months ago | One readable file that describes the whole app |
| "Who added that worker?" | Git history and pull requests answer it |
| A new server means retyping everything | Deploy the same repository: the file recreates the setup |
| Staging and production drift apart | `cipi.yml` and `cipi-staging.yml`, side by side |
| A typo can half-change a server | Every change is planned first and applied all or nothing |

> [!tip] You don't have to adopt it all at once. A file with only `workers:` is valid: everything you don't write stays as it is on the server.

## Create your first cipi.yml 

### From an app you already have (recommended)

Cipi writes the file from the app's current setup, so the first plan changes nothing:

```bash
$ ssh cipi@your-server
$ sudo cipi yml generate shop > cipi.yml        # or --save to keep a copy on the server
```

Copy the output into `cipi.yml` at the root of your repository, commit, push, deploy. Then `sudo cipi yml plan shop` should say **Nothing to do**: the file and the server agree. From now on, change the file instead of running commands.

### From zero

Start from a commented template that already validates:

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml example shop
```

Or write the smallest useful file by hand:

```yaml
version: 1

workers:
  queues:
    - { queue: default, processes: 2 }

schedule: true
```

Validate it before committing, with the same rules as the server (needs [Cipi Agent](https://cipi.sh/docs/agent-yml)):

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ php artisan cipi:yml validate
```

### Where it goes

```tree
your-repository/
  app/
  composer.json
  cipi.yml              ← production (and any app without its own file)
  cipi-staging.yml      ← optional: apps created with --env=staging
```

## The workflow, step by step 

Click a step to jump to it. The map stays at the top while you read.

```flow
Edit cipi.yml | in a branch | #file
Review | in the pull request | #validate
Deploy | the file ships with the release | #environments
Plan | every change listed | #plan
Apply | all or nothing | #safe
```

## 1. Edit: the whole app, in one file 

```yaml
version: 1

app:
  php: "8.6"
  aliases: ["www.shop.example.com"]
  www: to-root
  ini: { upload_max_filesize: 50M }

workers:
  horizon: true
  reverb: true

schedule: true
search: true

health:
  url: "https://shop.example.com/up"
  rollback_on_unhealthy: true

deploy:
  predeploy_snapshot: true
  node_build: "npm ci && npm run build"
  post:
    - artisan scout:sync-index-settings

env: { required: [STRIPE_KEY, MAIL_HOST] }

backup:
  profiles:
    - { name: shop-nightly, scope: all, cron: "0 2 * * *", keep_days: 14, destinations: [s3], encrypt: true }
```

| Block | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `app` | PHP version, aliases, www/apex, `php.ini` values, resource limits, basic auth |
| `workers`, `schedule` | Queues, Horizon, Reverb, the scheduler |
| `search` | Meilisearch for Laravel Scout |
| `health` | URL probed every 5 minutes and after each deploy, with automatic rollback |
| `deploy` | Branch, releases kept, DB snapshot, asset build, post-deploy steps |
| `databases`, `backup` | Extra databases and backup profiles for this app |
| `redirects`, `proxies`, `crons`, `node` | Routes, scheduled commands, Node apps |

Full reference: [cipi.yml docs](https://cipi.sh/docs/yml). Ready-made files: [recipes](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-recipes).

## 2. Review: validate before you push 

```bash
$ composer require cipi/agent
$ php artisan cipi:yml validate          # same validator as the server
$ php artisan cipi:yml generate --write  # a first file inferred from your code
$ php artisan cipi:yml schema --write    # autocompletion in your editor
```

Add `php artisan cipi:yml validate --json` to CI and a broken file never reaches a server. AI assistants connected through the [agent's MCP](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-mcp-ai-agents) can validate drafts too.

## 3. Deploy: one repository, every environment 

The file ships inside each release: what you merged is what the server reads. Which file an app reads depends on its environment.

| File | Read by |
| --- | --- |
| `cipi.yml` | Production apps |
| `cipi-staging.yml` | Apps created with `--env=staging` |
| `cipi-preview.yml` | Preview apps per branch |

Walkthrough: [staging and production from one repository](https://cipi.sh/guides/cipi-yml-staging-production).

## 4. Plan: see every change first 

`plan` lists each change and each blocker. `apply` performs them in one transaction. `auto on` applies the file after every successful deploy, from the CLI, the webhook or the panel.

## 5. Apply: all or nothing, safe to accept from Git 

`cipi yml apply` performs the plan in one transaction: if any step fails, nothing is left half done. With `cipi yml auto  on` it runs after every deploy. Anyone who can push controls the file, so it's designed to fail closed.

| Guard | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Configure only | It can never create, rename or delete an app |
| Namespaced | Databases are `shop` or `shop_*`, backup profiles `shop` or `shop-*`: no reaching into other apps |
| No secrets | Required variables are names; generated credentials stay on the server |
| No shell | Only allowlisted runners (`artisan`, `composer`, `npm`, `php`…), no pipes or `;` |
| Small YAML | Anchors, tags, merges and block scalars are refused |
| Strict routes | Proxies can't target Cipi's own ports, link-local or cloud-metadata addresses |
| Server picks the file | Staging reads `cipi-staging.yml` because the server says so, never because a commit asks |

## Start in two minutes 

```bash
$ sudo cipi yml generate shop --save      # the app as it is today
$ cat /home/shop/cipi.yml                 # commit it at the repository root
$ sudo cipi deploy shop && sudo cipi yml plan shop
```

Step by step: [keep your server settings in the repository](https://cipi.sh/guides/manage-apps-with-cipi-yml).
